Select Committee Procedure
THURSDAY, 22 SEPTEMBER 1977
The House met at 3.18 p.m.
The Clerk Assistant (Mr McGhee) informed the House of the unavoidable absence of
Mr Acting Speaker, whereupon Mr Birch, the Acting Chairman of Committees, took the
chair as Acting Deputy Speaker pursuant to the Standing Order.
Prayers.
SELECT COMMITTEE PROCEDURE
Mr ACTING DEPUTY SPEAKER: This may be an appropriate time to rule on a point
of order raised by the member for New Lynn yesterday. The member for New Lynn raised as
a point of order the conduct of the member for Waitemata at a meeting of the Social Services
Committee that morning. The member for Waitemata is not a member of the Social Services
Committee, but was attending the meeting by virtue of Standing Order 360. It is important
to establish precisely what it is that the member for New Lynn complained of. He did not, I
think rightly, raise a matter of privilege or contempt, and the matters he described do not go
anywhere near establishing anything of that nature. He alleged that the member for
Waitemata had breached Standing Order 360 by taking part in the proceedings of the
committee.
Under Standing Order 377, the proceedings of a select committee are to be conducted
as nearly as possible in the same manner as those of the Committee of the Whole House.
Standing Order 321 deals with the general rules for the conduct of business in the Committee
of the Whole House, and, subject to the stated exceptions, these are to be the same as those
observed in the House itself. That Standing Order then provides: ". . . but disorder in a
committee may only be censured by the House on receiving a report." That provision is
repeated in Standing Order 154. The Standing Orders are amplified by Speaker's ruling
123/4: "The House has no cognisance of anything taking place before a select committee
unless it is reported by the committee through the chairman. The only way in which to raise a
point of order in the House on a matter taking place in such committee is to move that the
chairman report to the House in order to obtain the Speaker's opinion. If the motion were
declined, the only alternative would be to give notice of motion to move in the House that
the chairman's ruling be disagreed with. It has been the custom for the Speaker's ruling here
and in the House of Commons to be obtained privately through the chairman by arrange-
ment with the committee.'
It is quite clear that a matter of order such as this should be raised by the select
committee, and I understand that the member for New Lynn did raise this matter with the
chairman of the committee at the time. Usually, raising a matter in this way would be
sufficient to resolve it with the chairman, who would deal with the matter then and there.
However, exceptionally, when something cannot be cleared up in this way and it is desired to
bring the matter before the House, this must be done by means of the committee's reporting
to the House and the House's considering the select committee's report. In these circumst-
ances I rule that this matter must be raised, if at all, at the select committee, and, in the
absence of a report from the committee, cannot be brought before the House at this time.
PRIVILEGE
Mr D. M. J. JONES (Waitemata): A point of order, Mr Speaker. I want to raise a
matter of privilege in terms of Standing Order 366 and Standing Order 367, and as a result of
your ruling. When the member for New Lynn spoke yesterday on the matter on which you
have just ruled, he obviously referred to matters that had taken place at the select
committee.
Mr ACTING DEPUTY SPEAKER: Order! I am sorry to interrupt the honourable
member, but two aspects of what he is saying concern me. First, I have ruled on the question
that was brought before the House, and I want no further debate on it; secondly, matters
that occur before a committee are the responsibility of the committee itself, and there are
proper procedures to be followed.
Mr D. M. J. JONES: I am referring to Standing Order 366 and Standing Order 367.

Privilege
Standing order 366 states: "The proceedings of, or the evidence taken by, or the report of
any select committee, or any summary of such proceedings, evidence, or report shall be
strictly confidential and not published or divulged by any member of the committee or by
any other person, until the report of such committee has been presented to the House...".
Standing Order 367 states: "Any person committing a breach of Standing Order 366 shall be
deemed guilty of a breach of privilege, and may be dealt with by the House accordingly.”
The method adopted by the member for New Lynn is in contradiction to Speaker's ruling
123/4, as his method allows members of a select committee to come in to the House and
make allegations against members who would be unable to reply because of the provisions of
Standing Orders 366 and 367.
I am concerned that, as in this case, a member of a select committee may mention some
of the matters that took place in the select committee, and that other members who were
present could not reply. In terms of Standing Order 366, the member for New Lynn divulged
some of the proceedings; he admitted that he divulged some of the proceedings of the Social
Services Committee. Under Standing Order 367, he has therefore committed a breach. If
Speaker's ruling 123/4 is not strictly adhered to by all members of the House, and if the
procedure adopted by the member for New Lynn is taken up by other members, it will be
difficult for members who find themselves in the position I was placed in yesterday to say
anything about what happened in the select committee, and yet they will be faced with a
charge they cannot answer. I ask you to rule whether the member for New Lynn has
committed a prima facie breach of privilege by divulging the proceedings of the select
committee in the House yesterday.
Mr HUNT (New Lynn): When I raised the point of order yesterday, I said that I was not
going to mention any of the proceedings, and I did not refer to the subject before the select
committee. I thought in good faith that the incident was serious, because I had never before
seen a member come to the hearings of a select committee and try, not once or twice, but
seven or eight times, to interfere with the proceedings. When the chairman of the commit-
tee, the member for Pakuranga, spoke yesterday he agreed that what I had said was basically
what had happened. I emphasise those words, because he agreed then that what I had said
was in fact-
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: Order! I am sorry to interrupt the honourable member. I
remind the House that I have ruled that matters taking place before a select committee are
not to be debated in the House. The member for Waitemata has now asked whether the
honourable member for New Lynn, in raising the matter in the House, has committed a
breach of privilege. If the member for New Lynn wants to speak on that matter I am
prepared to listen to him.
Mr Hunt: I do not think that a question of privilege is involved. Nothing was revealed
about the subject under discussion by the select committee. If I am guilty of a breach of
privilege, I suggest that other members of the committee who spoke at that time are also
guilty. This matter comes very close to abusing the form of breach of privilege.
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): It may well be that technically divulging
part of the proceedings-and this is the point raised by the member for Waitemata-is
caught by our Standing Orders on privilege. The matter complained of by the member for
New Lynn having been dealt with, it should be taken as novel, interesting, and informative
to us all, and the member should not press the technicalities any further. I am sure that the
member for Waitemata would not want the House to spend too much time dancing on the
point of a legal pin about such an awesome matter as privilege.
Mr ACTING DEPUTY SPEAKER: The matter having been raised in the House, it will
require a ruling by me. I intend to consult the Clerk of the House about the interpretation of
the Standing Orders, and in due course I shall rule on the question raised.
ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS
Sugar Price
1. Rt. Hon. W. E. ROWLING (Leader of the Opposition), on behalf of Hon. W. W.
FREER (Mt. Albert), asked the Minister of Trade and Industry: How does the new price
negotiated with Fiji for bulk sugar compare with fluctuations in the world sugar price, and
what effect will it have on the price for Australian sugar?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Deputy Prime Minister): The Minister of Trade and
Industry replies as follows: "The world price for raw sugar is only one of the factors that have
had to be considered in the recent price negotiations with Fiji. Under the terms of the


## p. 3129 (#11) ############################################

22 September
3129
Oral Answers to Questions
agreement, approved by the previous Government, Fiji was entitled to argue for price
increases on the basis of prices received in other markets and factors such as increased costs
of production. We, for our part, had to seek a price reasonable in terms of the New Zealand
consumer and the overall balance of the agreement. The price that has been agreed involves
a slight increase in the return to the Fiji grower and is in the Government's view reasonable
in view of all the factors involved. I would not expect the outcome of the negotiations with
Fiji to have any effect on the price for Australian sugar. The Australian agreement operates
until the end of 1978."
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.
"White Man's Peace is Worse than His War"
2. Mr WELLINGTON (Manurewa) asked the Minister of Broadcasting: Could he
indicate whether the documentary "The White Man's Peace is Worse than His War" is
available for screening in New Zealand?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Broadcasting): This, of course, is a programme
matter, but I am informed by the Broadcasting Corporation that the film was offered to TV2
but was considered to be too subjective in its approach and not of sufficiently high quality to
warrant screening in New Zealand.
Mr Wellington: Is the Minister aware in what way the film was considered to be too
subjective, and does he know who makes decisions about the lack of quality in a prog-
ramme?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: No, I have no information on the basis on which it was
decided that the film was too subjective, but I understand from the supplementary material
that it was made with a view to export and to use overseas. Presumably the makers will
follow up with TV1, or the other users of films in New Zealand, if there is a possibility of a
sale here.
Mr Wellington: Does the Minister consider that a film about New Zealand race
relations, if it is shown abroad, should equally be available to a wide variety of New Zealand
viewers?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: This is a matter for the makers of the film and the users of
films in New Zealand, but I hope the producers think it worth while to pursue sales
possibilities in New Zealand.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.
Law Graduates
3. Mr BLANCHFIELD (West Coast) asked the Minister of Education: As approxi-
mately 1618 students have graduated in law since 1972, could he tell the House the number
expected to graduate this year, and whether there are or will be enough positions available
for their legal talents?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): It is not possible to be certain how many
students will pass their examinations this year, but on past figures it is likely that approxi-
mately 360 will complete a degree in law. In the last year or two there have been insufficient
positions in law firms, particularly in the university centres, for all law graduates wishing to
take up such employment. However, there has always been a gap between the number of law
graduates and the number finding employment with private law practices. The explanation
for this is that many students study law as a general education and seek careers in
administration, in business, or in local or central government.
Mr Blanchfield: Could the Minister enlighten the House about the number of students
likely to enrol at universities for law courses in 1978, and because of the desperate shortage
of doctors, would he consider adivising the students that the field of medicine as a career
could be recommended?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: No, I could not forecast accurately the number who might offer
themselves as students in law, although I presume it would be roughly the same number as
this year. As for the suggestions that I should advise them to take up medicine, the member
ought to know that the number of students accepted in the medical schools is restricted. The
intake is highly competitive, and is based on a number that is forecast to be the requirements
for New Zealand in the future.
Mr Blanchfield: Are there many students who wish to take up medicine but do not get
the opportunity?

Hon. L. W. GANDAR: I am not certain of the proportion, but I would hazard a guess

places in medical schools.

Medical Panels
4. Mr D. M. J. JONES (Waitemata) asked the Minister of Health: Has he seen the
statement in the New Zealand Tablet of 14 September that 33 doctors have listed fields in
which panels are commonly used, one of these being health centres and medical centres
where public health nurses and social workers work together with doctors in managing a
variety of problems, and is this correct?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare): I reply on behalf of the Minister of
Health. His answer is as follows. "I have seen the statement in the New Zealand Tablet of 14
September 1977 to which the member refers. It is true that in medical and health centres
multi-disciplinary teams of health professionals, headed by doctors, work together in the
management of patients suffering from a variety of conditions. The combined use of the
different skills which each discipline possesses leads to improved patient care and rehabilita-
tion."
Dr Shearer: Are the panels referred to in the question statutory panels appointed by and
under the supervision of a supervisory committee, as outlined in the Contraception,
Sterilisation, and Abortion Bill?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: No.
Mr D. M. J. Jones: Has the Minister received any complaints from the general
practitioners' society, the nursing society, or the social workers' organisations about these
panels?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: That question should be referred to the Minister of Health. I do
not know of any complaint.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.
Geothermal Power Station, Broadlands
5. Hon. MICHAEL CONNELLY (Wigram) asked the Minister of Electricity: In view of
the need for some additional employment in Taupo and surrounding districts and the
Government's promise of accelerated geothermal power development, is there any possibil-
ity of speeding up the construction of the Broadlands geothermal power station rather than
the delay suggested in the report of the Planning Committee on Electric Power Develop-
ment?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): I reply on behalf of the Minister of
Electricity. The report of the Planning Committee on Electric Power Development for 1977
shows a delay of 6 months on the previous year's target for approval to construct the
Broadlands geothermal power station. The target date is now October 1978. It is expected
that the environmental impact report will be ready to publish by the end of October, and,
following this, application for statutory clearances will be made. In general, the statutory
procedures, including objection and appeal hearings, require up to 12 months. If there were
no objections or appeals, it would be possible to advance the approval date by several
months.
Hon. Michael Connelly: Notwithstanding the need to go through these procedures, how
does the Government reconcile its stated objective of accelerated development with the
proposal of the power planning committee to delay this project for a further 6 months?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: That is fairly easily reconciled. We are dealing with a planning
committee's report on power development. The plan now includes a re-evaluation of the
time of commencement and the lead times required to complete the various power projects,
and this plan is reviewed annually. The planned requirement for this year is a commence-
ment about October 1978, and this will then take care of total power requirements in the light
of all the other projects that are being commenced or are in the process of being built.
Hon. Michael Connelly: As a major contractor is reported to be in difficulties because of
the Government's policy on this project, could the Government investigate the possibility of
providing other work urgently in that area in order to maintain employment of plant,

Mr ACTING DEPUTY SPEAKER: That is a little wide of the original question.
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: The original question referred to power development, and this
must take its place in a total planning policy. The question of whether a firm is having
difficulties is irrelevant to the national needs for electric power development in an orderly
way.

Recreational Regional Survey, Marlborough
6. Mr LATTER (Marlborough) asked the Minister of Lands: Who will follow up the
recently issued Marlborough recreational survey, and is it the first regional survey to be
completed?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Lands): The Marlborough outdoor planning pilot study
was released at a public meeting in Blenheim on 22 August 1977, and interested bodies were
given 3 months to submit their comments or criticism. The report will be evaluated in the
light of these comments, and my department will then discuss the implementation of the
recommendations with the local bodies affected. The report is not seen as a final plan. It
emphasises the need for continual and co-ordinated planning, and it will undoubtedly
provide a valuable basis for planning for the proposed united council for the Marlborough
region. I can confirm that this is the first regional survey to be completed.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.
East-West Center, Honolulu
7. Mr ROGERS (Onehunga), on behalf of Mr KIRK (Sydenham) asked the Minister of
Foreign Affairs: Will he inform the House the number of New Zealanders who have
benefited from courses run at the East-West Center in Honolulu?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Minister of Foreign Affairs): I quote from a brief prepared
by the East-West Center in May 1977: "From 1960 to 30 September 1976, New Zealand has
had a total of 316 participants in East-West Center programmes. Of this number, 31 were
degree students, including 4 Ph.D. candidates, and 27 were seeking masters' degrees. Of the
271 professional associates, 76 participated in projects held in Hawaii, while 195 were in field
based projects. There were 12 senior fellows and visiting researchers."
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.
Liquid Fuel from Trees
8. Mr LITHGOW (Palmerston North) asked the Minister of Forests: Where will the
research into the production of liquid fuel from trees take place, and to what extent will this
research differ from other similar projects overseas?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Forests): Research into the production of ethanol from
wood has already been carried out at the Forest Research Institute, but only on a small
laboratory scale. Provision is made in departmental estimates this year for the scaling up of
this work in a cellulose-hydrolysis plant. Some associated research is being undertaken at
Auckland University and the Cawthron Institute. The Department of Scientific and Indus-
trial Research is also exploring overseas work in producing methanol from wood. The Forest
Research Institute research will differ from projects overseas in the techniques used and the
type of wood available.
Mr Lithgow: Have any results of overseas research been made available to New
Zealand?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: The country most advanced in the production of ethanol from
wood is the USSR. However, so far it has been difficult to obtain research material from that
country on the process we are interested in.
Mr Wetere: What is the extent of the research at present being carried out by the DSIR?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: I cannot answer on behalf of the DSIR, but a small amount of
laboratory research has been carried out by the Forest Research Institute. One hundred
thousand dollars has been provided in the estimates to increase the extent of the research
into the use of pine wood for this purpose.
Mr Prebble: I understand that at present the Forest Service is investigating the

hydrolysis process. Has the service investigated the DSIR's work on the physical gas
vacation process of getting methanol from wood?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: The research activities of the DSIR, the universities, and the

I am sure there will be an exchange of views and research material between the DSIR and

Mr Blanchfield: In the event of the research proving successful, does the Government

Hon. V. S. YOUNG: I think the member for West Coast is asking whether the beech
trees would be taken from the West Coast and processed in Rotorua. One of the values of
producing liquid fuel is its easy transportation, and one of the disadvantages of having solid
fuel and other materials is the cost of transportation. Obviously, any plant to be established
would be sited close to the source of the raw material-in this case, the timber or the logs.

Diplomatic Representatives-Appointment of PR Consultants
9. Mr O'BRIEN (Island Bay) asked the Minister of Foreign Affairs: Is it an approved or
customary practice for foreign governments which have diplomatic or consular representa-
tion in New Zealand to appoint public relations consultants to conduct propaganda
campaigns on their behalf; and, if it is an accepted ethical practice, does the New Zealand
Government have to be notified and approve of such appointments?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Minister of Foreign Affairs): It is not uncommon anywhere
in the world for a diplomatic or consular mission to employ a public relations agency to assist
it with some part of its information work. This is perhaps especially true where the
information function is important in relation to the size of the mission. In any case, the
decision is a matter within the discretion of the mission, and the host Government need not
be informed or approve.
Mr O'Brien: Does the Government intend to change its policy in this respect in light of
the Prime Minister's definition of subversion as serving the interest of a foreign government;
what is the Government's attitude towards, for example, Mr Peter Isaacs, who is reported to
have taken the job of public relations consultant for the Chilean military junta and will thus
be serving a foreign government; and does this mean that foreign governments can openly
pay New Zealanders to freely propagandise on their behalf?
Mr ACTING DEPUTY SPEAKER: That is rather wide of the original question.
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS: All I can do is repeat what I have already said. It is not
uncommon for a diplomatic or consular mission to employ a public relations agency to assist
it. This is done in many parts of the world.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.
Industrial Actions by Meat Inspectors
10. Mr FALLOON (Pahiatua) asked the Minister of Labour: How many man days were
lost in the freezing industry over the past year due to industrial action by meat inspectors,
and what were the major reasons?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): Unfortunately, my department does not
compile detailed statistics pertaining to State employees. However, it is estimated that 713
working days were lost through industrial action by meat inspectors within the freezing
industry. The main reasons for this lost time were protests over wages, working conditions,
and facilities.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.

Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.
Medical Panels
12. Mr D. M. J. JONES (Waitemata) asked the Minister of Health: Has he seen the
statement in the New Zealand Tablet of 14 September that 33 doctors have listed fields in
which panels are commonly used, one of these being transplant surgery, and is this correct?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare): I reply on behalf of the Minister of
Health. His answer is as follows: "I have seen the statement referred to. It is not clear what
panels are referred in connection with transplant surgery or what type of transplants the

Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare): I reply on behalf of the Minister of

reception order committing a patient to a psychiatric hospital after receiving medical
certificates from two medical practitioners. The decision is made by the magistrate on the
advice of two doctors.
Mr D. M. J. Jones: As the decision is made by a statutorily appointed person, who is not
a doctor but is a magistrate, in a health matter affecting the future of a human being, has
the Minister received any complaints from the New Zealand Medical Association, the Social
Workers Association, or the Nurses Association about this statutory way of making
decisions?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: I have had the opportunity of turning up the Mental Health Act,
and see that this is a statutory decision. However, I am not aware that the Minister of Health
has received any complaints.
Hon. Dr A. M. Finlay: Is the magistrate's role in these proceedings medical or legal?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: This quotation from section 22 of the Mental Health Act may be
of assistance to the honourable gentleman: "Examination by magistrate and two medical
practitioners-(1) On the lodging of the application for a reception order a magistrate shall
examine the person alleged to be mentally disordered at his residence or elsewhere, and for
the purpose of further inquiry shall call to his assistance two medical practitioners who are
not prohibited by section 32 of this Act from signing a certificate, and those medical
practitioners shall either together or separately examine the person." I am not a legal man,
and perhaps the learned gentleman opposite can tell me whether I am right in assuming that
this is a legal decision, made on the advice of the medical profession.
Dr Shearer: Can the Minister confirm that, to his personal knowledge, this is the only
statutory panel referred to in the New Zealand Tablet, and that it relates specifically to
psychiatric hospitals?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: Yes, I can.
Mr Lange: Is the Minister suggesting that no one who has been committed under the
Mental Health Act has ever complained about it; and, is he not aware that litigation is
proceeding involving New Zealand and the Cook Islands at this very instant?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: Nobody has personally complained to me. I suggest that the
honourable gentleman should contact the Minister of Health who, possibly, could give him
more information.

Christchurch or the Auckland Metropolitan College, which are spoken of as "community
schools". Some special staffing and support was given to four Auckland schools in 1974 to
develop community education programmes, but no firm policy was established by the
previous Administration. These programmes have been maintained. The Nga Tapuwae
College opened in 1976, and includes planned additional community facilities to be jointly

funded by the Department of Internal Affairs and the Manukau City Council. Similar

ANIMALS PROTECTION AND CARE AMENDMENT BILL
Mr MacDONELL (Dunedin Central): I move, That leave be given to introduce the
Animals Protection and Care Amendment Bill. I apologise to the Minister of Agriculture, as I
had intended that a copy of this Bill should be delivered to his office yesterday, but I had
only the one proof copy. However, I understand that he did receive a copy this morning.
This Bill is the result of some months' work. Last year I suggested there should be a ministry
of animal welfare, and the response was quite remarkable; I received letters from all parts of
the country. I was particularly heartened by the following letter sent to me by the New
Zealand Veterinary Association: "At a recent meeting of the council of this association your
proposal was discussed with great interest. This association has been concerned for some
time with the lack of adequate, informed legislative action in the general field of animal
welfare. Accordingly, I am pleased to offer the association's co-operation and technical
resources in any appropriate manner that will help achieve the highest possible standard of
animal welfare in this country."
Although this Bill does not establish a ministry, it provides for a Minister of Animal
Protection and Care. One of his functions would be to co-ordinate the efforts of animal
welfare agencies in New Zealand, and to liaise with other departments. The Bill also
impinges on the protection of wild animals. Mrs Rowe, of Arapawa Island in the Marl-
borough Sounds, has entered into correspondence with me about a rare breed of goat that is
under threat of death by the Forest Service. The Minister of Lands will be well aware of Mrs
Rowe's representations to him over a long period. I envisage that this Bill would give the
Minister of Animal Protection and Care power to intervene in that particular matter.
For some time I have been concerned about the increasing number of offences against
animals which, in most cases, are unable to defend themselves. Animals have rights too, and
I am always suspicious of those people who do not like animals; Hitler was one, probably
because he did not want to be dominated by a cat or a dog, both of which have a disarming
habit of doing just that. I shall quote from an editorial in the Evening Post of 16 September,
praising the work of the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals: "Starving,
neglected, sick or injured animals attract the sympathy of most people. When it comes to
doing something effective towards easing their suffering it is too often a very different
matter. The plight of thousands of dogs, cats and other domesticated animals would be much
worse were it not for the untiring efforts of the SPCA, which in methodical and often
dedicated manner gives practical help to stricken creatures." Why should the SPCA and
other animal agencies have to depend on voluntary assistance and legacies? Why do they not
receive help from the State?
The chairman of Animal Welfare Year in Great Britain in 1977 said recently, "Will this
century be remembered for its political upheavals and debates about the economy, or for its
realisation that mankind's treatment of the other animals is a matter of the greatest moral
importance?" Those words are very important.
I have in my possession documentation of a number of examples of cruelty perpetrated
on animals in the name of science. One hair shampoo in Great Britain was tested by painting


## p. 3139 (#21) ############################################

22 September
3139
Animals Protection and Care Amendment Bill
it over the taped-open eyes of rabbits to see if it would affect those eyes, and consequently
the eyes of the end user. However, that example is mild compared with other experiments
carried out in the name of research and for medical knowledge. In Britain, work is being
done to establish a universal declaration of the rights of animals, and many prominent
people in Britain support that move. In 1975 experiments on animals in Britain rose to about
5 500 000, 3 500 000 of which were carried out by commercial organisations; such figures
make one wonder what is happening in our own country.
The Evening Post recently carried a large news report about animals being neglected in
Wanganui. Three dogs were left chained for about 2 weeks without food, water, or shelter,
until they were little more than skeletons. The people were named in court, and the animals
had to be destroyed. The present law provides a maximum penalty of 3 months' imprison-
ment. I have done nothing about altering the imprisonment provisions of the principal Act,
but I have done something about the fines.
Clause 3 provides for the establishment of a Minister of Animal Protection and Care,
and this Minister will be under the umbrella of the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries.
Rt. Hon. B. E. Talboys: That would involve an appropriation.
Mr MacDONELL: It could do. Clause 4 prohibits the use of steel-jawed traps,
commonly known as gin traps. Nearly all the pest destruction councils use other means, such
as shooting or poisoning, to destroy rabbits, so there is no great need to retain those traps in
the country. I have had an animal of mine caught in one of those traps, and I know of
children who have had their hands caught in them. The time has come when they should be
outlawed. One of my colleagues will go into more detail about that.
Clause 6(3)(b) concerns animals that are tethered and confined for a time without food
or water. The principal Act allows an inspector to enter a property either to feed or to water
the animals affected if they have been left for more than 24 hours. This provision would
reduce that time to 12 hours. Clause 7(b) provides for an increase from 12 months to 24
months in the disqualification period imposed upon a person who has offended against the
Act and who has been prohibited from owning an animal or a particular animal for 12
months. This provision extends that time to 24 months.
Clause 8 provides that funds are to be made available to animal welfare societies. It
states: "In each financial year the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries shall make provision
for, and grant to, suitable animal welfare organisations such amounts as will assist them to
carry out their respective objects effectively." That means that animal welfare societies such
as the SPCA would be able to receive direct assistance from the State.
Clause 9 deals with research and experiments on animals, and tightens up the present
provisions in the Act. It states: "No research or experiment on animals which, apart from the
provisions of subsection (1A) of this section, would constitute an offence against this Act or
would otherwise cause pain, suffering, or distress to an animal, shall be commenced without
the prior written consent of the secretary, who, before giving or refusing his consent, shall
consult not less than two veterinary practitioners or surgeons." That means that if research
must be carried out on animals-and I am not very happy about that—two veterinary
surgeons would have to be consulted by the secretary before a warrant was issued. The
provisions for penalties have been updated and, in most instances, doubled. As I said earlier,
I have done nothing about altering the imprisonment provisions.
I have been particularly heartened by the number of messages I have received from
around the country in the last 24 hours, all in support of the Bill. I hope that Parliament will
seriously consider this measure, which I feel is timely. Members must be concerned about
the increasing number of offences against animals which, in many instances, as I said earlier,
cannot defend themselves. I hope that Parliament will consider passing this legislation.
Mr COMBER (Wellington Central): First, I commend the member for Dunedin Central
for bringing this matter to the attention of the House. I am sure that in doing so I echo the
concern of all members about cruelty to animals and the need to protect and care for them. It
is rather sad to reflect that we should be obliged to introduce a measure such as this. Most of
us would hope that there would never be any need for such legislation, as indeed we would
hope that there would never be any need to legislate against crimes of violence against the
human animal. However, we must face up to the facts of life.

entitled. So often that is overlooked, and those small puppies that have become large dogs

wander the streets, sometimes attacking other animals and even human beings. I take the

Clause 3(1)(b) states that the secretary will be the Director-General of Agriculture and

The use of gin traps has been debated in the House in the past, and at least one petition
has been presented on this issue. The Counties Act and the Municipal Corporations Act
provide that local authorities may control the use of such traps in their bylaws, which, in
turn, must be approved by the Minister of Local Government in consultation with the
Minister of Forests and the Minister of Agriculture. The use of gin traps has been retained in
the interests of pest control, and one local authority, which had banned their use, recently
removed that ban because of the damage caused by bait-shy oppossums that could not be
controlled by other means. However, investigations are continuing to find a more humane
alternative to the use of gin traps.
Clause 5 states that the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries will administer the Act.
However, many cruelty prosecutions are brought by the SPCA quite independently of the
ministry, and the Police also have certain powers. I am advised that the SPCA is the only
outside organisation concerned with animal welfare that is officially recognised by the
ministry. Inspectors, other than ministry officers and Police officers, are appointed only after
recommendations from that organisation. I am sure the member for Dunedin Central knows
that all veterinarians and livestock officers employed in the animal health division, and all
veterinarians and senior meat inspectors in the meat division, are inspectors under the
present Act. That point is well controlled, but I am sure the Minister has no hard-and-fast
rule.
The member referred to an editorial in the Evening Post of Friday last, which covered
the question of funds for animal welfare societies. No one appreciates more than I do the
work done by voluntary welfare organisations in this field. I believe it is one of the strengths
of our society that so many people are prepared to work in a voluntary capacity to look after
the interests of people and animals. I want to clear up a misconception regarding the refusal
of the Minister of Internal Affairs to make a grant to the SPCA from the funds of the Lottery
Board of Control. In 1973 the royal federation received a bequest of $115,000. The most
recent figures available to the department show that the federation had an excess of income
over expenditure of about $4,700.
It is true that some local SPCA branches are experiencing financial difficulties. One of
the arguments against making further grants to the national organisation is that in the past
the moneys made available have not been paid to local SPCA branches; only a small
proportion of the most recent $4,000 grant reached the local branches. I know that this is a
bipartisan debate, but I must point out that the decision to discontinue the payment of grants
to the SPCA was made by the former Minister of Internal Affairs, Hon. Henry May, in 1975,
and his action has been endorsed by the present Minister.
Local authorities can play an important and constructive role in the funding of the
SPCA, which provides a very worth-while service and helps to keep down the expenses of
local government by attending to stray dogs and other animals on the streets. I commend to
local authorities the idea of assisting these organisations, instead of their feeling that they
must always turn to central government.
I congratulate the member for Dunedin Central on his deep concern for animal care and
protection. I believe that as a result of this debate more people will be aware of the need to
love and care for their animals.

Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East): I congratulate the member introducing the Bill. It

The member for Dunedin Central mentioned the painting of shampoo on rabbits' eyes,
as an example of the callous attitude of some experimentalists to animals. He did not say that
the dilution principle is most frequently used nowadays. The shampoo is diluted to different
strengths and used on humans, because it is for use by humans, not by rabbits. The member
for Dunedin Central spoke about research costing $3.5 million being carried out in Britain by
commercial organisations, and implied that the research of a nature similar to that with
shampoo was being done at a cost of $3.5 million a year. I spent 3 years in Britain operating
on and working with animals under the British laws. Almost 90 percent of the $3.5 million
used by commercial organisations is spent on the cat and dog food market in Britain. I visited
experimental stations where the sole ambition was to find the best tucker for dogs. The
amount of money spent on giving animals the best possible diet must be put in perspective.
When speaking about clause 6 the member for Dunedin Central mentioned the
appointment and powers of inspectors. It is my understanding that the existing legislation

Why does the member want more inspectors? Clause 5 states: "The Ministry of Agriculture
and Fisheries shall be responsible for the enforcement and the administration of this Act and

country. What would be done about a continuing offence under clause 7(a), which repeals
section 16(1), if a person refused to dispose of an animal, or actually had an animal when he
had been told by the court that he was not permitted to keep one?

Animals Protection and Care Amendment Bill
research or experimental work carried out on an animal by a bona fide research worker."
The Bill clearly attempts to limit, control, or restrict-one can choose whichever word one
wishes-the powers of people engaged in research with animals. If passed in this form the
Bill could harm agricultural and medical research conducted in New Zealand, which is
internationally recognised. I know from correspondence with scientists in Russia, Poland,
and Czechoslovakia that our research, particularly at Ruakura, is well established and world
renowned.
There is a lot of clouded emotional ignorance about some of our experimentation, and I
make that point to the member who has introduced the Bill. I remember reading of the
horror expressed by the former member for Hamilton West when she was confronted by a
cow with a fistula. To her it was a terrible thing to see a cow with a plug in its side, but any
cow is likely to die of bloat and if the alternative to a dead cow-which is not worth very
much—is a live cow that is still producing but has a hole in its side I suspect, and in fact I
know, that every farmer worth his salt would prefer a cow with a hole in its side. I was
interested to hear the comment of the former member for Hamilton West when she found a
cow with a permanent hole in its side—a hole that is very much needed for research so that
we can find out what is going on inside the animal, and find out all about bloat, which kills
off large numbers of our cattle and costs thousands of dollars each year. Nevertheless, we
had a supposedly knowledgeable member of Parliament saying we should stop such
operations.
There is also a suggestion here that we should not conduct any experiments causing
pain, suffering, or distress to animals. I take issue with the third point-distress-because, as
a physiologist working in this field, I know from many years of experience that it is very
difficult to define the state of stress. In fact, scientists throughout the world are trying to
define stress, and to define it they must be able to induce a stress condition so that they can
measure what stress does to the animal, measure physiological effects, measure the actions
in the blood of the animal, and in every other way. So it is impossible to learn more about the
stress phenomenon unless we have an animal that can be stressed.
Mr Couch: Come to the Wairarapa.
Dr SHEARER: Yes, there is natural stress in the Wairarapa because of climatic
conditions. It is rather limiting, therefore, if a Bill provides that we cannot stress an animal in
order to find out what physiological changes caused the stress to show. Stress can be defined
in a dozen different ways. When I was in Britain, stress was defined by British legislation in
the Cruelty of Animals Act 1876, the Protection of Animals Act 1911, the Protection of
Animals Anaesthesics Act 1954, the Protection of Animals Anaesthesics Act 1964, and the
Medicines Act 1968. All those Acts referred in part to experimentation on animals. I found
that you were not allowed, without a ticket, to inject an animal. You were not allowed to
reduce the food of a rat by 10 percent without someone descending on you from a great
height. You could not cage a pig for any period without permission. A pig lives in a cage
quite happily. He is a most genial fellow when he is sitting in a cage getting plenty of food;
but that is the sort of legislation they have in Britain.
Finally, the Bill proposes that if you do not get this certificate you must appeal to the
Supreme Court for a review. I can imagine a research post-graduate fellow over here for a
year sitting around cooling his heels for 12 months while his appeal goes through the
Supreme Court to give him a ticket so that he can have an animal to experiment on. These
are the matters I am most concerned about in the Bill. I am prepared to accept some of the
provisions about gin traps and other matters, but I feel the member must look very carefully
at the continuance of the conditions for research on animals.

INCOME TAX (ANNUAL) BILL
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Acting Minister of Finance): I move, That this Bill be now
read a second time. This is the usual measure to fix the rates of income tax, excess retention
tax, and bonus issue tax for the year of assessment which began on 1 April 1977. As I
explained to members on the first reading, the rates are the same as those fixed last year.
Clause 1 is the short title. Clause 2 fixes the rates of income tax for the current year, the
rates being specified in the first schedule to the principal Act. Clause 3 fixes the rate of
excess retention tax at the rate specified in the first schedule to the principal Act. This tax


## p. 3146 (#28) ############################################

3146
22 September
Income Tax (Annual) Bill
has a very restricted application, and applies only to privately controlled investment
companies. Clause 4 specifies the rate of bonus issue tax as set out in the first schedule to the
principal Act. The amount of any bonus issue made by the company will continue to be taxed
but at the rate of 17c in the dollar.
I should repeat that the existing rates of income tax for individuals are those set by the
Labour Government in July 1975, but measures have been taken, as set out in the Income
Tax Amendment Bill, to provide rebate relief for young and single-income families. As I
said last night, this relief will assist some 220 000 families. This Government is aware, as any
Government must be, of the burden of taxation. Our concern, therefore, has been for a
Budget based on a strategy of restraint, to maintain restraint in Government expenditure
and so limit increases in taxation. Such restraint plays an essential and vital part in helping to
limit tax requirements. Our success is clear from the figures. In 1972-73, taxation was 77
percent of public expenditure, the same percentage that the present Government achieved in
1976-77.
It was very different during the 3 years of the Labour Government. In its first 2 years the
percentage of taxation for public expenditure was 80 and 82. It dropped to 66 in 1975, but
that was the year when the financial system really went out of control with a huge
unauthorised expenditure of $176 million. In what was effectively a period of inflation, the
Labour Government ran a Budget deficit projected at $1,200 million, and simply failed to
cover that deficit adequately with taxation. It was irresponsible and inflationary, and it poses
a problem for any subsequent Government to keep taxation at a reasonable level, but I
believe that the percentage at which we have maintained it is an earnest of our intention to
restrain Government expenditure, and so limit taxation.
However, a country like New Zealand has a high continuing demand for Government
services and for State support and action of all kinds. It is therefore necessary to maintain
reasonable levels of taxation in order to cover those obligations. The State, which is at the
service of all our people, has particular obligations in the care of the aged, and this has been
a matter for debate. I remind the House that we have met a policy of national superannua-
tion within the present rates. I remind members of the need to cover increases in wages and
salaries within Government services that constitute a very big proportion of the increases in
Government expenditure. The Government accepts the need to provide funds for efficient
social and Government services. Our objective has been to restrain Government expendi-
ture and to limit total tax requirements, while helping those most in need by maintaining
services essential to our social and economic progress.
The clearest example of the Government's determination to restrain taxes is in the
changing amount of tax paid as a percentage of the average ordinary weekly wage. It is very
difficult to evaluate the ordinary man, but, in terms of statistics, I believe it is reasonable to
take the average ordinary-time weekly wage. In October 1972, in terms of tax rates, the
average ordinary-time weekly wage earner paid 15 percent of his wages in taxation. In
October 1975 the figure was 18 percent. In October 1976 it fell to 16.3 percent. In April
1977, with the rebates introduced in this Budget, the same man's taxation as a percentage of
his wages overall for the year will fall to 10.9. There are, of course, different statistics, but,
taking the average total weekly wage, we find that in October 1972 the tax as a percentage of
the wage was 15.5. In October 1975 it was 19.2. In October 1976 it had fallen to 16.6, and at
April 1977, with the rebates applied, it was 11.4.
The Government intends to assist those most in need. The Bill reflects a fair and
reasonable effort, in a time of considerable economic difficulty, to limit tax burdens and help
those with the greatest need. What is more, taxpayers no longer bear the burden of the
Labour Government's superannuation scheme, which today would have been running at
about $3 a week for the average wage earner. Ratepayers can also look forward to rate relief
as from 1 April 1978. I do not claim that that is a major move, but it provides significant help
in an area where there has been consistent demand for assistance over the years. The
Government is concerned with tax relief, tax reform, and tax change, but, as all Govern-
ments discover, there is limited room for action. The Bill is a fair and reasonable approach to
the country's tax needs while at the same time meeting its economic requirements.
Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition): I do not know what fairyland

absolute terms and as a percentage of the estimated gross national product. The Minister
very carefully avoided those points. The taxation rates have not been changed, but the scales

$129 a week according to ministerial statements, attracts a marginal rate of tax that was

is now paying for the promises made by the Government when it bought its way into office.
The Minister's remarks emphasised the Government's priorities, and it is obvious that
provision for the well-to-do aged between 60 and 65 years takes priority over housing, social
services, and the other responsibilities the Government has to the community. In 3 years the
Labour Government collected $6,129 million in income tax, but in 2 years the National
Government will have collected $6,389 million. The Government has not given income
earners the relief it promised. Worse than that, it is positively harming effort. It is causing
people to slacken off, because they object to paying the rate of tax on average earnings and
resent the amount they have to pay on overtime earnings. In 1973-74, total tax as a
proportion of the gross national product was 27.7 percent. It increased to 30.5 percent in
1974-75, and fell by 1 percent the next year. Under the National Government it increased to
30.7 percent-some of these figures are estimated, because we do not have final figures for
the gross national product, but they are fairly close-and for the current financial year the
figure is estimated at 33.4 percent.
This will be the first year ever in which $1 in every $3 of the gross national product will
be taken in tax. That is the achievement of the National Government, and there are two
reasons for it. The first is the obsession with the deficit before borrowing, and with what the
Government sees as the need to reduce it; the second is the promises made by the National
Party in order to gain office. The deficit is a relatively small item this year, but unemploy-
ment, social unrest, and the lack of productivity which have resulted from the Government's
so-called success in reducing the deficit are serious and increasing problems. The figure for
unemployment is well beyond 15 000. No one really knows how far beyond that it is, because
the statistics are hidden. Many people who should properly be shown as unemployed are on
benefits other than the unemployment benefit. Many married women are not shown in the
statistics, but the unemployment total is 15 300-and the Government talks of its success in
reducing the deficit.
The National Party put out three forms of its manifesto. No one yet knows which one to
believe, but I suggest that anyone would be a fool to believe any. One statement appears in
most of them: "The growth of Government spending will be curbed, thus enabling tax
increases to be less than the 87 percent total rise in the last 3 years." The figures were
phoney, anyway. The tax increases under the Labour Government were not 87 percent, but
about 65 percent. The National Government, with its Budget and these tables, will have
achieved a 49 percent increase in 2 years; and if that is compounded at the present rate of
increase it will become 82.4 percent for 3 years.
That manifesto statement was deceitful in itself, but the next statement on superannua-
tion is even worse: "The National Party is satisfied that the money required can be found
from the increased volume of taxation which naturally accrues every year by the growth of
incomes." The Prime Minister had finally to admit in the House the other day that there will
be no real growth in income. The growth is purely in monetary terms; it represents no extra
wealth or real gain to people, but they will pay from that bigger amount of cash not only
more in tax but a bigger proportion of their earnings. They will be a lot worse off financing
the promises-specifically the promises about superannuation—that the National Party said
could be financed out of the natural increase in revenue. I want to give two examples to
illustrate what I mean.
Last year wages rose by 14.9 percent and the income tax take by 23 percent. The
expected wage rise for next year is about 15 percent. If the Government is more successful
than the Opposition believes it will be, the wage rise will not be as much as that, but if it is
what the Opposition expects, it could be more. The tax increase on the expected 15 percent
will be 26 percent. The Opposition objects to that figure. The Government is trying to fool
the people by stating that it is using the same tax rates as were used by the Labour
Government. In general they are the same tax rates, but the basis upon which tax is levied
has been changed, to the disadvantage of almost every taxpayer. Because of the recovery in
export prices last year a few farmers had a little more cash income, and they may have had an
increase in their real income. However, their income will be down this year, and they will not

22 September
have an increase in real income.
The Government is exploiting inflation and using propaganda to hide what it is doing. It
is building on a false basis. The Government talks about its determination to fight inflation,
but inflation is the basis of its policy. It must have inflation to obtain the extra money;
without the extra money it cannot reduce the deficit before borrowing and finance its
grandiose spending programmes. The Opposition suggests that certain elements of Govern-
ment spending are wrong and that its tax programme also is wrong. A 4.8 percent increase in
the consumer price index for the June quarter is not a sign that the Government's predictions
will come true. If inflation is 20 percent this year the tax rate will not be 26 percent out of the
15 percent wage increase; it will be more than 30 percent on top of the 20 percent.
The effect on low-income families is serious. When the tax rates first applied in 1975 the
person on the average wage of about $105 paid a marginal rate of 37c in the dollar. Today the
marginal tax for the average ordinary-time wage of $129 and some cents is 46c in every
dollar, or an increase of 9c in the dollar to stay on the average wage. When people do
overtime, extra work at penal rates, or a secondary job they object to almost half of the
money they earn being paid in tax, without getting beyond the average wage. If a person is
fortunate to earn a little more than the average wage he soon finds that he is giving half of
the earnings back. One of the basic causes of inflation is the Government's obsession with
the tax rates and its effort to reduce the deficit before borrowing.
In conclusion, I challenge members opposite to say how they will reduce the tax scales,
because if the tax rates are not changed the wage and salary earners on the average
wage-which has been inflated by cost rises-will in 10 years be in the top tax bracket,
paying 60c in the dollar. That is where New Zealand is heading at present. With the
deceptively simple clauses in this Bill-that the income tax rates shall be as shown in the
schedule the marginal rate for the man on the average wage is already 46c in the dollar.
Two years ago it was 37c, and it can hit the maximum of 60c within 10 years. That is the
tragedy of the so-called economic miracle perpetrated by honourable members opposite.

maximum tax rate, the rate was increased in two jumps.

PRIVILEGE
Mr ACTING DEPUTY SPEAKER: This may be an appropriate time to rule on a matter
of a breach of privilege raised in the House yesterday by the member for Waitemata.
Allegations of a breach of privilege are regarded very seriously in the House, because,
among other matters, Standing Order 429 awards precedence to them. They are not to be
raised lightly, nor on the spur of the moment, nor without adequate reason supported by the
Standing Orders and customs of the House. Yesterday the member for Waitemata raised a
matter of privilege about comments made in the House on Wednesday by the member for
New Lynn, who had alleged that the member for Waitemata contravened Standing Order
360 in that he took part in the proceedings of the Social Services Committee, although not a
member.
The matter of privilege raised by the member for Waitemata alleges that the member
for New Lynn divulged the proceedings of a committee contrary to Standing Order 366. The
point involves matters of some difficulty, as it raises the question of whether a member who
refers to the proceedings of a committee in the House commits a breach of privilege. I find
this a difficult question to answer, for I am sure members will recall many instances when
reference to the proceedings of a committee that has not reported has been made in the
House, yet has not been treated as if it were a matter of privilege. Members in discussing,
and the Speaker in ruling on, matters of privilege under Standing Order 366 almost
inevitably refer to the proceedings of a committee in a manner that, on the face of it, might
appear to contravene the Standing Order. The question then arises, does the Standing Order
apply to disclosures made in the House or are such disclosures to be dealt with as breaches of
order as they have been in the past? Fortunately I am not called upon to resolve this question
for I can rule on another ground.
The member for New Lynn, when speaking on Wednesday, referred to certain actions
of the member for Waitemata at the Social Services Committee. It was his contention that
the member took part in the proceedings of the committee, although he was not entitled to
do so. As I indicated in ruling yesterday, whether the member for Waitemata took part in
those proceedings can be determined by the House only when it has received a report from
the committee. Until the House considers such a report from the committee, if indeed one is
forthcoming, the member for Waitemata cannot be said to be in breach of Standing Order
360. Consequently his conduct at the committee cannot be regarded as part of the
proceedings of that committee. It follows that the member for New Lynn did not divulge the
proceedings of the committee by referring to this conduct. I rule that no prima facie breach
of privilege has been established.
GAMING AND LOTTERIES BILL
Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister of Internal Affairs): I move, That the Gaming and
Lotteries Bill be introduced. The Bill represents a new body of law relating to gaming in New
Zealand. It completely revises and updates a body of law which most people would now
acknowledge to be archaic. The most important change is one of emphasis. The old


## p. 3157 (#39) ############################################

23 September
3157
Gaming and Lotteries Bill
legislation, relying as it did in the main on nineteenth century tradition and a large measure
of prerogative and case law, was based on the premise that all forms of gambling should be
declared to be illegal unless they were made legal. The only major form of gambling not
dealt with in the Bill is betting on horses and greyhounds, which is governed by the Racing
Act 1971.
As I have indicated, the present law-the Gaming Act 1908-dates back to 1881. The
principles on which it is based certainly reflect problems and attitudes of the last quarter of
the nineteenth century. There have, of course, been many amendments since 1908 in an
attempt to bring the law into a closer relationship with developing public opinion, but these
changes have been mainly in permitting new and specified forms of gambling, such as
legalising raffles and housie, the introduction of an off-course betting scheme, and, more
recently, the development of a national lottery. No attempt has been made throughout the
years to change the emphasis of the legislation itself.
Today not only the public but, I venture to say, the courts themselves have been
frustrated in their attempts to interpret the confused situation that such outdated law has
created. One could say that these amendments to the law have been merely grafted on to the
legislation, the original purpose of which was to prohibit almost completely any oppor-
tunities to gamble, even in a most modest form. I venture to say that if the existing provisions
had been enforced in their entirety most of us in this House would have been quite
unwittingly guilty of some minor infringement of the gaming laws, which went so far as to
make illegal even modest forms of gambling in one's own home.
It is for that reason that my department, working in association with the Police and the
Department of Justice, has tried to bring a new look into the legislation, and one that reflects
present-day attitudes. I want to emphasise, however, that this does not mean that the Bill
promotes any great liberalisation of gambling. In fact, the forms of gambling-such as poker
machines, casinos, and the like—which most of us would still regard as undesirable, are
prohibited under the new Bill. What the Bill does is ensure that every person who takes part
in any form of gambling will do so with a much clearer idea of whether or not he is breaching
the law.
The Bill applies to four types of gambling-games of chance, bookmaking and betting,
prize competitions, and lotteries-and then only when consideration in one form or another
is required to take part in these forms of gambling; that is, when some stake, either money or
money's worth, is involved. The new draft legislation is not concerned with where a game of
chance is played, but rather with how and for what purpose it is played. Accordingly, the
concept of a common gaming house-an old-fashioned expression, surely—which conjures
up visions of dimly-lit, smoke-shrouded rooms in city back alleys, need no longer be
continued in the law.
As I have said, it is no longer important where the game of chance is played. The
important thing is the type of game being played and the purposes for which it is being
played. For example, a family game of poker for stakes, modest or otherwise, within one's
own home and among friends-which definitely would be illegal under the present law-will
no longer be so. A similar game played in other circumstances, with somebody conducting it
for personal gain, would definitely be in breach of the law.
The bookmaking provisions in the Gaming Act are mainly unchanged. Bookmaking will
still be an offence, no matter where it is undertaken, and I am sure most in the House would
agree that this should be so. I take this opportunity to comment on remarks made by one or
two people from overseas who have been in New Zealand lately, and who have suggested
that we could lend colour to our racing scene by permitting bookmakers to operate on
course. There is no intention by me or the Government to legalise bookmaking in any shape
or form or in any circumstances, either on course or off course.
The degree of control to be exercised over lotteries—or raffles, as they have been called
in the past has been greatly reduced by exempting from the requirements of licensing any
lottery or raffle for which the total value of prizes does not exceed $50, providing that the
requirements of the Bill as to the conditions under which these rather harmless competitions
can be carried out are met. In general, a more realistic view is being taken of small-scale
gambling, or what most people would regard as a mild flutter. The office raffle for the
benefit of the social club, the sweep on the Melbourne Cup, and other traditional forms of
gambling in a very mild form that take place in every office in the country, particularly on
Melbourne Cup day, will no longer be illegal providing they are not being run for personal
gain.
The Bill introduces a new concept to gaming legislation in this country-that of the prize


## p. 3158 (#40) ############################################

3158
23 September
Gaming and Lotteries Bill
competition. At present there is a grey area in the legislation. It concerns competitions that
are really not lotteries on the one hand, or games of chance on the other. Everyone will
know the kind of game I refer to-how far will the car travel on X litres of petrol, and "spot
the ball" are common examples of what are now defined in the Bill as prize competitions. In
the past there has been doubt as to whether individual competitions come within the purview
of the gaming legislation. The courts have held that the presence of any element of
skill-even if only a scintilla-means that the particular competition is not a game of chance.
To clear up this idea of the present law, the Bill provides that this type of scheme will be a
prize competition and subject to controls in very much the same way as are lotteries. Minor
competitions complying with the conditions of the law will be exempt from licensing, but
large-scale competitions will, as with lotteries, be subject to licensing.
The Bill also covers trade competitions. In future a competition run as a means of
promoting trade will in general not be subject to the law relating to gambling, with the
important proviso that the only fee or consideration required to be paid to enter the
competition is the purchase of the product or the services being promoted.
Another innovation of some importance, and of interest to members I am sure, is an
entirely new part of the Bill covering the engagement of professional promoters to assist
organisations in raising funds by way of lotteries or similar fund-raising schemes. Until now,
the employment of professional fund raisers has been prohibited by virtue of the conditions
under which licences were granted. The new provisions of the Bill will help greatly in
clearing up what has been a matter of some concern to many organisations that do not have
the resources to organise large-scale fund-raising projects. Promoters or professional fund
raisers will now be required to be licensed by the courts, and will be subject to stringent
controls regarding the proper accounting for and handling of the money raised on behalf of
their client organisations. Provision is made in the Bill for complaints against the operation
of such professional fund raisers to be dealt with by the courts, and the Secretary for Internal
Affairs is given power to investigate the operations of any such fund raisers if there is cause
to do so.
The 1962 legislation covering the operations of the Golden Kiwi lotteries is continued in
the Bill with little amendment.
Under the Bill a number of United Kingdom laws will cease to apply to New Zealand.
In practical effect they have not been applicable for many years, although the courts might
have been obliged to draw on the precedents of English case law established under these old
English statutes. Their continued application to New Zealand would be quite ridiculous, and
references to English Acts have accordingly been removed from the legislation.
Because of the many changes in the Bill and the difficulty of understanding the
background to the changes, I have had my department prepare an explanatory statement on
the Bill, and I have arranged for copies of this statement to be distributed to all members.
Further copies are readily available from my office or the department to anyone who may be
interested. I have dealt with the major changes the Bill proposes. I am sure there will be
widespread interest in the legislation, and because it makes such fundamental changes I
think it is appropriate that it should go to a select committee for consideration and the
hearing of submissions. In this case, it will be the Statutes Revision Committee.

EEC and Dublin Declaration
4. Miss DEWE (Lyttelton) asked the Minister of Overseas Trade: Has he seen in the

Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): I reply on behalf of the Minister of Overseas


## p. 3164 (#46) ############################################

3164
23 September
Oral Answers to Questions
Trade. His answer is as follows: "I have seen the article referred to in the September 1977
issue of the New Zealand Economist titled “A Minister for Europe?", and the reference in it
to"... the assertion made in New Zealand that the EEC had, by omitting to approve the
price rise, not honoured the Dublin Declaration". The EEC has not failed to honour the
Dublin Declaration. The article actually confirms this. In terms of the Dublin Declaration,
the Community is obliged to review periodically and, as necessary, to adjust the prices New
Zealand received for its exports of butter and cheese to Britain under Protocol 18 to the
EEC Treaty of Accession. While I was in Europe in July, the EEC Commission put a
proposal to the Council of Agriculture Ministers that the Protocol 18 guaranteed prices
should be increased by 10 percent. This proposal was considered at the 18-19 July meeting of
the council, and will be discussed again at this month's council meeting, which is scheduled
for Monday and Tuesday of next week. I am hopeful that the council will reach a favourable
decision on the commission's proposal then."

8. Mr ELWORTHY (Oamaru), on behalf of Mr ELLIOTT (Whangarei), asked the

met?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Forests): Planting under the forestry encouragement
loans scheme and forestry encouragement grants scheme has totalled 45 914 hectares to 31
March 1977. This is made up of 14 479 hectares under loans which were commenced in 1964,
and 31 435 hectares under grants introduced in 1971. It is expected that a further 8500
hectares will be planted under both schemes during the 1977 year. Cabinet approved on 1
July 1974 a target level of 10 000 hectares of new planting per annum under both of these
schemes. Although annual project approvals are made up to this target level, actual
performance has been only 70 percent to 80 percent since the target was introduced. The
reasons for this shortfall by private planters have been both physical and financial. It is
expected that a gradual increase in the level of performance will occur during future planting
seasons.
Mr Wetere: Have Maori incorporations taken advantage of the forestry encouragement
loans scheme?

type of encouragement and assistance from the Crown for planting schemes on Maori
incorporation land.

conservancy in comparison to other parts of New Zealand, has the Minister plans for

Hon. V. S. YOUNG: The member for West Coast is referring to the Reefton area of the
Nelson conservancy. A great deal depends on the initiative aken by landowners. Their
applications to the Forest Service determine to what degree for st encouragement grants will
be taken up. I agree with the implied suggestion that more planting of exotics should be done
on private land in that part of the West Coast.
Mr Bell: Does the Forest Service, in considering whether or not to make forestry
encouragement grants, take into account the type of land, soil stability, and alternative land
use?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: Obviously, the Forest Service must take into account areas to be

Clothing Factory Closures
11. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) asked the Minister of Trade and Industry: Which
clothing factories have closed in the last 18 months, and how many people have lost their
positions in each case?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry): My department
does not collect such statistics—
Hon. M. Rata: It ought to.
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: It did not do so under the Labour Government; it
has never done so. As I have said, my department does not collect such statistics, nor does it
hear of all the company closures as not all firms come and discuss their problems and seek
help. They are welcome to do so, and are encouraged to do so. Also, there is no statutory
requirement to notify the Department of Labour of redundancies. I can only supply the
figures from that department's half-yearly surveys, and am therefore unable to provide the
information exactly as required by the honourable gentleman, but the survey figures reveal
that between 15 April 1976 and 15 April 1977 the work force in the clothing industry rose
from 19 221 full-time workers to 20 552, and part-timers from 3048 to 4082. In April 1976
there were 873 clothing factory units, and in April 1977, 880.
Mr Marshall: Is the Minister satisfied that those figures would still be the same 5 months
afterwards; and is there any indication that the NAFTA terms would have any influence on
the closure of a number of clothing factories?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: Dealing with the latter part of the question first,
possibly in some cases it has had an effect, such as where a factory did not have a firm
commitment to supply the Australian market with a quantity of goods. That has been taken
care of in recent negotiations, and I would be pleased to answer a question on that from the
honourable member. In regard to the other part of the question, I have taken it a little
further. I have asked my department to get up-to-date figures as far as it is possible to do so,
but I can tell the honourable member that during the first 6 months of 1977—that is, not to
April-29 factory closures involving 240 positions were notified to the Department of
Labour. That position compares with 1975, when there were 67 closures involving a staff of
700.
Mr Bell: How many new factories have opened and how many existing factories have
expanded in the same period because of assistance through the Government's regional
development programme, and also how many positions have resulted from that?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: I do not have the exact information with me, but I
am aware that new factories have opened and that other factories have expanded. When we
get the figures we will find that there has been very little drop in staff in the last 8 months.
Probably there will be a slight increase overall.
Hon. F. M. Colman: Could there be as many as 2000 jobs in jeopardy in the clothing
trade if the present recession in that industry continues?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: I cannot give a categorical answer, but I do not
believe it is correct because I know of new opportunities which are opening up in the clothing
trade. Figures from the Department of Labour show that for April 1977 454 vacancies were
recorded for sewing machinists. I have been informed by units in the industry that they are
looking for sewing machinists, and that there are jobs for those skilled people usually quite
near to factories which have ceased production. My information is that the skilled people are
getting those jobs at present, and that jobs are available.
Mr Comber: Can the Minister state if the management of at least two of the factories
which have closed most recently, the Supreme factory and the House of Raymonde, spoke to
officials of his department about the intending closures?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: I have no information about that, but I am
concerned that in recent reported closures my department has informed me no approach was
made concerning them. As I said in my original reply, I welcome such inquiries and hope
that we will be informed of any such proposals by units. Many of those units which operate in
the larger cities have some part of the work being carried out in the smaller rural areas, and I
would appreciate those firms informing my department of their intentions because we are
aware of jobs that are available in the industry nearby and could be of help.

Overseas Borrowing
12. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) asked the (Minister of Finance): How much has the
Government borrowed overseas so far this calendar year?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Acting Minister of Finance): Since the beginning of the
calendar year the Government's gross direct overseas borrowing-that is, Public Account
and Reserve Bank-excluding capital equipment credits, has been about $NZ319.4 million.
Of this $319.4 million, $194.7 million was used to repay loans raised under the Labour
Administration, leaving a net figure to date of $124 million. In addition, the Government is
at present arranging a United States loan to the value of $NZ103 million-$US 100 million.
The total net borrowing this calendar year is estimated at $227.7 million, but this does not
include the yen loan of approximately $NZ115 million, which is in the process of negotiation.
This would give a total of $340 million.
Mr Marshall: Can the Minister say what the figure would be if capital equipment credits
and non-Government borrowing were included?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: No, I do not have those figures, but there has been a
considerable decline in the amount of gross Government borrowing. In the first 18 months in
office the Government reduced the amount of borrowing by one-third of the amount
borrowed during the Labour Government's last 18 months, and the figures I have just given
suggest that the reduction is continuing.
Mr D. M. J. Jones: Are the loans arranged by the National Government at a lower rate
of interest and for a longer term than the loans arranged by the Labour Government?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: Yes, that is correct. The loans have been changed over
because of the better terms and interest rates that the Government has been able to arrange.
