more than they were under the Labour Government, how does the Minister justify the
present level of overseas borrowing?
Hon. M. Rata: They've squandered them.
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: I am surprised that the member for Wigram should ask such
a question. He must be well aware that import costs and the costs of our invisibles have
continued to rise. The Government has exercised restraint in the interests of the economy.
The Labour Government took over our economy when it was at its strongest, and it
squandered a balance of payments of $1,000 million and borrowed $1,240 million. Opposi-
tion members should be ashamed to use the word "squandered" in relation to this
Government. The Government has had to try to repair the damage caused by that excessive
mismanagement of the economy.
Mr Bell: Can the Minister give the total amount borrowed by the Labour Government,
and show the comparison on an annual basis to the $340 million he mentioned in reply to the
original question?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: I think members can calculate that for themselves. In the
last 18 months of office the Labour Government borrowed $1,240 million, which is about
$800 million a year, and that compares with a total of $340 million this calendar year if the
yen loan goes through. The Government's major aim is to try to get the country back to an
external balance. Reasonable levels of borrowing are essential to maintain the economy.
Mr ACTING DEPUTY SPEAKER: May I remind the Minister that his replies should be
concise and not provocative.
Mr Rogers: Does the Government intend to borrow any more money this calendar year,

OECD Economic Survey
14. Hon. R. O. DOUGLAS (Manukau) asked the Minister of Finance: Is it correct, as
reported in the National Business Review of 7 September, that paragraphs referring to
indexation of wage adjustments in the original draft of the OECD economic survey of New

to the word "indexation”, and, if so, can he confirm that the reason for the changes made
which is advanced in that journal is also correct?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Acting Minister of Finance): The reasons are not correct.
As I explained to the Deputy Leader of the Opposition yesterday, the differences between
the original draft of the survey and the final version were the work of the OECD secretariat.
As the term "indexation" is generally used internationally to describe the automatic linkage
between movement in a price index and wage rates, and this is not used in New Zealand, I
can only assume the term was removed by the secretariat when it discovered the error. The
reasons given in the National Business Review are therefore incorrect.
Hon. R. O. Douglas: Does the Minister deny the quote in the National Business Review:
"Neither Treasury nor the Government is prepared to use the word 'indexation' for fear of
frightening the natives. By accepting the concept of indexation Government takes the first
step to living with inflation; to admit as much would be political suicide."?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: I have said twice that the National Business Review is
incorrect.
Hon. Michael Connelly: Is the Minister prepared to table the file containing correspond-
ence between the Government and the Government departments about the OECD?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: In all respects the 1977 review has been treated in the same

3170
23 September

way as the 1975 and 1976 reviews. I do not propose to table the correspondence on a matter
that has been handled by officials and which was settled by the secretariat. The secretariat of

Hon. Michael Connelly: Is it not a fact that the Government officials are acting under
Government policy, and, in view of the controversy about this issue, will the Minister table

Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: I do not see that there is a controversy. The member is

Mr ACTING DEPUTY SPEAKER: I remind honourable members that a large number

in compiling the report. The system of giving information to the secretariat has operated for
3 years. There is no reason for the House to have any additional information. The OECD

Hospitals Geriatric Means Test
15. Mr MINOGUE (Hamilton West), on behalf of Mr MALCOLM (Eden), asked the

understood and implemented in the fashion intended at the time the original decision to
remove the "geriatric means test" was announced?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare): I reply on behalf of the Minister of
Health. There was some misunderstanding about this scheme when it was introduced. The
purpose of the special assistance scheme was to provide financial assistance to geriatric
patients in private hospitals who were over the age of 65, who could not be accommodated in
public hospitals, and who had insufficient income to meet the private hospital fees even after
payment of the $11 a day Government subsidy by way of private hospital daily patients
benefit. The Government has decided that from 9 February 1977 the Government will
subsidise the patients by up to a maximum fee, which will take into account the patient's
income less $5 a week for personal and incidental expenses. On 1 July the maximum fee to
which subsidy would be available was reviewed, and the scheme is now working as intended,
and earlier misunderstandings have been resolved.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.

I want to take up briefly the point I advanced about the power contained to extend the
operation of the Bill to the Ross Dependency. I accept the construction placed on the
conventional words "peace, order, and good government by the Minister's advisers", but I
should also refer to some problems of enforcing the Act as a whole. The Minister declined to
enter into a discussion on the ground that this would disclose a bargaining position we might
take up. That is fair enough, and I accept it unreservedly. However, for the record, I want to
mention briefly two points. First, whatever jurisdiction was conferred on us by the British
Government in 1923 is now of a very distinctly unfashionable character. Britain's own right
to legislate for the Antarctic rests on discovery; and, of course, the general principle is that
discovery must be coupled with settlement to confer such a right. Until recent years at any
rate, settlement was at best episodic and generally non-existent, and if a right exists and has
properly been delegated to us by Britain, it is at best of a colonial nature. I know of no other
claim to wide fishing rights made on behalf of a non-selfgoverning colony. If at any time in
the future we do rely on the right conferred by clause 9(3) and seek to exert it, I believe we
will be breaking new ground, which at that time might well be regarded as anachronistic.
The second point is that any claim to extra territorial rights is absolute and uncondi-
tional. The 200-mile extension is a recent development, and, although still disputed by land-
locked countries, is widely accepted, although I am sure full understanding has far from been
reached. Even the conventional 3-mile limit was not free from doubt and difficulties. The
Minister's advisers will be well aware of many of the cases brought forward in the United
States during prohibition that distinguished between a right associated with national security
and a right to seek protection of the revenue. Even the 3-mile limit was not absolute, and
had restrictions built into it. It may well be that different attitudes will be taken to actions
clearly designed to exploit the resources of the sea for the benefit of mankind generally—a
"dog in the manger, what is in our back yard is ours" kind of attitude. That is what the open-
ended law of the sea conference is all about-the differing attitudes taken by countries like
New Zealand, which claims the fourth largest zone in the world compared with, say,

The member for Henderson seems to have some special interest in seeking to establish
that there is doubt about New Zealand's sovereignty in the Ross Dependency. I do not know
what his purpose is, but he has some varied legal arguments. In the second reading debate
the member for Henderson suggested that New Zealand jurisdiction over the Ross Depen-
dency was limited to the land area. He argued on the basis that the 1923 Order in Council by
which sovereignty was transferred from the United Kingdom to New Zealand made no
reference to the seas. The order empowered the making of regulations for the peace, order,
and good government of the Ross Dependency, but it made no specific reference to the seas
in the area. I pointed out to him that the phrase "peace, order, and good government" is
well and truly established in Commonwealth case law as indicating full sovereign powers. I
do not know what limitations may have been inherent in the phrase initially, but certainly it
has never been suggested by anyone that the phrase "peace, order, and good government"
included some limitation on the right of the State to legislate for its off-shore maritime
spaces.
I referred the honourable member to the New Zealand Constitution Act 1852, the point
being that until 1973 section 53 of the Constitution Act empowered this Parliament to make
laws for the peace, order, and good government of New Zealand. If the Act empowered
Parliament to make such laws and the member suggests that there is some weakness in
seeking to apply that power to the maritime area of the Ross Dependency, then he is
suggesting that any law that has been written by Parliament relating to maritime areas
around New Zealand would be invalid. That is the sort of circle that the member carries
himself through, and he did it again this Friday morning.
The Territorial Sea and Exclusive Economic Zone Bill is of very considerable import-
ance to New Zealand. In complete conformity with the negotiating techniques produced by
the Conference on the Law of the Sea, it provides an opportunity to make provision for the
exploitation of the resources of the sea surrounding New Zealand. What we are writing into
law reflects the wide agreement achieved by the conference. I pay the warmest possible
tribute to the work done by a select but very well informed group of New Zealand officials
who have, year after year, attended the Conference on the Law of the Sea. They have made
very significant contributions to the general debates about the law of the sea, and have also
worked to protect New Zealand's interests and to provide an opportunity for the New
Zealand fishing industry to exercise its skills and its determination to exploit, and at the same
time conserve, our resources. The two concepts are compatible one with the other-the
exploitation of the sustainable yield, and at the same time the preservation of the fish stock
so that it will be available not only for New Zealand's economic benefit, and not only to feed
New Zealand people, but also as an industry upon which we can base a considerable foreign
exchange income. I thank those who have taken part in the debate.

It is a substantial move where help is needed most. In the Committee stage I gave the
example of a married man with a dependent child under 5. At 1 April 1974, under the former
Labour Government's 1973 Budget, the level at which he started to pay tax was $1,362. At
15 July 1975, under the Labour Government's 1975 Budget, that level was lifted to $1,560.
At 1 October 1976, under the National Government's 1976 Budget, the level was lifted to
$3,016. At 1 October 1977, as a result of the 1977 Budget, the starting level at which tax will
be paid by a married man with a dependent child—and we are emphasising the family
man-will be $4,316. I should have thought that it would be obvious that the Bill provides
substantial help for the family man with young children.
As I said in Committee, this can be demonstrated in another way. In 1975 a married
man with a child under 5 would have received only the family benefit of $156. In 1976, if one
adds the family benefit of $156 to the first young-family rebate, the sum was increased to
$348. As a result of the 1977 Budget and the Bill we are now considering, which provides for
the single-income and young-family rebates for 1977-78, very substantial assistance is
provided, as, if we add to the $156 family benefit $468 for the young-family rebate plus $208
for the single-family rebate, that represents a total of $832.
During the discussion in the Committee, the Opposition tended to emphasise the
marginal rates of tax, but it is the total percentage of tax paid by the taxpayer that is the
critical point. On the average wage of, say, $5,000, the tax paid is 24.5 percent, or $1,217,
not the marginal figure of 38.5 percent the Deputy Leader of the Opposition emphasised.
For the taxpayer earning $6,000, another low wage earner, the total tax of $1,597 still
represents only 26.6 percent of his total wage, as I emphasised to the Committee.
Several Opposition members criticised the fact that the single-income rebate applies
only to those with a child under 10 years. The argument could go on endlessly. If you can
give more, you do give more, but the emphasis on resource management made it impossible
for the Government to lift the rebates beyond certain levels, and so that age level was fixed.
The rationale was clear: there is more scope to earn a supplementary income when the
youngest child reaches the age of 10. I believe most members have experience of that fact. It
can be argued, of course—and, indeed, one would generally expect—that as children grow
they eat more and need more clothing, and so on; but as a whole families tend to be better
off after the youngest child reaches the age of 10.
Hon. Sir Basil Arthur: That's just not so.
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: The member for Timaru can argue as much as he likes, but
that is the rationale, which I believe is fair and reasonable. However, I have never yet heard
a reasonable argument from the member for Timaru. Earlier in the day, he could not
understand the answer to a question on how officials worked, even though he has been a
Minister. I do not, therefore, expect him to understand the rationale behind the measures to
be implemented in this Bill, but I am stating them to the House as a whole, which I believe is
understanding and responsible.
There was some criticism that the adjustment would be made at the end of the tax year.
Again, I want to make it clear, as I said in the Committee, that it was decided that the

in the battle against inflation. When people decide whether or not to work overtime or

work that extra time, of course, but, when they get their overtime earnings in a week or even

University Acts Amendment Bill
UNIVERSITY ACTS AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. This Bill is made up of eight different parts, which, when the Bill is passed, will
emerge as eight separate amendment Acts. They will bring about changes in the legislation
applying to the University Grants Committee, to each university, and to Lincoln College.
The Bill results from a number of requests made by the University Grants Committee and
individual institutions over the last few years. Most of them reflect the views developed
within these independent institutions about the constitution and functions of their governing
bodies and administrative structures. Some of the amendments are of a minor machinery
nature, and there are, of course, consequential clauses. The amendments do not represent
any major restructuring or radical departures in the development of the universities. They
do, however, give effect to wishes arising from matters of internal concern and importance
locally, and I know that their resolution by the passing of this Bill will give considerable
satisfaction to the universities.
Because of the nature of the Bill, I shall go through some of the clauses more carefully.
Some clauses deal with the Universities Act itself, and the first two correct an anachronism
that has existed since 1963. In that year Massey became a full university after going through
an extraordinary series of name changes, such names including Massey College, Massey
University College, Massey University College of Manawatu, Massey University of
Manawatu, and finally Massey University. It is no longer appropriate to refer to that
institution as the Massey College of Agriculture, but the tradition has died very hard.
However, the change in the name does not alter the fact that the university still has a very
strong tradition of research into and the teaching of agriculture. Some clauses also ensure
that the chairman of the council of Lincoln College is included in the procedure for the
appointment of the chairman and members of the University Grants Committee. This
remedies a strange anomaly, in which the chairman of the council was omitted from the list
of those whom the Minister of Education should consult—that is, the chancellors and vice-
chancellors of the universities and the principal of Lincoln College.
The two clauses relating to the curriculum committee of the University Grants Commit-
tee allow the professors on that committee to appoint deputies to attend the meetings. This
will avoid the necessity of members having to resign if briefly out of the country and of new
appointments having to be made. The extension from five to seven of the number of
members of the research committee of the University Grants Committee will enable each of
the university institutions to be represented on the committee as of right. I am sure that the
universities will welcome my recent announcement that the research grant, which was not
paid in part of each of the last 2 years, will be restored in full next year. This will enable
evaluation of the research applications to begin very soon, so that allocations may be made
in time for next year.
I shall now move to matters that affect individual universities. Clause 10 adds a full-time
lecturer, to be elected by his fellows and the president of the students association, to the
membership of the council of the University of Auckland. It also allows the Mayor of
Auckland, who is mentioned in the Act, to nominate another councillor as his deputy. The
University of Auckland has encountered some difficulty in its existing powers to appoint and
to remove, and these provisions will eliminate that difficulty.
Most of the universities have professorial boards, but in the case of Auckland it is a
senate. The membership of that senate or professorial board has been altered in the Bill, and
there are a number of variations in each of the clauses dealing with individual universities.
For example, in the case of the University of Waikato there is a restriction on the eligibility
of non-academic employees of the university for office as council members. The restriction
depends on the amount of remuneration received from the council, and was expressed as a
fixed sum of money. Clause 19 allows the Minister of Education to determine what that
amount should be. Also in the case of the University of Waikato, the professorial board is
replaced by an academic board with a wider membership than academic staff. The new
members include student representatives, the university librarian, the liaison officer, and the
principal of Hamilton Teachers College.
Only two clauses affect Massey University, and they are similar in substance to some of
those to which I have already drawn attention. One adds the president of the students
association to the council, and the other allows for contracts with staff. For many years the⚫

3181
University Acts Amendment Bill
president of the students association has been a member of the council, but only by co-
option; this Bill will put him there as of right.
The clauses that deal with Victoria University of Wellington are similar in some respects
to the others. One of the clauses deals with the membership of the council and the
professorial board, and another deals with contracts, in much the same way as in the other
Acts.
An interesting provision relates to the constitution of the council of Lincoln College. It
has been normal in the past for two members of Parliament to be elected to the board by

functions of a vice-chancellor delegated to him and in certain circumstances will be the acting
vice-chancellor.
I have discussed Supplementary Order Paper 31 with the member for Wanganui, and I
thank him for his co-operation. We agreed that the Supplementary Order Paper should lie
on the table for a time, and, although the University of Waikato had some reservations, the
other universities were in general agreement with its provisions. Under the principal Act it is
not clear whether university councils have the power to decline to enrol certain students
because of an insufficiency of accommodation or teachers. The Supplementary Order Paper
clarifies that point, and I do not see it as a severe limitation on student enrolments. Students
will not be excluded from other courses or classes at the university, and it is similar to the
position in which, for some reason, a university does not offer a particular course in a
particular year. I am sure that universities will take great care to see that students are not
penalised and that alternative courses can be found after consultation with the dean of the
faculty. The Supplementary Order Paper also contains some minor consequential changes,
which were not foreseen when the Bill was introduced. One of the amendments adds a
student to the professorial board of Lincoln College. The Bill contains many machinery
provisions, but it will go a long way towards tidying up the present position, and will enable
universities to function more satisfactorily.

TUESDAY, 27 SEPTEMBER 1977
Mr Acting Speaker took the chair at 2.30 p.m.

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS
Employment Service, Tokoroa
1. Mr REWETI (Eastern Maori), on behalf of Hon. M. RATA (Northern Maori), asked
the Minister of Labour: In view of the employment difficulties being experienced in
Tokoroa, has he any plans for improving departmental employment services, and in
particular for providing Tokoroa with a permanent employment service?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): An expansion of the operations of the
Department of Labour's employment service is currently under consideration by the
Government. A decision on a proposal to increase the number of employment officers is
expected shortly, following which I hope to be able to upgrade the service provided in
Tokoroa. This will, however, not be a full-time service. Whether such a service will be
provided at some time in the future is likely to depend, among other things, on the extent to
which the Government can make available additional staff and other resources for the
employment service.
Mr Hunt: To what extent is the proposed improvement in employment services in
Tokoroa due to the increasing amount of unemployment in that town?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: The original reply did not indicate an immediate upgrading of the
service in Tokoroa; it indicated that we were still applying for appropriate officers, and that
then we might be able to step up the service in Tokoroa. Regarding unemployment—and I

Otago University Staff
4. RICHARD WALLS (Dunedin North) asked the Minister of Education: How many
lecturers, readers, and technical staff were employed at the University of Otago in the years
ended 1974, 1975, and 1976, what is the figure for 1977, and how many took up postings
direct from overseas?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): In 1974, the University of Otago had
358 lecturers; in 1975, 349; in 1976, 346; and in 1977, 324. Of these, 22, 26, 27, and 22 were
appointed from overseas in the 4 years. The figures for associate professors, the grade used
by the University of Otago instead of reader, were 51 in 1974, 53 in 1975, 57 in 1976, and 61
in 1977, of whom 2 were appointed from overseas in 1975 and 1 in 1977. The numbers of
technical staff have been 250 in 1974 and 1975, 259 in 1976, and 276 in 1977. Of these, 2 were
appointed from overseas in 1975, 1 in 1976, and 3 in 1977.
Mr Hunt: Was the quite alarming decrease in the number of lecturers between 1976 and
1977 because of a fall in the roll or because of other factors?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: The question asked for a return of full-time staff. Just the same
as any other university, Otago has many staff, and, in its case, a larger number of part-time
staff, particularly in the medical fields. That is the reason for the change in the staff numbers,
and I am certain that if the university had felt it was being understaffed it would have made
some representation.
Mr Hunt: Can the Minister assure us that the University of Otago has made no
representations to him or to the University Grants Committee for an increase in the number
of staff?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: The university has certainly made no representations to me. I do
not know whether it has made representations to the University Grants Committee. The
member should know that a university is given a block grant, out of which it is expected to
make provision for the students within the university. The university makes the decision
about how many staff will be employed within the total allocation.
Mr Hunt: In view of the Minister's answer that it is up to the university to make the staff
available out of the block grant over a 5-year period, could the Minister now answer the
supplementary question I asked him-namely, was the reason for the dramatic decline
between 1976 and 1977 a drop in the number of students attending the university?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: I would not call it a dramatic drop, because the number of
lecturers and associate professors does not include professors, and the total figures are not
available for the member to make that assumption.
Mr Hunt: A drop of 30 or so last year, isn't it?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: It is not a drop of 30. I repeat that in 1976 there were 346
lecturers plus 57 associate professors, which totals 403. In 1977 there were 324 lecturers and
61 associate professors, which totals 385. That is not a dramatic decrease, because at the
same time there was an increase in the number of part-time professors and lecturers from
outside the university, and this could well have made up the total number to teach those
students. The number at the University of Otago was, from memory, about the same as in
the previous year.

Energy Conservation, Tax Incentives
7. Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) asked the Minister of Energy Resources: Has he seen
the comments of Mr Lindsay Halliday, WRONZ chemical engineer, in Wool World for
August which describe "The Government's tax incentives as too limited in their scope" and
"should be extended to include all systems whose main aim was to save substantial amounts
of energy", and, if so, is he considering any extension of the tax incentives?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy Resources): The article referred to was obviously
written some time ago. As the member should know, a major extension of the tax incentive
scheme was announced in this year's Budget, and now covers the types of systems referred to
in the article. I remind the honourable member that some of the features were listed in a
press statement issued on the night of the Budget. As mentioned in the press statement, the
scheme has now been extended to include capital expenditure on the following: equipment
for recycling or re-using waste material; heat exchange equipment; equipment for recovery
of waste heat; insulation of industrial and commercial buildings; sealing of energy leaks; new
energy using plant which uses indigenous resources, for example, coal, waste, natural gas,
geothermal, LPG, solar or wind energy, but not plant using oil or electricity; conversion of
existing energy using plant from oil or electricity to other indigenous resources, for example,
coal, waste, natural gas, geothermal, LPG, and solar or wind energy; and, finally, plant and
ancillary equipment, which in association with approved energy using plant and equipment.
mitigates pollution effects.
Hon. F. M. Colman: Since the announcement of the tax incentives in July, what interest
has the industry taken in the incentives, how many applications have there been, and for
what amounts?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: It will not be possible to know this at least until after the end of the
financial year, because most of them relate directly to the opportunity of writing off certain
investments against tax liability. Until such time as that applies, and the records are known, I
cannot give an indication. However, I can assure the honourable member that inquiries
made to the office and to the Ministry of Energy Resources have been healthy.

Social Welfare Counselling of Unmarried Mothers
9. Hon. MICHAEL CONNELLY (Wigram), on behalf of Mrs BATCHELOR (Avon),
asked the Minister of Social Welfare: Has he seen a report in the Evening Post of 21
September 1977 in which he is quoted as saying that increased counselling would be given to
unmarried mothers who choose to keep their babies, and could he explain what the emphasis
of such counselling will be and what effect it may have on unmarried mothers?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare): Yes, I have seen the report referred
to. The Domestic Purposes Benefit Review Committee recommended that counselling
should be provided for unmarried mothers before the birth of the child with a view to
ensuring that she is fully aware of all the considerations on which her own decision of
whether to keep the child or make it available for adoption is made. I referred to the
implementation of this recommendation when I spoke to the Dominion Federation of
Townswomen's Guilds recently. Emphasis will be placed on informing the unmarried
mother of her rights and the likely consequences of any decision she may make. The effect of
the counselling will be that unmarried mothers will be able to make a more informed and
reasoned decision on the future of their children.
Hon. Michael Connelly: When the mothers have made the informed and reasoned
decision after being counselled, what justification is there for reducing the benefits paid to
them?
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: That has nothing to do with the question or the answer given.
Hon. Michael Connelly: A point of order, Mr Speaker.
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: Is it in relation to the ruling I have just given?
Hon. Michael Connelly: It is a point of order in relation to the general issue.
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: Order! This is question time, but it is not the time for
questioning rulings given. If the honourable member has another matter he wants to raise
with me he is entitled to do that, but I am not prepared to hear a discussion, on a point of
order, on a ruling I have just given. A ruling given is a ruling given, and that is that. We want
to get on with the questions. If it is not clear in the honourable member's mind it is perfectly
clear in mine that when a question is asked the answer given must be relevant to the
question. Occasionally Ministers stray a little, but if I can I try to encourage them not to do
so; but the supplementary question must be designed to elucidate further relevant material
based on the answer given by the Minister and, in turn, must be relevant to the main
question. The main question simply asked the Minister if he had seen a report, and if he
could explain what the emphasis of such counselling will be; it had nothing to do with the
amount of benefit. The answer given related to the type of counselling to be given to
unmarried mothers.
Hon. Michael Connelly: A point of order, Mr Speaker. I raise this point on the general
question of what is involved in this case. In his reply, the Minister referred to the advice that
will be given to people. The tenor of my question to him was if, having received that advice,
a person pursued a certain course of action, what was the justification for certain action on
the part of the Minister. I based that supplementary question on the final part of the original
question, which asked if the Minister could explain what the emphasis of such counselling
will be and what effect it may have on unmarried mothers. The point I make is simply that
the Minister is making decisions that affect the well-being of unmarried mothers. On the
other hand, he is saying that they are given advice to enable them to make a correct decision.
I want him to relate the correct decision they would make on that advice to other action
taken, apart from any advice on the decision that may be made. I believe that is a proper
question.
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: The honourable member is coming very closing to trifling with
the Chair and wasting the time of the House. I have given him my ruling, and I told him why
I had so ruled. I explained it in very simple language. He is questioning my ruling, and this is
not the time to do that—and a point of order is certainly not the method by which to do it. I
am not prepared to accept that type of comment on rulings I have given. The question was
quite clear to me, and the Minister's answer was also clear. I know the honourable member
would like to have some further information, but the question he asked was not related to
the answer given by the Minister. He is entitled to ask the Minister for that information in a
separate question if he still wants to do so, but this is not the appropriate question to ask it
on. If I were to allow the honourable member to ask that supplementary question other
members would be able to ask supplementary questions on any matter touching on social
welfare-benefits, the lot. The question is a specific one dealing with counselling and advice
given by the counselling services.

Imports—Volume
12. Mr ELWORTHY (Oamaru) asked the Minister of Trade and Industry: Has he seen
the comment by the New Zealand Institute of Economic Research, on page 17 of its latest
report, that “it is difficult to see that the volume of imports could fall much further”, and, if
so, (a) does he agree with this statement, and (b) could he indicate what evidence there is to
support this view?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Minister of Overseas Trade): I reply on behalf of the
Minister of Trade and Industry. His reply is as follows: "I have seen the comment referred
to. I cannot disagree with this statement when it is read in its proper context, for the
paragraph goes on immediately to point out that 'Opportunities for import replacement are
limited, in the short term at least, and any marked reduction in the quantity of imports would
probably be precipitated only if there were a substantial fall in the volume of production.'
With most of the goods currently imported into New Zealand being essential inputs into the
manufacturing process, the Government would certainly not consider further restricting the
level of imports if, by doing so, the viability of our economy, in terms of both production and
employment, would be endangered.”
Mr Elworthy: Would further restrictions on imports have any adverse effect on
employment opportunities?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS: Inasmuch as the great weight of our imports relates to raw
materials, it certainly would.
Richard Walls: Does the Minister agree with the comment made by Sir Frank Holmes,
that intensifying import controls would invite retaliation against New Zealand exporters?
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: That question seeks an opinion from the Minister, but he may
comment if he wishes.
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS: That view is widely held.
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: How does the Acting Prime Minister reconcile his current position
in this question with the election manifesto of the National Party?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS: I have no difficulty whatsoever. The National Party sought
to reduce the volume of imports into New Zealand and that, in fact, has occurred. If the
honourable member checks the statistics, he will find justification for that statement.
Hon. Michael Connelly: Does the Minister see any prospect of economies in expenditure
of overseas funds?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS: There could well be some areas. One suggestion I have made
on a number of occasions—I am not sure how effective it would be—is that importers might
well shop around in exercising their opportunity to import into New Zealand, and obtain a
better bargain in that way.

UNEMPLOYMENT-NOTICE UNDER STANDING ORDER 89
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: I have received from the Leader of the Opposition a letter
bearing today's date, which reads as follows:
"Pursuant to Standing Order 89, I give notice that I propose to move on Tuesday 27
September, that the House be now adjourned for the purpose of discussing a definite matter
of urgent public importance. This is the increase in the numbers of those out of work and on
special Government relief work, as revealed by the Minister of Labour on Friday 23
September, to 15 838, the highest level since World War II. This increase of 10 percent in 2
weeks of registered unemployed runs completely contrary to the normal seasonal trend,
which traditionally shows a decline at this time of year, and, as such, is a matter of recent
occurrence and of urgent concern facing the country.
"This rise is attributable to a whole series of fiscal, monetary, and economic measures
taken by the present Government during its term in office, all aimed at depressing the
economy with the inevitable result being an increase in unemployment. These measures, for
which the Government is responsible, include: (1) Rises in interest rates, slowing invest-
ment, at least partly due to actions by the Government; (2) Steep increases in the amount of
tax collected, thus leaving less for expenditure and hence cutting demand. Tax collected this
year is estimated to rise by $913 million, or 6.5 percent of gross national product; (3) Failure
to safeguard New Zealand's interests in trade negotiations, especially with Australia, leading
to cuts in, among others, the clothing industry; (4) Increases in Government charges, further
depressing the amount consumers have to spend, and thus cutting demand; and (5) Cuts in
regional development expenditure, from $5,047,000 in 1974-75 to $4.32 million in 1977-78.
"Unless these measures are reversed or other counteracting action taken, the situation
can only deteriorate as the end of the school year approaches and many thousands of school
leavers enter the labour force in search of employment. This constitutes a very serious threat
to the country and, as such, requires the immediate attention of the House and the
Government."
The letter was submitted more than 1 hour before the time fixed for the meeting of the
House, and so complies with the requirement of Standing Order 89 in that respect. In terms
of Standing Order 90, I have to consider, in deciding whether the matter is one contemplated
by Standing Order 89, if the statement I have read to the House satisfies Standing Order 90.
In considering this I immediately called to mind the remarks of Mr Speaker Jack earlier this
session when he received notice of a similar adjournment motion proposed to be moved
concerning a rise in the consumer price index. That was on 8 July, and the Speaker's remarks
are contained in issue No. 11 of the Hansard "pinks" at page 1289. As on that occasion, I
feel no difficulty in holding that one of the three criteria set out in Standing Order 90 is
satisfied in that this matter does involve the administrative or ministerial responsibility of the
Government.
In respect of the other two requirements of Standing Order 90—that the matter must be
a particular case of recent occurrence, and that it requires the immediate attention of the
House-I must turn to the ruling of 8 July for guidance. Mr Speaker Jack quoted a precedent
from the United Kingdom in which an adjournment motion concerned with rising unemploy-
ment was declined under the corresponding Standing Orders of the House of Commons. The


## p. 3193 (#75) ############################################

27 September
3193
Unemployment-Notice Under Standing Order 89
reason was that unemployment was a continuing problem, and not a particular case requiring
immediate attention. The Speaker pointed out that in New Zealand we had given some
weight to other factors-for example, whether the Address in Reply debate is
continuing-by which the matter proposed to be discussed could be raised in the House.
None of those factors is present here; as also they were not in the case he was considering.
He felt that matters such as this, which refer to continuing problems, were not strictly
contemplated by the Standing Order.
After weighing all these considerations Mr Speaker Jack said: “Therefore, bending my
legal conscience a bit and bending the meaning of the word 'case' and of the word
'immediate' a bit, I propose to give the Leader of the Opposition the benefit of an enormous
doubt and let him move his motion." He concluded, "My decision to accept the motion is, I
believe, right in instinct, though probably wrong at law, and I should not like it to be treated
as a precedent."
Following the Speaker's admonition on that occasion that his decision on the merits of
the application before him should not be treated as a precedent, I think it is inescapable that
a proposal to move the adjournment of the House to discuss a continuing problem such as
increasing unemployment is not one contemplated by Standing Order 90 in that it is not a
particular case of recent occurrence, nor does it require the immediate attention of the
House. I must therefore decline to accept the motion. Were I to do otherwise, I would in
effect be setting a precedent, which Mr Speaker Jack said specifically should not happen.
Mr HUNT (New Lynn): A point of order, Mr Speaker. I wonder if you might have a
look at the precedents set over the years, particularly between 1966 when I came into the
House and when Mr Speaker Jack himself set a precedent with the ruling he gave in 1977. I
am not in any way suggesting that you should comment at this stage, but I remember that in
the past a number of adjournment debates sought by both sides of the House have been
allowed precisely because this very statistic has been published. If that is the case, and if
there is a recommendation from the Standing Orders Committee that we should have
another look at it, then that is a desirable point at which you could set a new precedent.
I thought the precedent had been established by Speakers as far back as Mr Speaker
Oram, Mr Speaker Algie, and subsequent Speakers including Mr Speaker Jack himself in
the late 1960s, and then by Mr Speaker Whitehead, the member for Heretaunga when he
was Acting Speaker, and myself. On a number of occasions exactly the same statistic has
been the occasion of the acceptance by Speakers of a motion for an adjournment debate. If
we are to have a precedent then perhaps it should be the subject of a recommendation from
the Standing Orders Committee, because what happened in the past must presumably have
some bearing on what is happening in the present unless there is a specific recommendation
to the contrary.
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: I am grateful to the honourable member for giving me his
advice. I had a look at this with my advisers, and it seemed quite clear to me that on this
occasion the precedent to which I would turn was the most recent ruling, given in a very
similar case, which Mr Speaker Jack took from a similar case that had occurred recently in
the House of Commons in Britain. As the honourable member knows, rulings in the House
of Commons are not binding, but they are a guide that we follow very often. It seemed to me
that the latest ruling by Mr Speaker Jack was such that were I to set it aside I would be
creating an undesirable precedent. I am not justified in setting aside any ruling he has
recently given. However, I shall have a look at the matter in the broader context.

the word "crisis" had become synonomous with the words "National” and “housing”. In its
1975 report the National Housing Commission had said that New Zealanders' housing needs
would be met only if sufficient long-term finance at reasonable rates of interest was
constantly available. That point could not be emphasised too strongly, because mortgage
finance was the life blood of the housing industry.

a greater degree, and to take the State out of housing. Last year the amount of mortgage

wished Mr and Mrs Futter much happiness in their retirement.

Taxation-Direct
1. Mr TALBOT (South Canterbury), on behalf of Miss DEWE (Lyttelton), asked the

Ross, as reported in the Dominion of 21 September, in which he refers to the proportion of
tax yield received from direct taxation and notes "the peak was reached in 1975 where the
proportion of direct taxes to the total tax revenue reached 79 percent", and, if so, could he
indicate whether this is correct?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister in Charge of the Inland Revenue Department): I
have seen the report in the Dominion. I can confirm that the proportion of direct taxes to the
total tax revenue was the highest in the year ended 31 March 1975, and that the proportion in
that year was 79 percent of the total tax revenue, excluding highways tax.
Mr Rogers: If the peak of direct taxation was reached in 1975, when does the Minister
expect to reach the peak of the amount of indirect taxation that is now being foisted on New
Zealand?
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: That question is quite unrelated.
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: I cannot give the figures for indirect tax, but the peak of
direct tax relates in the following way: 1972-73, 73.5 percent; 1973-74, 75.7 percent; 1974-75,
79 percent. In 1975-76 it fell to 76.3 percent, and in 1976-77 it was 77.3 percent.
Hon. P. I. Wilkinson: Bearing in mind that the peak year fell when the Labour
Government was in power, can the Minister confirm that it fell particularly heavily on the
low and middle income groups, which Labour is now protesting require further taxation

Hon. R. L. Bailey: In monetary terms, what were the taxation figures?

Horohoro Forest
5. Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East) asked the Minister of Forests: Now that the milling of
the Horohoro Forest is to cease in November next, can he indicate when the original
contract was due to terminate, and what new management proposals have been formulated
for this area?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Forests): The original Cabinet decision to provide
wood to the New Zealand Railways Mamaku sawmill was for 40 years, and was due to expire
on 16 November 1984. The future management of the Horohoro Forest is now being
examined by the Conservator of Forests, Rotorua, with the object of defining the future role
of the forest for various uses. Before any final decision is made, areas which should be
reserved for scientific and other purposes will be considered by the scientific co-ordinating
committee, together with proposals for neighbouring forests.

service for refitting from 13 May 1976 to 13 December 1976. Wages payments to cooks and
stewards for the 5 months that the vessel was in service during the year ended 31 March 1977
totalled $185,724.
Mr Latter: How many more cooks and stewards were employed after the refit, and what
would be the amount paid for a full year's wages, at the higher level?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN: Seventeen provedore staff were kept on the Aratika
during her refit, at a cost of $158,900. For the current staffing level-and these are the only
figures available to me—it is estimated that the annual cost of wages for provedore staff on
the Aratika will be about $745,000, and that revenue earned by the ship for the carriage of
passengers and passengers' cars, and for catering, will total about $3.6 million during 1977-
78.
Hon. F. M. Colman: Can the Minister confirm that wages paid to personnel on the
Aratika are the subject of award negotiations between the cooks and stewards and the
Railways Department?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN: Yes, I can confirm that. I gave the total wages paid, but
individuals earn different incomes in accordance with the class of cook or steward.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.

Oral Answers to Questions
Auckland Hospital—Unused Wards
14. Hon. MICHAEL CONNELLY (Wigram), on behalf of Mr HUNT (New Lynn),
asked the Minister of Health: Has he seen a statement in the New Zealand Herald of 2
September 1977 that "Three brand-new wards at Auckland Hospital are still standing empty,
nearly 4 years after the main building at the hospital was completed", and, if so, (a) is the
statement correct, and (b) is there any possibility that these wards could be used to upgrade
provisions for hospitalisation of children?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): I have seen the statement. It is slightly
misleading. Although the main structure of the building was completed some years ago, the
wards referred to were not available for occupation until the end of 1975. Since then, there
has been progressive commissioning of stage III, leaving only the three wards to be
commissioned within the next 9 to 12 months. These will provide an increase in existing
services namely, E. N. T., urology, and orthopaedics. The possibility of using these wards
temporarily for children was examined in great detail. It was decided that the lack of
facilities suitable for children, and the necessity of having life-support systems, laboratory
services, and so on, especially geared for children, made this undesirable.
Hon. Michael Connelly: Will the Minister confirm that the main reason for the wards not
being put into operation is that the Auckland Hospital Board has not received the
commissioning grant which it requested 5 months ago and to which it has not received a
reply?
Hon. T. F. GILL: I cannot comment in detail on that without notice. I have seen the
chairman of the Auckland Hospital Board at least once a month over the last 5 months, and
he has never mentioned to me that he was awaiting a reply of that nature. Obviously, the
commissioning of a large new hospital which requires staffing and equipment is part of a
programme, and it is proceeding in accordance with that programme.
Hon. Michael Connelly: Will the Minister discuss with his department the application by
the Auckland Hospital Board for a commissioning grant, and instruct his department to
prepare the necessary papers for making the financial arrangements forthwith?
Hon. T. F. GILL: I cannot agree that we should proceed forthwith with a proposition
involving a lot of money which has been put to me in the House by a member of the
Opposition. I can assure the member that we are administering the Health vote, and the
moneys available to us are being used very sensibly and properly.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.

permanent position are married. To be eligible to apply for permanent positions in primary
schools certificated teachers who have been out of the service for 3 or more years are
required to undergo retraining. I cannot ensure that married women who retrain will obtain
permanent positions. Appointments are made on the basis of overall suitability for a position

WRITTEN QUESTIONS
Racing Broadcasts
Survey
1. Mr LITHGOW (Palmerston North) asked the Minister of Broadcasting: How many
people were questioned in the sample taken in the recent survey on race broadcasting, was
the sample the same as that in previous surveys, and what percentage of people in the survey
came from towns with a population of less than 5000?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Broadcasting) replied: The Broadcasting Corpora-
tion informs me that 2725 people returned questionnaires in the recent survey, a number
strictly comparable with the 2823 who responded to the 1969 questionnaire. Respondents to
the 1977 survey, who came from rural areas or towns of less than 5000, amounted to 34
percent of the total. This proportion is 4 percent higher than the overall percentage of the
population living in such localities.
(8/9/77)
Racing Broadcasts-Scratching Service
2. Mr LITHGOW (Palmerston North) asked the Minister of Broadcasting: What is the
cost to a sponsor to run a BCNZ broadcasting network scratching service each morning for
the racing public on a 12-month basis?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Broadcasting) replied: As I indicated in my reply
to an earlier question, the Broadcasting Corporation can assess costs for such a service only
if the potential purchaser supplies all the relevant details of the proposal.
(8/9/77)
Racing Broadcasts-Scratching Service
3. Mr LITHGOW (Palmerston North) asked the Minister of Broadcasting: What is the
cost to an interested party to buy time to give a daily scratching service to the racing public
on BCNZ radio network each morning on a 12-month basis?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Broadcasting) replied: The Broadcasting Corpora-
tion advises that no such service has been sold and a cost for it could not be assessed until
such factors as its actual time placement and duration, the degree of broadcasting staff
participation in obtaining and presenting the information, and the cost of telephone links
were finalised. Any such session would have to satisfy programme acceptability criteria and
would depend on the availability of commercial time.

Christchurch Neurosurgical Unit-Operations
5. RICHARD WALLS (Dunedin North) asked the Minister of Health: Following the
announcement that a neurosurgery unit is to be established at Christchurch, would he
advise: (a) what was the number of major cases operated on at the Christchurch Hospital
over the past year, and from which areas did those come; (b) how many were transferred
from Christchurch to Dunedin for operating; and (c) what was the number of other cases
treated at the Christchurch neurosurgical unit last year, and from which areas did those cases
come?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health) replied: The answers to these questions are as
follows: (a) During 1976, there was a total of 165 operations which might be classified as
neurosurgical operations undertaken in the Christchurch, Princess Margaret, and Burwood
Hospitals. These were operations undertaken by general surgeons, orthopaedic surgeons,
and paediatric surgeons. These patients would all have been drawn from the North
Canterbury, West Coast, Ashburton, and South Canterbury Hospital Board areas. (b) In the
same period 63 patients were transferred from Christchurch to Dunedin. (c) This question is
not relevant, because there was no neurosurgical unit at Christchurch.

9. Mr BRUCE BARCLAY (Christchurch Central) asked the Minister in Charge of the
Rural Banking and Finance Corporation: Can he give a guarantee that technical changes in
farm ownership, such as where a farmer brings his children into the business as a partner-
ship, will not result in a review, and a consequent raising, of the interest rate on mortgages
provided by the Rural Banking and Finance Corporation?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister in Charge of the Rural Banking and Finance Corporation)

Rural Banking and Finance Corporation and the Department of Maori Affairs, and
advances made through the Land Settlement and Marginal Lands Boards of the Department
of Lands and Survey. In addition the new rates will also apply to all interest review notices
issued on or after 22 July 1977 and when any change is made in the loan arrangement at the
request and benefit of the mortgagor."

Armed Offenders Squad-Dog Culling
20. Mr KIRK (Sydenham) asked the Minister of Police: Can he confirm that the armed
offenders squad is being considered for or has been used in some areas to cull dogs that have
molested sheep, and, if so, will he state the occasions and background for this?
Hon. ALLAN MCCREADY (Minister of Police) replied: The armed offenders squads have
never been used as suggested, nor has it ever been contemplated that they would be used in
such a situation. Due to concern over the actions of stray dogs in the Auckland area, there
was discussion by the city council that such assistance should be requested. No approach has

Dog Control
23. Mr KIRK (Sydenham) asked the Minister of Local Government: Is he aware that some
sheep farmers bordering on the Wellington urban area have suffered serious harassment to
their flocks by marauding dogs, and, if so, what action does he intend to take to reduce the
serious stock losses which are occurring?
Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister of Local Government) replied: I am aware of the problem
of marauding dogs harassing sheep on some farms near Wellington and elsewhere. It is, of
course, the responsibility of local authorities to provide and enforce in their districts dog
control measures within the provisions of the Dogs Registration Act 1955, the Hydatids Act
1968, and other relevant legislation. Property owners also have certain powers, one of which
is to destroy immediately dogs attacking people or stock, or running at large among stock.
Nevertheless, I know there are shortcomings in the present law that need attention. As I
have recently indicated to a number of organisations and individuals interested in the dog
control issue, an investigation is to be carried out into all aspects of this, including the
problem of dangerous, straying, unwanted, and neglected dogs.

Maori Land Alienations

section leases; and 1 scenic reserve lease to the Crown.

Genetic Engineering-DSIR Experiments
27. Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central) asked the Minister of Science and Technology: Has
he read the article by Mr Wilson in the August 1977 issue of New Zealand Environment
entitled "Genetic Engineering: Ultimate Environmental Hazard?", which states on page 23
that a DSIR experiment conducted in 1974 with a genetically created fungus killed all the
trees it was tested on, and, if so, can he confirm whether this story is correct, and, if it is, can
he say what precautions the DSIR took then and is taking now to ensure that genetically
created substances cannot escape into the environment?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Science and Technology) replied: I have read the
article referred to. It is correct that, in the course of some experiments carried out by the
DSIR in late 1974, a single modified strain of mycorrhizal fungus was produced which might
have been the cause of the death of 10 1-in.-high pine seedlings. Following normal
precautionary procedures, all experiments with the modified strain were carried out under
contained conditions to ensure that the fungus did not escape, and subsequently both
seedlings and fungus were totally destroyed and sterilised. New Zealand guidelines for the
safe conduct of research using novel genetic techniques have since been developed by the
New Zealand Medical Research Council and modified and extended by the DSIR, and are in
force in the DSIR by my direction. DSIR containment facilities for the 1974 experiment
would have complied with the guidelines. I am satisfied precautions have been adequate at
all times.
(21/9/77)

Higher Salaries Commission
29. Mr BRILL (Kapiti) asked the Minister of State Services: How many job classifications
and approximately how many positions fall within the jurisdiction of the Higher Salaries
Commission, and what is the minimum salary of persons falling within the jurisdiction of the
commission?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of State Services) replied: The Higher Salaries Commis-
sion is required, under regulation 23 of the Wage Adjustment Regulations 1974, to
determine the salaries of specified persons. The positions and job classifications include: (a)
the salaries and allowances of members of Parliament; (b) the salary of the highest-paid
executive officer of public corporations and other public bodies; (c) the salaries of the
highest-paid administrative professional and technical officer of local authorities; (d) the
salaries of State servants who are subject to section 18(2) of the State Services Remuneration
and Conditions of Employment Act 1969; generally this includes administrative and profes-
sional persons whose salaries exceeded $19,556 as at 15 May 1977; (e) the salaries of doctors
employed by hospital boards; (f) the salaries of university academic staff. No minimum
salary is prescribed, but in small county councils a salary as low as $6,000 may be set by the
commission. The precise number of persons falling within the jurisdiction of the commission
is not available. However, the commission has made 1200 determinations; one determina-
tion covers groups such as medical doctors, 2009, university academic staff, 2900, and State
servants, over 200 positions.
(21/9/77)
Common Fund Proposal
30. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) asked the Minister of Overseas Trade: What is New
Zealand's present position on the proposal to establish a Common Fund?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Minister of Overseas Trade) replied: I have commented fully
on New Zealand's position on the Common Fund in the past. Basically, this is that we
recognise the problems of commodity trade and are prepared to support practical efforts to
alleviate the difficulties that fluctuations in commodity prices can cause. We have also
expressed our support for the principle of some common financing arrangement. We have
not, however, been able to support all aspects of the Common Fund proposal as prepared by
the secretariat of UNCTAD. Currently we are participating in a series of meetings under
OECD auspices to discuss the possible elements and framework of a fund which would be of
practical assistance in dealing with commodity problems, and these discussions will continue
over the next few weeks. I understand that the developing countries will be holding similar
discussions. A further negotiating conference on the Common Fund is to be held in
November, and, as there are now signs of greater flexibility on both sides, I am hopeful that
it will be possible to make some worth-while progress at that time.
(21/9/77)

Unit Titles Act
33. Mr HUNT (New Lynn) asked the Minister of Justice: Has he seen a comment in the
Western Leader of 30 August 1977 by Glen Eden Councillor Mr Peter Trim that the Unit
Titles Act is a "horrible mess" that has been thrust upon local authorities and should be
pushed right back on the Government, and that the council is in the "ridiculous situation
where it can be sued for not issuing a certificate for a unit title, just as it could be sued for
issuing one, and, if so, have complaints been received about this matter from other councils,
and are there any proposals for amending the Act?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice) replied: I had not hitherto seen the
comment referred to. I would certainly not agree that the Act is a "terrible mess", as Mr
Trim terms it. The Government is aware that there are some problem areas in the Unit Titles
Act, and in particular has noted the difficulties local authorities are experiencing with the
Act in that there seems to be a lack of uniformity among local authorities as to their
requirements. Because of this, and in order to honour its election undertaking to review the
Unit Titles Act, the Government has set up a special committee to carry out this task. This
special committee, which was set up earlier this year, is made up of departmental representa-
tives and representatives from the professions and other interested bodies, and includes a
representative from the local authority organisations. The committee is, I am informed, now
nearing the end of a full review of the Act, and will report back to me with a suggested draft
amendment to the Act. Among the amendments that will be included will be a provision
clarifying the duties and obligations of a local body under the Act.

Remand Prisoners-Use of Police Cells
35. Mr KIRK (Sydenham) asked the Minister of Police: Will he approve the use of Police
Department cells, staffed by prison service staff, for short-term remand prisoners from the
courts, in order to overcome the serious overcrowding problems which exist at Addington
Remand Prison and at Mount Eden Jail?
Hon. ALLAN MCCREADY (Minister of Police) replied: No official approaches have been
made about this, but in any event the position is that cell accommodation at the Christchurch
Police Station was designed for the detention of persons arrested pending their appearance
before a court, and for those who have been sentenced to some form of detention and have
to be escorted elsewhere. The facilities would be totally inadequate for use as a remand
prison. Some police stations were formerly used for the detention of prisoners, but because
of numerous complaints about the standard of facilities must have now reverted to overnight
lockups. The use of the Christchurch Police Station cells for remand prisoners would be most
undesirable and disruptive to the normal policing function. Accordingly, I would not agree
to the proposal. The same comments apply to the cells at the Auckland Police Station.

Housing-Second Mortgage Lending by POSB
47. Mr ROGERS (Onehunga) asked the Postmaster-General: Can he confirm that to
qualify for a second mortgage through the recently introduced Post Office scheme the total
outgoings under first and second mortgages must not exceed 33 percent of the income of the
applicant, or, if both parties are working, 33 percent of the income of both applicants?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Postmaster-General) replied: Generally, a person wishing to
borrow under the Post Office Savings Bank's personal housing loans second mortgage
scheme must not be overcommitted with regular payments for items such as mortgages,
rates, insurance, hire purchase, and so on. However, no percentage figure that these
payments bear to income is laid down, each case being considered on its merits by the Post
Office Personal Loans Board. There is no 33 percent limit for housing loans. The member
appears to be referring to unsecured personal loans. Approval to authorise unsecured
personal loans within prescribed limits has been delegated to district officers. In the case of
an unsecured personal loan, if the level of commitment exceeds 33 percent of the net
income of the applicant, or the joint net income in the case of an application from two people
jointly, the application must be forwarded to the loans board for decision.

Exports to Australia
56. Mr DOWNIE (Pakuranga) asked the Minister of Trade and Industry: What was the
value of exports to Australia for the years ended June 1975, June 1976, and June 1977, what
were the trade imbalance figures for those years, and what percentage of this trade is under
NAFTA arrangements?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry) replied: The value of
New Zealand exports to Australia for the years ended June 1975, 1976, and 1977 were as
follows: June 1975, $166.8 million; June 1976, $263.7 million; June 1977, $365.6 million. The
balance of trade figures for those years were: in 1975, 1:3.01 in favour of Australia; in 1976,
1:1.95; and in 1977, 1:1.79. We do not have available schedule A figures for the year ended
June 1977. In the year ended June 1976, however, A$172.2 million, or 68.7 percent of New
Zealand imports into Australia, were covered by schedule A of NAFTA. In addition, there
was NZ$35.58 million of trade carried on under company-to-company article 3:7 arrange-
ments. Thus for the year ended June 1976 the total amount of our exports to Australia
covered by the NAFTA agreement was 78.8 percent. Since the 1975-76 trade year furniture
and luggage products have been brought under schedule B of NAFTA, and in April 1977 a
3:7 arrangement was concluded on apparel.

60. RICHARD WALLS (Dunedin North) asked the Minister of Health: Will the develop-
ment of faster scanning techniques mean a revision of the originally planned installation of
three body scanners at Auckland, Dunedin, and Wellington by 1979?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health) replied: No. The faster scanning time reduces the

causing artefacts in the resulting image. The number of patients who can be examined in any
period of time is more dependent on the time taken to reconstruct the image, and the time
taken to prepare the patient for the examination. The machine to be purchased has an
excellent record in both these respects.

Housing Corporation Assistance to Doctors
82. Mr WELLINGTON (Manurewa) asked the Minister of Housing: Can he outline the
nature of the scheme whereby Housing Corporation assistance is available to doctors wishing
to practise in urban areas where general practitioner shortages exist?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing) replied: This scheme-which involves
loans by the Housing Corporation to local authorities at local body rates of interest where
the sanction of the Local Authorities Loans Board has been obtained—was introduced in
1969, and was originally confined to rural areas. More recently, it has been extended to
urban areas, where the Department of Health confirms that there are problems in obtaining
or retaining doctors because of a lack of house and surgery facilities. In practice, the local
authority builds the facilities and leases or rents them to doctors.

Housing Corporation Loan Freeze
83. Hon. W. A. FRASER (St. Kilda) asked the Minister of Housing: Why did he not make
public until August 1977 the findings of a survey carried out in September 1976, and referred
to in the Housing Corporation's 1977 annual report, which confirms that the Government's
decision to freeze the basic Housing Corporation loan at $13,000 has not only created the
biggest "deposit gap" in the corporation's lending history, but has led to a situation in which
"outgoings on home ownership have . . . doubled inside 2 years"-in other words, during
the term of this National Government?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing) replied: The survey was limited in scope
and carried out for the corporation's own purposes. The honourable member should be well
aware that the basic loan provided by the Housing Corporation is not frozen and that the
Government's policy is to adjust loan limits as and when economic circumstances permit.
The Government has concentrated on helping those most in need, and has made significant
improvements to the loan supplement scheme whereby both the range of those qualifying
and the amount of supplements have been increased. Supplements up to $6,000 are now
available, and in addition, in its August package, an additional supplement of $3,000 for
single-income one-child families was introduced. In brief, these adjustments are to be seen
as steps in the process towards achieving a larger basic loan.

Mortgagee Sale-Threat by Trustee Company
87. Mr T. J. YOUNG (Hutt) asked the Minister of Justice: Has he considered the
implications of a letter he will have received from Messrs Gazley and Black, solicitors,
relating to a threatened mortgagee sale by a trustee company, and can he take any action to
prevent the company from using its financial position to secure an unjustified profit by
evicting a widow and family from a home that provides ample security for a renewal of the
existing loan at market rates?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Minister of Customs) replied on behalf of the Minister of
Justice. This is a complex matter and entails a fairly lengthy reply which, with the leave of
the House, I shall give. The Minister has given preliminary consideration to the letter from
Messrs Gazley and Black, and, from my understanding of the situation, there is no way in
which he can intervene. The honourable member's information is obviously far from
complete. The brief facts are that about 2 years ago the widow purchased a property for
$97,000. The purchase was financed by taking over the existing first mortgage of $30,000 to
the executors trustees, and by raising a second mortgage for $10,000 through her solicitor's
nominee company. The balance of $57,000 consisted of her own cash contribution.
The first mortgage had been raised in 1972 by the prior owner of the property. The 5-year
term was due to expire on 7 July 1977, and as the conditions of the mortgage did not require
regular repayments of principal this meant that only interest at 9.5 percent had to be paid.
This is not a case where personal circumstances have changed after the property was first
purchased, nor does it involve a widow and a young family. The house is plainly in the high-
price bracket. I understand that the widow and her married daughter's family both live in the
same home, and indeed her son-in-law is a covenantor to the mortgage. At the time the
contract was entered into the owner and her solicitor would have known that there was a
possibility that refinancing would be necessary once the balance of the term had expired.


## p. 3241 (#123) ###########################################

28 September
3241
Questions and Replies
The company is not evicting the family. As long ago as last February it was made clear to
the owner that repayment had to be made on due date. Despite further reminders, the only
response was a request for a 2-year extension. At no stage was any explanation regarding
possible difficulties mentioned, and since there was no dialogue the company had no
alternative but to follow its present course. As the honourable member will appreciate,
moneys lent on mortgage by trustee companies represent in the main investments with them
by their clients, in accordance with whose instructions the companies must at all times abide.
If the worst did happen and there was a mortgagee's sale, the company itself would make no
profit at all from it. Naturally, I sympathise with any person in this predicament, but on this
occasion it is simply not true to label the trustee company as the villain of the peace.

Penal Institutions-
-Overcrowding
93. Mr KIRK (Sydenham) asked the Minister of Justice: What positive steps has he taken
to overcome the serious overcrowding that has existed in penal institutions in New Zealand
for the last 6 years and has been reported in every annual report of the Department of Justice
since 1971?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Minister of Customs) replied on behalf of the Minister of
Justice. The Government has no control over the number of offenders sentenced to penal
institutions. This is always an important unknown factor affecting forward planning. Its
responsibility is, therefore, on the one hand to provide and encourage the use of alternative
sentences for cases where the public interest does not require full-time detention, and on the
other hand to ensure as far as our resources permit that prison accommodation is provided to
cope with future needs to the extent that these can be forecast. The first responsibility has
been met by a continued development of the periodic detention scheme, a scheme inaugu-
rated by a previous National Government in 1962. The Minister of Justice is exploring other
proposals involving leisure time detention. The second responsibility is being discharged by
pressing ahead vigorously with additional accommodation to relieve overcrowding in institu-
tions. The member will find details of developments in accommodation in the department's
annual report.

OECD Economic Survey Draft
121. Hon. R. O. DOUGLAS (Manukau) asked the Minister of Finance: Is he prepared to
table the draft of the OECD economic survey of New Zealand so that it can be compared
with the final version?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance) replied: The OECD draft economic
survey of New Zealand is a confidential OECD secretariat working paper circulated to all
member countries, including the country under review. The final document is issued under
the sole responsibility of the OECD secretariat, after being considered at the annual review,
which, on this occasion, took place on 20 June. New Zealand, was, of course, represented.
Since the text in question is the first draft of a confidential report of an international
organisation, it would be wrong to table the draft. This is precisely the procedure which has
obtained in previous years, including 1975, when the honourable gentleman asking the
question was a member of the New Zealand Cabinet. Exactly the same procedure took place
on that occasion, and similar amendments were made.

generated, and state by how much per unit the departmental receipts fell short of the unit

1978-79?

## p. 3254 (#136) ###########################################

3254
28 September
Questions and Replies
period it has been considered entirely appropriate that expenditure should be scrutinised by
Parliament. This was clearly the case when broadcasting operated as a Government

of the Broadcasting Corporation Act 1961, section 10 (3) of the Broadcasting Act 1973, and
section 11 (3) of the Broadcasting Act 1976-for an appropriation by Parliament from the
Consolidated Revenue Account to cover the remuneration and expenses of board members.

Parliament. Taken jointly, those provisions ensure scrutiny by Parliament, and the Public
Expenditure Committee exercises this function on behalf of the House.

lished?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Forests) replied: Ruatoria, Mangatu, Wharerata, and

Native Timber Exports
160. Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East) asked the Minister of Forests: What limitations are
there on the export of native timber?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Forests) replied: On 3 July 1967 Cabinet approved of the
removal of prohibition on the export of native timbers, with the exception of kauri. Exports
are approved only under a permit system if sawmills are accumulating stocks-in excess of
local demand—and are not cutting above their normal capacity or working over 40 hours a
week or in any other way increasing their output to supply any export orders. Major
shipments are approved only after consultation with the Department of Trade and Industry.
This Cabinet approval is reviewed periodically on the basis of recommendations by the
Indigenous Forest Timber Advisory Commitee.

King Country Land Use Study
162. Mr LUXTON (Piako) asked the Minister of Lands: Why has the King Country land
use study extended further than the area originally considered by New Zealand Forest
Products Ltd as appropriate for its afforestation plans for the King Country, and when will
these surveys be complete?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Lands) replied: The boundaries for the King Country
land use study area were extended to better assist the resolution of conflicts of land use,
guide resource developments, and aid decision making. It was recognised that sufficient land
would not be available for the establishment of a viable afforestation industry in the New
Zealand Forest Products study area without conversion of existing farm land. Therefore, the
study area was extended in order to better illustrate the extent of unused land with potential
for afforestation that exists in the enlarged region. Work on stage 1, incorporating the
company's study areas, has been completed and the report will be printed by early October.
However, the full study will not be completed until March 1978, although the maps for the
whole area are likely to be available in November.

Import Deposit Scheme
163. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) asked the Minister of Customs: What effect has the
import deposit scheme had since its introduction on the volume of imports?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry) replied on behalf of
the Minister of Customs. Volume statistics are not recorded by the Department of Statistics
for all of the items at present covered by the import deposit scheme. In those items where
volumes are recorded it is revealed that the volumes imported decreased by an average of 30
percent during the period February 1976 to January 1977, being the first year of operation of
the import deposit scheme, when compared to the previous 12-month period. A comparison
of the latest available statistics, covering the 12 months ended 30 June 1977, indicates that
imports have been reduced by volume to a level 25 percent below that pertaining before the
introduction of the import deposit scheme.
