Police Patrol Base, Avondale
165. Mr HUNT (New Lynn) asked the Minister of Police: Is the Avondale police patrol
base manned on a 24-hour basis, and, if not, in view of the increasing population in this area,
when will it be so manned?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice) replied on behalf of the Minister of Police.
The Avondale patrol base is not manned on a 24-hour basis. At present the base has a staff
of seven constables under the control of a sergeant. These members carry out inquiries, foot
patrols, hotel visits, and similar duties on a rostered basis between the hours of 7 a.m. to
11 p.m. 7 days a week, as well as manning the public office of the base during normal
business hours, including late shopping night. In addition, the full resources of the Auckland
Central Police Station are available. Twenty-four-hour crime and incident patrols are
deployed in the areas of Avondale and Mt. Albert to ensure a rapid response to complaints,
and also provide an additional preventive service. When the base is unmanned personal
callers may receive immediate assistance by medium of a telephone provided in the foyer of
the base, which connects the caller direct to the central operations room. It is considered that
the service provided to this suburban area is of the highest possible standard, and indeed is
more than adequate to meet present demands. Any extension of the service provided at the
patrol base cannot be justified at this time, but the matter will, in accordance with
departmental policy, be kept under constant review.

Livestock Improvement Schemes, Waihora
166. Mr LITHGOW (Palmerston North) asked the Minister of Lands: What increase in
animal productivity has been established as a result of the Department of Lands and Survey's
livestock improvement schemes at Waihora, near Lake Taupo?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Lands) replied: The livestock improvement scheme at
Waihora commenced in 1968, and sire progeny have been available to sheep flocks on most
Rotorua blocks for the past 4 years. In this period the lambing for this district has increased
by 12 percent. It is considered that most of this increase is attributable to breeding, and both
the Department of Lands and Survey and the Ministry of Agriculture are satisfied with the
results achieved. Comparisons between Waihora and commercial rams have revealed an
advantage in favour of the former of up to 14 percent in lambs docked. It is also a fact that
the use of Waihora rams has resulted in lambs fattening earlier. As regards the beef
improvement scheme, the aim has been to improve the weight gain in progeny, and results to
date show that Waihora bred bulls compare favourably with top commercial sires.

169. Mr T. J. YOUNG (Hutt), on behalf of Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central), asked the
Minister of Immigration: Is it correct that certain countries are designated as traditional-
source countries for immigration purposes?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Immigration) replied: Yes, it is correct that certain countries
are designated traditional-source countries for immigration purposes. They are countries
from which most of our skilled migrants have come, and where the vocational training
systems and work methods are compatible with our own. Migrants from such countries are
well fitted by training and experience to adapt to life and work in New Zealand. In addition,
the traditional migrant source countries are industrialised rather than developing countries
which have need of skilled people. No countries have been added to the list of traditional-
source countries in recent years.

Immigration—Traditional-source Countries
175. Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central) asked the Minister of Immigration: What is the
effect of a country being designated as a traditional-source country for immigration
purposes?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Immigration) replied: As the House will be aware, certain
occupations have been determined to be in sufficient continuing demand in New Zealand to
warrant recruitment from overseas. Nationals of traditional migrant countries may be
recruited in the full range of 243 occupations on the occupational priority list, while the list
that applies to nationals of non-traditional migration-source countries is very much smaller
with only 4 occupations. One of the main reasons for this distinction is that New Zealand
agreed at the World Employment Conference not to recruit skills from developing countries,
which themselves have need of them.

Matches Research into Native Timber Usage
178. Mr FENTON (Hastings), on behalf of Mr LITHGOW (Palmerston North), asked the
Minister of Forests: In view of the interest by Bryant and May N.Z. Ltd. in manufacturing
matches from indigenous timber, can he indicate what research has been done into the
species and the volume of wood required?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Forests) replied: Bryant and May N.Z. Ltd. became
interested in the possibility of using indigenous timbers-namely, beeches-for matches
early in 1975. Trial splints of red, silver, mountain, and hard beeches were produced in an
associated company's plant in Australia. Good results were obtained except with hard
beech, which presented some problems in absorbing paraffin wax. The matches produced
were stronger than the imported Canadian aspen, which is currently used. Timber require-
ments for New Zealand consumption would be 4000 m³ annually. As a result of its research
the company is interested in obtaining beech from the West Coast. At present a major
problem in supply is the lack of outlets for lower grade logs arising during the production of
the veneer grade match splint logs. The disposal of lower grade beech logs is currently under
consideration.

Forest Products, Taupo
179. Mr LANGE (Mangere) asked the Minister of Forests: What plans has he for the
development of forestry and forest products usage in the Taupo basin, particularly from the
area east of the lake, and does he propose to give the local authority in the area any
information about such use and how the products will be transported from the district?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Forests) replied: The exotic forests of the Taupo basin
are mainly immature at this stage. Not until the late 1980s or the 1990s will their potential for
major industrial development be realised. Until then the limited quantity of forest produce is
most likely to continue to be processed in existing installations at Taupo or outside the basin
itself. The centres of processing for the greatly expanded quantities of wood that will come
on stream as the forests mature is speculative at present. The forests of the Taupo basin are
well placed to deliver saw logs to mills throughout the central North Island and pulpwood to
the industry in the Bay of Plenty, Hawke's Bay, and the King Country. Planning for the
State and Maori lease forests is based on achieving high proportions of quality saw logs and
veneer logs through intensive silviculture with pulpwood simply as an arising. Private forest
might be grown as pulpwood crops, particularly those associated with the proposed King
Country development. As the timing and nature of likely major increases in production
become more definite, discussions will continue with local authorities. However, until
specific proposals are received in response to invitations it is not possible to define the
processing or export centre, and hence the direction in which various qualities and quantities
of wood will be transported.

Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Transport) replied: Discussions have been held

essential foods and fuel to the island. If the dispute is prolonged, permits may be issued by
the ministry to allow fishing boats to carry essentials. Directions issued by the tribunal will
require the members of the union to perform normal duties, including the loading of cargo
and taking the vessel to sea.

DISCUSSION OF QUESTIONS—ADJOURNMENT
[Note The questions and the replies referred to in this discussion appear on the
preceding pages, and are numbered consecutively from 1 to 189.]
Mrs BATCHELOR (Avon): For the purpose of discussing Ministers' replies to ques-
tions, I move, That the House do now adjourn.
In question 6 I asked the Minister of Social Welfare if he could give the names and
locations of the 74 child-care centres which had been closed since December 1975, and the
reasons for the closures. I was somewhat startled at the length of the answer, which takes up
a page and a half. That surely shows the lack of interest in this whole question of child care,
and that there is a need for financial assistance so that those who need child care should be
able to avail themselves of it.
I agree with those people who think—and I am sure that some Government members
would agree there is room for activity on the part of local bodies, voluntary agencies, and
private business, but most people who know anything about child care will agree that the key
role must be played by central government, which has the largest source of funds. It should
also be in control of providing for future needs. Higher standards are required, as is co-
ordinated action; these can best be provided through a Government agency. In today's
economic climate, the provision of child-care facilities is a means of social support for
families generally, and for women in particular.
The Government should recognise that it has a responsibility to provide for women to
enable them to broaden their lives, and therefore the lives of their families. It would help the
country through the economic and social benefit that comes from the effective use of higher
education and training of women, which is being increasingly undertaken today. It would
also provide another avenue of employment for the many women who are interested in
training for a career in child care-and, my word, there is certainly a need for the provision
of new work areas. Under this Government the work opportunities for women have
continued to diminish, and the situation has now been reached when hardly a day goes by
without another factory closing in some part of New Zealand.
Of course, usually it is the women, and often the married women, who are affected. I
think of the woollen mills at Kaiapoi outside Christchurch, or the clothing factories that are
traditionally female-labour oriented, which are being forced to close through this Govern-
ment's policies. It is the female labour force that is being affected. The situation is so bad
now that recently when a firm placed a small advertisement for a part-time receptionist in a
Christchurch paper 186 desperate women applied for the job. We have never had such a
situation since the grim days of the 1930s, when it was indeed difficult to get work. Now,
because of this Government's policies, we are back in that situation.
Women, because of their need to obtain some kind of work in today's economic
circumstances, are now so desperate that they are even offering to take a wage cut to get a
job. I fail to see how any Government can do nothing about such a situation. It is disgusting.
On 2 September statistics released in Christchurch showed a total of 1974 unemployed. Of
that number 681 were females, and those were only the females who had registered as
unemployed. That does not include the married women who have lost their jobs but who did
not bother to register. Those figures do not include young people and others who have left
the country because they cannot get employment. It is time the Government recognised that
the policies it has implemented during the last few months have made people desperate for
work.
Mr ALLEN (Tauranga): I cannot see how the member for Avon can reconcile her
statements about child care and women at work. Perhaps she might explain later just what

However, the picture will have already changed by the year 2006, when the baby boom


## p. 3268 (#150) ###########################################

3268
28 September
Discussion of Questions-Adjournment
after World War II turns into the grey power of the twentyfirst century. We then see
statistics giving us 18 percent of the population aged over 60. By the year 2006 the projected
ratio of labour force to population aged 60 and over is already 3.3. The ratio declines steeply
after the turn of the century. The basic reason is the working out of the age-structure effects
of the assumed relative fertility rates with the recent-and near-future lower births entering
the labour force, which will, by the twenty-first century, have a significantly higher average
age and a small proportion of members aged under 30, and later 40.
While the pattern of decline will vary if alternative fertility and external migration and
labour force participation rate assumptions are used, the overriding pattern of decline in the
first 25 to 30 years of the next century is still present, so that by the year 2031 the projected
ratio of labour force to population aged 60 years of age and over is 1.8. It is probably fair to
point out that these figures could be up to plus or minus 10 percent, even by the year 2000;
and of course there are other variants to be borne in mind-declining fertility, for instance.
The fact is often lost sight of that before low fertility results in a rapidly increasing population
of the aged, there is a period of more than 25 years during which the proportion of the
working-age population will rise from 56 percent to 60 percent. At the same time the
proportion of the total population in the dependent young—and I might say expensive-age
group is steadily diminishing. The proportion of the total population less than 15 years of age
may decline more than the 30 percent it was in 1974 to the 16 percent in the year 2031.
However, it is important to remember that because we have a large non-active old
population, that population also supports economic activities through its purchasing power.
Its role is not merely that of an economic burden. The net effect with current levels of
mortality and consumption among developing countries is that it costs about one-third more
to bring up an average baby to the age of 20 than it does to support an average 60-year-old
for the rest of his or her life.
In these projections there are also further developments that are not, and cannot, be
built into the sums given by the Minister of Statistics. We can expect further development in
longevity expectation. Over the last 20 years longevity expectations of New Zealand males
and females have increased 5 years, and with medical science sustaining life we may expect
further increases there. There will be a larger proportion of women in the work force. About
35 percent of our total labour force at the moment is female, and half of those women are
married. If we follow the next decade or 20 years we can look toward having 46 percent or 50
percent of all New Zealand women in the work force.

Question 33 deals with unit titles. On the face of it, the question seems innocuous and to
deal with rather unimportant legislation. Nothing could be further from the truth, because
the Unit Titles Act deals with the possibility that we will be able to realise the ideals or
policies that people are propounding about the containment of urban expansion on to good
farmland, and the better use of New Zealand's resources in the provision of urban services.
It is necessary to prevent urban sprawl for the two main reasons of avoiding encroachment
on to some of our better farmland, and reducing the cost of supplying main urban services
such as water and sewerage.
The means to this is not necessarily high-rise type residential development, but rather
higher density development, which at present, in physical terms, can take two main forms:
first, unit housing, which consists of a block of inter-connected apartments for which special
separate titles are issued; secondly, cluster housing, which means conventional houses built
at ground level, not on separately subdivided sections, but in accordance with a form of
layout that provides better living conditions and higher densities without requiring the
severance of the individual quarter acre. But separate home titles are required.
The present problem is that both unit housing and cluster housing is inhibited by the
existing legislation, because no title can be issued until each dwelling unit is completed.
Builders are finding it impossible to finance the construction of housing of this type because
of this present restriction. It is vitally important that when the Act is amended as the
Minister assured his questioner it would be, following the committee's report—we remedy
not only the title situation relating to unit housing, but also that relating to cluster housing. If
those changes are not achieved, our housing forms and the ideas of our planners will have
outrun the law and its capacity to facilitate desirable development. I was interested to learn
that the committee set up by the Minister will be reporting this year. I look forward to that
report with keen anticipation, because it is of vital interest to all who are concerned with
urban planning.

low or nil number of unemployed. Women fit into some other categories, but for typists,
shorthand typists, and office machinists in the three areas where the total of unemployed was
700, there were only 8 in those three categories.
Surely the school leaver, when considering what sort of employment he or she will take
up, does a little research and looks at figures like these to find areas where traditionally there
is a very low number of registered unemployed. The position is not as grim perhaps, when
we look at it in detail, as members opposite try to make it appear, because there are areas in
all parts of New Zealand where a shortage of labour exists. We have this background of
rolling over of unemployed people.
Hon. M. Rata: Where?
Mr BELL: Certainly we have a background of rolling over of unemployed people. I
have just told the House that there are very few unemployed in Gisborne and other areas
who have been unemployed for longer than 4 weeks, and so qualify for the private sector
special employment.
The time allowed for the discussion of questions and replies having expired, the motion
lapsed.

TRANSPORT AMENDMENT BILL (NO. 2)
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Transport): I move, That this Bill be now read
a third time.
Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR (Timaru): The Opposition is opposed to this Bill in its
present form. During the Committee stage we on this side opposed clause 1—the short
title-clause 2, and clause 5, specifically for reasons that I and other members on this side of
the House will detail during the third reading debate. The Opposition is not rigidly opposed
to an extension of what has become known as the 40-mile limit, but is certainly opposed to
the mandatory limit in clause 2 being increased from 40 miles to 93.5 miles, or 150 km. Open
competition between road and rail transport will lead to anomalies, highlighted during the
earlier debates on this Bill.
The road transport industry shares the Opposition's view that the decision to increase
the mandatory limit to a set distance, no matter at what point, must lead to anomalies.
Flexibility should have been allowed, regarding both the limit and the commodities to be
carried in various regions. During the Committee stage such areas were cited. With a cut-off
point of 150 km on the main highway corridor between Palmerston North and Wellington,
we find this is just short of the major capital area. Another such example is the highway
between Timaru and Christchurch, with those two major cities being outside the 150 km
limit. Such anomalies would not have occurred had some flexibility been left to the Minister
and the Government.
In preceding debates on this measure we have suggested to the Minister that the
extension be phased in over a period, enabling the Railways Department to adjust its
operations to the new area of competition, and giving both the road transport industry and
the Railways the opportunity to foresee anomalous situations that might arise. The flexibility
advocated by the Opposition would have enabled the Government, the Railways Depart-
ment, and the Road Transport Association to make the required adjustments in various
regions. Something more might have been required for transport of fertiliser in Southland to
avoid duplication of handling and to ensure that the most economic mode of transport was


## p. 3274 (#156) ###########################################

3274
28 September
Transport Amendment Bill (No. 2)
used.
The Labour Opposition would have supported the Government in any proposal leading
to economy of transport charges for a given commodity in a given region. However, that will
not be the situation under this proposed legislation. Only 12 months ago the Minister of
Transport was strongly opposed to any new mandatory limit being set. He was widely quoted
as an advocate of flexibility between road and rail in any extension of the 40-mile limit. We
on this side are only sorry that the Minister did not continue to have his way in Cabinet,
because then the Bill would have been in line with our views.
We opposed the short title because of the provision in clause 2, and also opposed, very
strongly, clause 5, because, with the deletion from the principal Act of the provision for a
minimum charge, it is clear that the major road transport through-operators will use the
period between 1 October 1977 and 1 April 1978—when the tandem provisions of a distance
tax and a mileage fee become applicable-to undercut rural and provincial transport
operators, as is already happening. Many small operators will go out of business very quickly
indeed because they just cannot face this type of competition from the major freight-
forwarding combines, such as Freightways Express, which, with its subsidiaries, covers from
Auckland to Invercargill. The smaller transport businesses will not have the financial
resources to compete for any length of time.
We suggested that the Minister should withdraw clause 5. This was described as an
orphan clause in that it had no strict relationship to the rest of the Bill. However, the
Minister and the Government would not agree, and for that reason we had no alternative but
to oppose it. The road transport industry and those associated with it-such as consumers
and manufacturers-believe it would have been desirable if this legislation had been brought
in at the same time as legislation covering the proposed distance tax and the mileage fee
forecast in the Budget. In fact, it was a new transport policy outlined in the Budget. If that
had happened then many of the problems that will arise in the next 6 months would have
been overcome.
At present the major transport operators see an opportunity to move in and undercut
the rural and provincial operators. The proposed distance charge would discourage such a
practice. I believe it will, no matter at what level it is set. At present discussions are going on
between the road transport industry and the Government, but no one, apart from those
involved in the negotiations, knows exactly at what level the charges will be set. Naturally
that information is not public knowledge.
The new policy covered by this Bill goes back to the Budget announcement, and puts
into operation the recommendations in the Wilbur Smith report that was commissioned by
the previous National Government at a cost of $1 million. That report is outdated, and it was
outdated when it was considered by the Transport Advisory Council, mainly because
increased oil prices had come into effect, and had applied before the end of 1973. Despite
that, the Government still proposed to relax the 40-mile limit and to encourage extended
road transport competition against the Railways. In doing that it still hearkened back to the
recommendations contained in the Wilbur Smith report. During the Committee stage we
pointed out that that was an American solution being applied to a New Zealand problem.
That report was given in the Budget as the reason for introducing this legislation providing
for a mandatory limit of 150 kilometres of open competition between road and rail. The
Wilbur Smith report, which was supposed to be the justification for that recommendation,
had outlived its usefulness before it was considered in depth by the Transport Advisory
Council.
During the Committee stage the Government was criticised at length for its failure to
discuss the proposals with the road transport industry before they were put into the
Budget-the proposals on which this legislation is based. The Transport Advisory Council,
which is supposed to be the Government's principal adviser on transport matters, had not
met for 11 months, and the industry did not know what was intended until its members were
told just before the Budget was presented. That was criticised as one of the reasons for the
legislation coming down in the form it did. The industry maintains, and we believe, that
there should have been in-depth consultation and discussion between the Government and
the industry; then provisions such as those contained in clause 5 would not have been
brought in, because the practical people in the industry know of the problems that have
arisen in the past and will arise in the future. Only people involved in the transport industry
can truly appreciate that, and they can do so better than anyone in the Ministry of Transport,
the Treasury, or any other Government department.
The Road Transport Association made submissions to the Minister to delete or amend

clause 5, because it knew that its members would suffer and that some will not be in business

Mr BIRCH (Franklin): I support the Bill, the purpose of which is to establish a Ministry
of Energy that will be responsible for the formulation and administration of the Govern-
ment's energy policy. The ministry will also assume the functions, powers, and duties
undertaken at present by the Mines Department, the Ministry of Energy Resources, and the
New Zealand Electricity Department, all of which will be disestablished. The member for
Petone has criticised the proposals in the Bill, but I remind members opposite that a similar
proposal was contained in their 1972 election manifesto, deleted from the 1975 manifesto,
and reintroduced at this year's Labour Party conference. A Supplementary Order Paper will
be introduced covering a number of matters that have arisen since the Bill was introduced.
One of the provisions in the Supplementary Order Paper will allow the Ministry of
Energy to resolve disputes, and another provision covers a legal point arising out of the
expansion of the Marsden Point oil refinery. I think it would be helpful if the Minister
explained the reasons for including these two points in the Bill. Over the years, large sums of
money have been committed to capital works necessary to keep the wheels of New Zealand
turning. Set out on page 35 of the report of the New Zealand Electricity Department for the
year ended March 1977 are details of the investment in thermal and hydro-electric power
stations. Up to 31 March 1976, $649 million had been invested in hydro-electric stations,
$282 million in thermal power stations, $337 million on transmission lines, substations, and
communications, and $664 million in works under construction. That investment highlights
the need for a single ministry. The estimates also show an additional investment of $1,963
million for completion of the Arapuni dam, work on the Clyde dam, the Huntly power
station, the Marsden B station, the Te Anau and Manapouri control structures, the
Tongariro scheme, including Rangipo, and various Waitaki works. A further $500 million is
likely to be invested in the Auckland thermal station No.1. The Budget provides $80 million
for coal mines, an additional $300 million for the first stage of the Maui platform, and $200
million for the pipeline.
A very large amount of money is being invested in energy for New Zealand. It is
necessary that the administration of that investment and the work of the Ministry of Energy
Resources be controlled by a single ministry. The report of the New Zealand Electricity
Department indicates that the cost of electricity generated by hydro-electric stations is 0.47c
a unit, which is a very modest figure. Electricity generated by thermal power stations costs
four times as much-1.7c a unit. When those figures are compared one has some idea of the
future cost of providing energy for the country. I welcome the Bill and the consolidation of
the three portfolios into one ministry. I congratulate the Minister on his foresight and
leadership, and on introducing the Bill.

country's future, and for that he deserves full marks.

Minister, will be responsible for the formulation and administration of policies for energy
for
New Zealand". The one ministry will assume all the functions, powers, and duties at present
undertaken by the Mines Department, the Ministry of Energy Resources, and the New
Zealand Electricity Department, and, in addition, will administer the Geothermal Energy
Act 1953 and certain energy pricing policies at present under the jurisdiction of the
Department of Trade and Industry. The 1975 National Party manifesto stated, among many
of its promises, that the importance of energy demanded that energy policy be planned and
administered by a single authority-a promise accorded the country in 1972, I believe, but
still unfulfilled in 1975. The Bill gives effect to that policy promise, for National believes that
it is in the best interests of consumers and producers that all forms of energy production,
development, conservation, and distribution should be co-ordinated so that the most
efficient use is made of each resource. The Ministry will have to draw together the fragments
of energy options and policies into a cohesive entity.
There has been some criticism from the Labour Opposition of the energy pricing policy
announced last year by the former Minister of Energy, who said, when announcing that
policy, that pricing would be the foundation of our energy policy. The goals of that policy
were conservation of non-renewable resources, and increased efficiency of energy produc-
tion and use. A levy is imposed on resources such as petroleum, gas, and coal, and is used to
subsidise exploration, development, marketing, research, and conservation. If we, as a
House and as a country, accept conservation and increased efficiency as the long-term goals
of energy policy, we have to ask ourselves just how responsive to changes in price are the
major flows of energy throughout our economy, and how long it takes for these responses to
occur. The answer for this country is still essentially one of assessment. We do not know in
many cases, although we can point to a 1 percent decline in petroleum usage in the last year.
The international statistics of transport fuel demands show that huge price increases in the
last 3 years have dented demand just a little. However, a simultaneous world recession
makes it difficult to assess how much of the effect comes from price increases or from the
decline in real incomes.
At present, before the establishment of the Ministry of Energy, a variety of policy plans,
or future scenarios, or goals and alternatives, is being worked on by various departments and
committees. The Electricity Department, the Mines Department, and the Ministry of
Energy Resources are obviously involved. The Burns committee report was recently printed,
and is available for release. The Maiden committee recently released a group of energy
scenarios for New Zealand. The Royal Commission on Nuclear Power Generation has yet to

3291
Ministry of Energy Bill
present its report to Parliament. All these policy options and plans will be effectively co-
ordinated by the Ministry of Energy under clauses 11 to 15 of the Bill.
Any discussion of energy policy inevitably leads, as we found from the member for
Heretaunga, to a criticism of the power planning report and the projections of supply and
demand for electricity as an element of energy policy for the future. However, the
production of electricity is only one component of the major energy flow, the others being
gas, coal, and oil, and the future demand for each must be assessed in accordance with a
number of assumptions, each of which may be questioned on a number of grounds. These
grounds include the present population growth rate, the price of oil, energy supplies, and
new policies introduced by the Government, as well as any technological change. However,
the Government is concerned to have full and open discussion on questions, and has
announced the production of goals and guidelines-a public draft of the Government's
attempt to reconcile the economic, social, strategic, and environmental considerations in the
development of energy planning for New Zealand.
Oil accounts for about 60 percent of New Zealand's primary energy supply, only about 3
percent of which comes from indigenous production, mainly gas condensate. About 40
percent of the total New Zealand energy usage is in the transport sector. Therefore, one of
the most difficult decisions for the future is how to ensure transport fuel at a price we can
afford. This is an urgent and difficult problem, because there is no substitute for petrol,
diesel, or kerosene that gives a high-quality content per litre, the same cleanliness, and the
same consistency of quality and ease of burning. Since the first world war, Germany has
produced oil from coal, mainly because of the need to be independent of outside supplies
during a war. However, research done in New Zealand shows that we would require the use
of some 8 000 000 tonnes of coal a year to produce our present requirements. That is about
three times our present output, and the magnitude of the investment needed is obviously
very great.
Research is being done on the production of alcohol from agricultural chemicals. Early
results of this research show a lower energy density per unit volume of the fuel with
advantages in clean burning but a reduction in performance. It appears that alcohol from
agricultural chemicals would be competitive with oil from coal, and would have the added
advantage of being produced largely from solar energy, from water, and from carbon
dioxide. However, the whole project is dependent on an obvious complex between the use of
land for transport fuels and the production of fuel. The New Zealand group of the Institute
of Fuel and Research Studies has suggested that joint studies between the Ministry of Energy
Resources and, of course, the new Ministry of Energy--and the Ministry of Agriculture
and Fisheries should be started to allow land use to be optimised for energy farming.
One of the decisions that must be made soon is that on the utilisation of natural gas.
Clause 21 sees the Ministry of Energy taking over the present function of the Mines
Department and the Ministry of Energy Resources on gas usage. At present, most of our gas
is used to generate electricity in a series of large thermal power stations. This is not the most
efficient way of using natural gas, and on present estimates the Maui and Kapuni fields are
likely to be exhausted in about 30 years. It is, therefore, important that we use the gas
wisely. Many people speak of the high cost of gas reticulation. On completion, the Huntly
power station will probably cost about $500 million. I wonder just how much gas could have
been reticulated for that amount of money, and for what savings. I have not seen that
exercise explained on paper, and I should be very interested in the results of any such
exercise. The Maiden committee recently recommended that gas could be piped directly to
the forestry mill at Kinleith, which would save nearly $20 million in fuel imports.
For the benefit of the member for Heretaunga, the combined cycle stations are being
viewed as an alternative to Auckland thermal station No. 1, putting another 6 to 8 percent
efficiency on the use of gas compared with generation in a peak power station. We have to
ask ourselves if that is enough. If the combined heat from a combined cycle station is also
used in an industrial estate we could claim nearly 50 percent efficient usage from gas. Last
year the Ministry of Energy Resources announced a renewable priority for the use of Maui
and Kapuni gas and any derivatives. It was intended that the greatest emphasis should be
given to applications in which natural gas directly replaced electricity, and that some usage of
gas, such as for boiler fuel, could be given low priority. It must also be borne in mind that the
National Government has a number of commitments to LPG distribution, which must, of
course, be met by November 1978.
The member for Heretaunga also mentioned hydro-electricity development, and New
Zealand has been fortunate in this in the past. Most of our hydro power potential has now


## p. 3292 (#174) ###########################################

3292
28 September
Ministry of Energy Bill
been exploited, or is being developed. However, some major and minor rivers in both
islands have still to be investigated, and there is major scope for the development of small
hydro schemes. The potential, or otherwise, for the production of electricity of New
Zealand's remaining rivers will be realised only if the public accepts that they should be
developed. For example, it is recognised that about 1600 GW capacity has yet to be realised
on the Wanganui River. However, the scenic and recreational value of the river would
influence both the scope of the work that could be undertaken and its introduction. In
addition to major hydro schemes, it has been estimated that there is a potential of about 3000
GWs a year to be derived from new schemes of less than 50 MW capacity. The rate of
development is still largely dependent upon the recognition of suitable schemes by our
electricity supply authorities and their initiative in obtaining the necessary approvals for
finance to proceed with investigation and construction.
The generation of electrical power from geothermal steam has a low thermal efficiency
because the steam is not available at high temperatures. Geothermal steam is not an
immediately renewable resource, but a slowly regenerating one. Clause 22 amends enact-
ments relating to geothermal energy, and the new ministry will take over the administration
of the Geothermal Energy Act 1953 from the Ministry of Works and Development. This is a
very important function for the new ministry, because if heat is taken too quickly from the
geothermal fields the temperatures may begin to decrease. If we exercise restraint in
exploiting the geothermal fields they may last for centuries. However, if we use use too
much, the temperature may cool off much sooner.
Of particular interest to the members of the Raglan electorate is the further develop-
ment of coal resources. For some 100 years coal was New Zealand's major energy resource,
its position being eclipsed only in the 1950s. However, since 1974 the industrial demand for
coal has risen rapidly, due mainly to the increase in the price of oil products. To encourage
industrial conversion to coal, a loan scheme for the purchase of coal-burning plant was
introduced in April 1975. However, for the time being the coal-mining industry has reached
the limits of its capacity in the North Island, and for most preferred types in the South Island.
No one knows how much coal New Zealand has, and in its future development many
environmental dilemmas will have to be overcome. Increased investment in mining science is
very necessary so that we can develop the technology for greater rates of extraction of our
underground coal.
Today we are being asked to consider the co-ordination of all forms of energy into one
ministry. In a paper prepared for the Canterbury Chamber of Commerce, Dr J. B. Stott, a
reader in chemical engineering at the University of Canterbury, said that in 1973 we were
using, per capita, 84 percent more electricity than in 1963, and that the domestic use was 58
percent higher. Between 1967 and 1973 the combined use of oil, electricity, and gas
increased by 37 percent, and, by itself, the consumption of motor spirit increased by 53
percent. It cannot be said that in 1963 we were living impoverished lives lacking in energy,
yet a reduction of some 20 percent in energy consumption at present would be regarded as
miraculous, and for many people unthinkable.
Under the new Ministry of Energy we will hope to see exploration developed and co-
ordinated into resources such as the sun, the wind, the tide, and organic matter. We can
hope that other cities like Hamilton will be encouraged to build sewerage outlets to produce
a little power from time to time to feed on to the national grid in the production of methane.
The ministry will be able to contemplate what obligations, if any, should be imposed on such
bodies as the Auckland Regional Authority to produce energy from the disposal of its
rubbish.
The Government is determined to ensure that New Zealand's energy needs are given
the full attention they demand. The co-ordination of all energy resources under one ministry
is but one step towards that. The action now being taken to improve the Government's
administrative machinery will be followed by improvements and initiatives in energy policies
and operations.

Opposition members should have no argument with the Bill, because energy is high in

depend very largely upon energy options. Most people's jobs depend on the energy policy.
The implications of such a policy are immense, and Opposition members, one after another,
should stand up and congratulate the Minister of Energy on the Bill and the steps taken in
it-steps they were unable to take, despite their wish to do so, largely because of their lack of

The first step was taken before the introduction of this Bill, when the three energy
portfolios were given to one Minister to administer. The second step is the setting up of the
Ministry of Energy, which should have the support of all members. For example, the
ministry takes over the administration of geothermal power. It is a logical and practical step
to bring all resources under one administrative body, which will co-ordinate research,
planning, and development. It will bring about the more efficient management of energy
resources, the more efficient use of energy, and improved conservation of energy. Surely the
Opposition should support these objectives instead of producing curious side arguments
which it kicks around, thus avoiding the major issues.
It is quite obvious why the resources are to be brought together under one department.
Energy resources and uses are closely related. Coal can be used for electricity generation,
but it can be used also as a substitute for electricity. Gas can be used for electricity
generation, but it can be used also as an electricity substitute in some areas. Geothermal
steam can be used for electricity generation, but it can be used also as a substitute for the
energy that would come from electricity. Electricity is the substitute for all the other forms of
energy I have referred to.

transmission, and supply of electricity; to encourage the development and improvement of
systems of supply of electricity; to seek to ensure standards of safety, efficiency, and
economy of operation in respect of the production, transmission, and supply of electricity;
and to initiate and carry out surveys in respect of the supply and use of electricity. What it
does not say is that the duty of the Ministry of Energy should be to conserve electricity.
Possibly the biggest objection to the policies of the Electricity Department is that it has seen
its role as increasing the supply of electricity holus-bolus, without paying any regard to the
ability of the country to absorb the initial cost of building the plants, or to whether the
electricity is needed.

This Bill disappoints me. It is true that the Labour Government advocated, and was
moving towards, the setting up of a Ministry of Energy to co-ordinate the activities of the
various departments dealing with energy, but in this Bill we find that all the powers given to
the Minister of Energy can be delegated to his secretary. What responsibility will the
Minister have under this legislation? Clause 9(1) states: "The Minister may from time to
time, either generally or particularly, delegate to the secretary all or any of the powers
exercisable by him as Minister. . .". Various committees, probably dealing with different
forms of energy, are to be set up, but there appears to be little co-ordination under the
Minister. I do not know how the departments and committees are to be structured, but the
Minister's only responsibility seems to be the acceptance of their reports. All the powers
given to the Minister may be passed over to the Secretary of Energy, who, in turn, under
Clause 10, "may from time to time, either generally or particularly, delegate to such officer
or officers or employee or employees of the ministry as he thinks fit . . .".
I am concerned for the right of members of Parliament to get close to what is going on,
because it would appear that under this legislation we are setting up a monolith quite
unworthy of New Zealand, and that the policies of the Minister of Energy will be removed
even further from our knowledge. Instead of the Bill's being presented to the House in its
present form, it should have been sent to a committee. What part will the Minister play? The
committees to be set up may be paid by way of salary, and so no doubt they will comprise
civil servants, to whom will be delegated all the powers of the Minister. This is an
undesirable policy for any Government to bring forward. The Minister is shirking his
responsibilities by asking Parliament to pass legislation of this type.
Why is the construction team of the Ministry of Works and Development excluded from
the Ministry of Energy? Clause 11(4) in Part II states that the ministry shall "promote,
encourage, and stimulate exploration for and the discovery of any kinds, forms, and sources
of energy, and the co-ordination of such activities and, if the Minister so directs, itself
undertake or commission such activities". Will the ministry set up some other exploration
teams to carry out work that has already been done by the Ministry of Works and
Development in the building of power stations and other energy sources? The construction
section of the Ministry of Works and Development should have been included in this
legislation.
Clause 12 deals with the control of prices of goods and services. We read that, where
Part IV of the Commerce Act 1975 applies, the Minister of Energy will replace the Minister
of Trade and Industry, but subclause (5) states, "In any case where the exercise of any
function or power under this section by the Secretary of Energy may affect—(a) retail
margins for petroleum products; or (b) exports from New Zealand or industrial production
or industrial development in New Zealand-the Secretary of Energy shall consult with and
consider the views of the Secretary of Trade and Industry...". We were clearly told that the
Government's intention was to set up a Ministry of Energy that was to be completely free of
any other department, but the Minister of Trade and Industry is to carry out investigations
into petrochemical industries based on Maui gas.
Where is it shown that the functions of this Ministry of Energy will be any different from
those of the departments that existed under the Labour Government? The Labour Govern-
ment was criticised for having a Minister of Mines, a Minister of Energy Resources, and a
Minister of Electricity. In introducing this Bill the Minister said that the departments of
those Ministers were to come under one ministry, yet we now find that the Minister of Trade
and Industry is looking at firm proposals for a petrochemical industry based on Maui gas. It
has been stated that the Government's petrochemical project group has concluded that the
most favourable options appear to be based on nitrogenous fertiliser for either the export or
the domestic market, or on export-oriented methanol industries. That statement came not
from the Minister of Energy Resources, but from the Minister of Trade and Industry. Where
will the Minister divide his responsibilities between that same Minister of Trade and Industry
and his Secretary of Trade and Industry?
I am bitterly disappointed in this Bill, which does nothing to give us a constructive
energy policy. The Minister's responsibilities will be assigned to a number of committees,
which will probably comprise civil servants, to be set up to devise policies for the Govern-
ment. That will remove even further from members of Parliament the possibility of their
finding out our energy directives and the Government's energy policies. We are setting up a
monolith that is quite unnecessary, especially when the Minister is to be divested of his
powers to the extent that is provided for in the legislation. This Bill should have gone to a

more than a month ago, it makes a summary reply a little difficult, but I should like to

The member for Island Bay said that the Bill did not establish a Ministry of Energy

The member for Franklin asked me about the Supplementary Order Paper that will be
circulated in the morning. There were two Supplementary Order Papers printed, but not
circulated, that bore on the legislation and made some technical amendments. Two matters
of greater substance will be incorporated in a new Supplementary Order Paper, which will be
available before the Committee stage. Most of the amendments have been drafted to ensure
that all the associated legislation is correctly linked to the Bill. Two amendments have
greater significance, because they correct weaknesses in the existing law, rather than
improving co-ordination.
One of the amendments makes it clear that the agreements made from time to time
between the Government and the petroleum refinery operators may be taken into account
when the price for motor spirits is being determined. This amendment is necessary to
overcome the possibility, which was recently drawn to my attention by Crown counsel, that
the courts could set aside any agreement between the Government and the petroleum
refinery operators. The basis for such a decision would be that the agreement sought to
require the Government to take its provision into account when determining prices, while
the legislation gives the Governor-General in Council full discretion on the matter.
The second significant amendment empowers the Secretary of Energy to determine
disputes among or between electrical power authorities. This amendment is proposed

Natural Gas Corporation. The amendments I have just described, and those relating to
drafting matters in the Bill, will be moved as the clauses are considered.
The Bill amends 26 different Acts, either incidentally or in some important way. The
Government's intention is that the Ministry of Energy will not be a mere aggregation of
existing agencies, but will be a merger and a melding of the authorities and powers the
Government requires to ensure that the energy we need will be available. In view of the
number of Acts affected and the care needed to ensure that the Government's intentions
were properly reflected in the Bill, it was expected that continued re-examination of its
provisions would identify a number of matters needing correction or improvement. I believe
that the Supplementary Order Paper will provide the improvements considered necessary.

JUDICATURE AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. The Bill makes a number of amendments to the Judicature Act 1908 and the
Judicature Amendment Act 1972. Clause 2 relates to service or execution of a writ or process
on Sundays. At present, section 54 renders void any writ or other process served or executed
on a Sunday, and in addition a penal sanction is provided. In considering this ban the
Supreme Court Rules Committee did not recommend that the section be repealed in toto,
and I think that such a proposal would be generally opposed. None the less, the committee
saw a need for some relaxation of the absolute prohibition when cases of urgency arise.
Moreover, exemptions already exist in criminal matters, custody, and in admiralty.
Under clause 2 of the Bill, the prohibition in subsection (1) will remain, but will be subject to
any rules of court, and the penal sanction is removed. The exemption in admiralty was
inserted in 1974 and related to "The Supreme Court in its admiralty jurisdiction, or when
sitting as a Prize Court". Technically, the term "admiralty jurisdiction" includes prize
jurisdiction, so the words "or when sitting as a Prize Court" are superfluous. The opportun-
ity is taken to remove those words.
Clause 3 foreshadows changes in the new Code of Civil Procedure whereby writs of
subpoenas become orders of subpoenas; this is simply an updating of terminology. The
penalty for failing to attend court in answer to a subpoena is increased to $500. The clause
will not come into force until a date appointed by the Governor-General by Order in
Council, and this will allow the proposed changes in the code to be effected.
Clause 4 took up another recommendation of the rules committee. After hearing
evidence on the clause, the Statutes Revision Committee invited the rules committee to give
further consideration to the clause. That committee has now asked that the clause be not
proceeded with at this stage; it has accordingly been struck out.
Clause 5 abolishes the jury of four in civil cases. This jury was seldom used and has been
practically unknown in recent times. The rules committee recommended its abolition, which
is supported by the New Zealand Law Society. Subsection (2) of the proposed section 19A
gives a right of jury trial in all actions in which the amount claimed exceeds $1,000. For the
reasons given earlier, the words "or when sitting as a Prize Court" are also to be deleted.
Clauses 6 to 10 amend Part I of the Judicature Amendment Act 1972. Broadly, the
clauses embody the recommendations of the Public and Administrative Law Reform


## p. 3311 (#193) ###########################################

28 September
3311
Judicature Amendment Bill
Committee contained in its report of September 1975. Clause 6 amends the definitions of
"statutory power" and "statutory power of decision" in section 3 of the 1972 amendment so
as to ensure that the procedure of application for review is available in certain cases where
the older common law remedies are available. The existing definition of "statutory power"
limits the application of the Act to the exercise of functions under statutory authority. The
result is that the procedure for review under the Act is not available to a member of a non-
statutory body who wishes to challenge the exercise of a power by that body—for example, a
decision expelling or disciplining him. Such a person would need to resort to one of the old
forms of remedy—that is, of certiorari, mandamus, prohibition, and so on. This subclause
extends the definition to apply to the powers or rights specified in the definition if they are
conferred either under statute or under the constitution or other instrument of incorpora-
tion, rules, or bylaws of any body corporate.
The Statutes Revision Committee received a number of submissions from voluntary
bodies expressing fear at becoming subject to the oversight of the Supreme Court, and the
possible crippling effect of a flood of litigation. These fears seem to be based on a
misunderstanding of the effect of the Bill. It is procedural only, and extends to non-statutory
bodies the form of application for review. The Act was not intended to—and, in my view,
does not change the substantive law. As section 4(1) of the Act clearly states, relief on an
application for review may be granted only if the applicant was entitled to relief under one of
the old remedies. In short, if a person can not now obtain relief he will not be able to get it
when this Bill is enacted.
Another effect of the present definition of statutory power is to prevent the application
of the Act to a review of the legality of investigative functions as distinct from an act or
decision that has a final and determinative effect. This subclause extends the list of powers
set out in the definition to include the power to make an investigation or inquiry into the
rights, powers, privileges, immunities, duties, or liabilities of any person. The effect of the
amendment is that a review may be obtained in respect of the exercise of such a power. A
person's rights may be detrimentally affected by a decision without being actually decided or
prescribed by it. The definition of statutory power of decision is amended to include a
decision "affecting" those matters in subclause (2).
Clause 7 relaxes the jurisdictional threshold for an order of or in the nature of certiorari
or prohibition by removing the need to show that the tribunal whose decision is given under
review was obliged to act judicially. This follows recent judicial decisions. However, where
the ground for seeking a review is a breach of natural justice the applicant will still be obliged
to establish that the tribunal was bound to observe the principles of natural justice.
Subclause (2) clarifies the court's power under section 4(5) of the amendment Act to direct
the tribunal to reconsider the whole or part of its decision. The change makes it clear that, as
long as the court is satisfied that the applicant is entitled to relief, it may give a direction
under that provision. In short, the power is an independent not an ancillary one. If the court
directs reconsideration under section 4(5), it may make interim orders to preserve the status
quo pending the final determination of the matter.
The new subsections (5B) and (5c) of section 4 clarify the jurisdiction of a tribunal when
a matter is referred back to it. When the court does not make an interim order under that
power or section 8, the original act or omission shall continue to have effect until it is
amended or revoked. When any matter is referred back to any person under subsection (5),
that person is given jurisdiction to reconsider and determine the matter, notwithstanding any
enactment to the contrary.
Clause 8 clarifies the extent of the court's powers under section 8, which provides at
present that, on an application for review, the court may make such interim order as it thinks
proper pending the final determination of the application. This clause rewrites the section.
First, it is made clear that an interim order may be made at any time before the final
determination of an application for review. Secondly, in order to preserve the position of the
applicant, the court may, except against the Crown, make an interim order prohibiting the
respondent from taking further action that is or would be consequential on the exercise of
the statutory power, prohibiting or staying any civil or criminal proceedings in connection
with the matter, and continuing in force any licence that has been revoked or suspended in
the exercise of the statutory power or that would otherwise expire by effluxion of time.
When the Crown is the respondent, the court may make an order declaring that the Crown
should not take any such action in the interim.
Clause 9 sets out in greater detail the procedure to be followed on an application. This
clause replaces sections 9 and 12 by a new section 9, which removes uncertainty as to the


## p. 3312 (#194) ###########################################

3312
28 September
Judicature Amendment Bill
procedure on an application, in particular as to the statement of facts and of the grounds for
relief. Subject to any direction of a judge under the new section 10, the clause also requires
every respondent to file a statement of defence. Clause 10 rewrites section 10 so as to enable
a judge at any time-either on application or without an application-to call a conference of
parties or their counsel and to settle the issues and give directions on a number of specified
matters for the purpose of ensuring that an application or intended application for review
may be determined conveniently and expeditiously and that all matters in dispute may be
effectively and completely determined. The Statutes Revision Committee has made some
amendments to clarify the application of the power in certain circumstances.
I draw the attention of honourable members to Supplementary Order Paper 33, which
has been circulated. One of the Government's election promises was to "give attention to
expedients for improving the situation in the courts in the short term . . . and the long term."
Members will be aware that a royal commission is at present reviewing the structure of the
courts to ensure they are properly equipped and staffed to fulfil their proper role in our
society. In the short term, we have been concerned at the growth of the work of the courts
and the capacity of the present Bench to cope with it. Last year we increased the maximum
number of Supreme Court judges by two, and, notwithstanding appointments to fill those
positions, the need for temporary appointments continues. The situation in the Court of
Appeal has given concern for some time. The work of that court reflects the volume of
business in the Surpeme Court and magistrates' court. Civil appeals must at present wait
almost a year for a hearing, and criminal appeals, while enjoying a measure of priority,
suffer a delay of about 6 months.
Delays of this magnitude cannot be tolerated. The situation demands prompt action;
this is the purpose of the Supplementary Order Paper. It is, however, only a holding position
until the recommendations of the Royal Commission on the Courts have been received and
action taken after their consideration. The Supplementary Order Paper provides, first, for
the number of ordinary judges of appeal to be increased from two to three. As the judges of
the Court of Appeal must be judges of the Supreme Court, the maximum number of
Supreme Court judges allowable under the Act must be increased by one, and this is
provided for; secondly, for the court to sit in divisions; and, thirdly, for additional judges to
be appointed. The extra permanent judge will not enable the court to sit in divisions, and for
this purpose the new subsection 1(C) to be inserted in section 58 of the principal Act provides
for additional judges to be appointed. The Government is aware that this must necessarily be
a short-term expedient, and this is acknowledged by the judges and the legal profession. For
this reason, the clause has been narrowly drawn and, by subsection 1(D) is expressly stated to
cease to have effect after 2 years.
The opportunity is also being taken to include two other measures. The new section 61A
will enable a single judge of the Court of Appeal to make incidental—and I stress the word
incidental orders, and give incidental directions. These orders and directions will affect
preliminary matters, and at present can be given only by the three judges sitting as a court.
This provision should help, though in a minor way, to ease the burden on the court.
Finally, the first opportunity is being taken to remedy an oversight when a defendent
pleads guilty to a charge before or during the preliminary hearing of the charge. Because the
right of appeal in the Supreme Court is available only to a person “convicted on indictment”,
and because a person in the situation mentioned does not come within the meaning of that
term, he does not have a right to appeal. This omission is rectified by amending the
definition of the term "convicted on indictment" in section 3 of the Crimes Act. It is
backdated to the date of the last year's amendment to preserve the right of appeal.

I simply want to say a word about the Supplementary Order Paper, to which the

establishment of a country's superior judicial tribunal is of considerable constitutional
importance, as people will recall from President Roosevelt's attempt to pack the Supreme
Court of the United States. This move is being brought in by a Supplementary Order Paper,
which gives it the appearance of an afterthought; it is a matter to which we have not given
sufficient consideration. The Minister told me that the explanation is that we have before us

Order Paper were to be given the status of a full Bill, it would have to be the Judicature
Amendment Bill (No. 3). It does seem a little untidy to have three amendments in one year
to an Act that is not often amended.

treated as one of considerable importance. It is unfortunate that we go back to giving the
appearance of diluting the strength of the Court of Appeal. When set up, it was intended to
be a permanent court consisting only of the judges of the Court of Appeal. Since then,
members of the Supreme Court have on occasions been seconded for service on the Court of
Appeal for brief periods. That has generally been regretted and, for my part, while I concede
I was driven to it, it was done with reluctance. I am reluctant to agree to a repetition of this;
it is only on the score of the extreme pressure under which the Court of Appeal is placed at

Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Attorney-General): I wish to comment on the provisions of
the Supplementary Order Paper relating to the judiciary as they concern my portfolio of
Attorney-General. The work pressure in the Supreme Court has expanded in a quite
dramatic fashion in the last year or two, and I regret that it has not been possible to bring this
authorisation for the fourth Court of Appeal judge into the House before now; but this has
been unavoidable, for reasons some of my colleagues are familiar with. I hope that once the
Bill is through, we will be able to announce the new fourth member of the Court of Appeal
with a minimum of delay. The choice will be influenced by my belief that we should plan on
the assumption that, in the not too distant future, there is a possibility that the Court of
Appeal could be our final appellant court. We cannot see it in the immediate future, but we
must be ready to move on the assumption that it could happen.
It always interests me, when any discussion on the future of the Court of Appeal comes
up and people talk about the link with the Privy Council, how often it is assumed that what
happens in the future is entirely in our hands. The British legal system is becoming more and
more enmeshed with the European system, and it could be that the first break in the natal
cord comes from the other end, not from ours. So the choice of Court of Appeal judges is
particularly important now, and the choice of the next member will be made only after very
deep consideration.
It is appropriate that I should express very great appreciation of the work that has been
done by the present members of the Court of Appeal, in conditions that have been,
admittedly, testing and difficult. It has been a great feat of will and dedication to apply the
meticulous deliberation and reflection required in appellate court work in a situation of
increasing work pressure. To break the back of this wholly untenable situation, the
Government is taking two measures in this Bill: first, to appoint the extra judge, and,
secondly, to make provision for the court to sit in divisions, which previous speakers have
alluded to. To enable the court to sit in divisions is a sensible expedient, which will definitely
expedite the work flow and give the court more room to manoeuvre in its division of work.
The legislation is designed with the report of the Royal Commission on the Courts very
much in mind. The commission could well recommend major structural changes to our court
system. The power conferred in the Supplementary Order Paper to appoint additional

difficult. When the two new appointments authorised by the Supplementary Order Paper

permanent or temporary Supreme Court or Court of Appeal appointments within its first 2
years of office. I do not know of any period in the history of the country when more judicial
appointments have been made within a 2-year time span. It gives me very great pleasure to
support the Minister of Justice in presenting the Supplementary Order Paper on the Bill.

WOOL INDUSTRY BILL
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Agriculture): I move, That the Wool Industry Bill be
introduced. The Bill is being introduced at the request of the farming industry, and I intend
to refer it to the Lands and Agriculture Committee. Its main purpose is to provide for the
amalgamation of the present Wool Board and the Wool Marketing Corporation into a new
body to be called the New Zealand Wool Board. The Bill also incorporates the main
provisions governing wool income stabilisation, as currently contained in the Wool Income
Stabilisation Regulations 1976.
The Wool Board has proposed the amalgamation of the board and the corporation,
because it recognises the desirability of removing areas of overlapping work, and the need to
increase the efficiency of New Zealand's wool marketing effort. Wool marketing, promo-
tion, and research are all interrelated, and it is necessary to have a unified effort in all phases
of those areas if New Zealand is to obtain the best returns for its wool. The marketing efforts
of the industry continue to provide for the development and maintenance of an efficient
marketing system. This is in the interests of all New Zealanders, not just wool growers, as
the economic state of the country is very dependent on the revenue earned from our exports.
The Wool Industry Bill contains little that is new. It is essentially a merger of the
provisions of the Wool Industry Act 1944, the Wool Marketing Corporation Act 1972, and
the Wool Income Stabilisation Regulations 1976. The new board will have the same
objective as the corporation—that is, the obtaining, in the interests of growers, of the best
possible long-term returns for New Zealand wool. The board will be a producer organisation
with 10 directors; 6 elected by growers and 1 appointed on the nomination of the board on
the basis of his commercial experience. The chairman of the board will be elected by the
directors from among their number.
The board will have the same powers as the Wool Marketing Corporation over the
licensing of premises for the receival, storage, or appraisal of wool, and on the export of
wool. Provision is also made for appeals about licences. The board will have the power to
negotiate freight rates for the shipping of wool from New Zealand. The Bill provides for the
board to administer a minimum prices scheme along the same lines as the corporation is
doing at present. The minimum price funding scheme, as incorporated in the Bill, is to
provide finance for the board to pay supplementation to growers under the minimum prices
scheme when prices are less favourable. The funding scheme is equivalent to that currently
operating under the Wool Income Stabilisation Regulations. The rate of the minimum price
funding levy will be set by regulations, and it is intended that it remain at 3 percent for this
season.
Part IV of the Bill, providing for the individual grower income levy retention scheme,
contains further provisions apart from the stabilisation regulations. Provision has been made
to set different trigger prices for different wool types should the industry wish to change to
such a system. In the meantime, however, it is intended to continue with the present
averaging system, with just one trigger price. Provisions governing refunds for the grower
retention levy will be made in regulations.
Part V of the Bill, on annual pooling and marketing of wool contains the provisions of
Part III of the Wool Marketing Corporation Act 1972. The intention to pool the wool
purchased by the board under this part, and for the profits from its trading operations
properly to reflect the prices received for the various types of wool, are, however, more
clearly spelt out in this Bill than in the 1972 Act. The Bill provides for this part to come into
effect only after the board has held a referendum on the matter among growers owning 100
or more sheep, and only if 60 percent or more of the valid votes cast are in favour of the
proposal to bring Part V into operation. This provision has the same effect as that originally
contained in the Wool Marketing Corporation Act and will allow the question to be fully
debated among the growers, and for growers themselves to make the decision on the future
marketing system for their wool.
The proposals embodied in the Bill have been widely discussed within the industry. The
Wool Board has advised me that the electoral committee of the Meat Producers Board and
the Wool Board, and the meat and wool section of Federated Farmers broadly support the
proposals. The Bill will be referred to a select committee, before which all interested parties
will have the opportunity of making representations or presenting submissions.

consultations with woolgrowers been? We know, because of a Bill now before the Lands and
Agriculture Committee, how widely split the industry can be over a measure such as this. It
would be regrettable if that was to be the fate of the Bill now before us.
Would it not have been more appropriate to hold the referendum among growers before
the Bill came back to the House? What time scale does the Minister envisage for the
implementation of this measure-the time the Bill will be before the select committee and
for it to become law, and then for the referendum among growers so that it can become
operative? What is the urgency about the Bill? Government members have had the benefit
of discussing the measure for many weeks, and even months, in their caucus, but the
Opposition first sees a Bill when it is introduced, and we have a duty to the people affected
by this Bill to ensure that we provide the best machinery to handle it and to hear the voice of
the growers and those in the industry affected—and that Parliament itself gives adequate
attention to the industry's needs.
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Agriculture): Because the Bill is being sent to a
select committee it will have wide publication. It will lie until such time as farmers have had a
chance to study it. If the Lands and Agriculture Committee is so bogged down with
representations made to it before the end of this session, the Bill will not become law. The
Wool Board has indicated to me that, if possible, it would like the Bill to be passed this year
so that the board can obtain the advantage it sees in the amalgamation for the coming major
wool season. The Bill contains very few new concepts. The member asked how wide
consultations with the industry have been. Comments have appeared in the press; the Wool
Board's publications have commented on and explained the letter; the Wool Board itself has
explained the principles to the electoral college, which, in turn, has explained them to its
constituents; the meat and wool section of Federated Farmers has explained them to its
constituents; and I myself have been up and down the country and been questioned on the
concept. Nowhere have I found opposition to it.
Rt. Hon. W. E. ROWLING (Leader of the Opposition): I have one or two questions to
ask the Minister about Part II of the Bill, which is the acquisition section that would not
come into force until a referendum among growers had been conducted; and such a
referendum would require a 60 percent majority of those who actually voted. On what
initiative will the Minister take such a referendum? I note that the Bill states that this can
happen at the request of the board, but is there any other way in which the Minister might
take such an initiative? How does the board propose to monitor grower opinion on this issue,
which proved to be highly controversial at the time of the 1972 Act? This is an area in which
there has been, and is likely to be, changing opinions. The attitude of growers in one year

two-way structure.

Auckland Hospital Board-Surgical Waiting List
4. Mr HUNT (New Lynn) asked the Minister of Health: Has he seen a statement in the
New Zealand Herald of 6 September 1977 that, at a recent meeting of the Auckland Hospital
Board, it was revealed that "in the last 12 months since July last year the general surgical
waiting list increased by nearly 1000, to a total of 2422", and, if so, (a) is the statement
correct, and (b) in what way will the Government be assisting the Auckland Hospital Board
to reduce the waiting list?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): I have seen the statement. There is a further
statement in the New Zealand Herald of 27 September which gives an explanation of the
increased waiting list, and I would draw this to the member's attention. Briefly, the total
increase in the general waiting list is 950, of which 680 are on the surgical list. The remainder
are on the geriatric non-surgical list, and this is considered to be due to the greater eligibility
of geriatric patients to receive a subsidy for private hospital fees. I am advised that many of
these patients are in private hospitals. The paediatric surgical list is composed of patients
with mainly minor conditions, and no urgent cases are on it. The greatest single cause is a
shortage of anaesthetists. This is worldwide. Two extra specialists have been appointed and
approvals have been given for further increases. The situation should improve as further
areas of stage III of the Auckland Hospital are commissioned in the next 9 to 12 months and
by the return of the eye department to the Wallace block, which has been upgraded.
Hon. Michael Connelly: What steps have been taken to ensure that the shortage of
anaesthetists does not create similar problems in other districts, and to increase the number
of surgeons for the Auckland district?
