Health-Advertisement
9. Mr HUNT (New Lynn) asked the Minister of Health: Would he detail to the House
the measures he has taken to correct the unnecessarily alarming information given in an
advertisement headed "Parents-Send that teenager to the Doctor", published in the June
issue of Health magazine and signed by the medical superintendent of Lake Alice Psychiatric
Hospital?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): I wish to stress that the item entitled
"Parents-Send that teenager to the Doctor" was not an advertisement. The layout of the
item may have contributed to the misconception, but under no circumstances would Health
carry any advertising. It has been the Department of Health's experience that people do not
think that health may be a factor in some adolescent behaviour. Some of the points may be
typical of teenagers, but they may also indicate general medical disorders, and that is why
the item was published. While it attracted a certain amount of publicity and criticism, the
department stands by its original intention in publishing and feels that any other comment
would attract further unnecessary and confusing publicity.
Mr Hunt: How can it possibly be construed that the pupil who becomes silent and
withdrawn, or philosophical, or excessively religious in his outlook should automatically be
sent to a doctor?
Hon. T. F. GILL: I do not think that it can be construed in that way. The suggestion is
that when teenagers have a change of mood, character, or habits there could be some
medical cause, and, therefore, a medical check-up is desirable. That is what the department
is saying in this statement.
Mr Hunt: Why is the statement signed by the medical superintendent of Lake Alice
Psychiatric Hospital? The statement does not mention that there could be a disorder, but
simply says that parents should send the teenager to the doctor, and then lists 14 things, the
last of which is a girl who frequently faints.
Hon. T. F. GILL: The item is not signed by anybody.
Hon. Sir Basil Arthur: It is, it has his name at the bottom.
Hon. T. F. GILL: It has his name at the bottom, but it is not signed by anybody. The
article is a suggestion that parents should send their teenager to a doctor, and it states the
sort of complaints that teenagers might be suffering from that would warrant a medical
check.
Hon. Sir Basil Arthur: Did somebody forge his name?
Hon. T. F. GILL: That is a rather silly interjection. The name S. L. Pugmire is printed
at the bottom of the statement, but it is not a signature. The article is not attributed to him in
any way, and it is simply a suggestion that when teenagers are showing certain symptoms
parents should consider sending them to a doctor.
Mr Prebble: Is the Minister saying that the article was not written by Dr Pugmire?
Hon. T. F. GILL: I have forgotten his name, but I am sure that somewhere in this
document we will find the name of the Government Printer. His name is on most documents.
That does not mean that everything published under the auspices of the Government Printer
was written by the Government Printer. From what I have seen in the magazine the article
was printed with the authority of S. L. Pugmire. I am unable to say whether the article was
written by him, but I would think probably it was not.
Mr Hunt: Notwithstanding the comments that have been made about this page in the
Health journal, will the Minister assure us that he will consult with the Director-General of
Health, Dr Hiddlestone, before this type of advertisement or statement appears in future?
Hon. T. F. GILL: By no means. I am not aware of the criticism. Because of my lack of

Consumer Price Index
10. Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central) asked the Minister of Statistics: Has he seen the
recent article in the Evening Post of 21 September in which Mr L. N. Ross discussed the
exclusion of direct taxation from the consumer price index, and has consideration been given
to including income tax in the calculation of the index?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Statistics): I have seen the article referred to by
the honourable member. Consideration has been given to including income tax in the
consumer price index whenever the compilation of the index has been reviewed. The 1971
report of the consumer price index revision advisory committee recommended that the
consumer price index cover direct personal expenditure on goods and services only, and in
keeping with this definition the committee recommended the exclusion of direct taxation.
That is in line with international practice.
Mr Prebble: Is the Minister aware of Mr Ross's statement that it is an incontrovertible
fact that whether or not direct taxation should be included in the CPI, it does enter into the
pricing system, that the tax on the average wage has gone up from 20 percent to 26 percent,
and that this should be reflected in the CPI?
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: The question is seeking an opinion from the Minister. The
Minister may comment briefly if he wishes.
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: It is extremely difficult to measure the cost of Government
goods and services and reflect them exactly. The matter has been reviewed, and it will be
reviewed again when the index is next considered.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.
Hospital Board Financial Allocations
11. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) asked the Minister of Health: In view of comments by
the treasurer of the Wellington Hospital Board, supported by the executive of the Wanganui
Hospital Board, to the effect that financial allocations are received too late for effective
control over spending, can he assure hospital boards that in future they will be notified of
these allocations earlier?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): The Government is keen to notify hospital
boards of all of the elements of their allocations earlier than has been possible in the past. In
fact, last December I personally notified all board chairmen of the basis on which they could
prepare their budgets for the 1977-78 financial year. I do not believe that boards have
received this information earlier than they did on this occasion. The Government is also
conscious of the need to provide the earliest possible advice to boards of other provisions,
such as those to cover increased costs and the development of services, and means of
achieving this are constantly being reviewed.
Mr Marshall: Notwithstanding the Minister's early notification, boards are still dissatis-
fied. Does he intend to give notification at a still earlier date?
Hon. T. F. GILL: May I take a minute to outline the problem. The board is advised that
its expenditure next year will be based on the previous year's expenditure with allowances
for increases in the cost of supplies in accordance with the hospital supplies index, and
increases in wages in accordance with any general wage order, and other matters. The Board
cannot be advised until the index figures are available and the general wage order has been
announced. One of the biggest problems is in the area of growth, and whether the board will
be allowed an additional amount for growth. The information for the balance of the year to
31 March is not available until just before the Budget, or at the time of the Budget. The basic
figures have to be established before any frills and additions can be arranged.

cases.

Hon. J. B. GORDON: The policy of the Government at present is the standard formula
for house rents that has been in existence for about 10 years. It was annulled once. I think
the warrant was signed the day after the last election.

article 3:7 arrangements have been for products which Australia already has under global
restriction. The New Zealand quotas constitute a special allocation tied to New Zealand
suppliers. They are additional to whatever sales New Zealand exporters may make by
competing for global quotas using their duty preference. Since sales to the Australian market
may still therefore be made outside the special quotas for New Zealand, it is not possible to
quantify in advance the extent to which the sales of New Zealand goods into the Australian
market will be restricted under the new regime. The fact that it has been possible to
negotiate special entitlements for New Zealand within the Australian quota system is itself a
testimony to the spirit of the NAFTA agreement.
Mr Schultz: Will the Minister confirm that opportunities to export to Australia will not
only continue but will continue to increase?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: There are continued opportunities for export to
Australia, but it gets more difficult in respect of products where New Zealand has no
NAFTA arrangement and has been increasing its exports for particular commodities. At that
point, as the commodity comes under a global quota, New Zealand can export, but if New
Zealand wants to go further it must negotiate a special quota that enables Australia to have
some access to New Zealand.
Hon. R. L. Bailey: In view of the Minister's final reply that we might be required to
renegotiate a special quota, will he immediately do so, particularly as many people in New
Zealand are losing their jobs, and I refer to Upper Hutt, where a factory that is completely
orientated towards the Australian market is to close down and the machinery is to be
transferred to Australia, with 41 people losing their jobs, only 7 of whom can get assistance?
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: Order! We have had enough speech. The question was asked
at the beginning.
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: I am concerned about the closing of factories, as I
have no doubt the Labour Government was when 97 factories in the apparel industry closed
during its last 2 years in office. Discussions are at present being held by my officers with the
Australian officers, and between me and the New Zealand garment industry.
Hon. R. L. Bailey: In view of the discussions the Minister is now having on the NAFTA
agreement, does he hold out any hope for these people in Upper Hutt being able to retain
their jobs?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: The Upper Hutt project is in the hands of the
company that has closed it down. My information is that the company has been considering
this move for the past 12 months as part of its total rationalisation of the industry in New
Zealand and in Australia. The company manufactures mainly in New Zealand, but will also
be manufacturing in Australia.

KAPITI BOROUGH (APPORTIONMENT OF INCOME AND
GENERAL EXPENSES) BILL
Mr BRILL (Kapiti): I move, That leave be given to introduce the Kapiti Borough
(Apportionment of Income and General Expenses) Bill. The Bill is a local Bill, and relates to
the situation pertaining in Kapiti Borough, which comprises three wards: Paraparaumu,
Paekakariki, and Weraroa-the rural ward—which is very small and, therefore, has a
restricted rating ability. Yet the requirements of the Order in Council that set up the
borough in 1974 require that all wards contribute to the administration account or the
general expenses of the borough in direct proportion to the rateable value of each ward, and
this has led to the Weraroa ward's having to contribute 83.7 percent of its rating income
towards the administration account.
The borough council is unanimous that this situation is unsatisfactory, and the percen-
tage is far greater than applies to either of the other two wards, but the position cannot be
changed at the moment as the council is tied by the direct ratio to rateable value that is set
out in the 1974 Order in Council. Only a few weeks after that Order in Council was
promulgated in 1974, the Local Government Act was passed, and introduced a new

provision allowing flexibility in determining contribution to the administration account.
Under the 1974 Act, the council is permitted to negotiate with individual wards the amount

the Bill, the gravamen of the Bill being contained in the second proviso set out in clause 3,
which, if I may put it in context, permits the share that is to be contributed to the
administration account to be "such amount as the council considers fair and reasonable
having regard to the direct or indirect benefit derived by each ward from the general
expenses of the borough". The intention is that the administration figure should be such
figure as is fair, rather than the inflexible figure fixed by the Order in Council.

years, and would have had to be terminated when the land was required by the institute.
There has been no continuing commitment, nor in fact any obligation, to provide recrea-
tional facilities for the local community. The obligations of the Technical Correspondence
Institute are to provide teaching and training for its 26 000 correspondents.

Technical Correspondence Institute. There was no way in which the committee could or
should recommend that the Technical Correspondence Institute accept responsibility to

AGRICULTURAL WORKERS BILL
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): I move, That this Bill be now read a second
time. This Bill makes fundamental changes to the structure which regulates industrial
relations in the agricultural sector. The present structure has proved inadequate and clumsy,
and ill fitted to cope with conflicting viewpoints in today's farming world. The existing
arrangements under the Agricultural Workers Act 1962 have proved to be a source of
dissatisfaction to farm workers generally. The one major factor counting against that system
is that duplication of representation can, and indeed does, exist. That duplication is a base
for conflict rather than meaningful negotiation and settlement, and indeed advancement of
agricultural workers.
Among other objectives, this new Bill aims to avoid conflict. It aims to provide a more
efficient and workable framework within which farm workers and their employers can
regulate their working relationships. It introduces a system of exclusive recognition for
organisations of employers and workers. Sole rights of representation will be given to the
organisation most representative of employers and to that most representative of workers in
each particular class of agricultural work. The representative organisations will be registered
under the Bill. The essential ingredient of the new system lies in the fact that for each class of
work there will be only one representative organisation for employers and one for workers.
Nine submissions were received by the select committee which considered the Bill, and
were alluded to when it was reported back. All but one of the parties making submissions
appeared before the committee to give oral evidence. A point that cannot be allowed to pass
without noting is that some scepticism was expressed about restricting those giving evidence.
However it worked out very well, and, I think, to the satisfaction of members on both sides
of the House. Proposals made at that stage certainly helped the committee to report back
what is fundamentally an improved Bill. Several amendments have been made.
A specialised agricultural tribunal will be established under this legislation. It will have a
role akin to that of the Aircrew Tribunal, and will be used to resolve disputes where
agreement cannot be reached, even after conciliation. The procedures for reaching volun-
tary and conciliated settlements must be exhausted first. The composition of the tribunal will
vary according to the dispute being heard. The president will always be the president of the
Industrial Commission. However, the other two members will be nominated by the parties
involved in the particular dispute. This method will lend an expert agricultural flavour to the
tribunal no matter what sector is involved.
The tribunal can settle a dispute by making an award. Voluntary and conciliated
agreements, when lodged with the tribunal, will be deemed to be awards. That is the same as
is provided under the Industrial Relations Act. In making an award the tribunal is to have
regard to the seasonal and climatic conditions, and any other characteristics of the work.
Because of an overall flexibility, the future wages and conditions of employment of industrial
farm workers should more accurately reflect the circumstances in which they work. It is
worth pointing out that shearers have always had their own Act, and will continue to have it.
The first step in dealing with an interpretation dispute will be the constitution of a disputes


## p. 3335 (#217) ###########################################

29 September
3335
Agricultural Workers Bill
committee in each case. When such a committee cannot agree, or when one of the parties
appeals against the decision, the Industrial Court-sitting as a judge alone-has the final
say. Such a decision is binding on all parties.
Three clauses in the Bill are designed to give agricultural workers similar protection to
that enjoyed by other workers under the Industrial Relations Act. The first establishes a
personal grievance procedure to be used by farm workers. The other two clauses are
designed to protect farm workers from victimisation and discrimination because of their
membership or non-membership of any agricultural organisation or other body. A signific-
ant new clause in this legislation is that relating to the safety and health of workers. It is new
to the agricultural industry in that it is written in a separate part of the legislation.
The Government is determined—and I think the approach of members is bipartisan
here to reduce the high rate of accidents in industry as a whole, and in the agricultural
industry in particular. The accident rate has a direct effect on productivity. If productivity is
to increase, then the accident rate in the work place must be reduced. As Minister in charge
of accident compensation, I know there are many factors involved. At present the Govern-
ment is preparing amendments to industrial safety legislation in other sectors of industry in
an attempt to reduce accidents. It would not have been logical to have omitted similar
preventive measures from this Bill. I have no reluctance in advancing this because I believe
there will be full support from both sides of the House for at least this part of the Bill.
The remainder of the Bill is practically a direct take from the 1962 Act. All the
provisions dealing with the accommodation of farm workers have been retained, and so have
most of the machinery and procedural provisions. Clauses 1 to 8 are merely machinery
provisions and, apart from the necessary modifications, are the same as in the existing Act.
Clause 9 relates to the application of those parts of the Act that set out the new system of
representation, conciliation, and arbitration. Those parts will not apply to any class of
worker to which there applied, immediately before the commencement of the Act, an award
or collective agreement under the Industrial Relations Act, nor shall those parts apply to a
class of worker whose conditions of employment, immediately before the Act, were fixed by
the State Services Commission.
Clauses 10 to 14 establish the system of exclusive recognition to which I referred earlier.
A class of work becomes a recognised category. One employers' organisation and one
workers' organisation become registered with sole rights to represent that category—and the
categories are set out in the schedules. The first schedule sets out those recognised categories
that are to prevail when the Bill comes into force, and also the organisations registered for
each of those categories. Clause 14A sets out the effect of registration as an agricultural
organisation under the Act. Clause 15 requires each registered organisation to nominate a
person to be a member of the Agricultural Tribunal for occasions when the tribunal is
considering matters with which the organisation is concerned.
Clauses 16 to 26 all relate to the establishment of the Agricultural Tribunal, and deal
with procedural and related machinery matters. Clause 27 allows for voluntary settlement of
any dispute. Clause 28 deals with disputes over the interpretation of awards, and clause 29
provides that unsettled disputes, except disputes over the interpretation of awards, be
submitted to conciliation. Clause 30 sets out how a conciliation council established under the
Act is to operate. By clause 31, if a dispute is not settled in conciliation, it can be referred to
the tribunal for settlement. The tribunal can resolve the dispute by making an award, or,
when appropriate, it may decline to make an award. Clause 32 sets out the scope and
application of awards. Clause 33 requires a written copy of every voluntary settlement and
every conciliated agreement to be lodged with the registrar, and they are thereby deemed to
be awards. That provision is common to the Industrial Relations Act. Clause 35 limits the
reasons for which deductions can be made from the wages of a worker.
Clause 38 sets out the personal grievance procedure, which is available to a farm worker
whether or not he is a member of an agricultural organisation. Clauses 38A and 38B make
victimisation and discrimination in certain cases offences against the Act, and clause 39
makes contempt or obstruction of a council or the tribunal an offence. Clause 41 sets out the
procedure for the recovery of arrears of wages, and clause 42 places a limitation period of 6
years on actions to recover wages. Clauses 43 to 48 deal with the accommodation of farm
workers, and are taken almost unchanged from the 1962 Act.
Clause 49 is the provision I discussed earlier requiring employers to take reasonable
precautions for the safety and health of their workers. The committee spent considerable
time on this provision, and a Supplementary Order Paper will be introduced to bring the
employees of agricultural contractors within the provisions as set out in this clause for farm


## p. 3336 (#218) ###########################################

3336
29 September
Agricultural Workers Bill
workers. The committee was unanimous in wanting that provision included. Clause 50 places
restrictions on the employment of children in agricultural work. Clause 54 requires every
employer to provide a first-aid kit. Clauses 55 to 58 cover procedural and machinery matters.
The first schedule, which is the real key to the Bill, sets out the classes of work deemed
to be recognised categories when the Bill comes into force, and also sets out the employers'
and workers' organisations deemed to be registered in respect of those categories. These are
fairly widespread, but are self-explanatory. One of the registered organisations under the
first schedule is the New Zealand Farm Workers Association Incorporated. I draw the
attention of the House to the National Party's manifesto-
Mr Isbey: Which one?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: The manifesto.
Hon. Dr A. M. Finlay: Leave us a choice. Make it "a manifesto".
Hon. J. B. GORDON: The manifesto is the manifesto, although there have been
adaptations of it. I can remember very well excerpts of the "little red book", but we do not
want to digress into that. The National Party's manifesto stated that on becoming the
Government steps would be taken to accord the Farm Workers Association full rights of
representation of its members.
Mr Reweti: What about the amalgamation of unions?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: We will come to that later; it is going very well on the waterfront.
Just to digress for a moment, the amalgamation of the four railway workers' unions would
have solved a lot of the recent industrial trouble. The association was formed to oppose the
Agricultural Workers Amendment Bill introduced by the Labour Government in 1973.
Mr Wetere: Why?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: It did not get very far, and would not have given farm workers the
specialised attention called for and recognised by this Bill. The association has developed
since then, and its objectives are not only to protect and further the interests of members on
conditions of employment, but also to help farm workers on a wide variety of welfare and
educational matters; and I hope the association will foster the settlement of farm workers on
their own land. It has also been active in pressing for a retirement housing scheme for farm
workers. The second schedule sets out the enactments that have been consequentially
amended.
The present system of representation under the Agricultural Workers Act has proved
inadequate to meet the special needs of the farming sector today. The Government has done
what it promised, and has done it with a clear conscience, and has remedied the defects in
the present system of representation. The emphasis is on voluntary and conciliated agree-
ments, and the parties should be able to negotiate without direct Government involvement.
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: That sounds unusual.
Hon. J. B. GORDON: I thought I would hear from the member for Roskill before too
long. I am sure he will endorse my view that this should be done without direct Government
involvement. Negotiations should, therefore, prove more fruitful now that the Government
has moved to prevent duplication of representation and the source of conflict within the
agricultural industry. The legislation will lead to better conditions, better coverage, and
better industrial relations, which farm workers have not been able to get until now. It will
also advance the character and the stature of farm workers. It should also help many more
young New Zealanders to appreciate the full educational value they need in the agricultural
industry, and, in expressing my best wishes to the association, I hope that it leads to their
becoming young farmers in the interests of not only themselves but also New Zealand.
Hon. A. J. FAULKNER (Roskill): During his speech the Minister said that the

The member for Roskill spoke at some length about the manifesto, suggesting that the
statements made in it were incorrect and, for that reason, the Government should change its
mind. However, the Government is still convinced of the need for a special tribunal and
special legislation applying to farm workers. The Bill provides for an industrial framework
designed to cater specifically for the requirements of the agricultural industry, the creation of
a system of representation for agricultural workers and their employers, and the establish-
ment of an improved structure for the negotiation and settlement of terms and conditions
that will prevail in the recognised categories of agricultural work.
Traditionally, the wages and conditions for farm workers have been established at
farmer level; negotiations on terms and conditions have taken place at the level of employer
and employee. However, the conditions that have existed on farms for many years are not in
line with the awards that have been agreed to, because in many cases those awards have not
been updated. Those conditions, however, will be remedied with the passing of the Bill.
Every employee has, as an objective, ownership somewhere in the future. I know that for
many years the farm worker has moved towards farm ownership, and this should continue in
the future.
Mr Wetere: What has the relationship been?
Mr LUXTON: A very good relationship has existed between farm employee and farm
employer. The title of the Bill provides for just that: "An Act to provide for the
improvement of industrial relations between agricultural workers and their employers and to
consolidate and amend the law relating to the employment, and the safety, health, welfare,
and accommodation, of agricultural workers."
The Bill is divided into seven parts, and does more for farm workers than past
legislation. The broad outline of the Bill can be divided into three parts: first, it establishes a
new system for determining wages and conditions of employment for agricultural workers;
secondly, it provides for exclusive recognition of organisations of employers and employees
for different classes of agricultural work; and, thirdly, it makes general provision to ensure
the safety and health of persons employed in agricultural work. If we look at the new system
for determining wages and conditions of employment of the agricultural worker, and
recognise his special needs and demands, it is seen that a special tribunal is required when
the employer and the employee cannot reach agreement; that is covered in Part III of the
Bill.
Then there are provisions for safety, which were discussed fully by the select committee.
Clause 49 of the Bill is new, and the Government believed it was necessary for the safety,
health, and welfare of the worker: "Every employer shall take all reasonable precautions for
the safety and health of workers employed by him. . .". Many submissions were made about
this clause. The employer is required to provide adequate instruction and take reasonable
precautions for workers undertaking many of the jobs on a farm. The noise factor is covered;
it will be necessary for the farmer to ensure that his employee does not work in a place where
the noise level is likely to impair his hearing, and to take all practical steps to reduce the
noise.

course, some Government members make fun about presidents who are peanut farmers, but

Under the Industrial Relations Act the Industrial Court, the Industrial Commission,
and a whole series of conciliation commissioners and industrial mediators have been set up.
According to one of the provisions in the Bill before us, the president of the new tribunal will
be able to appoint his own conciliation chairman, in line with a section in the Industrial
Relations Act. Will he select one of the present conciliation commissioners? If that is to be
the case, the claim made by the Minister of Labour, the National Government, Federated
Farmers, and the self-appointed farm workers' organisation that people with a certain
special expertise are required to act in negotiations between farmers and farm workers is
nonsense.
Obviously the whole structure-the conciliation commissioners, the mediators, the
Industrial Commission, and the Industrial Court-that has been so carefully established
under the Industrial Relations Act means nothing. The Minister of Labour and other
Government members have said in glowing terms that the farming industry needs its own
special tribunal. Why? We have the Industrial Commission and the Industrial Court, which
put their stamp of approval on awards for a multiplicity of industries and organisations,
including agricultural ones. The Bill is a subterfuge for the setting up of a new organisation,
under the pretext that only people with special expertise will be able to sit on the new
tribunal to be appointed to negotiate conditions of employment between farmers and farm
workers.
Let us forget the pretensions and all the nonsense uttered about the Bill, and consider
the measure carefully. Federated Farmers, employers in the farming industry, and the
National Government claim that many farm workers are employed under poor conditions;
they want to set up a stooge organisation-a stooge union, an appendage of Federated
Farmers, and a satellite of the employers. The Bill has been drafted by the National
Government with the combined help of Federated Farmers and the farm workers' organisa-
tions. It will deprive the farm workers of a negotiation procedure used in every other
industry throughout New Zealand, whereby the industrial courts and commissions are
required to give their stamp of approval to awards and conditions arranged. The farm
workers will have their awards and conditions negotiated in a nice little corner, behind
closed doors, before a new tribunal of specialised personnel, with a president sitting as
chairman. In fact, I can see that tribunal introducing a new code of slavery for the farm
worker; and, of course, the Industrial Court and the Industrial Commission will have no part
to play, and will certainly have no opportunity to approve or reject the arrangement. Farm
workers will be subject to completely different legislation, and to a tribunal set up for a
particular purpose.
The whole country should see clearly: first, that the Bill is aimed at establishing a tame-
cat organisation that will do nothing to help improve the conditions of farm workers;
secondly, one could call the measure the "Smash the New Zealand Workers Union Bill",
because that union already covers the agricultural industry, among others; thirdly, the Bill
directly attacks the whole structure of the organised trade union movement; and, fourthly, it
is a vote of no confidence in the whole of our present industrial legislation.

relationship one with another than do those who live in urban areas. Of course, that is not
true on some farms and the boss may remain the boss on a big industrial farm; that is the

not work in large groups, and rarely meet except socially-perhaps at the weekend, or down

was standing room only at meetings held up and down the country to protest against such a
possibility, and they formed their own association. That is democracy at work, and this Bill
will help to make that law.

strike was broken because many of the shearers were not members of the union; they were
people who went out shearing in the weekends, and they kept on shearing in spite of threats
of intimidation and victimisation. We do not want that to happen for our farm workers in the
future, because they are looking after livestock, which is an important factor and an
important difference between farm workers and factory workers. You can stop a factory, but
you cannot stop a sheep eating; it has to be shifted when it is necessary and when it is hungry.
In this legislation we are trying to encourage voluntary unionism rather than compulsory
unionism. The member for Roskill talked about amalgamation of unions and the prolifera-
tion of unions, and said that we were just adding another one. Surely it is right that a group
of people who are determined to be in their own organisation should have the opportunity to
belong to it voluntarily. Surely this is a better form of legislation. It follows the principles of
this Government, which believes that people should have the opportunity to join a union if
they wish.
The Farm Workers Association has gone from strength to strength, and earlier this year
negotiated the first agricultural workers' award for some years. It covered many avenues,
including conditions of employment, and the termination of employment, which had not
been covered before. This legislation is noteworthy for the fact that it covers not only these
conditions, but also safety and protection. For the first time in our history farm workers will
be safeguarded, and that is an important aspect of the Bill. Their accommodation also will be
safeguarded, and the member for Porirua, who talked about the fowl runs in shearers'
quarters, should read the last part of the Bill and note that we are safeguarding farm
workers.
This legislation is very important in the farming history of New Zealand. No longer will
a farmer be able to victimise a member of his work force, because he will have to answer to
the Agricultural Tribunal. That is an important safeguard in the Bill, which I strongly
support. But, as well as that, a farm worker has the right to join a union if he wishes. He does
not have to go on strike unless he wants to do so. He will not be forced by victimisation or
intimidation to do so, because he has a responsible attitude, and the Government believes
that people should have a responsible attitude towards their work. I support the Bill.

traditional shell-backed Tory attitudes that I hoped were dying out in this country.
Unfortunately, that is not the case, and I and my colleagues resent the patronising attitude

When the Labour Government introduced legislation, the then Opposition encouraged

The union made very real attempts to work out an industrial agreement with Federated
Farmers, but did not get very far, because the leaders of Federated Farmers made it quite
obvious that they were not interested in meaningful negotiations with the workers' union. In
1966 a meeting took place between the New Zealand Workers Industrial Union, the dairy
employers' association, the sheepowners' union of employers, the town milk producers'
federation, and Federated Farmers. The stumbling block was the employers' prerequisite
that the unrestricted hours of work clause should be retained. No member on the union's
side of the table attempted to talk about the 40-hour week, as they all realised that farm
work is seasonal and has to be flexible. They knew that, when the crops have to come in,
when the stock has to be loaded to be sent away, when it is lambing time or harvesting time,
you have to work long hours. Anyone who knows anything at all about farming knows that.
However, if a farmer does require his workers to work extra hours during these times,
the workers should be entitled to compensation in the slack part of the year when work is not
as intensive. This is the sort of quid pro quo that the union has always wanted and asked for
in negotiations. Federated Farmers would not come to the party on those reasonable terms,
yet members opposite ask what the union did in the past to try to protect farm workers. The
union had no encouragement from the National Government in the 1960s and the early
1970s to give coverage and protection to agricultural workers, nor was there any sign from
the National Government that it would extend the Industrial Relations Act to give such
coverage. Together with members of Federated Farmers, the National Government set out
to encourage the growth of the Farm Workers Association.

Waikato Valley Authority Amendment Bill
WAIKATO VALLEY AUTHORITY AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. W. L. YOUNG (Minister of Works and Development): I move, That this Bill be
now read a second time. The Bill was introduced at the request of the Waikato Valley
Authority, and contains two relatively minor amendments concerning membership and
administration. It improves the provisions for the representation of constituent local
authorities on the Waikato Valley Authority, and for assessing the local authorities' share of
the authority's administrative expenses.
Under the Act as it stands at present members are elected to represent those constituent
districts which are specified in the Act. There is also provision for the Governor-General to
provide by Order in Council that any other constituent district in the valley may be
represented on the authority, either separately or as part of a combined district. This power
has been exercised in the past to increase the membership from 11 to its present total of 14
members representing constituent districts. This Bill provides that not more than 14
members may be elected to represent constituent districts, either separately or as part of a
combined district. Provision for representation of the various constituent districts will be
made by Order in Council, in accordance with any agreement between the authority and the
councils of its constituent districts. The provisions relating to the representation of the
Ministry of Works and Development, the New Zealand Electricity Department, and the
local drainage and river boards remain unchanged.
The changes were made necessary by the amalgamation of Te Kuiti Borough and
Waitomo County, and Otorohanga Borough and Otorohanga County. The new provisions
will also improve the distribution of membership among the various constituent authorities.
The Bill also alters the provisions determining the constituent local authorities' share of
the authority's administrative expenses. At present, each authority's contribution is assessed
as follows: one-half in proportion to the adjusted capital value of those parts of its district
that lie within the valley, and one-half in proportion to the assessed loading of the proposed
works and services for the district. The Bill provides that the local authorities' share of the
administrative expenses will be apportioned solely on the basis of adjusted rateable capital
value. This amendment will bring the authority into line with most other catchment
authorities.
In the debate on the introduction of the Bill the Deputy Leader of the Opposition asked
me about the amount of the authority's administrative expenses. The latest figures I have are
for the financial year ended 31 March 1976. The authority's administrative expenses for that
year totalled $314,000, of which the local authorities contributed just under half. As I said
when introducing this Bill, it has the full support of the Waikato Valley Authority, its
constituent councils, and the National Water and Soil Conservation Authority.
Mr WETERE (Western Maori): As I said in the debate on the introduction, I welcome
the measures proposed in this Bill, which has to be passed before the forthcoming local body
elections. The Bill primarily concerns two local authorities-Waitomo County and Te Kuiti
Borough, and Otorohanga County and Otorohanga Borough. They are to be included, on
the basis of amalgamation, in the Waikato Valley Authority. In welcoming this amendment
to the 1956 Act, I note that the provisions of the Bill conform to the suggestions outlined in a
submission made to the Minister by the Waikato Valley Authority in April this year. The
authority has one of the largest catchment areas to oversee in New Zealand—a total area of
18 000 square kilometres, equivalent to one-tenth of the North Island's total land area. The
catchment area for which the authority is responsible includes many pumice-based soils,
which are particularly susceptible to erosion. The need to safeguard the responsibilities of
the authority in a form that does not differ greatly from that at present constituted in the
1956 Act cannot be overemphasised.
The wisdom of the original Act is borne out by the achievements of the Waikato Valley
Authority to date. In the north of the authority's catchment district in Franklin County, parts
of the Motukaraka swamp lands have been drained and brought into productive use. The
authority deserves much of the credit for the success of this venutre. Onion production in
these former swamp lands now exceeds the production per acre in Pukekohe. Returns of up
to 20 tons per acre have been achieved, and much of the crop is now exported. In the
southern parts of the authority's catchment area, where erosion is a problem, the authority
has worked to ensure that the land and water resources in the region are used efficiently and
economically to contain existing erosion problems and to prevent further problems develop-
ing. New Zealand can ill afford to pay millions of dollars to correct erosion damage that need
not occur, and which will not occur if we give catchment authorities the support they deserve


## p. 3357 (#239) ###########################################

29 September
3357
Waikato Valley Authority Amendment Bill
in carrying out the necessary preventive measures and identifying potential trouble spots
well in advance.
After a recent visit by the Labour caucus committee as guest of the Waikato Valley
Authority, I am convinced that the authority is doing an excellent job that will ultimately
benefit all New Zealand. The effectiveness of the authority has depended on the ability of its
members to establish harmonious working relationships with all territorial authorities, the
New Zealand catchment boards, those who farm the Waikato Valley region, and the
management of industries in the area. These relationships have been developed and have

Zealand's export income and, virtually, our basic livelihood. Obviously, the Opposition is of
one mind with the Government in promoting this Bill, which ensures that the Waikato

The amendments set out in Supplementary Order Paper 35 were read into the Bill.
Clause 1. Short title and commencement.
(3) The Governor-General may, by the same or a separate Order in Council, bring into force the

BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Acting Prime Minister): I shall give an indication of the
business proposed for next week. It is intended to take 2 days on estimates-Tuesday and

PERSONAL EXPLANATION
Mr FENTON (Hastings): With the leave of the House, I wish to make a personal
explanation in response to a notice of motion given on 29 September by the member for
Auckland Central, which was phrased: "That this House notes the comments in the
September 30 issue of Far Eastern Economic Review in an article on race relations in New
Zealand which discusses the extreme racist national front organisation, and states on page
33, 'Yet in Robert Fenton the Government has a back-bencher in whom National Front
members may have confidence, and calls on the member for Hastings to explain in what
manner the national front may have confidence in him, and asks him to explain exactly
where he stands in regard to the national front."
I cannot see any reason for confidence in me by the national front and, apart from this, I
do not know members of the organisation concerned, am unaware of its aims and objects,
have not read any material it may have distributed, and have had no communication of any
kind with it. On perusal of the article by Denis Wederell in the Far Eastern Economic
Review, which was supplied to me late yesterday afternoon, I noted that the member for
Auckland Central had failed to complete the quotation he chose to use, and that the same
paragraph, directly after the words selected by the member, went on to say, "He is among
those who hold that there should be no political interference in sport."
In addition to what I have said, I can think of no reason for the author of the article to
arrive at a conclusion that a particular organisation, which has been spurned by the president
of the National Party, should have confidence in me. In such a supposition there is the same
element of innuendo and insinuation which prompted my objection to the notice of motion
given by the member for Auckland Central. There is therefore no ethical purpose in the call
for me to tell the House where I stand in the matter, because I am as unacquainted now as I
have been before with the reasoning of the author of the article. I consider the implications
in the article as they relate to me to be odious and to give rise to vindictive and unsavoury
suggestions by shoddy and unscrupulous persons.

SAFETY OF CHILDREN'S NIGHT CLOTHES BILL
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry): I move, That the
Safety of Children's Night Clothes Bill be introduced. It was intended that the Consumer
Protection Amendment Bill currently before the Commerce and Mining Committee would
be the vehicle for product safety regulations, and that the first of these regulations would
relate to protection in respect of children's night attire. However, in the select committee it
became clear that virtually all the organisations making submissions preferred separate
legislation or regulations to deal with this particular matter, and the introduction later of
provisions dealing with product safety generally.
At that point I arranged, with the agreement of members from both sides of the House
represented on the committee, to set up a small working party consisting of senior
administrative officers of the Consumers Institute, the New Zealand Manufacturers Federa-
tion, and the New Zealand Retailers Federation, to study the provisions of the Bill and of
the 1975 report of the committee on flammability, and to work out fair and equitable
procedures. The Bill is the result. In fact, it implements both the recommendations of the
working party and those of the 1975 Flammable Fabrics Committee.
The Bill proposes the adoption of Standards Association of New Zealand recommenda-
tions, and that children's nightwear be either of two classes of material—that is, low
flammability or designed to reduce the risk of burning. The range of materials available is
limited, but in case it is found necessary the Bill also provides for descriptive labelling
requirements. Because of the lead time of the clothing industry, particularly the manufactur-
ing industry-
Mr Hunt: What's left of it.
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: Well, if the member for New Lynn would like to
initiate a debate on the clothing industry, I shall be very happy to take part in it, but I do not
think Mr Speaker would allow such a debate at this time. Therefore I shall not be tempted to
answer the interjection. The clothing industry, as I said, has a fairly long lead time, and
because of that lead time the measure will not become fully effective until 1 January 1980. It
is intended to refer the Bill, along with the one I mentioned previously, to the Commerce
and Mining Committee.
Mr Mac DONELL (Dunedin Central): I notice that in the interpretation clause it is
stated that a "fabric that melts" means thermoplastic fabric that, when tested by the method
described in Part 2 of the Standard Specification for Methods of Test for Combustion
Charateristics of Textile Materials—and it refers to the number NZS 8703-shows any
tendency to melt or to allow drops of molten material to fall. That does not seem a very wide
definition; has consideration been given to the point that other fabrics may be coming into
the country that do not come within that definition and would not therefore be covered by
this measure.
I believe that, generally, the Bill will be welcomed. We have had this problem for a long
time, and accidents have caused very bad injuries to and even the deaths of young children.
Legislation that will help prevent accidents is necessary. The Minister mentioned that the
Bill will not come into operation until 1 January 1980. I am sure that will be accepted,
because many orders are placed some time ahead, and we must ensure that the manufactur-
ers at least have the chance of discharging orders placed overseas before the legislation
comes into operation. The Minister also said that the Bill is to be referred to the Commerce
and Mining Committee. It is right that interested parties should be able to present
submissions on it. I am particularly concerned about the point I raised earlier, the
interpretations clause, and about the types of fabric covered by the Bill. I should be grateful
if the Minister would comment on that.

Safety of Children's Night Clothes Bill
Mr HUNT (New Lynn): I also welcome this measure, which is a move in what could

measure will provide just a little extra protection for children.
I should like to direct two or three questions to the Minister. Clause 11 provides that
"Nothing in this Act shall, before the 1st day of January 1980, apply to or in relation to any
garment manufactured in or imported into New Zealand on or before the 1st day of January

exempt from the provisions, and not subject to legal action on the safety aspect? Does it
mean that any very poor quality garments imported at this time will be absolutely protected?
That is a point I hope the committee will examine-to ensure that we do not protect shoddy
imports. I am not suggesting that locally manufactured goods are shoddy, but am referring to
those that may be imported before 1 January 1980.

Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry): The honourable
member for Dunedin Central raised the matter of definition of a fabric that melts. As he
rightly said, this is a technical matter, and it would be pursued in some depth in the
committee with the law draftsmen and other officers, and the appropriate people making
submissions to the committee. We are concerned, not only with the fabric that goes into
night attire, but also with other attire worn with it-such as a dressing gown-made of a
fabric that melts. There is provision in the Bill for these two matters, but the effectiveness of
them is properly a matter for the select committee.
The honourable member for New Lynn asked several questions. Overall provision to
protect goods available now has been discussed in great depth with the trade associations
concerned and the consumer groups. There is a general protection, but I believe that once
the legislation is passed the public, who are very well aware of the problem-the public's
attention has been drawn to this problem for some time by the Consumers Institute-will
virtually make an immediate request for an assurance about the safety of garments, and we
shall find the garment industry moving rapidly in that direction.
Mr Hunt: Perhaps a simple little label on the outside of the garment would suffice.
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: Certainly, we can look into that matter. The Bill
provides that labelling of a garment must be exact in terms of the Bill so that there will be no
subterfuge.
I pay tribute to the trade associations. This matter has been very difficult, and I
commend to the House the way in which we have been able, in the last year or two, to
develop the joint working party approach, with the Consumers Institute, importers, manu-
facturers, and retailers working together in the public interest. The Consumer Council has
been involved in negotiations right from the beginning and has been consulted at every turn.
The working party was chaired by Mr Dick Smithies, Director of the Consumer Council,
which fully supports the Bill. I believe that, when the Bill is before the select committee, we
shall find that the National Council of Women, the Country Women's Institute, and the
other organisations that gave evidence on the original Bill will be pleased with the Bill as it
now stands. The Department of Health made submissions, and representatives will appear
before the select committee.

NAC-Use of Aircraft
3. Mr KIRK (Sydenham) asked the Minister of Civil Aviation and Meteorological
Services: Will he explain the justification for the sale of ZKNAQ earlier this year for reasons
of non-utilisation when it is reported that NAC is considering the purchase of a further
Boeing 737 as the ninth in its fleet?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Civil Aviation and Meteorological Services):
NAC's ninth Boeing, ZKNAQ, was bought ahead of demand for it in order to avoid a
substantial price increase-NZ$329,929-and to ensure that it was available to meet the
considerable passenger growth forecast at that time. The aircraft entered service in
December 1975. Due to an unforeseen falling off in traffic it was leased to Nigeria in June
1976. This lease expired on 31 March 1977, and because traffic had not recovered by this
time the aircraft was sold to Nigeria on 15 April 1977 for a substantial profit. Traffic growth
on trunk routes is now exceeding predictions, and there is every indication that an additional
aircraft will be required by December 1978. A special arrangement has been negotiated by
NAC with the Boeing Aircraft Corporation whereby NAC will be able to use the cheaper
Dash 7 engines instead of the Dash 15 variety. The Government is at present studying the
whole proposal.
Mr Kirk: Why was it impossible for NAC to carry on the leasing when the company to
which the aircraft was sold itself subsequently leased it at a profit?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN: I can only say that this was an NAC proposal. I am
unable to tell the member why it was not possible to carry on the lease. If he puts down
another question I will find out from the corporation. I remind him again that these things
are done, as he knows, and the Government approves them, but the actual negotiations are
done by a corporation, whether it be the Shipping Corporation, NAC, or Air New Zealand.

LANDSLIP AND WATER AND SOIL MANAGEMENT ASSISTANCE BILL
Hon. MICHAEL CONNELLY (Wigram): I move, That leave be given to introduce the
Landslip and Water and Soil Management Assistance Bill. The Bill is being introduced in
default of action by the Government, and also-because of the unsatisfactory nature of
present protection and assistance for home owners against landslip-there is now an urgent
need for further relief to be made available under the Earthquake and War Damage Act and
regulations. At present compensation cannot be paid for damage to a section or for a
dwelling that, although not destroyed, is no longer suitable for habitation.
The Bill is introduced also because of the urgent need for better planning of water
management and soil conservation in land development work, both rural and urban, and
because the action to remedy developments which were not fully adequate in providing for
hydrological changes caused by urban land development. The Bill is here today as well
because the time has come when the Government, through the National Water and Soil
Conservation Authority, should where appropriate grant direct financial assistance and
encouragement to local authorities and developers to assist and encourage them to follow
sound water management and soil conservation practices.
The Bill is here also because some local authorities have not been giving sufficient
consideration to potential landslip hazards when issuing building permits-indeed permits


## p. 3372 (#254) ###########################################

3372
Landslip and Water and Soil Management Assistance Bill 30 September
have been issued for sites that should not have been built on. In that respect, provision is
made in the Bill for the Governor-General by Order in Council to make regulations
providing for local authorities to be legally responsible for the consequences of instability
arising on developed sections that have been approved by them as being suitable for housing.
The Bill authorises local authorities to provide and maintain a special fund to meet the
cost of repairing sections damaged by landslips. This could be a means of ensuring that local
authorities take greater care in future when considering the suitability of land for a building
site. The Bill is introduced also to permit the Earthquake and War Damage Commission to
meet for home owners the cost of relocating to some other site provided by the owner an
insured building used as a dwelling place that is irretrievably threatened by landslips-to
allow the commission to act before the building becomes a total loss and the commission has
to pay out. That is a logical provision, and will save the commission's money-and the home
owners', in certain circumstances.
The Bill will also permit a home owner, in respect of an insured building used as a
dwelling place, irretrievably threatened by landslip, and a total loss constructively, to qualify
for a claim for the total loss, notwithstanding that the structure is not a total loss materially.
At present, compensation covers only the cost of repairing the actual damage to a building,
regardless of whether that building remains suitable as a dwelling. This new provision would
allow the commission to offset more completely the effect of landslip by paying for a house
rendered uninhabitable by the chronic instability of land, to be moved to a more suitable
site, or to be written off as a total loss.
The Bill also permits the Earthquake and War Damage Commission to contribute
towards the cost of section repairs carried out with the approval of the commission to
prevent damage or further damage to an insured building used as a dwelling place, but
limited to 10 percent of the sum insured on the building preserved from damage or further
damage by the site restoration work. This also is a logical approach, which again could save
the commission and home owners money. Until land development and water and soil
management is tackled realistically, each year we will continue to have serious losses of
homes, commercial properties, valuable farm land, and public installations, and also
unnecessary soil erosion resulting in hardship. Therefore, there is need for the further
provisions I have suggested.
Last year I introduced a Bill to which the Government refused to give a second reading.
I hope the Government will act this year, because since it refused to acknowledge the need
for my previous Bill, some parts of the country have experienced the worst and wettest
winter for 100 years, which has resulted in severe damage. If such a Bill as this had been in
operation, much needed relief could have been given. Local authorities and others could
have been given some incentive to follow sound water and soil management practices. The
past year has been one of lost opportunity for the Government and, in some cases, of
unnecessary loss and hardship to people. I hope the Government will face up to its
responsibilities and support the Bill, and take it, or some modification, through all its stages.
If so, I and my colleagues will undertake to give the Government the utmost assistance.
When I was Minister, I had similar action under way, which was unfortunately
interrupted by the election. Does the Government have any recommendations for action?
About 2 years ago, following the submissions I made to the Labour Cabinet, an officials
committee was set up to consider ways and means of giving greater assistance to owners of
property damaged because of landslip. Has that committee reported to the present Minister
in Charge of the Earthquake and War Damage Commission? If so, when, and what did it
recommend? I notice that in the commission's annual report, which was recently tabled in
the House, it states that it has put proposals to the Government. It also states: "The
December floods and the resultant damage to many sections through landslips again raises
the question of the desirability of providing some further form of relief. This should be
divorced entirely from the cover on insured property under the existing legislation. Local
authorities, with their local knowledge and expertise through their engineering staffs, are
best able to investigate the many problems associated with remedial measures and the
administration of a local relief scheme. The commission has outlined a scheme to the
Government . . .“
Which scheme was referred to in the report, when was the Government advised of it,
and what action does the Government propose to take? Late in 1975, I asked the National
Water and Soil Conservation Authority to make recommendations for a subsidy designed to
encourage and assist local authorities and private developers to follow sound water manage-
ment and soil conservation practices. Has that report been received? If so, when; what


## p. 3373 (#255) ###########################################

30 September Landslip and Water and Soil Management Assistance Bill

Hon. Mrs T. W. M. TIRIKATENE-SULLIVAN (Southern Maori): In saying that it is
timely to take another look at this problem, the member for Lyttelton has, by implication,
commended the initiative of my tenacious colleague in presenting his Bill. The purpose of
the Bill is to prevent the human heartbreak, hardship, and tragedy suffered by home owners
who lose their houses because of landslip. Almost every New Zealand family aspires to
owning their own home eventually. To strive to attain that goal has become a part of our
national character, and is as much a part of our culture as is the drive by Maori New
Zealanders to stand on their own turangawaewae. The need to strengthen existing legislation
is explicitly stressed by the Earthquake and War Damage Commission in this year's annual
report. In referring to the floods in Wellington and the Hutt Valley on 20 December 1976,
Mr Blackwood, Deputy Chairman of the Commission, commented on the desirability of
providing some further form of relief, and observed that clearly the present conditions are
indequate to cover the problem. The current New Zealand Official Yearbook points out that
the present cover for landslip does not apply automatically, and that there is neither a
comprehensive and complete cover nor an automatic cover for damage caused by landslips.
The Earthquake and War Damage Commission also observed that this winter was the
wettest recorded this century, pointed to the weaknesses in the local authority system of
approving subdivisions and issuing building permits, and confirmed that the inadequacies


## p. 3380 (#262) ###########################################

3380
Landslip and Water and Soil Management Assistance Bill 30 September
were more apparent this year because of the excessive floods. Furthermore, a publication
put out by the New Zealand Geomechanics Society and the DSIR points out that present
landslip cover applies only to property covered by fire insurance, that a minimum franchise
of $200 applies, and that landslip insurance does not cover a property owner for loss of land,
or damage to paths, fences, or retaining walls, nor for the cost of stabilising a section or
clearing landslip debris. The publication points out that the responsibilities of local govern-
ment are not adequately coped with. That is why the problems have been so great. Therefore
those official sources confirm the need for further legislation, and clearly this Bill goes a long
way towards completing the comprehensive cover.
The member for Lyttelton suggested that more could be done, and there is nothing to
prevent the Government from adding to the Bill's provisions, and where possible, improving
them. Clause 3 refers to rural land, and is concerned with the failure to provide adequate
guidelines for home owners who buy houses in new subdividions in urban areas. Under
clause 4 the National Water and Soil Conservation Authority will be able to provide, by way
of subsidy, such direct financial assistance as may be required to remedy developments that
are not fully adequate in providing for hydrological and other changes caused by urban land
development.
The schedule permits the Earthquake and War Damage Commission to relocate an
insured building used as a dwelling place if it has been irretrievably threatened by landslip.
The schedule provides also that that building qualifies for material total loss notwithstanding
the structure of the building.
The Bill provides sensible measures to cope with the tragedy to home owners caused by

Dogs Registration Amendment Bill
DOGS REGISTRATION AMENDMENT BILL
Mr ELLIOTT (Whangarei): I move, That leave be given to introduce the Dogs Registra-
tion Amendment Bill. This is a short but important Bill of five effective clauses that aim to
tighten legislation on dog ownership. Some months ago representations were made to me in
Whangarei about the stray dog problem throughout New Zealand and about the problem of
young dogs in their first 3 months of life, which in law do not exist. Members may recall the
canine cavalcade that began in Whangarei and ended at Parliament Buildings, when
submissions were presented to the Minister of Internal Affairs. The Minister undertook to
investigate the submissions and to set up an inquiry into the Dogs Registration Act.
After discussions with my constituents, the Minister, and officials of the Department of
Internal Affairs, I decided to sponsor a private member's Bill, and ask that it be referred to a
select committee so that all interested persons could make submissions, examine my
proposals, and suggest any changes they considered desirable to the Dogs Registration Act
1975. The Minister of Internal Affairs kindly agreed to that procedure, and I thank him.
Mr Selwyn Knox, a dog ranger in Whangarei, estimates that many thousands of stray
dogs were destroyed last year. The infection rate in stray dogs is unknown, but there is a risk
to human health and to the meat industry. People who breed dogs should be responsible for
them. I am sure most people are, but the right for people to breed dogs should carry with it a
corresponding duty to look after them. Pups eat meat from about 4 weeks of age, yet no
official recognition of their existence is required. Mr Knox suggested that every person who
possesses a dog should be required to notify the appropriate local authority within 7 days of
the dog's attaining the age of 4 weeks, and should notify also any disposal of the dog within
72 hours.
I have not included those suggestions. Although I believe they have some merit, they
would require a register to be kept by the local authority, and would in fact be another form
of registration. The notification of disposal, although a laudable suggestion, would be
difficult to enshrine in law-for instance, how would a telephone call be classed?-and
difficult to enforce. However, I have no doubt that pups given away after weaning and
passed from one temporary owner to another are often never registered and can easily
become strays.
My proposal, which I believe would help, is to require bitch owners to declare at the
time of registration any litter of pups born during the previous year, and to say how those
pups have been disposed of. This would be some check on what happens to unwanted dogs;
and, although it may not appear to be as effective as notification at birth, I consider it would
be more acceptable to dog owners and therefore more likely to be complied with.
Compliance with the registration provisions has always been a problem, and too many
additional requirements imposed on dog owners would only bring further problems in
enforcement. I note the comments of the Auckland Dog Protection Society, which states
that dogs are handed out willy-nilly to any home and that the problem is escalated. The Dog
Owners Group-DOG-also based in Auckland, has expressed concern, as has the Kennel
Club of New Zealand. I hope that all those groups will present submissions to the select
committee. Clause 1 of the Bill is the short title. Clause 2 requires the owner of an unspeyed
bitch to declare at the time of registration all pups born alive during the preceding 12
months. It also provides for a fine not exceeding $100 for non-compliance. Clause 3 deals
with wandering dogs. The principal Act provides that an unregistered dog over 3 months can
be destroyed or seized and impounded. Clause 3 goes further than that. It still provides for
the destruction of an unregistered dog over 3 months, but it provides also the right for
authorised persons to seize any other dog and impound it. These provisions would now be
enshrined in the Act rather than being available for local authorities to include in bylaws if
they so desire.
Clause 4 provides for a bond not exceeding $200 when an owner is required to keep a
dog under proper control. Clause 5 empowers a local authority to include in its bylaws
provision for a fine up to $100 for any breach relating to the impounding of a dog. At present
only the costs of keeping a dog can be recovered. Clause 6 provides for a dog to be seized
and destroyed as soon as reasonably practicable. That is an alteration to the existing
legislation, under which a dog must be destroyed forthwith. One can envisage authorised
people going down the road and shooting a dog on sight. The provisions in the Bill will
provide an opportunity for the dog to be seized and destroyed as soon as practicable within 3
months.
Hon. R. L. BAILEY (Heretaunga): I propose to make one or two brief comments on the


## p. 3387 (#269) ###########################################

30 September
3387
Dogs Registration Amendment Bill
Bill. I believe that in the main the House will support the principles enunciated, but the
member for Whangarei made one or two comments that I think should be considered. We
know that throughout the country local authorities and the Hydatids Council are undertak-
ing a vigorous programme, and have been for a number of years, to control and eradicate
hydatids and sheep measles. The member for Whangarei claimed that a dog can be a risk to
human health. I suppose one could argue that to a minor degree, but I wonder if the risk is
any greater than contact between one human and another. I am wondering whether the
member has, or can produce, any figures to give an indication of the actual risk from a
domestic dog, or any other type of dog for that matter. He said that hydatids and other
diseases can be picked up from handling a dog. If he can make any figures available I should
like them to be broken down into the various categories.
The other question I raise relates to clause 2. The member for Whangarei said that the
dog owner would be required to declare the birth of pups. The proposed new section
7A(1)(a) provides that, on a form provided, the local authority may require a description and
such further reasonable particulars as may be specified. That is a fairly wide provision. What
is meant by "further reasonable particulars"? When I turn over the page I find that, in effect,
the member is asking for a register to be set up recording the births and deaths of dogs.
Perhaps the member would tell the House whether that is his intention. An owner of an
unspeyed bitch must, at registration time, register any pups born during the year, and say
whether the pups have died or how they have been disposed of. I see that as a register of
births and deaths for dogs, and believe it would be almost impossible to administer.
I know that some local authorities are making tremendous efforts to overcome the dog
problem, and I have every sympathy with those who are taking measures. I am a dog lover,
and I own a dog myself. I know that dog owners have many responsibilities, but unfortu-
nately in this day and age, when many families require a double income to meet their needs,
the pets are often left unattended during the day. That is usually the cause of the problems
that arise. As I have pointed out, I am aware that local authorities in some areas are doing
their best to try to overcome the problem. The member for Whangarei spoke of strays and
wandering dogs. I believe the greatest problem is the wandering dog rather than the stray;
although the latter can cause considerable damage at times, he is usually caught up with. I
emphasise that it is the wandering dog that causes the problems, and I am concerned that
some people in our community will allow their dogs to wander.
I am pleased to see that the member is not waging an all-out war on dogs. The dog has
been looked upon as man's best friend for a long time now, and I think the proposals for
coping with wandering dogs and the provision for impounding them are reasonable enough.
However, I feel the member may be a little ambitious in clause 2, which provides for the
registration of pups. As it is the member's intention to move that the Bill be referred to a
select committee for consideration, we will have the opportunity of looking at that provision
in greater detail, and perhaps be able to make it a little more workable. I think everyone
agrees with the sentiments expressed by the member for Whangarei, but, as he himself said,
the Bill may be amended considerably during its consideration by the Local Bills Committee.

Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East): We have just heard a typically negative speech from

The member for Heretaunga asked about the risks to health from dogs. Although I have
not the figures for New Zealand, I have some figures for Australia. Last year there were over
2000 cases of hydatids in Australia. All of them required surgery, and most of them required
several operations. Another disease, toxoplasmosis, is the most common infectious disease
throughout the world. Over 60 percent of the blood donors in Tasmania were found to be
infected by toxoplasmosis, as were over 44 percent in the Australian Capital Territory. That
is the type of situation we have to look at fairly carefully. Another common disease is
visceral larva migrans-and that is world wide. That disease can cause severe liver damage. I
am sure the member for Heretaunga will be interested to hear that. The Leader of the
Opposition asked a question about the age of dogs. I suggest he look at the dogs' teeth, or
alternatively at the marks where a dog's teeth have been.
I am particularly pleased to see that some action is suggested to deal with the problem of

matter was being discussed with the local authority it was not clear how far the law went in
allowing the destruction of that animal. I am pleased, therefore, that the Bill is to go to a
select committee so that people who are concerned will see how far the law goes and how far
it needs to go. There will also be an opportunity for qualified people to give evidence.
