Mr ELLIOTT (Whangarei): I thank the members who have taken part in the debate,
including Opposition members who have spoken in favour of the intention of the Bill. I
agree with the member for Heretaunga that local authorities are doing their best in difficult
circumstances to control the stray dog population, and to ensure that dog owners are
responsible. With so many stray dogs around, the disease factor is difficult to gauge. The
exact number of stray dogs is not known, but some estimates have put it at 100 000, so the
disease factor is quite considerable. Dogs begin eating meat from the age of 4 weeks and can
then contract hydatids and run wild undetected, with no known owner, until they are 3
months of age.
I make it very clear that clause 2 does not call for the registration of pups. Opposition
speakers have mentioned the provision of a births and deaths register, but death is not
mentioned at all. Clause 2 does not provide for pups to be registered at birth, but simply
provides for the owners of bitches to fill in a few extra clauses on their registration forms
each year stating whether the bitch has had pups, and, if so, how they were disposed of. This
will give local authorities some check on the number of pups born in their district, and where
the pups have gone. I admit that not all dogs will be able to be traced in this way, because
some dog owners will give pups away to a person they have met in a hotel and do not know. I
do not pretend that this provision will control all dogs, but it will give some further measure
of control without being bureaucratic or dictatorial.
The comments made by Opposition speakers on clause 3 highlighted their ignorance of
the principal Act, which enables authorised people to destroy dogs that are found wander-
ing. This Bill re-enacts those provisions, which can be embodied in by-laws, although that
practice is by no means widespread or mandatory. The suggestion that I plucked this
provision out of the air without any thought is unfounded. The Leader of the Opposition
asked how it would be decided whether a dog was over 3 months old. It is not envisaged that
a dog ranger, on sighting a dog at 100 yards, would imagine it was over 3 months old and
shoot it on sight. Dogs will be seized, taken to a pound, and examined, and people who
know about these things-and the Leader of the Opposition would probably not be able to
tell the age of a dog, and neither would I—will decide the age of the dog. Under clause 6 a
dog need not be destroyed forthwith, but as soon as practicable after seizure. The local
authority or the owner will have 3 days in which to destroy a dog, and that is a reasonable
time after the heat of the chase so to speak.
The member for Auckland Central criticised clauses 2 and 3, and I think I have
adequately answered his criticism. There is no bureaucratic provision for the setting up of a
register of birth. I accept that the whole problem will not be solved, but I believe that dog
rangers, local authorities, and responsible dog owners will be assisted in the control of stray
dogs. I assure the member for Nelson that there will be no register of pups. There will be no
extra costs, because only a few extra clauses will be needed on the registration form. The
information will be available to dog rangers and dog owners. The Animals Protection Act
provides that animals must be destroyed humanely-not by being hit over the head with a
hammer. I hope that the SPCA will take note of the Bill, and perhaps present submissions to
the select committee.
Although the Bill will not solve all the problems with stray dogs it will solve some,
particularly in urban areas. Once again I thank members, and particularly the Minister of
Local Government, for speaking in favour of the Bill and agreeing to its being sent to a select
committee, subject to the approval of the House. I thank the people who made representa-
tions to me on this matter, and I am sure that in the next few months further representations
will be made to me by my constituents in Whangarei and by other interested people
throughout the country.
Motion agreed to.

Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson): A point of order, Mr Speaker. I believe this is
the proper time to raise the point, because it is the first opportunity I have to do so. I seek
your guidance on a situation that has arisen between committees, and ask you to rule on a
procedure to be followed when there is a clash or a conflict between the sittings of different
committees of the House. As you know, we have a number of select committees, some of
which are specifically referred to in the Standing Orders-the Local Bills Committee, the
Statutes Revision Committee, and the Lands and Agriculture Committee; but I think
particularly of the Local Bills Committee. There are also other committees that I do not
believe are specifically mentioned in the Standing Orders, but it is our custom to set them up
regularly.
Seven of these committees are to sit tomorrow, and in addition an ad hoc committee, to
which the Town and Country Planning Bill has been referred, is to hold a sitting. All
members are on at least one select committee, and all members will be sitting on a
committee tomorrow. However, it will be necessary for some members to leave their
appointed responsibilities to try to attend the sittings of the ad hoc committee. That will
mean a particular clash, because one of the Bills before the Local Bills Committee is the
Local Government Bill and there is a great deal of coincidence between the town and
country legislation and that Bill. I cannot refer to anything that has happened in a committee
hearing, but I have reason to believe that there is a good case for the two measures to be
considered together, and, of necessity, there is a coincidence of personnel on those
committees.
As I say, I cannot refer to what has happened in a committee, but it is plain that the
Town and Country Planning Bill is very important, being the result of about 5 years' work,
and the committee considering it ought to sit continuously. On the agenda this morning we
had a notice of change of committee personnel, showing that Messrs Quigley, Brill, and
Latter were to replace Messrs Bell, Malcolm, and Minogue. In point of fact, however, the
member for Eden was present and no substitution for him was necessary. I suggest that this
Bill, above all others, requires a continuity of application, and if members have to leave the
committee to honour the responsibilities they have to the ordinary standing committees, the
procedure necessarily followed by the ad hoc committee will be highly unsatisfactory.
I seek your guidance. Where should priority lie? Should a member's responsibilities to a
standing committee supersede those he has to an ad hoc committee, or should each member
weigh up in his own mind the importance of the occasion and try to deploy his individual
forces where he feels they would be best employed? I can find no guidance in the Standing
Orders. This appears to be one of the residual matters that falls to your discretion, but it is an
important one, and for the guidance of members I should like your ruling on whether we

sibilities by attending both committee meetings.

Dr WALL (Porirua): A point of order, Mr Speaker.

Mr ACTING SPEAKER: A point of order may arise from it, but certainly not at this
stage. I draw honourable members' attention to Standing Order 350, which states, "A Select
Committee may adjourn from time to time and, by direction of the House, from place to
place." The House has set up select committees, to which it has referred appropriate
legislation, to hear submissions and report back to the House on those submissions,
including recommendations for amendments. In my opinion, until such time as the chairman
of a select committee reports back to the House, what takes place in select committees is of
no interest to the House, provided, of course, that the business is carried on in accordance
with the rules of the House.
I am reinforced in that view by Speaker's ruling 123/4, which states, "The House has no
cognisance of anything taking place before a Select Committee unless it is reported by the
Committee through the Chairman. The only way in which to raise a point of order in the
House on a matter taking place in such Committee is to move that the chairman report to the
House in order to obtain the Speaker's opinion. If the motion were declined"—that is, in the
select committee-"the only alternative would be to give notice of motion to move in the
House that the Chairman's ruling be disagreed with"-the same sort of procedure that
applies with the Chairman of the Committee of the Whole. "It has been the custom for the
Speaker's ruling here and in the House of Commons to be obtained privately through the
Chairman by arrangement with the Committee."
If the committee were having doubt as to the procedure to be followed within the
committee and wished to seek advice from the Speaker, the committee should instruct its
chairman to see me privately. It is not a matter for discussion in the House at this stage,
unless of course the committee decided to instruct its chairman to report progress, or for a
particular purpose, in which case we discuss again what has been handed over to the
committee to deal with.
Regarding the advice sought by the member for Henderson, I am sure he is more
competent than I to decide for himself, and far be it from me to advise him what priority he
should give one Bill or another, or one committee or another, if he happens to be sitting on
two committees. The general procedure in the House in these matters is that we leave it to
the chairman of select committees to arrange, with the overall supervision of the Whips who
are given the general supervision of running the business of the House in this way.
Dr WALL (Porirua): A point of order, Mr Speaker. I had intended raising the same
Speaker's ruling because it no longer has the relevance it did when put down for our
guidance in 1926. At that time, procedure for the debate of notices of motion was not as
restricted, and the statement, "I intend to move next sitting day" had very definite
relevance. Privilege stops me from reporting any fact or bringing to the House some
criticism—or at least some questioning of the chairman's ruling. All that can be done in this
Parliament is to give notice of a motion, without any explanation and with no prospect of
debate. I cannot report what occurred in the committee. Your opinion may or may not have
been sought in private, and such opinion may or may not have been obtained and there is no
recourse from the ruling of a chairman guided by a majority of Government members in the
select committee.
I found myself having to move from one committee to another, both of which were
discussing town planning in total isolation, although both committees were discussing
legislation dealing with local government planning objectives. Surely the work of those two
committees should have been co-ordinated. It is not a question of co-operation or willingness
to serve on the committees, but the physical impossibility of doing justice to the obligation
put on me by this House. It would have made no difference whatsoever if I had been
replaced on one of those committees, because the two separate and unrelated committees
were handling matters which bore direct relationship to one another. With no common
membership the purposes of the House-I am not talking about the purposes of the
Government; the Government does not set up the committees, it only provides the work for
them—were not being served, and will not be served as long as this impossible situation
continues.

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS
Local Authority Loan Finance
1. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) asked the Minister of Finance: Is he aware that the
Taupo Borough Council had a loan for $500,000 on the market at 10.5 percent, but attracted
only $250, that the loan is the largest launched by the council and has one of the highest
interest rates ever offered by a local authority in New Zealand (New Zealand Herald, 27
September), and, in view of the importance of loan finance for local authority capital works,
what advice is he giving to local authorities wishing to borrow at the present high interest
rates?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance): I have not been advised of the results
of the Taupo Borough Council's recent public loan issue. The increase in the maximum local
authority loan rate announced in the Budget was necessary to maintain a margin over and
above the rate for Government loan issues. The member will realise that 10.5 percent
taxable is still considerably less than the rate of inflation. The changes in these interest rates
have had some effect on loan raising by local authorities. The Government is watching what
is happening, and will take such measures as may be necessary to rectify the position. As in
the past, it is the Government's intention to see that local authorities are able to secure
sufficient loan money to carry out a reasonable level of capital works.
Hon. R. J. Tizard. The Minister referred to the need to raise interest rates, but can he
refer to any local body loan at the old rate of interest that was less successful than this one?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: I have no details of local body loan rates, but the member
will know that local bodies receive very small amounts from public subscription. This
particular loan was underwritten to the extent of $210,000, and the National Provident Fund
underwrote $125,000. I have no comparative statistics, but this loan closed on 30 September
and the returns are not yet available. I do not know where the sum of $250 came from, but it
certainly is not the final figure of the loan.

Education-Primary School Library Books
2. RICHARD WALLS (Dunedin North) asked the Minister of Education: Has he seen
the claim made in the August newsletter of the Concerned Parents Association that two
books which are said to encourage masturbation "are being displayed and promoted for sale
for primary school libraries in the North Island" and, if so, is this claim correct, and how are
books purchased for school libraries?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): Members will be aware that there are
2234 primary and intermediate schools, all of which have the power to make decisions in
these matters. I am not aware of any sales promotions. Books for primary school libraries
may be purchased either from the library grant-an allocation made to each school by
education boards from funds provided by the department for this purpose or from funds
raised locally. In both instances selections are made by the principal and his staff, sometimes
with the assistance of parents. Where the subject-matter of a book is controversial or touches
a sensitive issue the principal might seek the guidance of his school committee. Financial
control of the library grant is exercised by education boards, and locally raised funds are
controlled by school committees.
Mr Lithgow: Would there be times when librarians could purchase these books on their
own account?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: I can only repeat that in primary and intermediate schools these
books would be bought by the committee, and the librarian, if there was one-and very few
schools have them—would be consulted. It seems extraordinary to me that a school would
want to buy these two books. I find them most unattractive, and I cannot imagine a library
purchasing them. These books are available in book shops, but so are thousands of other
books. Any school is at liberty to choose from all of the books available, and to select these
two and suggest that schools will use these books is quite erroneous.

Hire Purchase Regulations for Motor Vehicles
5. Mr MacDONELL (Dunedin Central) asked the Minister of Trade and Industry: Has
the Government received any evidence to suggest that employment in the motor-vehicle
assembly industry has been adversely affected by the car hire purchase regulations?
Mr ALLEN (Parliamentary Under-Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Industry):
No. While employment in the motor-vehicle assembly industry is marginally down on the
corresponding period in 1976, the hire purchase regulations are only one of a number of
factors that might have caused this. Others are the lower level of economic activity, the sharp

Mr MacDonell: How does the Minister's reply tie in with the comment made by Mr

comment that employment is marginally down on the same period last year?
Mr ALLEN: A survey compiled by local assemblers shows that for the week ended 16
September 1977, which is the latest date we have, about 5200 people were employed in the
industry, compared with 5400 at the same time last year.
Mr Prebble: Did the original answer suggest that the hire purchase regulations are not
having an adverse effect on the car industry?
Mr ALLEN: I will repeat that part of the answer. The hire purchase regulations are only
one of a number of factors that might have caused this.

10. Mr LAMBERT (Western Hutt) asked the Minister of Education: Can he provide

Drugs in Prisons
11. Mr KIRK (Sydenham) asked the Minister of Justice: What immediate action has he
taken to prevent hard drugs entering New Zealand prisons since the death by drug overdose
of an inmate at Addington Prison?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): Experience both here and overseas
shows that it is not possible to exclude illicit drugs completely from penal institutions, even
those designed for maximum security. For obvious reasons I shall not describe publicly some
of the methods that can be used. It is enough to say that they do not depend simply upon
conveyance by visitors, although that is the usual channel at present. I imagine that,
theoretically, a totally sterile environment could be produced by severing every form of
contact a prisoner has with the outside world. In practice it would be impossible. Prisons are
now dependent upon many incoming supplies and services that can be used to breach
security by those who are so determined. To eliminate every possible channel would mean
disregarding practical difficulties and the enormous cost factor, as well as humanitarian
principles. Small quantities of drugs are easy to conceal, and no prison can be made self-
sufficient and isolated from the community. I am indeed concerned about the recent death of


## p. 3401 (#283) ###########################################

4 October
3401
Oral Answers to Questions
an inmate by presumed drug overdose at Addington Prison, but a hasty emotional reaction is
unlikely to assist matters. Hence, no immediate action has been taken. My department
depends on the continued vigilance of staff and the imposition of salutory penalties by the
courts upon those who are caught introducing contraband into penal institutions.
Mr Kirk: As the person who died was on remand for serious drug charges, can the
Minister say why he was not under tighter security?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: No. The police are investigating the death of the inmate, and
of course I myself cannot take any action on a police matter. Certainly I shall be interested in
the outcome of the police investigations and of the coroner's court upon the death.
Mr Kirk: Can the Minister confirm that this is the second serious event at Addington
Prison in the last 6 weeks?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: If the honourable member is referring to the breakout and
the injuring of a number of prison officers, including the superintendent, yes, it is the second
serious incident at Addington Prison. I shall be going down later this month to meet the
staff.

Down Under the Plum Trees
14. Mr LUXTON (Piako), on behalf of Mr MALCOLM (Eden), asked the Minister of
Education: Is he in a position to give an undertaking that the book Down Under the Plum
Trees will not be used in New Zealand schools, and, if not, can he explain why, although he is
Minister of Education, he cannot give an assurance of that type?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): It should be obvious that I am unable to
give the undertaking that is sought in the honourable member's question. Part of the findings
of the Indecent Publications Tribunal, as amended by the Supreme Court, read, "This book
is indecent unless circulation is restricted to persons over the age of 18 years." In my view,
this means that the unrestricted availability of the book in any library in New Zealand,
including school libraries, would be illegal and subject to prosecution if this age restriction is
not enforced. It is only necessary to remind members that there are 2525 primary and
secondary schools, and it must be apparent why I cannot give a categorical undertaking that
the book referred to in the question will not be found in a school library somewhere in New
Zealand. If any information is available to anyone that might indicate that the book is at
present in a specific school library, that information should be brought to the attention of the
authorities.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.
National Superannuation—TV and Telephone Concessions
15. Mr LANGE (Mangere) asked the Minister of Social Welfare: When does he intend
to phase out the TV and telephone concessions?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare): The Government has no intention of
phasing out the concessions for income-tested social security beneficiaries. In accordance
with its election manifesto, the Government is, however, phasing out concessions for
persons receiving national superannuation, on the grounds that when national superannua-
tion reaches 80 percent of the average ordinary-time weekly wage in August 1978 the
relationships between the income of a big percentage of the work force and national
superannuitants will be such that there will no longer be any justification for the concessions.
As explained in the manifesto, the phasing out is being effected by applying the same income
test to the concessions as applied when the National Government took office. These limits
are $88.20 a week for married couples, and $60.80 a week for unmarried persons. The phase-
out will be completed when there are no national superannuitants with income less than the
limits.
Mr Lange: When the means test becomes the sole criterion for determining the
availability of those concessions, will the Minister give the member for Hobson and the
member for Waitemata the opportunity to make a retraction of their election promises that
the concessions would not be phased out before that policy becomes effective?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: Because of the substantial increases being given under national
superannuation, when national superannuation is fully implemented on 31 August next there
will not be the need for concessions, as there was under the Labour Government when the
benefit paid was only 53 percent of the average wage.
Mr Comber: If the concessions mentioned in the original question were available to
recipients of national superannuation after the scheme is fully phased in, would this not give
them a financial advantage over other members of the work force who may be receiving less
than the average income?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: Yes, and we do not believe it would be proper to tax people in
receipt of a lower income, with dependent wives and families, to give concessions to those
receiving an income or a benefit of an amount equivalent to the wages earned by the lower-
income employees.
Hon. Michael Connelly: Does the Government intend to withdraw these concessions,
notwithstanding that spokesmen for the National Party said that the concessions would not
be withdrawn, and that the National Party's manifesto made no reference to the proposals
that the concessions would be withdrawn?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: To help the honourable member, I should like to quote from the
National Party's official election manifesto.
Hon. Michael Connelly: Which one?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: This is in the Government's 1975 election manifesto. "Tele-
phone, television, and rates concessions will continue for the same categories of

Mr HUNT (New Lynn) said that the annual report of the Department of Justice made
gloomy reading. The department seemed to be in a state of seige, with a diminishing staff
struggling to maintain New Zealand's system of justice. Staff cutbacks and restraints had
been imposed in spite of the unprecedented increase in the number of cases and work loads
carried by the department. In August 1976, New Zealand prisons had had the record number
of 3062 inmates. Of the 25 penal institutions, 15 had had more inmates than they were built
to take. At 6 June 1977, Addington prison had had 51 inmates instead of the 25 it would
normally hold. How many inmates were in that prison at the date of the most recent survey?
Criminal prosecutions had increased by 34 000. An increase in problems of law and
order in any country was a sign of depression. The Secretary for Justice had pointed out in
his report that if present trends continued, by 1990 there would be one criminal prosecution
for every six New Zealanders. The department's commercial affairs division had in train up
to nine times as many liquidations as it had had in 1973. There had been a 100 percent annual
turnover of head office staff during the past 2 years. In his report, the Secretary for Justice

Resignations from the probation service had been unprecedented during the past year,
and in the long run society was likely to be the loser, both in terms of more offending, and

Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) said that the sinking-lid principle-reducing staff
numbers by 1.5 percent-had had a more serious effect on the Department of Justice than on
any other department, because it made it impossible for the department to do its job
effectively in some areas. In the last year, 186 extra people had been appointed—many for
the new prison at Kaitoke—but the effect of the 1.5 percent sinking lid meant that staff
numbers were reduced to about the previous level. Prison staff and probation staff had been
adversely affected. In 1976 more probation officers had been lost than had been recruited,
and there had been a 19 percent turnover rate.
In the Auckland probation service there were at present 25 basic grade officers with an
average length of service of 1 year. In the Lower Hutt office there had been a 100 percent
staff turnover during the last 3 years. The industrial action taken earlier in the year, when
probation officers had limited their case loads, had shown how much pressure the service
operated under. The 15 extra staff allocated after the service had been forced to take that
industrial action would not be sufficient.
The 6 September issue of the Law Journal had stated that, like other Government
departments, the Department of Justice had had problems with staff shortages, and had
asked whether, if both could not be done well, emphasis should be placed on pre-sentence
reports or on counselling and supervision work. It had pointed out that, if the latter suffered
at the expense of the former, judges and magistrates could lose confidence in the efficiency
of probation as opposed to custodial detention. On relinquishing his office the former Chief
Ombudsman had said he was concerned and worried that New Zealand had one of the
highest rates of incarceration in the Western World, and twice the proportionate prison
population of Australia. He had also been concerned that about half New Zealand's prison
population was Polynesian. The commercial affairs section of the department was under
considerable pressure, and had had almost a six-fold increase in work. There were nine times
as many liquidations now as there had been in 1973.
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice) said that as at 26 September 1977 the
prison population had been 2846, compared with 2910 a year earlier. Addington was a
remand prison, and therefore the numbers changed every day, but as at 26 September the
number there had been 52. The Department of Justice staff had totalled 3521 at 31 March
1976, with a staff ceiling of 3517. On 31 March 1977 it had been 3614, with a staff ceiling of
3633. Staff numbers had increased, not diminished. The same was true for the penal division.
In the past 12 months the number of staff in the penal division had been increased from 1471
to 1515.

Hon. MICHAEL CONNELLY (Wigram) said that in its annual report the Earthquake
and War Damage Commission had pointed out that, because of quite unsatisfactory water
and soil management and land development procedures, slips occurred following heavy rain
and flooding. If nothing were done, the fund would increasingly have to bear a greater
burden than it was able to meet. The Government could assist by encouraging better water
and soil management and land development procedures and by helping to remedy develop-
ments that had not proved fully adequate. That could help to minimise the prospect of loss
after heavy rain and flooding.
In addition, the Government could assist home owners and at the same time help to
prevent some of the burden that was at present falling on the commission by, for instance,
facilitating the shifting of buildings to another site, as had been suggested in legislation he
had introduced in the previous week. It was also in the commission's interest for home
owners to be assisted with repairs to sections where, if erosion continued, it would result in
the total loss of the section and the buildings. Why had the Government not provided some
incentives to encourage better land development practices? Why had the Government not
offered assistance to home owners, which would save the commission money in the long run?
Would the Minister make available the report of the officials' committee which had
been set up under the Labour Government? The commission had reported on an unsatisfac-
tory state of affairs and had suggested how improvements could be made. That would assist
the commission in meeting the calls on its fund.
Mr McLAY (Birkenhead) said that landslip cover had first been introduced in 1970 in an
amendment to the 1944 Earthquake and War Damage Act. That cover had been fairly
limited; it had applied to the house itself, but had not extended to developed residential
sections. The provisions had been extended a little in the Building Performance Guarantee
Corporation Bill introduced by the National Government in the present session.

legislation introduced by the National Government in 1970. In 1974, when the member for
Wigram was the Minister in Charge of the Earthquake and War Damage Commission, a

dations to include damage caused by floods and sea erosion.
The member for Wigram had asked that a report, which he said had been brought down
in 1974, be tabled. No such report had been presented, because the officials' committee
established by the member for Wigram in 1974 had not got off the ground.
The scheme the Government was considering would enable local authorities to set up
their own relief schemes, which would be funded and administered at local community level
and tailored to meet the special needs of the community. After the December floods, local
bodies had been faced with tremendous bills for repairing roads and the reticulation of
various services. The scheme would also assist local bodies to meet the cost of such repairs. It
had been estimated that a levy of 1c on each $100 of land value would be sufficient to cover
the cost of repairing damage. The money would be invested in the National Provident Fund
and would be available on demand.

Hon. Michael Connelly: You were quoting from a report given to you by your adviser.
Hon. H. J. WALKER said that the only report he had contained the 1974 landslip
recommendations. Those recommendations had been: first, that the present concept of
cover under the Earthquake and War Damage Act, which provided landslip cover only in
respect of an insured building and its contents, should be retained; secondly, that the
Earthquake and War Damage Regulations should be amended to allow the commission to
meet the cost of resiting a building that had been irretrievably threatened by landslip, if such
resiting was physically and economically feasible; thirdly, that provision should be made so
that an insured building that had been irretrievably threatened by landslip, and which was a
constructive total loss, could qualify for a total loss settlement regardless of whether the
structure was a material total loss; fourthly, that the local authorities should be charged with
responsibility for instability problems affecting sections they had approved as being suitable
for housing, and that they be authorised to set up a local fund to meet the cost of repairing
developed residential land affected by landslip; and, fifthly, that provision should be made in
the Landslip Regulations to permit the commission to contribute towards the expense
incurred by a local authority in carrying out work on a landslip-damaged section when it
could be shown that such work had mitigated a loss that would otherwise have fallen as a
liability on the commission. The 1974 recommendations had covered only landslip. The
proposals now being considered were much wider, and would be of much greater assistance
to people who suffered loss caused by landslip, flooding, or sea erosion.

New Zealand Post Office
Mr ROGERS (Onehunga) said that the National Government had slashed the services
provided by the Post Office and doubled the charges. In 20 months the Government had
increased postal charges twice. On 1 October, only days after the Post Office had announced
a profit of more than $21 million, its charges had been increased. The Labour Government
had held Post Office charges in its 3 years in office. In 1974 it had introduced the Post Office
home ownership and farm ownership accounts, and had laid the second Tasman submarine
telephone cable for communications between Australia and New Zealand. The Labour
Government had introduced the computerised savings account system, and had completed a
large number of building contracts. New post offices had been built in Gisborne, Mangere,
Onehunga, Paraparaumu, and Martinborough. In 1975, 140 new building projects had been
completed. That had been the year of greatest achievement for the Post Office, despite the
freeze on charges for 3 years. The 1975-76 deficit had been held to $38 million.
The National Government had promised to make the Post Office more efficient by
making the user pay. Since January 1976 the Government had increased postal charges three
times, stopped rural mail deliveries in Otago, closed down 32 rural post offices, and deferred
38 capital development projects for new post offices and telephone exchanges. It had slashed
$10.3 million from the capital investment programme, reduced the number of suburban mail
clearances, and halved the building programme for all new projects. In 1975, the charge for
ordinary surface mail had been 4c, in 1976 it had been 8c, and it was now 10c-an increase of
150 percent. In 1975 the charge for airmail letters had been 5c, in 1976 it had been 10c, and it
was now 12c-an increase of 140 percent. In 1975 the annual telephone rental had been
$61.60, in 1976 it had been $95.20, and it was now up to $120.50. He paid tribute to Mr Ivan
Reddish of the Post Office Association.
Mr BRILL (Kapiti) said that the Post Office had had a net loss of $38.7 million in 1975.

returned a profit of $21 million. The Government was to be congratulated on that.
Opposition members had castigated the Post Office for showing a return of about 8 percent
on the funds employed. He hoped that any public enterprise operated by the National
Government would work on a profitable basis, balance its budget, and maintain an efficient
operation.
In its last year in office the Labour Government had spent $78.3 million on capital
works. Of that amount, $62 million had had to be borrowed. The Labour Government had
felt that it was able to borrow $62 million and to provide only $16 million from the Post
Office's own resources. In the last year of the Labour Administration, $38.7 million of
taxpayers' money had gone down the drain. A large amount of capital work had been carried
out during the year, but most of it had been financed from Post Office resources. Of the
$67.9 million that had been spent, about $26 million had been borrowed.
With the increases in postal charges that had taken effect on 1 October, it was expected
that the Post Office's profit for the year would be $19.5 million. What would a Labour
Government have done about Post Office losses? Would the Post Office have been
subsidised again? Would Labour have used funny money? If the money did not come from
Post Office charges or from the taxpayer, the Post Office did not operate.

continued; the net gain in connected main station telephones had been 29 277; additional toll
circuits had been provided on main routes; free-calling areas had been extended; the telex
service had been improved; an order had been placed for a new international telephone
exchange, which would increase the capacity of international circuits from 208 to 500 and
permit the introduction of international subscriber dialling; and 92 buildings had been
completed.
The staff ceiling had been reduced during the previous year, partly because of the need
to economise, and partly because of the fall-off of demand in some fields—for example,
automation in subscriber toll dialling. It was predicted that by March 1978 the number of
staff would be only 200 below the staff ceiling, an insignificant figure when compared with
the total Post Office staff of 38 230.
The new subscriber toll dialling service brought with it other advantages, and a city-wide
radio paging system had been introduced whereby telephone subscribers, by calling a
number unique to each pager, could alert the user to call his house, office or his own special
number. That service was bound to be popular, but the Post Office had estimated that by the
end of 1979 it should be able to cater in full for the expected demand. From 1 October the
present public telex system had been expanded to provide for the acceptance by telephone of
messages for direct transmission by telex to addresses overseas and in New Zealand. That
system was known as the phonatelex. Another new service was the rapid-box system, which
was a special service at main offices and at main counters of small offices, delivery being
made within the hour to private boxes at the office of posting.
The Southland Times had stated that, by applying the user-pays principle, the Post
Office seemed to be doing what was required to restore its finances. That was very
heartening, and indicated that the fourth estate was aware of the difficulties of financing the
Post Office, even if the Opposition was not. The growth in the demand for telephones, which
was normally less than 4 percent per annum, had risen to a peak of 6 percent during the
period when heavy subsidies had been applied. The demand had now dropped back to 3
percent.

to the people when there were cuts in the building programme, in suburban postal

under the present Government it was merely a means of making money. Would the profit be
used to give services to the people and to provide better facilities for Post Office staff? How
much of the $21 million profit would be spent on providing a new Post Office at New
Brighton? People in New Brighton were being told that they would have to wait up to 3 years
for a telephone. It was imperative that elderly people living alone should have a telephone.
The Government was still placing restraints on Post Office staff numbers, on overtime, and
on spending, but no restraint was being placed on increased charges for telephone rentals,
postal rates, and private boxes. The recently increased charges were another attack on living
standards which the Minister could not possibly justify.

16.1c for first-class mail and 12.5c for second-class mail in the United Kingdom. The cost of
connecting a new telephone service in New Zealand was $50, in Australia $135.84, and in the

No one could claim that New Zealand Post Office charges were excessive by world
standards. It had been necessary to increase charges because all costs had been rising,
particularly wages and salaries. Increased costs had to be recouped either by increased
charges or by a return to massive subsidy payments, such as those that occurred under the

administration had been brought back to reality could be gained by comparing the $21.2
million profit in 1976-77-assuming there were no further wage increases-and the $26.7

Westport Dredge Contract
1. Mr ELLIOTT (Whangarei) asked the Minister of Transport: When will work on the
new Westport dredge begin at the Whangarei Engineering Company, and when is the
contract expected to be completed?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): I reply on behalf of the Minister of Transport.
Some steel has been ordered, and the latest information from the shipbuilder's yard is that
fabrication will commence towards the end of this year. Preparation of detailed working
drawings has already commenced. Completion is scheduled for April 1979.
Mr Reweti: What other active role has the Minister of Transport played regarding this
contract?
Hon. T. F. GILL: I cannot say. The member could put down a further question for the
Minister of Transport to answer when he is here.
Hon. R. J. Tizard: If fabrication is not to start until the time indicated by the Minister,
will there be any change in the amount on the estimates for this purpose-I think about $2.5
million?
Hon. T. F. GILL: A good deal of the cost, of course, is in the procurement, and in my
answer I stated that some steel had been ordered. The latest information is that fabrication
will commence towards the end of this year. Many contracts for supply of materials have
been placed and will come to charge this year. If fabrication commences towards the end of
the year, perhaps 4 to 5 months' labour will be involved during this financial year.
Hon. W. W. Freer: Does the fact that the member for Whangarei had to ask a question
of this nature of the Minister concerning the Whangarei Engineering Co. indicate a
breakdown in relationships between the member and the company?
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: That question is barely related to the original question and the
answer.
Hon. T. F. GILL: No, I am sure that the situation is that, as the company would not be
in a position to make public announcements, the member for Whangarei, in carrying out his
normal responsibilities of watching closely and jealously the interests of his electorate, has
sought to obtain this information from the Minister.

Pacific Aid
3. Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn) asked the Minister of Foreign Affairs: Has he seen the
statement by New Zealand's former immigration officer in Tonga, Mr D. Gordon, in the
Dominion of 30 September that aid projects did not solve immediate social problems, and, if
so, what does the external aid division of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs intend to do to
make New Zealand aid to the Pacific more effective in the short term?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Acting Minister of Foreign Affairs): I have seen the
article. It is simplistic to talk about the effects of aid projects in this way. New Zealand
responds to the wishes and priorities of recipient governments, and the New Zealand aid
programme in Tonga is no exception. In many cases we are asked to help in long-term
infrastructural projects. Many of them emphasise economic growth because the recipient
government has decided that such growth offers the best means of eliminating the causes of
social problems. The choice of approach and method is a matter for the Tongan Govern-
ment. Through the aid programme New Zealand will continue to respond to requests for
assistance in this field.

5. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) asked the Minister of Education: What curtailment has

the travel allocation was not balanced according to the requirements for the whole year.

reallocations can be made, or whether some other money can be allocated.
Mr Marshall: Does this mean that courses for which commitments have already been
made will also be cancelled?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: I cannot answer that question positively. We are examining the
commitments to see whether they can be fulfilled. There is not much of the year left, but
once the position has been fully examined the district senior inspector will be asked to
provide full details of the commitments to date and any proposed expenditure on in-service
training for the rest of the year so we can then allocate or reallocate as the case may be.

Primary Schools—“Human Development and Relationships" Courses
6. RICHARD WALLS (Dunedin North) asked the Minister of Education: Is it correct
that two Christchurch primary schools have this year introduced pilot courses entitled
"Human Development and Relationships", as mentioned on page 6 of the Concerned

Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): No Christchurch primary school has
introduced a pilot course entitled "Human Development and Relationships".
Mr D. M. J. Jones: Is it correct that the Cotswold Primary School and the Sydenham
Primary School have either introduced a course along the lines of the ``Human Development
and Relationships course, or are intending to introduce one?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: No course has been introduced into any school, or has been
planned to be introduced, which does not comply with the restraints that have been
established over many years that there is no place in a primary school for group or class
instruction in sex education. The only course that may be taught at present, and is in fact
being taught in those schools, would include material that lies within the present scope of the
handbook of suggestions on health education, which was first issued in 1969.
Mr D. M. J. Jones: Does the pamphlet also say at page 6, The courses involve mainly
relationships and family life; no sex education is included."?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: Perhaps I could explain the instruction given. The courses would
involve family and social living, and the topics that would be discussed would be sharing with
other members of the family, helping at home and taking turns, taking care of younger
family members, and teaching children to do things for themselves. The courses also include
instructions on the care of pets, and teach children that a pet depends on its owner for
comfort and safety. Another topic is safety, and the course stresses the fact that children
need instruction and guidance on safety hazards, as well as assistance to acquire skills and to
apply common sense if they are to avoid dangers. Teachers also help children in a class to
develop new friendships, or strengthen old ones, by encouraging them to bring their hobbies
to school. If people have fears about the instruction given, they should discuss them with the
principal to see just what is in the course, and what has been in the course for the last 7 or 8
years.
Richard Walls; Would the Minister agree that there is no basis for the further claim
made in the newsletter that these courses clearly indicate that the main purpose of the bill

schools?
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: This is seeking an opinion, but the Minister may comment
briefly if he wants to.
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: No decision has been made by Parliament, and it will be left
entirely up to members of the House to make any decisions about sex education. Guidelines
have been laid down and are being adhered to, and those guidelines have been in force since
1969.

industry, which has been held in Parliament Buildings during the past 2 days, in an

Facial Eczema Research
14. Mr LUXTON (Piako), on behalf of Mr SCHULTZ (Coromandel), asked the
Minister of Agriculture: To what extent is research being conducted into facial eczema in
sheep and cattle, and will further work be continued next year?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Agriculture): Officers of the Ministry of Agriculture
and Fisheries are carrying out extensive research into facial eczema, including work in the
following areas: (1) genetic resistance; (2) relative resistance to sporidesmin; (3) effects of
sporidesmin intoxication on milking cows; (4) incidence of subclinical facial eczema in dairy
herds; (5) zinc residues in milk and general work on fungi. This work is part of an on-going
programme started over 25 years ago, and until the cure has been found it will not be
terminated. The Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries now has a great deal of evidence to
show that controlled procedures are effective in preventing substantial stock losses.
Mr Luxton: How many people are involved in the research programme?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE: I do not have that figure in my mind, but Ruakura is putting in
substantial research on sheep and cattle. At a guess, I should say the number would be about
10.

MINISTRY OF ENERGY BILL
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Acting Minister of Energy Resources): I move, That this
Bill be now read a third time. The debate in the Committee stage confirmed that this is an
important Bill, with important administrative consequences and wide-ranging economic
overtones. It is designed to ensure the more effective administration of New Zealand's
energy policies, and there was considerable debate about this in the Committee stage. It
brings in two major changes: the formation of the Ministry of Energy by amalgamation of
three departments, and the replacement of the Natural Gas Corporation. The Minister made
clear in the Committee stage that these changes are designed to improve the quality of
energy forecasting, planning, and administration, and I am sure that they will do this. I
commend the Bill to the House.
Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone): As the Minister moving the third reading has said, this
is an important Bill on the New Zealand energy scene. While Opposition members generally
support the Bill, one or two aspects were contested in the Committee stage. It is to be hoped
that the Bill achieves the objects set out by the Government. There will be a major change in
the administration of energy in this country, and, resulting from that change, the real test
will come with the implementation of the Bill. During the Committee stage, the Government
introduced a series of amendments-in fact several pages of amendments were moved by the
Government-and the Opposition pointed out that the Bill has been hastily conceived, and
was being rushed through the House. The Opposition moved two amendments, which were
not agreed to by the Government.
The Bill is in line with Labour Party policy-policy that was re-endorsed at the annual
conference of the party this year. The commencement date is to be decided by Order in
Council, and during the Committee stage Opposition members pointed out that, while the
Bill should be given maximum urgency—because the second reading had been held up for
more than 1 month and applications for the position of secretary of this new ministry had
long since closed-it did not appear that the Government had a sense of urgency about
implementing the provisions of the Bill.
Clause 2, the interpretation clause, defines "energy" as "work or heat that is or may be
produced or derived from coal, electricity, gas, geothermal activity, petroleum products,
uranium . . .". The Opposition moved to delete the word "uranium", because, during the
second reading debate and the Committee stage, Government members claimed that the
1972-75 Labour Government had favoured introducing nuclear energy into New Zealand for
the very flimsy reason that it was part of a power planning committee report, despite a
similar provision's having been included in reports of the former national Government.


## p. 3431 (#313) ###########################################

5 October
3431
Ministry of Energy Bill
For reasons best known to themselves, National members placed great weight on their
arguments that the Labour Government was committed to nuclear energy programme,
when all the report meant was that it was one of the options being studied by the power
planners, the advisers to the Government-nothing more, nothing less. It would have been
totally irresponsible if this country had not examined all the energy options open to it, just as
the present Government is examining a wide range of options-including wind and wave
power. If we are to have knowledge of the total energy scene, we must be up with the play
and know what the prospects and the likely benefits are.
The Burns committee set up by the Labour Government resulted in a wide-ranging
public debate on the nuclear energy option, and the conclusion was that New Zealand did
not need to look seriously at nuclear energy for many years. This year's power planning
report substantiated that finding, and the nuclear energy option has been taken out of the
programme for the next 15 years. The Opposition moved during the Committee stage that
the word "uranium" in the interpretation clause be struck out, for the very good purpose of
testing the feeling of the Government-if in fact what it was saying during the second reading
and the Committee stage was that it was not committed to a position on nuclear energy.
Opposition members made it abundantly clear that they did not believe New Zealand
needed that particular option for many years. In fact, the advice from committees such as the
Maiden committee on power planning and development was that until at least the year 2020
New Zealand had a range of options open, and there was no need to include nuclear energy
as one of them. It was for that reason that we moved during the Committee stage to strike
out the word "uranium" from the interpretation. It is only right and proper that the
background be recorded in the third reading debate. It is also significant that, when put to
the test, Government members voted against that word being struck out of the clause. While
the Opposition knew where it stood on the nuclear question, the Government, when it came
to the test, backed down and supported the retention of "uranium" in clause 2.
During the second reading and Committee stage, Opposition members expressed their
concern about clause 12, which deals with the control of prices, and transfers from the
Department of Trade and Industry to the new Ministry of Energy the right to set prices for a
wide range of energy sources or products. The opposition considered that if the Government
was serious about a pricing and stabilisation policy such matters should be left with the
department that traditionally handles most pricing, not transferred to a department that will
be its own judge and jury. During the Committee stage it was pointed out that already
the Mines Department had tarnished its copybook by withholding briquettes from the
market until a suitable price could be obtained. The Opposition pointed out that if the
Ministry of Energy was to set the energy price the needs of the consumers could be
overlooked. That was seen as a disturbing feature of the Bill, and not in the best interests of
the country. It was also pointed out that the Government's policy had been one of getting the
maximum price, rather than of conservation.
The Opposition called for a division when dealing with the fourth schedule and the
matters arising from clause 15, which makes provision for the Natural Gas Corporation to be
formed into a private company; this will also involve the Maui development company as
well as developing the Maui gasfield and bringing gas ashore, provision is made for the
company to mine and prospect for oil or gas on shore, as announced in the Budget. The
Opposition saw no reason why this should be incorporated in this Bill, and pointed out that
the matter was one for separate legislation. However, in its wisdom the Government has
included these measures in the Bill, which is a retrograde step for the Natural Gas
Corporation, especially as less than 12 months ago the Government had a measure before
the House that drastically restructured the corporation. It was thought at the time that that
part of the Government's energy policy would hold for many years. The Natural Gas
Corporation is doing a good job, and made its first profit this year. The amendment to the
fourth schedule moved by the Opposition was defeated by the weight of the Government
vote.
Other matters raised during the Committee stage will be mentioned by Opposition
speakers who participated in the debate, but, generally speaking, members on this side
believe the Bill would have been better with the incorporation of the amendments and
suggestions put forward by them. For the future progress and well-being of this country it is
vital to have an energy policy that will work. The Opposition has some doubts about the
super Ministry of Energy that will be set up, and made the point that bigger is not always
better. Many people are convinced that the transport sector is no more efficient or working
any better since the reorganisation of the Ministry of Transport to include the former marine

Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Acting Minister of Energy Resources): In this Bill the

experience of members on both sides of the House would confirm—and the Opposition has
agreed with the principles of the Bill-that this is a necessary measure; there is some
disagreement about the details, but in principle we are agreed that the Bill should proceed
without delay. It is a good Bill.
In the Committee stage Opposition members played politics with the concept of nuclear
energy and the nuclear energy option, and sought to remove the word "uranium" from the
definition of "energy". That was nonsensical. There is no need to delete that word. Indeed,
even if it had been removed it would still have been included in the broad definition of
energy, which covers all sources of heat and energy. I believe I should write into the record a
point made by the Minister in the Committee stage-that the former Labour Government
considered the nuclear option and possible sites for the development of nuclear power. The
National Government, as the record shows, has not proceeded with that work, but has set up
a royal commission to examine the nuclear energy option for New Zealand.
Opposition spokesmen have confirmed that pricing is a complex matter. I was surprised
indeed that, with their experience and background, they did not realise the desirability of
bringing energy pricing under one department. With the multiciplicity of Acts and regula-
tions, it was common sense-in my view, speaking with my finance hat on-to ensure that
the ministry was able to work on the whole area of energy costs, to direct energy patterns, to
look at the technical possibilities, and to consider production costs, in developing proper
energy pricing policies.
I was puzzled by the opposition to the merger of the petroleum company and the
Natural Gas Corporation. Again, I should have thought that, when we are beginning to
develop a wider-ranging exploration programme, it was a common-sense move to bring
together the National Gas Corporation, with its experience, and the petroleum company,
with its role in developing and managing an on-shore programme for the State.
I turn now to staff matters. In terms of the development of legislation over the last 8
years, the Bill provides for reasonable oversight of a State agency by the State Services
Commission. In legislation establishing State agencies provision for oversight is generally
made. That applies, for instance, to the Accident Compensation Commission, which is a
good parallel to the proposed petroleum corporation. In general, I argue that such oversight
is necessary, and I repeat that I am puzzled by the opposition to it. This is a good Bill; it is
necessary and timely, and I hope the House will pass it.

Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition): Even though the Committee
stage of this Bill was taken at a very late hour, Opposition members made many points about
the short title and on clause 2, which fixes the actual rates of tax for the current year. Our
concern is that, although the rates of tax are the same as those fixed 2 years ago, the base to
which they apply has not been changed. We spent some time in showing the effect this would
have on the taxpayer and on the community. The first point we made was that, despite the
Government's claim that there had been no change in the rates, these provisions will mean
the collection this year of $742 million more than was collected under the same provisions
last year-a clear indication that there have been substantial changes in some part of the
financial structure in the interval.
Everyone knows there has been no real growth of incomes in that period. There has
been greater unemployment, greater migration, and no increase in productivity, either in
total or per head of population, in that period. Hence, it is clear that the effects of the two
clauses we discussed were on money incomes and on the product, in the tax sense, of those


## p. 3435 (#317) ###########################################

5 October
3435
Income Tax (Annual) Bill
money incomes. We relied to some extent on a talk given to the Wellington Manufacturers
Association by the chairman of the 1967 Tax Review Committee. He gave chapter and verse
for how the proposed tax rates, when applied to today's incomes, would drastically change
average tax impositions.
One of the most serious situations revealed was that for the first time, the total tax take
will be more than one-third of the gross national product; the estimated figures for taxation
and for the GNP this year show that the tax take is likely to be about 33.4 percent of the
GNP. Percentages may not mean very much to some people, and therefore we used other
statistics to illustrate how much the present Government is taking in tax. During the Labour
Government's 3 years in office the total income tax take was $6,129,000,000, but, in the first
2 years of the present National Government-using the provisions in the first two clauses of
this Bill, and without changing the basis to which they apply-$6,398,000,000 will have been
produced from income tax; in other words, using these provisions, the National Government
in 2 years will have collected more in income tax than the Labour Government collected in 3
years. No more obvious example of the tax-grabbing policies of this Government need be
cited.
This Bill is part of the price the public has to pay for the Government's election
promises. The Opposition referred to the Government's promise on page 1 of its glossy 1975
manifesto: "The growth of Government spending will be curbed, thus enabling tax increases
to be less than the 87 percent total rise of the last 3 years." The figures I have quoted
emphasise that the National Government has failed miserably in the first promise it made in
that glossy manifesto. It is no wonder that the Prime Minister disowned that manifesto and
blamed it on his advertising agents.
From the debate emerged the fact that Government members are deluding themselves
about the meaning of words and the effect of tax provisions. When replying to one part of
the debate, the Minister in charge of the Bill asserted that the Labour Government had been
responsible in 1975 for increasing the tax rates and that therefore, as a poor victim of
circumstances, he was only carrying them on. I explained to him that although the Labour
Government did adjust the tax rates as he said, it gave other forms of relief to people on
lower incomes. Of course, he did not mention those and tried to imply instead that the tax
rates decided what tax people would pay. That is only one of three factors, the second being
the graduated scale on which tax rates are applied, and the third being the exemptions and
rebates that are applied also.
Just as the Minister was implying that, because these rates are the same as they were in
1975, they are therefore all right or it is the Labour Government's fault, so in the Committee
stage he alleged that, because the Labour Government had changed the rates, it increased
the tax the people on lower incomes had to pay. Of course, the opposite is the truth. The
Labour Government applied these rates selectively, with consequent tax reductions for
everyone earning less than $150 a week. The reduction was given not just to some taxpayers,
as is happening under this Government, but to every taxpayer. Labour members were at
some pains to make that clear, but I think that, perhaps because of the late hour, the
utterances of the Minister mislead a considerable section of the community.
I come back to the point with which I started this discussion. The provisions in this Bill
will increase this year's income tax take by $742 million more than was collected last year. It
does this through inflation. The rates set out in the Bill are the same as those that applied in
1975 and 1976, and only a limited number of taxpayers is benefiting from changes in
exemptions and a few other adjusments. Although they receive some concessions as
individuals, the total effect is that the tax take has been grossly increased, at a time when the
Government has been talking at great length about its determination to grapple with
inflation. We discussed that point at length. Unless inflation continues, these tables will not
produce the return predicted. In order to finance Government expenditure-because that is
certain—and to reduce the deficit before borrowing-and that is almost an obsession with
some Government members-these tax tables must produce the level of income tax we were
talking about. In other words, inflation must persist at about 15 percent; otherwise, these
rates will not produce the results that have been claimed.
Despite the late hour, Opposition members argued at some length in the Committee
stage about the first two clauses of the Bill. The statistics measuring increases in the
consumer price index were referred to. In 1975 we had a decent early Budget, but the figures
used were those for December 1974, as they were the last reliable figures with which the
Government could work. If we take the figure then as 1000, we find that the June 1977 figure
for the consumer price index was 1439; in other words, the increase in costs has been almost

44 percent. Wages have increased also. In the course of the discussion we showed that, even
though wages might have increased in gross terms to parallel the increase in the consumer
price index I mentioned, the tax take has increased by a much higher percentage. An
examination of those facts was the central theme of Mr Ross's talk, to which I referred
earlier.
If a taxpayer has an income of $5,000 per annum, or a little over $96 a week, he pays an
average of 24.5 percent of that income in tax, but if he earns another $1,000 a year, or a little
over another $19 a week, the tax on that part of his income is increased spectacularly to 38
percent by the operation of these tables. The Opposition pointed to the effect this has had on
the willingness of people to work overtime, to accept shift work, or to work at penalty rates
in the weekends in terms of emergency. Opposition members said that one of the most
undesirable effects of this tax bill is to reduce the incentive to work, not just for people on
higher incomes, but right down the scale to those who earn little more than the average
wage, and for many people whose ordinary income is well below the average level-because
$5,000 a year, or $95 a week, is substantially below the average male wage, which
Government figures show to be about $129 a week. -An income of that level incurs taxation
of around 44c in the $1.
So, as soon as a person on the average wage works overtime, he has a feeling of
resentment that the taxgatherer is taking half his earnings-and that happens over and over
again. It is a direct result of this Government's refusal to change either the rates set out in
this Bill, or the personal rebate to which each taxpayer is entitled, or the graduated scale
upon which these rates are levied. The Opposition maintained that any of those three things
should have been changed, but that the Government was powerless to do anything, first,
because of its election promises and its extra spending; secondly, because of its obsession
with the deficit before borrowing; and, thirdly, because of its failure really to get to grips
with the problem of giving relief where needed. The Government is giving relief in some
areas that deserve it-such as low-income families-and in some areas where it is not
needed-such as the well-to-do aged over 60, who have perfectly adequate incomes from
other sources-but it has given nothing at all to the ordinary taxpayer.
The Government's income tax policy is an attempt to fool the public by quoting only a
selection of the figures; that is precisely the line the Minister took throughout the debate. He
said that the minimum tax had been increased from 18c to 20c in the dollar, but he failed to
mention the change in the personal rebate and the accompanying increase in all social
welfare benefits, and the fact that most people who are eligible for the minimum tax rates are
also beneficiaries—and very few of them would pay that, but even those who do pay, pay less
because of the operation of the rebate system. This bill will rebound to the Government's
discredit, because more people realise that the burden placed on the taxpayer by the
Government's policies on superannuation, employment, overseas trade, and migration come
back to the one simple fact that the average taxpayer today pays much more in total, and
much more as a proportion of his income, than he ever paid before.

schedule to the Income Tax Act. The schedule referred to in clause 2 of the Bill is the first
schedule to the principal Act, which is not the schedule we are dealing with here. We are
amending the first schedule to the principal Act. Reference can be made only to the clauses
of the Bill relating to the principal Act; that is the First Schedule of the principal Act as laid
down in the statute. We can refer to any amendment proposed to the Bill.
Hon. R. O. DOUGLAS: I shall stay close to clause 2, which states: "Rates of income tax
for the year commencing 1 April 1977—(1) Subject to this section, for the year commencing
on the 1st day of April 1977, income tax shall be assessed, levied, and paid pursuant to Part
IV of the principal Act . . .". During the Committee stage I spoke about the effect the
schedule would have on a married man with a young family. I took as my example a married
man with three children aged 10, 5, and 2. That family man was crippled by high interest
rates and mortgage repayments. I discussed how the taxation rates in clause 2 affected him.
I assumed the man was a fighter, and was prepared to work as much overtime as he could to
provide better conditions for his family.
It was pointed out that the taxation structure under this bill provides that a married man
with three children and on $3 an hour averages $21.91 net a day if he works 4 days a week, or
$87.64 for working Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, and Thursday. If the man works on the
fifth day his pay will drop to $14.72; in other words, he will earn $7.19 less on Friday than on
the other 4 days. It is no wonder that there has been a considerable decline in productivity
and an increase in absenteeism. At the outset I assumed the man was a fighter and that he
was prepared to work overtime to better his financial position. If the man worked on the
sixth day for $3 an hour, his rate of pay would be a little better than on the fifth day, but still
less than what he earned on the other 4 days. He would receive $21.64 for working all day
Saturday. If the man worked on the seventh day at double time he would receive $19.98,
which is marginally less than what he would receive for Saturday, and about $2 less than
what he would receive for Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, and Thursday. A married man
with three children and heavy mortgage commitments earning $48 gross on a Sunday-8
hours at $6 an hour-will pay $28.02 in tax.
During the Committee stage I suggested that this was the root cause of declining
productivity and the increase in absenteeism, and the other issues that labour experts are
talking about. The cold facts are that people are being penalised for daring to work harder.
They are being put into a poverty trap, and the Government is ensuring that they stay there.
People then wonder why the young family man reacts with despair. He faces interest rates of
18 percent to 23 percent, and pays up to $70 or $80 in interest payments on his mortgage.
Those prepared to work on Sunday pay more than 60 percent of their income in tax. Out of a
gross Sunday earning of $48, a mere $19.98 is retained. Those earning $3 an hour earn less
on Saturday and Sunday at double time or time and a half than they would earn on Monday,
Tuesday, Wednesday, or Thursday. It is a tragedy that people who can afford to do without
overtime, because their mortgages are repaid, are not prepared to work the extra hours. The
country is losing that potential productivity.
The person paying more than $60 a week in interest or with heavy rental commitments
has no alternative but to work the overtime, even though more than 60 percent of the
amount earned is taken in taxation. It is no wonder that people are resentful. Clause 2 of the

Clause 49. Safety and health of workers.
(1) Every employer shall take all reasonable precautions for the safety and health of workers
employed by him.
(3) Without limiting the generality of subsection (1) of this section, if, in the opinion of the
Medical Officer of Health, the noise arising from any process or activity carried out by an
agricultural worker, or by his employer or a person acting at the request or under the direction of
his employer, is likely to impair the hearing of that worker, the employer shall take all practicable
steps so to reduce the noise that it is no longer likely to do so, either by controlling it at source or by
isolating or insulating the process or activity; and until the noise is so reduced, or if in the opinion
of an Inspector it is impracticable so to reduce it, he shall, as soon as may be practicable, provide
every worker employed by him who is exposed to the noise with a personal ear protection device of
a type approved by the Director-General of Health.
(4) Without limiting the generality of subsection (1) of this section, every employer shall provide
for workers engaged in any process or activity that involves a risk of bodily injury to them, or a
danger to their health, from flying particles or fragments, or from falling objects, or from
corrosive, irritant, toxic, or explosive substances, or from harmful radiation. or from any similar
cause, such protective clothing and equipment as may be necessary to afford them reasonable
protection against that risk or danger.
Mr WETERE (Western Maori) moved to add to subclause (1) the words "and other
persons lawfully on his land or premises"; to delete from subclause (3) the words "as soon as
may be practicable"; to insert in subclause (4) the words "protect them from that risk or
danger; and to delete the words "afford them reasonable protection against that risk or
danger.

Mr Acting Speaker took the chair at 2.30 p.m.

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS
Roading Work on State Highway 1 at Glenavy
1. Mr ELWORTHY (Oamaru) asked the Minister of Works and Development: When
will the National Roads Board carry out works on State Highway 1 at Glenavy to remove the
dangerous hazard?
Hon. W. L. YOUNG (Minister of Works and Development): The delivery of culvert
pipes for the Glenavy dip is expected very shortly. The culvert should remove the hazard
caused by frequent flooding, and its installation is expected to be completed within 6
months.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.
Kaihu Multi-purpose Water Scheme
2. Hon. M. RATA (Northern Maori) asked the Minister of Works and Development:
What progress has been made on the Kaihu multi-purpose water scheme, and when will the
project get under way?
Hon. W. L. YOUNG (Minister of Works and Development): Progress on the Kaihu
multi-purpose scheme has been assisted by the Government by way of grants to the
Northland Catchment Commission for water allocation planning and operational surveys to
ensure that adequate water resource information is available to development agencies. The
Kaihu multi-purpose scheme is being promoted by the North Auckland Electric Power
Board largely as a hydro-electric development, and the timing of the project is really in the
hands of the power board.
Hon. M. Rata: Because of the obvious interest that the Government and the Ministry of
Works and Development have in this scheme, and because of its value, socially and
economically, to that district, exactly when will the scheme come into being?
Hon. W. L. YOUNG: I have already explained to the honourable member that the
timing is in the hands of the power board. On three occasions the Government has given
subsidies to the catchment board to allow it to carry out investigations. In the Budget which
has just been presented $400,000 was set aside to allow organisations such as the power
board to apply, and the Ministry of Works and Development will be glad to help them.
Mr H. N. Austin: Can the Minister confirm that the member for Hobson has been in
constant touch with him, in conjunction with the local authorities, over this Kaihu Valley
scheme?
Hon. W. L. YOUNG: Yes, and I have given the honourable member greater detail than
time permits me to give to the House on this occasion.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.
Abortion Admissions to Public Hospitals
3. Mr FENTON (Hastings), on behalf of Mr D. M. J. JONES (Waitemata), asked the
Minister of Health: Has he seen the statement on page 50 of the public health report that of
the 4500 abortion admissions to public hospitals annually about 3000 are the result of
"botched up back-street abortions", and can he confirm the accuracy of these figures?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): The statement made on page 50 of the public
health report quotes an article in the New Zealand Law Journal, No.15, of 22 August 1972,
by Mr W. A. P. Facer. In it the author refers to the average number of cases requiring public
hospital treatment for abortion between 1950 and 1968 as being 4488. Mr Facer has worked
for the Abortion Law Reform Association as a research officer. On the basis of an estimate
made by a British gynaecologist (Diggory, 1966), that two-thirds of British cases admitted to
hospitals were in his view due to criminal attempts, Mr Facer said that if this proportion is
valid in New Zealand it would mean an annual average of about 3000 criminal abortion

cases. There is no way of confirming the accuracy of these figures, as the true incidence of

Mortgage Lending by Solicitors Survey
4. Hon. R. O. DOUGLAS (Manukau) asked the Minister of Finance: When does he
