Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.
Butter Exports to EEC
5. Mr ELWORTHY (Oamaru) asked the Minister of Overseas Trade: What proportion
of our total butter exports will be sold to the EEC in 1977, and how does this figure compare
with the figures in 1975 and 1976?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Acting Minister of Overseas Trade): It is not yet
known exactly what proportion of our total butter exports will be sold to the EEC in 1977,
but for the 8 months ended 31 August 79.04 percent of our butter exports went to the EEC.
By comparison, for the full calendar years 1975 and 1976, 80.55 percent and 66.51 percent
respectively of our exports of butter went to the Community.
Mr Elworthy: What proportion of income resulted from these sales, and was there a big
difference in the butter price between the EEC and other markets?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: Those figures are not included in the brief I had.
Hon. W. W. Freer: What are the figures likely to be for this financial year and for next
year?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: We could sell 138 500 tonnes this year, but I have no
figure for next year.
Mr Luxton: Can the Minister give the tonnages for the 3 years mentioned?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: In 1975 total exports were 151 373 tonnes, and
exports to the EEC were 121 933 tonnes, which gives the 80.55 percent. In 1976 the total
exports were 171 853 tonnes, and exports to the EEC were 114 296 tonnes, which gives the
66.51 percent. For the 8 months to 31 August 1977 total exports were 85 919 tonnes, and
exports to the EEC were 67 915 tonnes, which gives the 79.04 percent.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.
Tongans in New Zealand
6. Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn) asked the Minister of Foreign Affairs: Has he seen the
statement by New Zealand's former immigration officer in Tonga, Mr D. Gordon, in the
Dominion of 30 September, that the money earned by Tongans in New Zealand is urgently
needed in the Islands and that letting people work in New Zealand is a more positive form of
aid for ordinary citizens than aid projects, and, if so, is he considering making representa-
tions to the Minister of Immigration to achieve this?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Acting Minister of Foreign Affairs): Few would
disagree that the money remitted home from Tongans working in New Zealand is a valuable
increment to incomes in Tonga. The Government has introduced special work arrangements
for people from the Islands. I would, however, disagree that to allow people to work in New
Zealand is in itself a more positive form of assistance than our official aid projects.
Remittances may ease hardship, but they do little to remedy its cause. Through our aid
programme, the priorities of which are set out in consultation with the Island Governments,
and through the Pacific Islands industrial development scheme, the Government is working
with the Island States to help them boost productivity, to create new jobs, and to expand the
opportunities available for people in their home countries, thereby offering people a real
alternative to having to leave their homes in search of work.

Mr Wetere: How many industrial schemes have been set up in Tonga?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: The question is similar to one answered previously
by the Minister of Foreign Affiars. One project is in the process of being established—the
Wiseman's scheme. The Rothmans scheme will shortly be established. Both schemes are in
Western Samoa. Another four or five schemes are on the stocks for establishment, but at this
stage I prefer not to give the details about them. A further 100 inquiries have been received,
though some of them are admittedly tentative. Within 12 months of the scheme being
announced four or five projects will be operating and another four or five should be being
prepared for commencement.
Hon. W. W. Freer: The Minister has referred to schemes for Western Samoa. How
many of these schemes apply to Tonga?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: Some inquiries have been made about Tonga, but I
cannot report about the finalisation of any scheme for Tonga. Western Samoa is leading with
the schemes being introduced. I hope that some schemes will be established in the other
Island States.
Hon. M. Rata: In view of the Minister's reply that at present there are no job

the Minister of Immigration the need for a continuation of income-related policies to aid the
people in Tonga?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: A scheme is operating under the Minister of
Immigration, and questions about that scheme should be addressed to him. The PIIDS
scheme for Tonga and other Island Governments is a matter of co-operation with those
Governments. It is impossible for the New Zealand Government or a New Zealand firm to
establish a business in the Islands without the agreement of the Governments there. I am
encouraging Island Governments to consult with the New Zealand Government about
establishing schemes in their Island States.

7. Mr FENTON (Hastings), on behalf of Mr D. M. J. JONES (Waitemata), asked the
Minister of Health: Has he seen the statement in the New Zealand Herald of 29 September
by the member for New Lynn that the present Government is spending only $4.8 million of
the beer and cigarettes tax on health, and can he reiterate the correct position?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): I have seen the member's assertions as
published. They are quite fallacious. For the current financial year it is estimated that $18
million will be received from the extra tax on tobacco and alcohol. Of this, $200,000 has been
transferred to the Education vote for the extension of nursing training in Waikato and
Southland, and $17.8 million to the Health vote for allocation as follows: additional costs on
established community care programmes, $6,171,000; new policies in community care,
$11,043,000; allocation towards supplementary estimates for community care, $586,000. The
total is $17.8 million. In the light of this, I am mystified by the member's reference to an
allocation of only $4.8 million from this tax for health purposes.
Mr Hunt: Did the Minister make a press statement earlier in the year that $4.8 million
would be spent on community health in the 1977-78 financial year?
Hon. T. F. GILL: I cannot categorically agree with that, nor can I deny it. It is possible
that I did. Of course, at the time of the Budget a new tax was introduced of 1c on a drink and
1c on a packet of 20 cigarettes, and so we were immediately into a new ball game. At the
time of the Budget it was said that this money would be spent on community health, and it is
being spent on community health. Earlier in the year, when I was advocating more money, I
might well have used the figure of $4.8 million, and this might well be in the estimates, but
since then the money from the new tax is being spent on community health.
Mr Hunt: Can we take it that the 1c on the glass of beer and the 1c on the packet of
cigarettes will, during this financial year, be totally devoted to community health?
Hon. T. F. GILL: Yes, at least that amount will be spent. A good deal more money will
be spent on community health, but $17.8 million, of which a small amount is yet to go to
closely allied organisations-for crippled children for instance-plus the $200,000 that is to
go to the Education vote to be used for training nurses in community health at technical
institutions, will be spent.
Mr Hunt: As the Minister's speech in which he mentioned the $4.8 million was made
very close to the time of the Budget, can the Minister say whether since the Budget the scope
of community health has been widened in accordance with the amount of money that has
been set aside?
Hon. T. F. GILL: It was the member who made the assertion that earlier this year I had
referred to $4.8 million. I said I could neither confirm nor deny that I had said it; I cannot
remember using that figure. Anyhow, it is quite irrelevant subsequent to the Budget. Most
of the money will go to projects as a result of a communication from the hospital boards.
They said how they would like the money to be spent. Some, we heard only yesterday, is to
go to the Plunket Society for its work in the South Auckland area for the nursing of young
children. I do not know how the member defines community health, but I know how the
normal New Zealander understands it, and that is where the money is going.

Fishing Vessels-Infringement of Economic Zone
12. Mr COURTNEY (Nelson) asked the Minister of Fisheries: What warnings about
future infringements are given to fishing vessels caught within the 200-mile economic zone?
Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Minister of Fisheries): The Exclusive Economic Zone (Interim
Measures for Foreign Fishing Craft) Regulations 1977 came into force on 1 October 1977.
Copies of these regulations, including maps showing the areas closed to trawling by foreign
fishing vessels, have been delivered to foreign boats, both at sea and in port. Foreign vessels
breaching these regulations would initially be given a warning, but if caught again they would
be liable for prosecution. Naturally, any foreign fishing vessels caught fishing within our 12-
mile territorial sea would be apprehended immediately.
Mr Courtney: How many warnings have been given, and to whom?
Hon. J. B. BOLGER: I do not have the exact number, but I believe it is five or six. They
were not strictly warnings. The vessels were inside the prohibited areas, but were not fishing.
Mr W. R. Austin: Is the Minister satisfied with the present planning for New Zealand's
capacity to cope with future infringements?
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: This is really outside the scope of the question and the
supplementary question.
Hon. M. Rata: In view of the need to ensure that the surveillance of New Zealand's
territorial and 200-mile economic zone is regarded seriously, do the warnings include
advising those who infringe of the likelihood of the confiscation of both ship and catch?
Hon. J. B. BOLGER: The advice given includes information about the penalty provi-
sions in the Act.
Mr Courtney: In the light of the Minister's answer that warnings were not strictly given,
is he telling the House that, although foreign vessels are within our 200-mile economic zone
and within restricted areas, they are not at present receiving a warning?
Hon. J. B. BOLGER: It is a word we are playing with. The vessels have been inside the
zone, but none has been fishing within the prohibited areas, so that it could be termed a
warning or the handing on of advice to the vessels that should they be caught fishing in that
zone they would be apprehended. The warning strictly means that they have infringed
already. To date they have not infringed.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.

would be that the relief committee would have taken all the requirements into account and
would have had some idea of the Inland Revenue Department's capacity for arranging relief.

Employment for School Leavers
20. Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn) asked the Minister of Labour: Has he seen the front page
story in the Christchurch Star of 28 September headlined "Job hunters face a bleak outlook",
which deals with the difficulties facing this year's school leavers; does he agree with the
analysis of the youth unemployment situation contained in that article; and what steps is he
taking to ensure that the estimated 65,000 plus school leavers and graduates who are due to
enter the job market in the next 3 months will be meaningfully employed?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): I have seen the article in the Christchurch
Star of 28 September referring to school leavers. The member for Grey Lynn will recall that I
have already indicated that unemployment levels, including those on special work, are not
expected to drop below 12 000 to 13 000 during the coming summer. As the honourable
member will know, several factors determine the number of school leavers entering the work
force in any year. These include examination results, the numbers proceeding to tertiary
education, the availability of the desired job, and parental concern that their sons and
daughters should not leave school unless they have a definite job arranged. Because of these
factors the actual number of school leavers entering the work force this year will not be
known until early next year. A survey of senior secondary school students' intentions is now
being undertaken, and this will give some indication of the numbers likely to be seeking to
enter the work force. When the results of this survey become available the school leaver
situation can be closely monitored and action taken if necessary.
Mr Isbey: The Minister stated that the number of unemployed, including those on
special work, will not drop below 12 000 or 13 000. Will he give the Department of Labour's
projected estimate for the number of unemployed at the end of this year or the beginning of
next year?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: I do not have such a projection, nor am I aware of it. The
member will have the chance to ask that question in a few minutes when I have my advisers
behind me.

BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): It is usual at this time on a Friday morning
to indicate the business of the House for next week. It is proposed that the House shall
devote itself entirely to legislation, starting on Tuesday with the Contraception, Sterilisation,
and Abortion Bill. On Wednesday afternoon the Supplementary Order Paper on questions
will be discussed, and then, subject to completing the second reading of the Bill, the House
would proceed to the Committee stage. The Minister of Justice has been trying to co-
ordinate Supplementary Order Papers to find out what amendments will be moved, and the
view has been expressed by several members that a long delay between the second reading
and the Committee stage of the Bill would not be desirable. I do not want to commit the
Prime Minister to that, but I understand that is his feeling and the feeling of several other
Government members.
CONTRACEPTION, STERILISATION, AND ABORTION BILL
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): With the leave of the House, I should
like to indicate what I have been doing. I have contacted several members to find out what
amendments will be moved, and I shall be in touch again this morning with those members
who have indicated their intention to move amendments, and ask their permission to release
a press statement later this morning—a copy of which I shall put in every member's box
before the House rises. I believe that will give us an idea of the size of our task in the
Committee stage, and will help to clear up any confusion that exists.
LAND TAX AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Associate Minister of Finance): I move, That the Land Tax
Amendment Bill be introduced. The Bill is a short one of only six clauses, and makes a
number of miscellaneous amendments to the Land Tax Act 1976. The amendments are of a
comparatively minor nature, and deal with such matters as fines for offences and remissions
of tax. None of the clauses calls for any detailed explanation, but I shall briefly outline the
amendments to indicate their effect. Clause 2 inserts a definition of superannuation fund,
which was overlooked last year when the Act was separated from the Income Tax Act.
Clause 3 relates to the meaning of "absentee", and was originally contained in the Human
Rights Commission Bill. Clauses 4 and 5 increase the amount of tax and penalty that the
Commissioner of Inland Revenue may remit. Clause 6 deals with increases in the maximum
fines that can be imposed for offences.
Bill introduced, and read a first time.
STAMP AND CHEQUE DUTIES AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Associate Minister of Finance): I move, That the Stamp and
Cheque Duties Amendment Bill be introduced. The main purpose of the Bill is to give effect
to the stamp duty exemptions announced in the Budget. Another matter of some importance
in this Bill is a provision to enable a simplified method of payment of stamp duty to be made
on shares sold to the various stock exchanges in this country. I shall now briefly discuss the
effect of each clause of the Bill.
Clause 1 is the short title and application date, and provides that exemptions from
conveyance duty will apply to transactions entered into on or after Budget night, 21 July
1977. Clause 2 gives effect to the Budget announcement to exempt from conveyance duty
three types of transactions: first, the purchase of a first home; secondly, the purchase of a
first farm; and, thirdly, transactions where older persons or individuals sell their large family
homes to growing families and purchase suitable smaller accommodation. Clause 3 is a


## p. 3471 (#353) ###########################################

7 October
3471
Stamp and Cheque Duties Amendment Bill
machinery provision to ensure that objection rights apply to the exercise of the commission-
er's discretion in regard to first homes and first farms.
Clause 4 authorises the commissioner to enter into an agreement with the stock
exchanges to enable sharebrokers to pay stamp duty on transfers of company securities
without the need to have the transfer documents presented to the Inland Revenue Depart-
ment. This is a matter that has been under discussion with the stock exchange for some time
now and could well involve the more expeditious handling of more than 300 000 share
transactions each year. Further details will be announced when the final agreement has been
reached. Clause 5 refers to the schedule in the Bill and brings present fines for offences more
in line with present-day values. Clause 6 is a machinery provision consequential upon the
proposed changed method of dealing with stock exchange transactions. There have been
problems in drafting the legislation because of the varied means under which property can be
owned and the wide-ranging nature of the reliefs given.
The delay in presenting the Bill to the House has probably meant that some transactions
have been held up awaiting details of the qualifications which will apply before the
exemption can be given. I assure members that all qualifying transactions entered into after
Budget night will get the exemption set out in the Bill. This means that shortly I expect the
Inland Revenue Department will be able to action documents, and in those cases where the
duty has been paid in full a refund will be arranged on application to the local branch of the
department.

Kauri Planting
2. Hon. M. RATA (Northern Maori) asked the Minister of Forests: In view of the recent
increase in the price of kauri timber and the limited amount available, has he any plans for
planting kauris as part of the afforestation programme?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Forests): The Government's objective is the perpetua-
tion of native forests both as natural forests and as managed stands. This policy requires that
the regeneration of species and stands will have high priority, and in certain circumstances
artificial enrichment of natural regeneration is beneficial. The present cut of kauri is quite
small, and it is the aim to sustain this by managing those stands that have regenerated over
the last 100 years, supplementing natural regeneration with enrichment planting.
Hon. M. Rata: What is the acreage involved, what money has been appropriated this
year, and what are the Minister's plans for the next 10 years?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: The direct establishment and enrichment of kauri forests is mainly
in the north, where kauri is regenerating and has been for a number of years, and to date 390
hectares have been treated. The current annual programme now runs at about 160 hectares a
year. In regard to the enrichment of all native species, there has been a considerable increase
in this method of managing our native forests.
Hon. M. Rata: Do I take it that the term "enrichment" simply means that these are trees
which come from natural growth and have not actually been planted by the Forest Service,
and that the aim is to intensify the natural growth instead of adding to it? In the original
question I asked whether the department had been planting trees along with the natural
growth.
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: Enrichment involves planting additional kauri trees in suitable
localities where there is already some regeneration-in other words, it is adding to the
strength of the regeneration.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.

Technical Institute Staffing
4. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) asked the Minister of Education: What are the broad
details of the new arrangements for staffing at technical institutes as notified to institute
principals on 29 June this year?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): I apologise for the length of this answer.
I have tried to keep it as short as possible, but I have been asked for broad details and it is
difficult to limit the answer. The arrangements for tutor staffing in technical institutes, as
notified in the circular of 29 June, are an outcome of discussions which have been held with
principals for some time. Each institute has been given an overall tutor staffing allocation for
the current 1977 teaching year. This allocation to each institute has taken into account the
growth in student numbers in courses for which there is a permanent commitment, and other
new developments, as well as the institute's proposals for other courses. In calculating the
increase over the 1976 staffing figures the Department of Education first took into account
for each institute its growth in courses taught towards examinations for the Trades Certifica-
tion Board, the Technicians Certification Authority, the Society of Accountants, and the
New Zealand Institute of Management, as well as all full-time courses. Institutes have been
asked to manage their provision of all other courses so that their total tutor staffing
allocation is not exceeded. Until this year, the department has controlled total tutor staffing
levels for all institutes by approving the staffing for each individual course. The new
arrangements enable the department to approve all acceptable course approvals for each
institute provided that it does not exceed its overall tutor staffing allocation. These
arrangements give institutes greater freedom in deciding upon which courses to offer.
Mr Marshall: I gather that there are now category A and category B courses. Would the
Minister confirm that, even if category B courses are approved, staff is not necessarily
guaranteed to be available for those courses?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: Category A courses are the full time courses of study that I
mentioned in my original answer-those which are being taught for examinations under the
various boards. Category B courses are all the others, whether vocational or not. Provided
they can be met within the staffing allocation they will be taught, but obviously this decision
will be made by the institute concerned in accordance with the allocation given to it.
Mr Marshall: There has been some suggestion that the statement of 29 June might
contravene regulation 5 of the Technical Institute Regulations. I do not know whether this
has been drawn to the Minister's attention. Has there been a contravention of the
regulations?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: I have no information about a contravention. I hope there has
not been.

considering whether protection similar to that given to land in the form of a national park
should be given to a river.
Hon. M. Rata: Who asked the Government department to do this?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: On the initiative of some of my advisers and myself arrangements
have been made for departmental officials from a number of departments to discuss this
question. As the member will know, similar legislation is on the statute books of other
countries, and it is worth our while considering whether protection should be extended to
limited areas of scenic and wild rivers.

Clothing Exports-U. S. Market Potential
10. Mr LUXTON (Piako) asked the Minister of Overseas Trade: What steps has the
Government taken to examine the potential for New Zealand apparel on the American
market?
Mr ALLEN (Parliamentary Under-Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Industry): I
reply on behalf of the Acting Minister of Overseas Trade: "My department has examined the
potential of the North American market on behalf of many individual apparel manufactur-
ers. While present prospects for developing sales of New Zealand apparel on the Canadian
market are not good because of the import quota system imposed by the Canadian
Government in late 1976, access to the United States market is unrestricted. Several New
Zealand manufacturers have proved that they can sell there competitively and that the
United States market can offer substantial prospects for increased exports of apparel.
Accordingly, it was recently decided that the Government would assist the New Zealand
Textile and Garment Manufacturers Federation to undertake an in-depth study of the
United States market. Details of the composition of the study team, the areas to be visited,
and the timing of the study are presently being discussed by officers of my department and
representatives of the federation."
Mr Luxton: Will the Under-Secretary indicate the monetary value of the present
apparel exports to the United States?
Mr ALLEN: New Zealand exported $744,000 worth of clothing items to the United
States in 1975-76, and $1.2 million worth in 1976-77.
Hon. W. W. Freer: Can the Under-Secretary advise whether the study team intends to
have clothing put on the whole of the American market or whether it will concentrate at first
on the major cities of the west coast?
Mr ALLEN: I believe this is being sorted out by the team at the moment. It may be wise
to attack one part of the American market at first and then move into the whole of the
United States. That is being discussed and will be decided before the team goes to the United
States to undertake the study.
Hon. W. W. Freer: Can the Under-Secretary give an assurance that the study will also
include an examination of the availability of production in New Zealand so that there is no
repetition of the previous incident when American orders were greater than the capacity of
supply by the New Zealand manufacturers?
Mr ALLEN: Yes.

Down Under the Plum Trees
17. Mr MacDONELL (Dunedin Central), on behalf of Mr BLANCHFIELD (West
Coast), asked the Minister of Education: Could he inform the House whether his department
will follow the Indecent Publications Tribunal decision that the book Down Under the Plum
Trees can be used for children of any age "while receiving instructions from parents or
professional advisers", and, if so, would he advise just who can be classed as a "professional
adviser"?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): My department has noted the decision
of the Indecent Publications Tribunal, and recognises that this book could, under the
conditions set down by the tribunal, be used in schools if a teacher were to be recognised as a
"professional adviser". The Supreme Court did, however, say this: "We consider that the
question of who is a 'professional adviser' is a question of fact to be determined by a court
faced with this question, particularly under prosecutions under section 21. It will be for the
person accused of committing an offence to justify himself under this section. It may be that
the term can be called 'imprecise', but it is deliberately designed, we think, to cover a great
variety of people who might legally have the advice and instruction of young people as their
responsibility." Any school contemplating using the book should, in my view, await a
decision from the court on the definition of a "professional adviser".

JUDICATURE AMENDMENT BILL (NO. 2)
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I move, That this Bill be now read a third
Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central): Opposition members raised a number of questions
in the Committee stage, and in particular we drew to the attention of the Committee the
effect of clause 6. I moved some amendments. Clause 6 has the effect of providing that an
individual can apply to the Supreme Court for the power of review against trade unions. The
effect is that non-statutory bodies corporate can now be subject to review, and all trade
unions come under that category. Opposition members brought to the attention of the
Committee the fact that we are drowning trade unions in laws. We are now asking trade
unions to be covered by a system of law that we, as a Parliament, have set up. In the past we
have passed statutes providing that trade unions should be subjected to legal controls over
and above what ordinary organisations are subjected to. No other friendly society has to
have its rules checked by the Registrar of Trade Unions. The registrar goes through the rules
of every trade union to make sure that they are fair, reasonable, and do not offend against
the rights of minorities, and to make sure that trade unions are democratic. I do not think
that any Government member can point to a trade union in New Zealand registered by the
Registrar of Trade Unions that is not democratic.
There are further safeguards for individuals with regard to trade unions-and I am
talking particularly about clause 6. Any person with a grievance can go to the Industrial
Court. That means that a person has two remedies against a trade union. But there is a
further remedy-and I mention this only in passing, because the Bill is next on the Order
Paper. Under the Human Rights Commission Bill it is proposed that an individual with a
grievance against a trade union can appeal. For that reason, in the Committee stage I moved
that clause 6(1) be deleted. I do not believe that, if we want trade unions to follow the law,
we should make them subject to clause 6(1), because that clause is an invitation to every


## p. 3490 (#372) ###########################################

3490
7 October
Judicature Amendment Bill (No. 2)
person who is a stirrer, who is anti-trade union, not to take advantage of the appeal rights
that this Parliament previously granted to him, but to decide to go to the Supreme Court.
I said in the Committee that the Supreme Court is not the best place to settle industrial
disputes. The whole procedure of the Supreme Court, with a judge, with expensive counsel,
and with attention on the particular common law advocacy system in the Supreme Court, is
not conducive to settling industrial disputes. For nearly 80 years New Zealanders have
agreed that the best way to settle industrial disputes is by a process of conciliation, and not
by a process of conflict-which I think is a fair way to describe Supreme Court actions.
Unfortunately, my amendment lost. I opposed clause 6(1), which amends section 3 of the
principal Act, because Parliament is actually issuing an invitation to individuals to take their
trade unions to the Supreme Court.
Trade unions will be affected by the provisions in clauses 6 to 10, which will be used
during industrial disputes. I do not think that ordinary bodies corporate will be affected by
the measure. No one on this side of the House is advocating that trade unions should not be
subject to the law. All we ask is that there should be a limit to the number of laws to which a
trade union should be subjected if it is to be able to function properly. Trade unions have a
role to play, and they should be able to carry out that role. They should not be hindered by
individuals who might be able to get finance from one source or another, and take the union
to court. As members opposite should be aware, trade unions in this country are not
wealthy. I know of no trade union that could afford injunctions or Supreme Court actions.
Nor do I know of any union officials who could afford to have their time taken up with
expensive Supreme Court actions. Yet this is what will happen. As a result, we can predict
industrial disputes becoming worse. I know of no injunction against a trade union that has
resulted in a dispute being solved. Two such cases in Auckland resulted in that city being
paralysed.
Parliament has a responsibility to try to solve industrial disputes. Stirrers who might
have access to money should not have an opportunity to bring a case against their trade
union in the Supreme Court. If a person is upset with his trade union he can take the matter
to the Industrial Court, or, in the future, to the Human Rights Commission. If he does not
like the rules, he can appeal to the Registrar of Trade Unions. He can also take the matter to
the Minister of Labour. We have now opened another door. The substantive law has not
been changed. The power of review is no greater than the prerogative writs. I am concerned
that the remedy should not be one of first resort, but a final one. However, under this
legislation, if a person falls out with his trade union he can go to the Supreme Court and
paralyse the union through litigation. Industrial disputes can blow up overnight, and must be
solved rapidly. No one could say that the Supreme Court procedure is rapid. A new division
of the Court of Appeal has been created because of the lengthy delays being experienced at
present. The ordinary working man will not wait for a whole year for an industrial dispute to
be resolved. If we want trade unions to follow the law we should set down a system of law
that is capable of being understood. Even though I do not like the present industrial law, it is
better than sending people to the Supreme Court.
This Bill undermines the Government's own industrial legislation. I am surprised that
the Minister of Labour did not speak during the second reading or the Committee stage, and
that the Minister of Justice did not apparently send the Bill to anyone who knows about
trade unions, especially when they will be affected. During the Committee stage the member
for Mangere and the member for Henderson drew attention to the concern expressed by the
Federation of Labour, a responsible organisation. The State unions have also expressed their
concern to me, and I understand they have made representations to the Minister. However,
we have not had an assurance from any Government member that the fears raised by the
trade union movement are not well-founded.
This measure is legislation for legislation's sake. At no stage have we been given any
evidence that any group has called for the change, unless Mr Harder has. Although the
Federation of Labour has stated that this legislation could result in the paralysis of efficient,
democratic trade unions, all we heard from members opposite was the strange argument that
the law would apply to everyone. That is absolute nonsense. Trade unions are subject to
more laws than any other organisation in New Zealand. No other organisation has its own
special court, or registrar, to make the rules more strict. If we want the trade unions to
follow the law, and are sincere about wanting good industrial relations, we should make the
laws clear and fair and capable of being understood.
In the past the Supreme Court has shown that it is not the right forum for the settlement
of industrial disputes, and I think even the Supreme Court judges would agree that they do

Mr ELLIOTT (Whangarei): The member for Roskill tried in his emotional few

union. At no time have more than 300 farm workers belonged to the workers' union. Now
there is to be a strong independent association and the workers will operate under their own
Act, as they deserve to.
The Bill provides for a special agricultural tribunal that will operate in the same way as
the Waterfront Industry Tribunal or the Air Crew Tribunal operates. A number of other
tribunals have been set up, so this new one will not be creating a precedent; and it will allow
people who know what the industry is all about to look at all the problems which exist
between agricultural workers and employers, but will recognise that there are differences
between agricultural workers and factory workers in cities. The people in the industry will be
catered for as a special industry-and this will relate to hours of work and the seasonal
nature of the work. The president of the tribunal will be the chairman of the Industrial
Commission, and two other members will be nominated by the parties involved in a dispute.
This will allow for a flexible understanding and appreciation of wages and conditions of
employment as well as the needs of the farm workers operating under their own Act.
There was a need for reform, and this legislation will provide it. It will create a
negotiating system that will fairly represent the special needs of farm workers, and will

3497
Agricultural Workers Bill
provide for the merger of negotiating procedures which, while they are within the general

members tried to move several amendments. I know I cannot refer to it on a third reading,

The member for Whangarei mentioned clause 49, which gives more protection to the
employer and the employee. During the Committee stage the Opposition moved amend-
ments to make it concise and specific that these precautions were to be taken. Clause 49(1)
states quite clearly that the employer must take all reasonable precautions to protect his
employee. The Opposition tried to be reasonable and to ensure that this clause was specific.
The amendments made to the Bill by the Government take the specific responsibility away
from the employer. The Government is opting out of its responsibility to ensure that
employees are protected as they should be. The new clause 9(a) states that Parts II to IV
shall not apply to agricultural worker of a class to which there applied, immediately before
the commencement of this Act, an award or collective agreement under the Industrial
Relations Act 1973.
Farm workers employed by the Department of Lands and Survey and the Department

are farm workers. Why are they excluded, and why was the clause written in this way? I was
asked yesterday whether they were included in the Bill, and I hesitated before I said I
thought they were excluded. The original clause has been struck out, and a new clause has
been inserted ensuring that they are excluded. The member for Roskill showed clearly why
the Opposition was against the Bill, and the Government has not justified its introduction.

I suggest that the Government's only justification is that, because the Labour Government

Mr FALLOON (Pahiatua): The member for Western Maori has spoken three or four

agricultural industry. The point he has tried to make is that, because of the lack of disputes,

each farm worker has the right, and has exercised the right, to leave his job and take another
job, and asked him to produce evidence-and the Opposition did not produce any-of
workers who have been unjustly discriminated against by employers.
The Government has introduced the Bill not only to protect farm workers from possible
discrimination by employers, but also to introduce safety provisions that have not previously
been available in legislation, and to provide a grievance committee to which farm workers
and employers can make representations. The Bill provides for the special needs of an
industry that cannot afford strikes and disputes as other industries seem to be able to;
indeed, no industry can afford stoppages, least of all the farming industry. If a crop is ready
for harvesting or stock has to be shifted, those matters must be urgently attended to in the
interests of the country's welfare. Because of the special nature of their work, farm workers
were adamant that they wanted to form their own voluntary association in 1973, when the
Labour Government tried to push them into compulsory unionism. Farm workers could see
what was happening as the result of port holdups and stoppages in freezing works. The
agricultural industry cannot afford such holdups, and the Bill has been introduced to allow
the farming industry to deal with problems between employers and employees.
Every safeguard for both employers and employees has been written into the Bill; more
opportunities than have ever been available are now provided for a farm worker to appear
before a grievance committee, to take a special dispute to a tribunal, and to act on behalf of
other members of his own organisation.
Clause 49, to which members opposite have referred, was amended by the Government
to give protection to employees of contractors, power boards, or catchment boards who go
on to farm properties. The Government has made certain that the employers of such
persons, and not just the farmers, are liable for their safety. During the Committee stage the
Minister spoke at length about a situation that could occur in which a farmer could be liable
for a worker employed by an entirely different organisation. The Bill affords protection for
the whole farming industry-both employer and employee. It is advanced legislation, in that
it allows grievances to be thoroughly discussed. It supports the Government's concept of
voluntary unionism, and is an excellent measure.

BROADCASTING AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Broadcasting): I move, That this Bill be now
read a third time.
Dr WALL (Porirua): In the Committee stage of the Broadcasting Amendment Bill the
Opposition concentrated on clause 3 as the essential point of its concern and, I believe, the
concern of every right-thinking person in the country. Under that provision the Minister of
Finance will be given the power to take control of the corporation's activities in considerable
detail. Our concern centres on the inclusion of the words "with the approval of the Minister
of Finance" in that clause, which appears to be a simple provision providing for the
establishment of reserves for general and special purposes. We could see the situation arising
where total financial control could be exerted by using the provisions in the main Act and in
this provision, which provides for control of the establishment of reserves.
As we see it, the machinery is likely to operate in the following way. It has become
obvious from the publicity given to the cost of "The Governor" that some of the produc-
tions, and particularly the major productions, of the Broadcasting Corporation will be
extremely expensive. This could happen when the corporation, in planning ahead, wanted to
establish reserves in one year to build up funds to use in the next year. It can be done only
with the approval of the Minister of Finance, who would want to know in considerable detail
the purpose for those funds. His approval or disapproval of any project gives him total
control over its life or death.
The provision could be used not only in the artistic production of drama, but also in a
decision on whether the corporations may plan and establish a fund to organise new services


## p. 3504 (#386) ###########################################

3504
7 October
Broadcasting Amendment Bill
in current affairs or in any of their activities. Very tight control is being given to the Minister
of Finance. The Opposition drew attention to the desirability of definitely re-establishing the
independence of this very important medium of public information.
It was also concerned at the effects of clause 2. Capitalisation of the major debts of the
corporations to the Government was laudable and the procedure met with no opposition
from this side of the House, but its inclusion in the Bill showed that the purpose of this
legislation was quite different from that of ordinary amending Bills, which are normally
introduced within 12 months of the original Bill to correct oversights or anomalies that have
arisen. The inclusion of this clause shows quite clearly that the original plan was to bankrupt
the corporations by excessively high interest rates, and on the basis of that pending
bankruptcy it imposed a tight control structure under the Act, as it did last year.
Having achieved that objective, which was part of the plan, then it was obvious that this
legislation would be required to take the financial pressure off the corporation by capitalising
the debts. Our only regret is that this legislation was not passed last year so that the processes
involved in this would have been taken at the beginning of last year, and not now. For those
reasons we opposed the passage of the clauses, and in particular the clauses giving control to
the Minister of Finance.

Demonstrations in Parliament Grounds
TUESDAY, 11 OCTOBER 1977
Mr Acting Speaker took the chair at 2.30 p.m.
Prayers.
DEMONSTRATIONS IN PARLIAMENT GROUNDS
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: It might be a convenient time to draw honourable members'
attention to a matter that has been exercising my mind, and that of the Speaker, for some
time. Recently I have had drawn to my attention incidents which have caused embarrass-
ment to members involved in some way with demonstrations in Parliament grounds. As
members will know, I, as Acting Speaker, am responsible for Parliament Buildings and
grounds. In line with past practice I see it as reasonable to allow people to hold rallies,
demonstrations, and meetings in the grounds in order to give them the opportunity to bring
their opinions to the attention of the Government and members. However, in the same way I
see it as my responsibility to ensure that those demonstrations are peaceful and orderly; and
consequently I have thought it desirable to enlist the co-operation of the police to make sure
that the House and its members are not disturbed, and that those of opposing views are not
brought to blows in our grounds.
Like Speakers before me, I have laid down certain conditions to regulate the demon-
strators and to guide the police. The conditions for the former comprise the following
standard rules for rallies in Parliament grounds: (1) participants assemble within and
disperse from the grounds in an orderly manner, using the pedestrian ways so as to avoid
damage to the lawns and flower beds, and not to interfere with the flow of vehicular traffic;
(2) participants do not mount the main steps nor interfere with the use of Parliament
Buildings by those entering or leaving in the normal course of their business; (3) the use of
sound amplification equipment is not acceptable; (4) the size of any deputation from the
rally waiting upon a Minister of the Crown is to be limited to five or six people; (5)
participants are to conduct themselves and the rally in such a manner as to avoid any breach
of the peace.
The question then arises as to the status of members of Parliament in these situations. I
have discussed this with the Acting Prime Minister-in the absence of the Prime Minister-
and the Leader of the Opposition, and both have agreed with me that while members should
not be prevented from taking part in demonstrations, nor from addressing crowds, they
should be prepared to abide by the same rules as apply to the public, and recognise the
instructions issued by the police under delegated authority from me as Acting Speaker. This
means that they may march, parade, and speak, but may not use any sound amplification
system, and should observe the instructions of the police officer in charge. I feel sure that I
can rely on the good sense of members to co-operate in this way.

1. Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn) asked the Minister of Immigration: In view of the statement

from coming to New Zealand on the off chance of finding employment, and the channelling
of prospective workers into the official work permit scheme. There has been no clamp down
in the last 2 years. The only changes that have been made have extended the period of stay
up to a maximum of 11 months, established a loan fund for the payment of fares, extended
the period of time for workers to repay fares to 20 weeks, and allowed specific workers to be

9. Mr O'BRIEN (Island Bay) asked the Minister of Statistics: What estimated increase

Immigrants from Pacific Islands
15. Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn) asked the Minister of Immigration: In view of the statement
in the Dominion of 30 September, in which New Zealand's former immigration officer in
Tonga, Mr D. Gordon, stated that his hardest task in Tonga was explaining to people why
they could not go to New Zealand even if they had job offers, could he specify the criteria
used for accepting permanent or temporary immigrants from the islands?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Immigration): Tongan citizens may come to New Zealand
for temporary employment, in accordance with the provisions of the official work permit
scheme agreed between the New Zealand and Tongan Governments. Under the scheme,
offers of employment from New Zealand employers are lodged with district offices of the
New Zealand Department of Labour for forwarding to the Tongan Department of Labour,
Industry and Commerce. There is no provision for employment offers to be made directly to
workers in Tonga, although employers may nominate particular workers. Employers are
required to make financial and other commitments, and the Department of Labour checks
that no suitably qualified workers are available locally to fill the vacancies. The Tongan
Government is responsible for the final selection of workers, who must be between 20 and 45
years of age and of good health and character. The policy covering the permanent entry of
Tongan citizens to New Zealand places a high priority on family reunification and other
humanitarian factors. New Zealand has given an undertaking that the migration of skilled
workers from Tonga, as with other developing countries, will not be encouraged. Applica-
tions solely on occupational grounds are therefore not accepted.

Broadcasting of Midweek Race Meetings
19. Hon. MICHAEL CONNELLY (Wigram) asked the Minister of Broadcasting: Has he
seen the TAB press release of 23 September stating that the board "has drawn attention to
the fact that recent published comments by broadcasting officials and others, claiming that
the curtailment of racing broadcasts has had no effect on off-course betting, cannot be
supported by the figures. . . . An examination of the turnover for the midweek galloping
meetings in August 1977, which can be properly compared with the same meetings in August
1976, reveals that there is a decline of 4.7 percent in the figures for the meetings on which
there was no network broadcast of the doubles races and the race for the third leg of the
treble", and, if so, will he urgently discuss with the BCNZ the need to review its recently
introduced midweek racing policy?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Broadcasting): As a result of a wide range of
approaches, I have raised the racing broadcasting question with the chairman of the
Broadcasting Corporation of New Zealand. Mr Cross has advised me that the corporation is
continuing to monitor the effect of changes. So far, the BCNZ feels that no clear evidence of
any trend has emerged, but the corporation has assured me that it will keep the matter under
review, and I will check the matter with the chairman when I see him next.
Hon. Michael Connelly: Am I to take it from the Minister that he refuses to accept the
TAB's figures as evidence of the fact that some racing clubs are worse off?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: The point I have made is that no clear trend has yet
emerged. In this particular period there has been a difference in the meetings. For example,
on the one hand, the Wellington Trotting Club meeting on 13 September, with no network
broadcast, recorded a decrease of $31,000 on last year's off-course betting total. On the
other hand, the Forbury Park trotting meeting on Wednesday, 7 September, and the
Geraldine Racing Club meeting on 26 September, also without network broadcasts,
recorded increases of $197,000 and $58,000 respectively on last year's total. So it is difficult
as yet to see a clear trend in relation to what the TAB is claiming.
Mr Latter: In his on-going discussion with Mr Cross, will the Minister endeavour to see
that the monitoring and assessing of the results is split into two areas-country clubs versus
metropolitan clubs?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: As a result of the representations the member has already
made to me on behalf of the country clubs he represents, and any others, I shall certainly
make this point very firmly to the corporation.
Mr Hunt: In view of the Minister's reply that he is waiting until a trend becomes
evident, could he indicate approximately how long the waiting period will be?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: As I have said in the House before, this is a programming
matter which is undoubtedly the responsibility of the corporation. All I can do is draw to the
attention of the corporation the issues in the questions that have been raised. But I have
been assured that the corporation will take those into account and will consult further with
the Racing Conference.
Hon. Michael Connelly: Is it not a fact that those racing clubs which have had the benefit
of midweek racing broadcasts have, in each instance, shown an increase in turnover?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: No, I do not have any such figures with me. But the point I
made in relation to those is that there has been one on each side, and two on one side. So I
think it is fair to give the corporation time. It is still the corporation's decision.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.
RESERVE BANK OF NEW ZEALAND AMENDMENT BILL
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance): I move, That the Reserve Bank of
New Zealand Amendment Bill be introduced. The proposed amendments to the Reserve
Bank of New Zealand Act 1964 cover three different functions of the bank. First, the
executive committee of the bank, secondly, exchange control provisions, and, thirdly, the
registration of securities. Section 6 of the Reserve Bank of New Zealand Act 1964, as
substituted by section 4 of the 1973 amendment Act, provides for the executive committee of
13.


## p. 3514 (#396) ###########################################

3514
11 October
Reserve Bank of New Zealand Amendment Bill
the bank to confer with the Minister of Finance, at his request, on any matter coming within
the scope of section 8 of the Act, and for any director common to both the Reserve Bank and
the Bank of New Zealand to be a member of the executive committee. Such an appointment
is unnecessary and has inherent dangers because of the conflict of interest which might arise.
Moreover, the appointment of a common director could adversely affect the reputation of
the Bank of New Zealand as an independent trading bank competing fairly and evenly with
other trading banks. In fact, no such appointment has ever been made, and it is proposed to
repeal the section substituted by the 1973 amendment and to replace it with the section in the
original Act.
A review of the exchange control provisions has been necessitated by a decision to
promulgate updated Exchange Control Regulations, which are made in terms of the Act.
This course was largely dictated by changes made to relevant legislation and procedures in
the United Kingdom, which reflect significantly in the administration of the Exchange
Control Regulations in New Zealand. Additionally, the opportunity has been taken to
correct some weaknesses in the regulations, with consequential amendments to the Act.
Clause 3 of the Bill amends the section of the Act relating to the control of overseas
exchange and other transactions. It clarifies the regulation-making powers in the section,
adds some definitions, including that of the term "borrowing money outside New Zealand",
and makes provision for the Minister of Finance to determine, in cases of doubt, whether a
person is deemed, for the purposes of the section, to be ordinarily resident in New Zealand.
Clause 6 amends section 50 of the principal Act so as to rectify weaknesses in the Reserve
Bank's legal powers to make inquiries into breaches of the Exchange Control Regulations.
Following the decision to introduce the Public Finance Bill, which consolidates and
amends the Public Revenues Act 1953 and the New Zealand Loans Act 1953, it was
considered desirable to incorporate in the Reserve Bank of New Zealand Act rather than in
the Public Finance Bill that section of the New Zealand Loans Act 1953-Part III—that
relates to the registration of Government stock. The Reserve Bank also acts as registrar for
loans raised by local authorities, and the Local Authorities Loans Act 1956 contains
provisions similar to those in the New Zealand Loans Act relating to the keeping of the
register of local authorities' stock. Clause 4 of the amendment takes these duplicated
provisions out of both these Acts and places them in one measure, for which the Reserve
Bank, as registrar for public sector securities, can be responsible. The Reserve Bank, under
its own Act, also acts as registrar for stock issued by other statutory organisations-for
example, the Housing Corporation and the New Zealand Dairy Board.
Clause 4 brings certain provisions relating to these operations within the Reserve Bank
Act. Any changes to existing legislation are of a minor nature only. They include a reduction
in the age of infants who may be registered as stockholders from 10 years and upwards to 7
years and upwards. This amendment will bring stockholders under the Act into line with
holders of inflation-adjusted bonds and various savings accounts.

will be discussed during the consideration of this Bill, but I should like the Minister to clarify
two points immediately, if he can. First, I should like to know whether the proposals in

considered whether some matters should be covered in the Reserve Bank of New Zealand

decisions reached by the Public Expenditure Committee have been followed precisely in the

Reserve Bank of New Zealand Amendment Bill
Public Expenditure Committee have not been changed in any way. Certainly that is my
belief from reading the notes I have on the Public Finance Bill, which we are not quite ready

Committee. I repeat that, to the best of my knowledge, there has been no change from the

The Deputy Leader of the Opposition spoke about the clarification of the regulations.
Curiously enough, borrowing has not previously been defined in the Act, and it is now
proposed to define what constitutes borrowing. That may sound rather silly, but, as the
Deputy Leader of the Opposition will realise, there could be some conflict or difference of
opinion as to whether or not a certain transaction was "borrowing" in terms of the
regulations. I think he will see the reference to that in the Bill, and by clarifying it we are
taking care of a possible difficulty in anticipation. As far as I am aware, it has not arisen from
a specific case, although I see it is to avoid the situation where a person who promises to
provide a consideration in New Zealand in exchange for a consideration outside New
Zealand is deemed to have completed the transaction outside New Zealand, thus escaping
the regulation which precludes the giving of a consideration inside New Zealand for a
consideration outside New Zealand-and there has been a judgment on that point. That is
the only specific case to which I can refer, but the clarification of the definition of
"borrowing" goes beyond that.

FISHING VESSEL OWNERSHIP SAVINGS BILL
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister in Charge of the Rural Banking and Finance Corpora-
tion): I move, That the Fishing Vessel Ownership Savings Bill be introduced. The purpose of
this Bill is to assist young fishermen and other suitably qualified and experienced persons to
save to acquire their first fishing vessel with a minimum registered length of 9 metres, for
their own operation, use, and benefit.
The scheme envisaged by the Bill is very similar to the farm ownership savings scheme
also administered by the Rural Bank. Persons who deposit money in an ordinary or special
fishing vessel ownership savings account with the Post Office or trustee savings banks or
certain building societies, will be able to receive a purchase grant or tax rebates on their
savings in these accounts; depositors who operate ordinary accounts will be able to receive a
purchase grant of up to $15,125 or such other amount as may be fixed by Order in Council
for the purpose of acquiring a fishing vessel. The amount of the grant, which is based on the
amount of savings and the length of the savings period, rises on a scale from 25 percent to 50
percent of eligible savings.
Alternatively, depositors in special fishing vessel ownership accounts can receive tax
rebates on their savings of up to $1,800 per annum and a maximum of $22,500. The
minimum savings period for ordinary and special accounts is 5 years. For the purposes of the
Bill, to open a fishing vessel ownership savings account a person must obtain the consent of
the Rural Banking and Finance Corporation. To qualify for a grant, or to retain tax rebates
received, a person must be a New Zealand citizen, must have had a good measure of
practical commercial fishing experience, must be suitably qualified, and must not be or have
been the owner of a substantial interest in a fishing vessel or, as a shareholder in a company,
have or have had control of such an interest. A person cannot, moreover, receive more than
one benefit. If a person receives benefits under the scheme he will, if he sells his fishing
vessel within 5 years after obtaining such benefits, have to repay them unless the Rural
Banking and Finance Corporation otherwise stipulates.
Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR (Timaru): The Minister will appreciate that I have not had an
opportunity to study the Bill in detail, but its provisions seem to indicate that the
Government is retracting some of the promises it made in the Budget. Following the Budget
announcement, Government members received a fair amount of publicity about this fishing
vessel ownership account scheme. If there has been any change in policy since the
announcement the Government will be able to correct me, but I believe that not only the
industry but people throughout the country will be interested to know if the Government has
backtracked on its word.
The Budget stated: "The tax rebate will be available on savings up to a maximum of
$4,000 per annum and $50,000 per account. Only one account may be operated by an
individual at any one time." The explanatory note to the Bill, dealing with clause 3, states in
regard to subclause (1): "Broadly the eligible savings consist of the first $250 saved,
including interest accumulated up to the date ('the qualifying date') that that figure is
reached, and the amount saved from that date up to a maximum of $3,000 a year, ('a
qualifying year'). Any amount saved in excess of that figure during any qualifying year can
be carried forward and taken into consideration in calculating the eligible savings for any
succeeding qualifying year, up to the maximum of $3,000 a year." So the figure is stated to
be $3,000 a year, while the figure mentioned in the Budget is $4,000 a year.

Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister in Charge of the Rural Banking and Finance Corpora-
tion): As the member for Timaru said, the Budget provided for a tax rebate to be available
on savings up to a maximum of $4,000 per annum, and $50,000 per account. These are
covered in the Bill, and are referred to as special accounts. When this measure was being
prepared it was remembered that in the legislation following the previous Budget we
introduced the special farm savings accounts, which ran parallel with the ordinary farm
savings accounts introduced by the previous Government, and so it was decided that it would
be wiser to give fishermen the same opportunities as had been given to farmers.
Part II of the Bill, which starts with clause 15, deals with the special fishing vessel
ownership accounts. However, in case some people preferred to have a savings system rather
than a tax rebate system, that was allowed in Part I, which starts with clause 3. The member
will see that there has to be a qualifying deposit of $250 and that $3,000 per year will have to
be saved in an ordinary savings account. That provision equates exactly with the one
introduced in 1974 in relation to ordinary farm savings accounts. With the special accounts a
person qualifies with a maximum of up to $4,000 per annum and up to $50,000 per account.
The member will remember that last year, when the special savings accounts were
introduced for farm savings, because in the Income Tax Act it was spelt out as being a rebate
of $1,800 per annum, the total amount was $4,000. Under the Bill the total sum that is able
to be saved in this way is about $22,000, which equates with the $1,800 that would have been
paid in tax, which is the $4,000 tax free.

CONTRACEPTION, STERILISATION, AND ABORTION BILL
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. When I introduced the Bill on 19 August I told the House that it expressed as
explicitly as possible the recommendations of the royal commission on the subject. I
described it not as the Government's Bill, but as Parliament's Bill. In the nearly 8 weeks
since, a further study of the Bill and the report has led to the need for one drafting
amendment to correct an inconsistency, and amendments of substance to have Parliament
instead of the Minister of Justice recommend the appointment of the proposed supervisory
committee and to receive its report as indicated in recommendation 1(12) on page 295 of the
report. These amendments are set out in Supplementary Order Paper 38 in my name.
Supplementary Order Paper 43, also in my name, proposes to set a commencement date of 1
January next for the establishment of the recommended supervisory committee, to enable
the committee to carry out its functions before the obligations imposed by clauses 21, 32, and
36 to 40 come into effect on 1 April 1978. Obviously this proposal depends on the Committee
of the Whole's agreeing to the recommended supervisory committee.
Members should recognise Supplementary Order Paper 15 in the name of the Minister
of Education as one that expresses the Government's policy commitment to give to parents
the right to be informed of the content of courses and classes on human development and
relationships each year before they begin, and the right to withdraw their children from
them. The remaining Supplementary Order Papers in the names of individual members are:
31, the Minister of Energy Resources; 38, the member for New Lynn; 39, the Minister of
Education; 42, the member for Franklin; 45, the member for Porirua; 46, the member for
Southern Maori; 47, the Minister of Social Welfare; and unnumbered amendments in the
names of the member for Wanganui, the member for Kapiti, and I understand from the
member for Wellington Central or the member for New Lynn.
I pay tribute to Mr Roger Barker of the Parliamentary Counsel Office for the long hours
he has worked to assist those members to get their Supplementary Order Papers drafted.
The acting Clerk has also made a valuable contribution to the debate by producing
annotated copies of the Bill for ready reference. These copies were annotated up to noon on
Friday last, so later amendments will not be marked on them. Then, in the explanatory note
to the Bill itself there are references to the page numbers of the royal commission's report
from which the recommended provisions come. I hope that these aids, which have not
previously been available to each member on an individual voting measure like this, will
enable us to produce clear and effective law with, I hope, an authoritative majority at its
passing, whatever the diversity of opinion now.
Before I leave these procedural matters I should refer to the order in which we shall
consider the clauses in the Committee of the Whole. The acting Clerk advises me that this is
set out in Standing Order 232. Standing Order 239 provides that the Committee may
postpone any clause "unless the same has already been considered and amended". As
clauses 1 and 2 are to an extent machinery clauses consequent upon the resolution of which
principles are given majority support, I shall move in the Committee stage to postpone
consideration of clauses 1 and 2 until after consideration of the remaining clauses. It will, of


## p. 3521 (#403) ###########################################

11 October
3521
Contraception, Sterilisation, and Abortion Bill
course, be necessary for me to so move at the end of whatever short title debate there may
be. I believe that there will be sufficient time between the end of the Committee stage and
the third reading to allow the Bill to be printed clean, as I am sure honourable members
would wish it to be.
Without attempting any detailed analysis of the Bill, which is not necessary because its
merits are argued in the royal commission's report, I believe I should now point up briefly
some of the aspects of the report and the Bill that seem to have been ignored or
misunderstood in the public debate that began when the report was published many months
ago. First, the emphasis in the report is on contraception and sterilisation; in the public
debate the emphasis has been on abortion. If the positive ideal of every pregnancy a wanted
pregnancy is to be achieved, I believe the commission's emphasis is right-we should
concentrate on contraception and sterilisation rather than on abortion. Nevertheless, the
question of the legality and control of abortions is of great moment to us. I think it was the
member for Porirua who remarked during the introduction debate that abortions are lawful
now in certain cases in New Zealand-they are not all illegal-but they have been
controlled, and the question before us is how wide should those controls go, not whether or
not there should be lawful abortion.
Most of the criticism has been directed at the provision on rape and the use of panels.
The recommendation on rape has been interpreted in some quarters as a requirement for a
woman who has become pregnant as a result of rape to bear the child. That is not so. What
the commission did say was that there is no need for any special provision for rape cases. It
did so because the evidence showed that the incidence of pregnancy resulting from rape is
almost nil. This conclusion is supported by a letter received by all members yesterday from a
Dunedin specialist gynaecologist of 20 years' standing who told us that she had never once
been asked to perform a termination of pregnancy on grounds of rape. It is her view,
considering the potential of physical injury, venereal disease, and mental and moral trauma,
that true rape cases are surgical emergencies requiring immediate treatment for all aspects at
that time. Termination of pregnancy 2 or 3 months later she regards as quite inadequate
treatment.
Members know that the commission held that on those very rare occasions where
women may become pregnant as a result of rape the existing mental health clause is
sufficient. Legislation in the United Kingdom and in South Australia-regarded as liberal in
both those jurisdictions-accepts that view. They have no special provision for pregnancy as
a result of rape. Our royal commission recognised the need for something to overcome a
woman's fear that she may become pregnant, hence the recommendations on the modern
medical aids to prevent implantation. I draw members' attention particularly to the commis-
sion's concern, expressed on page 213 of the report: "If the decision is to rest on the claim of
the complainant herself that she has been raped, it may fairly be expected that complaints of
rape will readily be made." The danger I see is one of law that encourages abortion on
dishonest request-abortion by subterfuge. Members will, of course, have to decide if that is
good law. I say, clearly and firmly, that it is not good law, and I shall vote against the
relevant amendments to clause 54 proposed in Supplementary Order Paper 31 by the
Minister of Energy Resources and in Supplementary Order Paper 36 by the member for New
Lynn.
On the criticism of the panels recommended by the commission, I need say little, for
their merits will be well canvassed by those members proposing alternatives. I believe that
the panel system, the commission's preference, would work if the medical profession wanted
it to. That is already demonstrated in the approach by the Southland Hospital Board. The
royal commission, however, offered an alternative, though not a preferred solution. It
involves the supervision of the statutory committee, the availability of counselling, and the
decision being made by two doctors. It is not necessary for me to canvass this as the merits of
the commission's alternatives are reasoned in pages 290 to 294 of the report.
It may be helpful, particularly to those not so familiar with Parliament's Standing
Orders, if I explained how the relevant clause on this issue and the proposed amendments
will be dealt with in the Committee stage. Standing Order 237 requires that amendments be
dealt with in the order in which they are lodged with the Clerk and circulated as Supplemen-
tary Order Papers. They are, therefore, taken in numerical order on each clause that they
advert to. However, subsequent proposals must not be inconsistent with decisions already
taken. Taking clause 32, entitled "Abortions not to be performed until cases reviewed by
panel", as an example, our procedures require us first to consider a proposed new clause
31A, set out in Supplementary Order Paper 31 in the name of the Minister of Energy

I conclude this opening speech on the second reading debate by saying that the three
women and three men who comprised the royal commission are deserving of the House's
gratitude, and indeed that of the country. They considered the views expressed in over 600
separate submissions. They identified defects in our present law and practice, and, despite
the great difficulties facing them when extreme contrary views were held on the subjects of
their inquiry, brought down a unanimous report recommending courses of action that,
despite the extremes, do represent, I believe, an achievable and acceptable goal to most
people. It is our duty in Parliament to translate it into clear and effective law.
Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson): I can give the Bill at least a guarded welcome,
certainly on one count anyway—that it adopts a proper approach. It is not circuitous or
devious, like some other attempts we have had to "interpret" or divert the law without
actually changing it. I certainly wish to take this early opportunity of echoing both the praise
and thanks that the Minister of Justice addressed to Mr Barker, parliamentary counsel,
whose work has been untiring and helpful to me, as I am sure it has been to everybody else
who has displayed an interest.
The Bill as originally introduced certainly has the merit of logic; and the respectable
parentage of the royal commission. Again I add my voice to that of the Minister in
expressing an appreciation of its work, although, as it happens, I do not agree with its
conclusions. It sets out quite deliberately to change the law, procedure, and practice relating
to abortion-but, in my judgment, for the worse. There is no doubt about the strong public
pressure that exists in the community today for some liberalisation of the abortion laws. I
believe the evidence of repeated polls is quite indisputable, however much some hard line
organisations have endeavoured to explain it away. The evidence of polls taken privately and
publicly-including one subscribed to at very considerable effort and personal expense by
the member for Onehunga-shows, unchallengeably, that there is a mood for liberalisation
of the law.
The controversy gives particular emphasis to the role a member of Parliament must
play, not only in this kind of legislation but in all legislation-however, particularly in
legislation of this conscience nature. If his duty is to represent-that is to say, to carry out the
views of his constituents-I believe it is difficult for him not to act in accord with the clear
evidence of directions as expressed by different parts of the community, and indeed on a
polling of the community as a whole. If one adopts the view that commended itself to Sir
Edmund Burke, and one that I adhere to, that he is a delegate entitled to give effect to his
own individual conclusions, then in my case there is a happy coincidence between my
