particular view, my personal view, and that which I believe to be the view of the community.
My own conviction is that, though the law has been strained for many years to give weight to
factors other than preserving the life of the mother-which is the wording of the
statute-even though it is strained to give effect to something more than that, it still does not
go far enough, and ought to go further.
The Bill follows the report in stating that “age and economic circumstances of the
woman or girl concerned may be taken into account"-whatever that means. Frankly, I do
not know, and I do not think anybody in this House knows what it means. However, that is
what the commission recommended, and what the Bill states. We are given no guidance on
how it is to be taken into account, and if we pass this legislation we will be giving no guidance
to the courts. Although these factors are not in themselves a specific ground for authorising
the termination of a pregnancy, I think they should be included in the relevant criteria.
Moreover, I believe those criteria should be judged by the woman concerned and her own
doctor, with a measure of counselling to which I shall refer later. That would be my first
preference.
However, despite the polls I have referred to, and after talking to individual members
on both sides of the House, my opinion is that that proposition is unlikely to command a
majority of members in the House today. I understand that the member for Southern Maori
intends to move an amendment along those lines, and that will no doubt reveal the actuality.
However, my feeling is that such an amendment would not be likely to attract a majority, so
I turn to the second option I prefer, what has become known as the Gair package—a series
of proposals in which I had a hand. I will not go into details of the procedure that would
follow the enactment of the Supplementary Order Paper standing in the name of the
Minister of Energy Resources. It has been fully discussed, and published in the papers, but,
briefly, it would require two doctors, adopting the terms of the law as amended by the Bill
and acting independently, both to recommend, not merely a referral for another opinion,
but a termination of pregnancy.
It is an important requirement of those proposals that the decision should be preceded
and followed by a mandatory offer of adequate counselling to the woman concerned. In my
opinion, that is an important and fundamental aspect of the proposal. I think a full
presentation to the woman concerned of all the factors that ought to occupy her mind in
coming to a rounded and full conclusion is an essential part of any consideration of the
operation we are considering.
Since the proposals by the Minister of Energy Resources were put forward, what is
known as the Birch Supplementary Order Paper has made its appearance. The first comment
I want to make about that is on its timing. It was put into our hands late last Friday morning,
shortly before the House adjourned, and at a time when I believe it was impossible for the
community—especially the medical section, whose views are very important on this
question to express a conclusive or professional view. Whether or not that was deliberate I
am unable to say. I suppose none of us really knows the medical consensus on this subject. I
am sure that all of us have had conversations with individual doctors, and been given
individual opinions and forecasts on what the consensus is likely to be, but none of us knows,
and none of us can know before we are asked to vote.
The timing of the paper was unfortunate—a word which inadequately describes the
situation. As to its content, I believe the purpose is transparent. It is intended to sidestep the
manifest unacceptability of panels. The community at large—including some people who
support the Bill in its original concept-has expressed more than just doubts about the panel
system, which clearly is an unpopular feature of the Bill. The panel proposals have attracted
little support, and have been openly rejected by nearly every organisation representing the
medical and nursing professions, and social and psychological workers. They have even been
deserted by some members of the commission. The Supplementary Order Paper in the name
of the member for Franklin substitutes for panels a similar procedure under a different name
and guise. In my judgment, the only real difference is that it would prove in practice to be
more clumsy and unworkable than panels.
At this stage, I want to stress one feature of the panels-as I believe they will still
be that I regard as objectionable, because it introduces a new and startling element, not
only into this discussion we are embarking on today but also to medical practice generally. It
contemplates a vital role being played in this procedure by people described as "certifying
consultants". The grounds upon which they are to be selected relate not just to the
professional competence of the people concerned but also to their political beliefs. They are
spoken of as practitioners who "hold views in relation to abortion generally that are

compatible with the tenor of this Act"—another phrase I have difficulty in interpreting. To
guide one in the interpretation, two specific criteria are set out in the paper: "the following
views shall be considered incompatible" with the tenor of the Bill-"(a) That an abortion

With regard to (a), I believe few doctors would make such a categorical and unqualified
statement. However, it is a fact that several doctors have admitted that they would
contemplate nothing but a grave danger to the mother's health as justifying termination of a
pregnancy. They go on to say, I believe quite justifiably, that there are few, if any,
indications of pregnancy that are not susceptible to modern medical science and that cannot
be either rectified or cured. In effect, these people are saying that there is no condition in
which the mother's health is really gravely endangered and there are no indicia for an
abortion. A test of this kind comes preciously close to thought control. Moreover, it is a test
that is to be applied and reviewed annually. A fair comparison would be if one were to
require that no lawyer should be involved in a criminal trial-much less be appointed to the
bench-if he or she believes that sentences currently being imposed are too short or too
long. That, to me, seems to be a similar kind of requirement the medical professional would
have to fit into to qualify for appointment to these panels.
Half the members appointed are required to be gynaecologists or obstetricians. I do not
have the statistics with me, but I understand the number in actual practice today would be
severely strained if they were to serve on these committees, assuming they are willing to do
so. I will come to that point in a moment. I believe—and I say this with respect—that this
paper is inspired by the Society for the Protection of the Unborn Child and by a group in that
society which would, if it had its own way, outlaw abortion entirely. They say that is not the
intent, but I believe it would be the effect. If the Supplementary Order Paper is agreed to
and passed into law, no woman could have her pregnancy terminated, for whatever reason,
by complying with the law. I say, with confidence, that she would find the required services
were unavailable. First, because there are insufficient specialists, if they were willing, to man
the panels-I must call them that-and secondly, there must be few doctors in the
community who have not taken up, in response to pressure put on them, some stance on the
various possibilities put forward by the Bill. Whether having taken up some stance or other
would then disqualify them by reference to the criteria set out, I do not know.
I believe that many members of SPUC are searching for a compromise, for the middle
ground. I do not believe that the Supplementary Order Paper of the member for Franklin is
the middle ground. It is an uncompromising and unyielding document. The true middle
ground is represented by the Supplementary Order Paper put forward by the Minister of
Energy Resources. I should like to see both papers considered as a whole. I acknowledge
and appreciate the move made by the Minister of Justice to try to focus the discussion away
from the trivia of definitions contained in clause 2, but even then we will be considering the
pieces that go to make up both packages, rather than the packages themselves. It would call
for a suspension of Standing Orders to do so, but I think it would be better if the House
could express its preference for one or other Supplementary Order Paper as a whole, and,
having done so, then consider the details.

I pay tribute to the work done by the Minister of Justice in bringing the Bill together. It
has been a particularly difficult exercise because, although he was acting on behalf of the
Government in bringing the Bill into the House, his task was to bring in a Bill that fairly
reflected the report of the royal commission. I think he has done that. It was necessary to
make some amendments, because the original draft was not seen to be precisely in
accordance with the recommendations, but I think we have that in front of us now. The royal
commission was set up by the former Labour Government and, at the time, I do not think
there was one word of criticism of the membership. When the commission reported, and
when some parts of its report did not meet with the approval of some people, there was a
certain amount of criticism of the membership. But that kind of criticism does not have very
much impact. It should have been made at the time the commission was set up if it was to
have validity. The commission gave these vexed questions the utmost attention in detail. It
heard evidence over a long period from all kinds of organisations. I do not think we will get a
better examination of the questions in our time. At the outset, to someone who approaches
the question in a totally unbiased manner-if that is possible—the recommendations of the
royal commission must be compelling, if only for the amount of detailed work that it put into
the task it was given.
Members have notified a number of amendments, and the member for Henderson
suggested that some had come in a bit late. We will have time to have a good look at them
after the second reading debate, and it may well be that this debate will throw new light on
some of the amendments. It is correct, I believe, that some members are working together in
groups to put forward an amendment and to support it, and I suppose to seek support for it.
In the peculiar circumstances in which I find myself, I feel that I should hold myself aloof
from any such group and simply vote on the Bill as a private member—and that I intend to
do.
Moving into the personal aspect, I see no reason why the law that comes out of the
debate on the Bill should not work, either in its original form or in accordance with the
various proposals that have been put forward. We are in a rather different position this time
from the position we have been in on other occasions when we have been dealing with
private members' Bills. We are now dealing with a Bill that has been deliberately
drafted as any other Government legislation would be—so that it will work. Providing that
the amendments are not too extreme I think that in the end we will get legislation that will
work.
Having given the matter a great deal of thought over the years, as have all members,
particularly those who were in the House in the last Parliament, I do not accept the excessive
emphasis on the rights of the woman that has come into some of the submissions on the
issue and I am speaking of abortion. There has been a tendency to ignore or to give
inadequate consideration to the other two parties. The obvious other party, of course, is the
unborn child; and the third party, who has had the least consideration of all, is, in many
cases, the husband, who has rights in the matter also.
I find it quite remarkable that in a society where in our time and in our generation we
have moved further towards consideration for the sanctity of human life, the welfare of the
individual, and the human rights of the individual, we can apparently contemplate with
equanimity the wholesale snuffing out of life before birth. I find those attitudes totally
illogical. Many years ago, against the votes of the majority of my colleagues on my side of
the House, I supported the repeal of capital punishment, very largely for the same reason
that today I support the right to life of an unborn child. It is a measure of the advance of
modern civilisation that we have greater and greater concern for the life, let alone the dignity
and welfare, of the individual.
I do not intend to speak at great length. I have always believed that the law on abortion
in New Zealand was fairly tight, and I believe most people have thought that, but in recent
years we have found that it is not so. I suppose the activities of the Auckland abortion clinic
have brought home to us the fact that those who are prepared to put an extremely liberal
interpretation on the law will find, in the event of a prosecution being brought, that no jury
will convict them. At that point we have a law that is effectively far more liberal than many
New Zealanders either believe it should be or are prepared to tolerate—and I am one of
those many New Zealanders.
The operation of the abortion clinic in Auckland is not in accordance with the law of
New Zealand as I would wish to see it. We have heard the slogan "Every child a wanted
child". I suggest that that slogan itself has a element of fallacy in it. We know that thousands

upon thousands of New Zealanders were not planned children. At the time of conception

The member for Henderson has criticised the proposal for panels. I know there is a
good deal of concern about whether the proposals made by the royal commission, and which

detail with doctors who serve regularly on panels that have been operating in New Zealand

panels operate and any reservations they may have about their operation. I believe it is not
generally known that panel systems do operate-and operate effectively-in this country;
and at that point I set aside the criticism of those who say they will not work. Not only will
they work, they are working. I hope that part of the Bill providing for panels will remain in

I cannot support the proposal that the decision should be made by two doctors and the
woman concerned. I put it to the House that every member knows that it would be very easy
to find two doctors whose attitude to abortion is such that it would be simply a matter of
course to obtain their endorsement. I am sure every member who faces the facts honestly
and has taken the trouble to investigate and research this matter knows that what I am saying
is true. One need look no further than the Auckland abortion clinic. But, quite apart from
that, as in every other profession the standards in the medical profession vary considerably;
attitudes to this matter vary considerably, and the great flaw in the two-doctor argument is
that it is well known, and would become more widely known, that such-and-such two doctors
would give an abortion certificate on the slimmest possible grounds. At that point you would
not have what I would wish to see in the law. I consider the Bill a good one, and believe it
should proceed, but I shall consider the various amendments as they are put forward one by
one.
I want to conclude by referring to the amount of mail I have received on this matter.
Yesterday, Monday, 10 October, 530 letters were received in my office, and I have to
apologise to those who have written to me and will not receive an acknowledgment. Until
yesterday I think everyone had been sent an acknowledgment, but my staff is simply not
capable of keeping up with that rate of representations. All representations are seen, and the
majority are read. I have received 2890 letters opposing liberalisation of abortion and 207
advocating the liberalisation of abortion. There were 62 other letters, but quite frankly, we

With other speakers, I recognise the work of the commission. Whether people disagree
or agree with its findings, at least it has laid the foundation for a substantive debate in
Parliament. As the Minister of Justice pointed out in his opening remarks, the emphasis in
that report was on education, contraception, and sterilisation. Those, in my view, are of vital
importance, but I think we must recognise as inevitable that public attention should turn to
the more controversial aspects of the report. Already, in the short time this debate has been
going, we have heard talk of packages. For my part, I reject the concept of packages,
because I can see in some of the amendments proposed something that I think has merit. I
see other areas that concern me. I for one would not be at all happy to accept a package
concept, although I can see some difficulties facing the House with regard to the order of
procedure in simply following the clauses of the Bill seriatim.
I doubt and this was certainly underlined by the comments of the Prime
Minister-whether ever before in the history of Parliament have members received so many
statistics, have been offered so much advice, or been quoted so many expert opinions as they
have on this measure. I have never received so many letters written from the heart as I have
on this Bill. By the same token-and I am bound to say this-never have I received so many
form letters, distant and impersonal—and I say this about both sides of the argument—often
much more indicative of prejudice than knowledge, than I have on this occasion, but I guess
that is the natural consequence of such a highly charged issue as that being discussed by
Parliament at present.
I have said on previous occasions that I believe Parliament is not well equipped to
handle issues of this kind, but such is the level of public protest and involvement that handle
the question it must. We are talking about the law of the land, and Parliament alone is
reponsible for making that law. The breakdown of the pluralistic approach, which in the past
has characterised New Zealand society, means that, like it or not, politicians will have to
grasp the nettle, and my guess is that it does not matter in which hand they grasp it—they are
still likely to feel the sting! Every member has to decide for himself or herself the balance
that must occur between the needs and the rights of the individual and the needs and the
rights of the society in which that individual lives, and, in the specific area of abortion, the
needs and rights of the women and the foetus which she carries within her. We are dealing
with the sanctity of life and, if Parliament lightly sets that aside, then the problems that most
of us see in society today will be compounded beyond all measure.
At this time, Parliament is charged with determining conditions under which an
abortion can take place, the decision makers, the reasons, and the place itself. Though many
times during this debate I will challenge the views of some of my colleagues, I will say this:
over the past month I have had sufficient opportunity to view at first hand their concern, no
matter what their viewpoint, to know that one must not challenge the sincerity with which
they hold their respective views. I hope those outside the House can contemplate a similar
attitude.
Before stating my opposition to some of the specific elements of the Bill, I make one
more slightly general observation. It seems to me that, once the conditions under which an
abortion can be performed are agreed to, then the doctor concerned and the place where the
patient is confined should be subject only to two major considerations. The first and obvious
one is the question of medical standards, which must be of the absolute kind. The second is
that the cost to the patient must be such as to eliminate even the remotest suggestion that


## p. 3528 (#410) ###########################################

3528
11 October
Contraception, Sterilisation, and Abortion Bill
there is profiting in the financial sense from the tragic state in which the patient finds herself.
I am saying in a sentence that the whole debate must surely turn on the conditions under
which an abortion can be authorised and who is to be given that authority. The clauses
relating to licensing and so on should surely be confined to matters of medical standards and
financial protection for the patient.
On a personal basis, I totally reject the concept of abortion on demand. Indeed, I
believe that most New Zealanders, with varying shades of opinion, hold that view. I would
not suggest for a moment that the amendment suggested by my colleague the member for
Southern Maori comes within that category, but I do see in that amendment a real danger;
and I thereby reject it, because I believe that such is the importance of the decisions we are
making, and such is the importance of the right of the foetus as well as of the mother, that
one medical opinion clearly is insufficient, even though I accept-and my colleague the
member for Henderson made this point-that counselling both before and after is of the
utmost importance.
I said a second medical opinion because I notice in the Bill that the opinion of the
women's family doctor appears to have been set aside, and the panel proposal in clause 33
fails immediately on that count, as it does on a number of others. Surely it must be assumed
that a woman seeking an abortion is in a state of very considerable distress. Her problem,
therefore must be approached in the most personal and humane way possible. In that respect
the panel proposal in clause 33 simply does not measure up.
I have mentioned the setting aside of the family doctor. It seems to me that the same
defects that the commission found in the panels to which the Prime Minister adverted are in
fact applicable to the panels proposed in the Bill. The commission talked about inefficiency
and a lack of consistency—and once gain these could apply. There is the question of the
cumbersome nature of the proposal and the danger that could accrue to the mother in this
respect. There is the matter of the composition of the panel itself. Some of those who,
according to the legislation, were to have been involved have already opted out—and I think
of the social workers. The final danger is that gynaecologists are likely to resist instruction
unless they feel they have a say in it.
The public view of the panel system is best summed up by a member of the royal
commission, Mr M. R. McGregor, who said on 15 June: "I took an active part in drafting the
panel procedures, which at that time I favoured because I thought they would provide a
uniform and impartial assessment. Subsequent informed statements made by doctors and
social workers have satisfied me that the panel system will not work effectively. I can no
longer see any justification for this depersonalising system." One must note the words of a
person who sat throughout the massive amount of evidence on the panels, who came to an
initial conclusion, and then, after further discussion and consideration, decided that it was
perhaps not the best direction after all.
Now I want to deal briefly with one or two of the other contentious points in the Bill.
The first relates to clause 14, which establishes the supervisory committee. In my refusal to
accept a package deal I must point out that, despite the widespread criticism—and, I think,
understandable fear of political direction of this committee-I feel that such a committee will
stand aloof from the department and Parliament, and has a place. If listening around has
anything to do with it, then I think its role might be rather diminished from that presently
envisaged in the Bill, because there could be quite significant changes relating particularly to
the panel system; but surely there is still a case for general oversight, and still a case for an
annual report so that the country and Parliament knows what is going on.
In this respect I accept the concept advanced by the member for Stratford, the Minister
of Justice, that the supervisory committee should not be appointed on the recommendation
of the Minister of Justice, but on the recommendation of Parliament in a way that is
comparable with the appointment of an ombudsman. In this way both personal and party
influences can be removed and the committee subject to less political direction than even a
department, because after all a department must be responsible to its Minister. The final
effectiveness of the committee will depend largely on the brief laid down by Parliament, and
on its actions on the rest of the Bill. I certainly oppose the committee's appointing panels as
provided for in clause 33, although I can see it maintaining a register of additional
consultants and additional opinions to those of the family doctor. Parliament's major
difficulty might arise in having to deal with a clause which establishes a supervisory
committee without knowing what the devil it will be supervising after the later stages of the
measure.
I now want to touch on clause 54, which covers ground on which abortion may be

Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy Resources): It is quite clear that Parliament will
serve the country best if it maintains throughout this debate a sincere and earnest effort to
find the answers to a problem which has bedevilled the country and Parliament now for 4

way he votes.
Neither the royal commission nor Parliament invented pregnancies or abortions, but I
would urge upon the House a realisation that any move which destroys or ends the Aotea
Hospital will not solve the problem of abortions; it will not solve the problem of unwanted or
rejected pregnancies. The problem of handling abortions is much easier when we face
reality, are prepared to bring the problem out into the light, and tackle it in the light of day.
I freely admit that the two-doctor formula that I have proposed in my so-called package
of amendments is not perfect. Any system is subject to the potential for abuse, but I most
sincerely believe, after the most earnest consideration and consultation with many
colleagues in this House-and their advice, for which I am most grateful-that the panel
alternative, either in the form of the Bill or in the form of the disguise in which my colleague
the member for Franklin has placed it, is even more subject to abuse. I am aware that there
are some people who feel the panel system has been successful in places like Kew Hospital,
but it has been successful only because most of the problems of abortion in the areas where
these panels certainly operate are exported to other parts of the country. A problem dodged
is not a problem solved.
This is the third legislative attempt for Parliament in recent years to find an answer.
There was the Hospitals Amendment Bill designed to tighten the situation with abortion by
choking the problem into the public hospitals. The House rejected it, the courts found it
defective, and it was placed in an amended form that did not solve the problem. The Health

Contraception, Sterilisation, and Abortion Bill
Amendment Bill was yet another attempt to seriously tighten the grounds upon which an

There are no doubt many features of the royal commission's report which are admir-
able, but there are some which, in my judgment—and I believe the judgment of most New
Zealanders-are quite unacceptable, would be unworkable if tried, and are in fact avoid-

debate the details of this committee I shall explain why I believe there is no way in which a
supervisory committee with the functions specified in the Bill can be anything but a pawn
between the forces of the hard line and of the soft line in the matter of abortion politics.
There there is the question of the panels. Whether they are panels, or whether they are
disguised by another name, like the proposal of the member for Franklin to call them
certifying consultants, makes little difference. The woman concerned is still exposed to the
Russian roulette of the panel's composition; and I was quietly appalled at the suggestion of
those who support the panel system that the supervisory committee would decide who would
be on the panel, or who would be one of the certifying consultants. In either case, a body
that is not accountable to the medical profession as such, like the medical council itself,
would be deciding which doctors could pass judgment, and which doctors could not.
The third feature of the Bill which my amendments seek to remove is the unwanted and
unhealthy intrusion of an administrative device into the relationship between doctor and
patient.
Some very real problems exist which we must tackle. In the time available to me I
should like to address my attention to an area in which I feel great confusion may arise unless
it is solved very early. I know that the member for Franklin realises that I have absolutely

Parliament may very well not be voting on the issue it wants to vote on. There is virtually no
difference in reality between the panel system and the certifying consultants. In some
respects, it makes the position even tighter because a specific requirement of the amendment
proposed by the member for Franklin is that not fewer than half these consultants should be
obstetricians and gynaecologists.

I have sought to show that, without the co-operation of the medical profession, the

I remind members of the provision for dual doctor approval in proposed clause 31a:
"(2)(a) The 2 medical practitioners shall be financially independent of one another; that is to

and give so much thought to a Bill as I have to the Contraception, Sterilisation, and
Abortion Bill; nor have I been bombarded with so many comments, both for and against, on
provisions understood and misunderstood, as I have on this measure. If I were asked to sum
up my attitude to the Bill, the correspondent whose views I find most sympathetic to my own
is a constituent who wrote to me: "As a 60-year-old woman I wish to add my opinions on the
abortion issue. I believe that the choice should be entirely up to the woman concerned. Men
will never be able to understand women's feelings in these matters, simply because they will

attendant results."
It is of considerable interest to me that since this issue was first discussed in the House in
1975, first by way of a private member's Bill and then through two Government Bills, the six
women members of the House of Representatives on those occasions have all had very much
the same point of view in that they do not support those who seek to make abortion more
difficult. Acknowledging, as we all must, that most members of this Parliament are male and
over the age of 45, it is incumbent on all of us to have regard for those who do not fall into
that category. In other words, we must have regard first for the wishes of women, and
secondly the wishes of younger people.
For that reason I should like to quote some comments that were discussed with me a few
hours ago by the University of Otago's Wellington Clinical School of Medicine branch, the
fourth-year class. Forty-six members of that class are in Wellington for their fourth-year
clinical studies, and 87 percent of them submitted to me a document that is well worth
noting. They say: "The Royal Commission has rejected more open definitions of health and
abortion in such a way as to disallow a more liberal interpretation of abortion legislation. We
believe that implementation of the Royal Commission's recommendations would put at risk
the health of many women seeking abortion. We feel that if a woman is prepared to risk
mutilation, and possible death, either at her own hands or at those of someone not qualified
to perform abortion, then there is more involved than simple self-indulgence. We feel that
more regard should be taken for her need in order to protect her health."
They further said that they felt that any tightening of the abortion law by the systems
proposed, either the panel outlined in the Bill or the panel proposed by the member for
Franklin, will bring the risk of intimidation. I add my own comment on this: it will
undoubtedly help the woman who is more articulate, better able to present a case, and less
nervous in front of people who are not her peers but to whom she will feel decidedly inferior.
To me the thought of a decision taken in that way does not reflect the type of humanity we
need.
Next I want to refer to some of the clauses of the Bill which have led me to object to its
overall provisions. Clause 3(5) states: "Every child under the age of 16 years who, knowing
its purpose, procures or attempts to procure any contraceptive from any person other than a
person who is authorised under this section to supply the contraceptive to that child commits
an offence and is liable on summary conviction—(a) In the case of a first offence, to have a
conviction recorded against him"-or her, presumably—“or (b) In the case of a second or
subsequent offence, to a fine not exceeding $4."
Let us take the case of a young person who goes into a toilet or some other place and
gets a contraceptive from a vending machine—and this could happen. Does the owner of
that machine, presumably a person, cause that young person to break the law? Should we be
legislating so that a conviction will be recorded against a 15-year-old who is doing something
probably for bravado, and allow no right of appeal? To me that appears to be inhumane, and
I shall certainly not support it.
Next I want to refer to the amendments in my name concerning the sterilisation of a
mentally subnormal person. I have a series of amendments, the first set being to delete
entirely clauses 7 to 11, because I believe they do not stand up to close scrutiny when we
examine the drafting—and I certainly do not in any way criticise Mr Barker, who did a
magnificent job in assisting me and other members to prepare amendments. The principle is
best summed up in evidence I received from the New Zealand Society for the Intellectually
Handicapped. Throughout New Zealand its 29 branches studied the Bill and came to the
general consensus, first, that it was totally opposed to any changes tending towards
euthenasia as an accepted policy and practice in the community at large. Secondly, the
prevention of intellectual handicap, whilst highly desirable, should not be sought at all costs.

The society's third point was that pregnancy and abortion are most undesirable for the

Next I want to turn-and I apologise to the House for moving quickly to different parts

Amendments have been provided by the member for Franklin to the proposals about

safeguards, the procedure will be very time consuming. The woman must first see her own
doctor. Then, if she wishes to be interviewed, she must make two separate appointments to
see two certifying consultants, at least one of these being a busy specialist. The consultants
may then wish to confer with the woman's doctor, with the operating surgeon, or with some
other person or persons. Basically the suggested clause 36 procedure is a panel that never
actually meets. The one advantage of a panel is that it is physically in one place at one time,
but that advantage is not carried forward into the amendments proposed by the member for
Franklin. This procedure sacrifices speed to gain privacy, but both are needed in any
humane proposal.
Secondly, in such a proposal any real doctor-patient relationships are negatived. The
woman's own doctor must refer her elsewhere, and must make representations on her
behalf, but is not allowed to take part in the decision making. Few busy general practitioners
would be ready to take the time away from their practice that might be involved in making
statements and representations on a woman's behalf, particularly if they are not considered
responsible enough to make the decision themselves. I interpolate here to say how much I
deplore that section of the amendments to be moved by the member for Franklin that states
that no one can take part who believes that the decision should be between a woman and her
doctor. A recent survey, the final results of which I understand the Minister of Energy
Resources will announce, shows that about two-thirds of obstetric and gynaecological
specialists would refuse to be appointed as certifying consultants; so the amendment will not
work.
Thirdly, clause 38 makes provision for counselling after the decision is made. This
ignores the purpose of counselling, which is to help the woman to clarify and understand her
needs and wishes. After counselling, a woman may decide not to have an abortion.
Counselling must take place before a final decision is made. Fourthly, and finally, clause
33(5) requires the supervisory committee to avoid appointing those whose views are

This debate is one of conscience. It is a debate on one of the most difficult social and
moral issues ever to come before the House. It is all about recognition and protection by
society of moral values. In it we consider the rights or convenience of the strong and whether
they should override the rights, or in some cases the lives, of the weak and unprotected.
Some would argue that a question of moral values is not a matter for the House. To them I
would say that many of our laws are based on moral questions and Christian ethics, and if
Parliament itself does not grapple with these matters and show leadership, then who in
society is to lead? One must recognise that there is a tide of change anxious to displace the
moral values of society. For those of us who want to stem the tide, this is a crucial debate and
critical legislation.
Many parts of the Bill deal with various aspects of those values, but tonight I want to
refer only to those parts that provide for changes in the abortion laws. Over the past 5 years
that separate issue has been the subject of wide controversy. We had the Wall Bill in 1975,
the Health Amendment Bill introduced by the Minister of Health in 1976, and now we have
the Contraception, Sterilisation, and Abortion Bill. All members have been exposed to wide
debate in their electorates and on public platforms. During those years I, like most other
members, have received more than 2000 letters. I have answered them all personally and
expressed my views on the subjects of the letters. This, then, is the third debate in 3 years on
essentially the same question-whether abortion should be permitted on demand or on
request, or whether, because it recognises the status of the unborn child, society, through the
law, should provide for its protection and preservation.
However, the Bill before us is different from its two predecessors, in that it has as its
basis a thorough inquiry into the whole matter by a royal commission established by the
Labour Government. I do not believe any member of the House should enter into the debate
without reading and having regard to the recommendations contained in chapters 9 to 28 of
the royal commission's report. Indeed, the commission's report deserves the fullest recogni-
tion as a thorough and comprehensive document expressed in precise language, and
undoubtedly it will be an invaluable reference on this important subject. I do not agree with
all the recommendations made-not many people do-but I believe that, in the general
tenor of the report, the commission has found the right spot for a caring and responsible
society-the sort of society this Parliament should be encouraging to flourish.
I want to give emphasis to three aspects of the report, because they bear very largely on
the content of the amendment I intend to move. The first is the conclusion on page 192:
"The fetus has a status from implantation which entitles it to preservation and protection." I
accept that that is fundamental to an ordered society. On page 198 the commission
questions, "Is it morally right to destroy a living fetus?" The commission then observes:
"There is a universal tradition concerning the absolute worth of any living human person.
That tradition finds its expression in the laws of many governments and in declarations of the
United Nations and related bodies.
The right to life is a sacred principle of civilisation. It is an indispensable guarantee of
the individual worth of the persons within it. Its universal denial would threaten civilisation
and would fail to recognise the dignity of man. A similar tradition, primarily Christian in
origin, exists with regard to the unborn child. Although this tradition has been eroded, we

think it to be still accepted that unborn life is entitled to a measure of protection and that it is
wrong, except for good reasons, to terminate it." In my view it would be an uncaring and
selfish society that disagreed with that philosophy or that statement.
The commission's report expresses the view on page 199 "that any moral code should
accept: (1) That society recognises a duty of protection towards the unborn child. (2) That
the standard of protection does not accord absolute protection to the child. (3) That society
recognises a duty of protection of the life and health of the pregnant woman. (4) That society
recognises the undesirability of children being born into a deprived state, but❞—and I
underline the word "but"-"that the life of the child should not be terminated in its unborn
state merely because ideal conditions for its upbringing in its born state may not be
attainable. Many well-adjusted people have been born and reared in circumstances of social
deprivation. History itself is a record of the success of people of poor circumstances. (5) It is
not immoral to terminate a pregnancy where the fetus is likely to be born with a severe
physical or mental handicap, because the burden of the handicapped person to himself and
to his parents may be greater than the sum total of their happiness." I have some disquiet
about that statement, but it is part of the commission's report. "(6) The termination of
unborn life for reasons of social convenience is morally wrong." I underline the words
"morally wrong".
Finally, the very aspect of the commission's report to which I wish to give emphasis is
chapter 25, on page 285, which states that today in New Zealand there exists wide variation
in the interpretation of the present law and in the procedures that are followed. The
commission's report goes on to say, "These vary substantially from place to place and
between one doctor or one committee and another. This is a matter fundamental to the
whole abortion issue, and every endeavour must be made to rectify conditions which at
present cause dissatisfaction and concern." Examination of these proposals led the commis-
sion in chapter 25 to recommend, in the interests of consistency in the interpretation and
administration of the law, the establishment of a supervisory committee, which is provided
for in the Bill.
Having made those observations, I turn now to Supplementary Order Paper 42, which I
propose to move in the Committee stage. The essence of the changes I propose, which have
been brought together with the assistance and support of a number of members on both sides
of this House, is to preserve the integrity of the commission's report, but they go a long way
towards meeting the criticism made of the Bill that the woman's own doctor is not
sufficiently involved and that the formality and inflexibility of the procedures associated with
the proposed panels are objectionable. These proposals have not been hastily put together,
as was stated by the member for Henderson, but represent many hours of work, and
examination, discussion, and consultation with a wide number of people. The changes
recognise that a woman and her doctor need to be involved in the decision, and that the final
decision should be made according to the criteria set within the law, the basis of which is
contained in the commission's report and restated in the Bill.
No attempt has been made to alter the basis of the criteria. The amendments provide
that the panels are to be replaced by a list of certifying consultants appointed by the
supervisory committee. The supervisory committee will determine the minimum number of
consultants necessary to ensure that every woman seeking an abortion has her case
considered expeditiously, but before making the appointments the supervisory committee
will consult the New Zealand Medical Association and may consult other professional or
other organisations before determining whom to appoint. In making the appointments, the
supervisory committee must ensure that at least one-half of the total number of appointees
are practising obstetricians and gynaecologists—but that is not to say that they need to be
members of the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists-and that there shall be
a sufficient number of appointees to ensure that every woman seeking an abortion shall have
her case considered without being involved in considerable travel or other inconvenience. It
is the responsibility of the supervisory committee to have regard to the desirability of
appointing medical practitioners who hold views in relation to abortion that generally are
compatible with the tenor of the Act. The amendment determines that views incompatible
with the tenor of the Act would be the view that an abortion should not be performed in any
circumstance or, alternatively, the view that the question of whether an abortion should or
should not be performed in any case is entirely a matter for the woman and her doctor to
decide.
The appointment of certifying consultants shall be for a term of 1 year, but the
consultants may be reappointed or their appointment may be revoked by the supervisory


## p. 3541 (#423) ###########################################

11 October
3541
Contraception, Sterilisation, and Abortion Bill
committtee at any time. The new clause 36 provides that every registered medical prac-
titioner who is consulted by a woman who wishes to have an abortion or who proposes to
perform an abortion on any woman if the abortion is authorised shall, if requested to do so
by the woman, refer the case to two certifying consultants, of whom at least one shall be a
practising obstetrician or gynaecologist, with a request that they determine whether or not to
authorise the performance of an abortion in accordance with the Bill. On referring the case
to the certifying consultants, the doctors shall submit in writing a statement that the woman
is pregnant, and the grounds on which she seeks an abortion. The certifying consultants shall
consider the case as soon as practicable and, if requested to do so, must interview the
patient. At any such interview she would be entitled to be accompanied by her doctor, but
the woman's own doctor and the patient shall also be entitled to make representations and
submissions if they think fit.
By amendments to clause 37, two certifying consultants must satisfy themselves that an
operating surgeon is available to the woman before they issue a certificate. The certifying
consultants must notify the supervisory committee if they are not able to reach a decision
within 14 days of the case being referred to them. I am satisfied that these procedures can be
completed within that time span. The existing clause 17(1)(e) requires the supervisory
committee to ensure that sufficient and adequate facilities are available for counselling
women throughout New Zealand, and Supplementary Order Paper 42 provides a new clause
38, which requires the certifying consultants to advise the woman seeking an abortion of her
right to have counselling from any of the appropriate agencies or persons, whether or not the
application for the abortion is approved.
Those, in brief, are the essential changes. They have been designed to preserve the
integrity of the royal commission's report. While introducing flexibility in the administrative
procedures, they are designed to involve the woman and her doctor in what is regarded as a
more normal medical approach to decision-making. Some members will argue during this
debate that a decision on abortion can be left to the woman and her doctor, or, as suggested
by the member for North Shore, to the woman and any two doctors.
I draw attention tonight to the 1977-78 handbook of the New Zealand Medical
Association, which on page 32 recognises the Declaration of Geneva, which states: "I will
maintain the utmost respect for human life from the time of conception even under threat. I
will not use my medical knowledge contrary to the laws of humanity." If every doctor
followed that declaration to the letter there would be no difficulty, but overseas experience
has shown that it is too much to expect the medical profession, without properly defined
procedures, to administer abortion laws consistently. Last week our own medical profession
was criticised for inconsistency by Sir Arnold Nordmeyer when he was talking about another
matter. As recently as 1970 the World Medical Association, in the Declaration of Oslo, laid
down for the guidance of the medical profession throughout the world the following
principles: "(1) Abortions should be performed only as a therapeutic measure. (2) A
decision to terminate a pregnancy should normally be approved in writing by at least two
doctors chosen for their professional competence. (3) The procedure should be followed by a
doctor competent to do so in premises approved by the appropriate authority."
The recommendations of the royal commission, which are provided for in this Bill and
which are carried into my amendments, have regard to those principles. Any lesser
provisions—and I know some would support only one certifying consultant—would not
maintain the integrity of the royal commission's report or the statement from the Oslo
conference or the Declaration of Geneva, and would lead virtually to abortion on demand.
Therefore the whole issue properly comes back to the simple question of whether members
support abortion on demand or whether they believe that society, through laws created by
this House, should offer protection for the preservation of the life of the unborn child. I
strongly take the latter view. I invite members to support the amendments set out in
Supplementary Order Paper 42.

The commission brought down its findings with absolute logic and in accordance with

by eminent scientists from all over the world. None of them suggested that human life begins
at any time other than conception, although the process of conception may not be
momentary, and it may not be possible to say whether it takes minutes or hours. By the time
the fertilised ovum has reached the uterus conception can be said to be complete." That is
the considered opinion of those whom the House set up to examine the matter for it. From

out through a sucker, or whether a woman should have her varicose veins-[Interruption.]

Hon. Mrs T. W. M. TIRIKATENE-SULLIVAN (Southern Maori): I remind the House
that abortion has been legal and part of the criminal law in this country since 1893, although
one would think, from some of the remarks made this evening, that this was not so. I have
been speaking on this subject throughout my 10 years in Parliament. Tonight I want to speak
on matters I have not mentioned before, so as to avoid repetition.
I refer immediately to my amendment, and point out that its principal effect is simply
that the decision about an abortion shall be that of the woman, in consultation with the
doctor of her choice. I was gratified to learn that more than 60 percent of the New Zealand
people surveyed support this view. My amendment implies that the code of ethics and
professional conduct we have come to expect from our medical practitioners will be
honoured and respected. As well as exercising his professional skill and competence, it
would be completely normal for a doctor to invite other appropriate specialists and
counsellors to join him in formulating his opinion, as a doctor normally does when he
considers it necessary. My amendment simply removes the compulsory imposition of such
normal professional requirements on both the woman and her doctor. We do not have to
legislate that specialists and counsellors are to be called in by the woman's doctor. He would
involve them if he considered their expertise necessary for the well-being and health of his
patient. Frankly, I consider that stipulation of each and every referral agent in the statute
book is overlegislating.
Any objection to my amendment also implies a vote of no confidence in the medical
practitioners. Are the doctors to be merely technicians at the end of the line, ordered by
statute to be almost less than professional? To be professional would be to be totally
involved in advising, and not merely a respondent of the bureaucratic panels envisaged in the
original Bill. If, and only if, the woman's doctor was totally acquiescent with her
demand-which would be tantamount to being totally unprofessional, to the extent that the
doctor would be offending against his code of ethics-could my amendment be validly
construed as amounting to abortion on demand. I repeat that my amendment implies
competent professional behaviour from the medical practitioner chosen by the woman
concerned. I am amazed that such a fundamental assumption has not been accepted by my
critics. We do not have to legislate to include each and every individual or professional
person who should be consulted. A competent medical practitioner would do all that.
The Bill as originally introduced sets pregnant women on a laborious, time-consuming,
demeaning obstacle course that is quite unnecessary; hence my amendment. The Bill in no
way guarantees that the woman will get over that obstacle course in time for a relatively safe
abortion-that is, within the first 3 months; indeed, the earlier the better. The Bill as
originally introduced provides for a panel system, an obstacle course, involving many
individuals: the woman's doctor, a counsellor, and a panel of three, probably complete
strangers to the woman-a specialist, another doctor (preferably a woman), and a social
worker without a vote. All that paraphernalia is unnecessary; it should certainly not be the
subject of legislation. It ignores the sensitive, human creature who is the subject of the Bill;
it ignores the pregnant woman. I believe that I am the only one in the Chamber to have
experienced the anxiety of pregnancy with risks involved. Because of that experience, and
for many other reasons, I have proposed my amendment.

commission, which I support in general, although not entirely.
I found great difficulty, both personally and in discussions in my electorate, in coming to
terms with the proposed panel system recommended in the Bill. I sought strenuously for a
suitable alternative. Many of those who oppose the panel system misinterpret the intention
in the original legislation and place an emotive emphasis on it. Other speakers in this debate
today have given examples of patients requiring surgery for certain complaints. Their
general practitioner refers them to a specialist, then to a surgeon, and so on. Perhaps three
or four opinions are obtained before surgery is undertaken. Is that not really a panel in a
different form? It is consultation between a patient and a range of doctors and specialists.
I certainly do not agree with those who tried to tell us that, if the Bill went through in its
draft form, a pregnant woman would be called upon to appear before a panel of men-and it
was always men who would be sitting on the panel-in starchy somnolence, and pour out her
soul. At no stage has that been intended, even though it was certainly the impression
mooted. For that reason, I do not find any difficulty in coming to terms with the amendment
put forward by the member for Franklin. It will have my support.
The member for New Lynn spoke very eloquently against this clause in the Bill. Even
though I do not agree with his argument, I respect his view that the proposal set out in what
is now known as the Birch amendment would assist the more articulate woman and would
not favour the more nervous and distraught woman in these circumstances. I shall read from
the explanatory note to the amendments put forward by the member for Franklin. I think we
must give them due regard. The procedure is as follows: "The woman's own doctor, or the
doctor who will perform the abortion if it is authorised, will refer the case to two certifying
consultants (at least one being a practising obstetrician or gynaecologist); the woman is
entitled to an interview with the consultants if she wishes, and, with her consent, her own
doctor and the operating surgeon is entitled to put forward his views of the case and any
medical reports for consideration by the consultants". With those provisos, if a woman's own
doctor knew that she could not adequately express her case, or if she was nervous or
distraught, he would certainly ensure that he was there to support her. He would point out
her right to have his counsel and that of the operating consultant if she so desired. I believe
those are adequate safeguards, and on that basis we can put to one side the objections raised
by the member for New Lynn.
I cannot accept his point that the doctor-patient relationship would be disturbed by the
amendments put forward by the member for Franklin. Throughout those amendments there
is reference to the woman's own doctor. For that reason, those amendments are an
acceptable alternative for me-although, as I have said, I found considerable difficulty in
coming to terms with the proposed panel system, not so much because of what the panels
would have been in practice, but because of the fear that they would operate in a somewhat
different manner.

Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): A point of order, Mr Speaker. This may
be an appropriate time to tell the House that the broadcasting of the debate will continue
beyond normal hours.
Mr BRILL (Kapiti): This Bill has been the subject of greater public interest than any
other measure introduced into the House during my limited time as a member. It is right that
this should be so, because it deals essentially with matters of life and death and also has a
direct bearing on the future health and happiness of many women, and indirectly of many
men, throughout New Zealand. But for many it also assumes a symbolic role as a
weathervane of the current attitudes of New Zealand society to traditional concepts of
morality. In this respect, the subject of abortion is becoming the great watershed for debate
on moral issues and changing values in our increasingly sophisticated society. In the same
way as conservationists flocked to the banner of Manapouri on the issue of the environment,
the debate on this Bill will be seen as a demarcation of the development or the decline of
moral standards in an avowedly Christian country.
Despite these overtones, I see it as the clear duty of members of the House to draw the
distinction between personal morality and the law of the land. A legislator clearly has no
fundamental right to impose his or her moral views on the entire population. In many so-
called "victimless crimes", the law should draw back and leave decisions to the consciences
of the individuals directly involved, however much we might disagree individually with the
practice involved. In my mind, the question before us is whether abortion can be regarded as
a "victimless crime". The entire crux of the abortion issue turns on the question of whether a
foetus can be regarded as a victim, or whether it can be regarded as some neutral object
having no claim to the protection of New Zealand law.
As I am certain that every member of the House has a fundamental belief in the sanctity
of life, the central question in turn is whether the foetus itself has life. If so, is it human,
animal, or plant, and is it a separate life before birth, or merely an extension of the life of its
mother? The royal commission assisted us in determining these fundamental questions. The
commission came unhesitatingly and unanimously to the conclusion that the foetus is a
separate human life from the time of conception. Even more persuasive than that is the
statement on page 364 of the commission's report: “All the witnesses who gave evidence
before us were agreed that life begins at conception, and pregnancy at implantation." When
one considers the range of medical, philosophical, theological, and outright partisan
witnesses who appeared before the commission, this statement becomes very persuasive,
especially when it is considered that more than 850 witnesses were heard and over 10 000
pages of evidence considered over a period of 21 months.
I can view with something akin to envy those who are able to sweep aside this viewpoint
and argue that life commences at some other point in the cycle. For them, no moral issue
arises, abortion becomes merely a simple surgical procedure, and no anguished balancing of
rights between the foetus and the mother is required. Every woman may make her own
decision, and society need take no interest in the matter because there is no second life to
protect. Unfortunately, the central question of whether the foetus has life, and therefore has
rights, must be decided one way or the other. This is not a question with different answers
depending on the attitudes of the mother. It is not a question that can be decided by women
alone, nor by men alone, nor even by majority opinion. Every member of the House must
decide that question for himself or herself, and only if it is decided that the foetus does have
some rights does it become necessary to consider the extent of those rights.
That brings us to the options that have been put before the House, both in the Bill and
the amendments proposed. The Deputy Leader of the Opposition said that there was no
difference between the Bill and the amendments proposed by the member for Franklin. I
should like to set that argument at rest from the outset. In making that statement, the
Deputy Leader of the Opposition ignored the fact that the delays inherent in the panel
system have been removed in the amendment proposed by the member for Franklin, and
that applicants will not have to wait until three persons, two of whom would be medical
practitioners, can get together to interview the applicant. He ignored the omission of an
additional step that required compulsory counselling, and the omission of the social worker
from the whole decision-making process. He ignored also the change from a compulsory
interview to an interview only if it is requested by the woman, and he ignored as well the fact
that the operating doctor must be on the panel, or must agree that the abortion is warranted.
The doctor cannot be reduced to the status of a technician under the amendment proposed
by the member for Franklin, and that is in contradistinction to the provisions of the Bill.

It is perfectly clear that there is a world of difference between the original panel system

I can only assume that the Deputy Leader of the Opposition, in saying that the two were

The test that was propounded earlier is the question of whether any rights whatever are
to be reposed in the foetus, and I believe that this should be applied to any amendments put
forward by the House. When one considers the amendment put forward by the member for
Southern Maori and raises the question whether it is intended in that amendment to accord
any rights whatever to the foetus, it becomes clear that the foetus is not a factor to be taken
into account. The member for Southern Maori would have the mother make the decision.
Naturally, the mother needs a doctor to carry out the operation, so it is not the mother alone
but the mother and the doctor who does the operation.
Despite the protestations of the member-and I accept that she sincerely believes that
this is not abortion on request-I believe it is generally accepted throughout the country that
it is abortion on request if the sole limitation on the right of the mother to have an abortion is
that she must find a doctor who is prepared to do it. The doctor does not have to apply any
criteria. No criminal law applies; indeed, no law applies. It would merely be incumbent on
the doctor to determine that she was medically fit to have an abortion. Certainly, no other
guidelines are suggested in that amendment. There seems to be no requirement that either
party-the woman or the doctor-should take account of any rights whatever that might be
reposed in a third party-the foetus-or, indeed, any rights that might be reposed in the
father of the child. Presumably, this amendment is based on the theory that a foetus has no
life and therefore has no rights whatever.
I commend the member for Southern Maori for the sincerity of her speech, although it

3557
Contraception, Sterilisation, and Abortion Bill
nor do I believe that an argument based on the fact that there is a world population explosion
should be upheld. If we were to go to those lengths we could say that there is a declining
birth rate in New Zealand—and, indeed, the birth rate is too low-but I think these are
matters that ought not to be taken into account in the essentially human question of whether
a particular foetus should live or whether a particular mother should be allowed an abortion.
I do not believe that, on those specific questions, we should be considering the world
population scale or the population within New Zealand.
I turn to the amendments that stand in the name of the Minister of Energy Resources.
This proposal differs slightly from that put forward by the member for Southern Maori in
that it requires another doctor-virtually any other doctor-to agree with the abortion
surgeon. Clearly, this is little more than a cosmetic difference from the extreme proposal.
The abortion surgeon may scour the city, or indeed the entire country, to find one other
medical practitioner-of any discipline whatsoever-who will countersign the application.
However, the amendment contains a further element that is more than cosmetic. It
introduces the notion that abortions must be justified. Unfortunately, the amendment
relates justification only to clause 54 of the Bill, which lays down an essentially subjective
test. The abortion surgeon and the woman's doctor or the other countersignatory must
believe that continuance of the pregnancy may result in serious danger to the mental health
of the woman, taking into account her social and economic circumstances. There is no
requirement that the belief be held on reasonable grounds. There is no way of disproving
that a particular doctor may have held such a belief. There is no protection against the 5
percent "rogue element" of the medical profession recently described by the President of the
New Zealand Medical Association, Dr Graham Gordon. There is no exclusion of those
doctors who are well known throughout the country as holding a ready belief that mental
health might be at risk. There is no provision for any effective supervision other than the
general role of the Department of Health, already found inadequate by the royal commis-
sion.
In the amendment in the name of the Minister of Energy Resources we have a curious
ambivalence. Lip service is paid to the fact that the foetus does have some rights, so we are
agreed on that score. However, when those rights fall to be determined vis-à-vis the mother,
the mother has an unlimited right to choose the judge from among the thousands of medical
practitioners throughout New Zealand. One such doctor will be found. That can be said with
near certainty, and has been established by recent history and by the accounts set out in the
royal commission's report. It is equally certain that the "judge" will then find a fellow
practitioner who is prepared to carry out the operation. Such a procedure makes a farce of
the suggestion that the abortion decision involves a balancing between the rights of the
mother and the rights of the unborn child. If it accords any rights to the foetus, such rights
are microscopic and almost derisory.
The Bill itself, incorporating the recommendations of the royal commission, and the
amendment proposed by the member for Franklin both presuppose that a balancing process
will be undertaken; both assume that medical practitioners with open minds will apply the
criteria set out in clause 54 and that doctors with extremely conservative or extremely
permissive views will be excluded. The two options provide the opportunity for members to
express a viewpoint as to the weight to be attached to the mother's rights on the one hand,
and the rights of the foetus on the other.
The member for Franklin has devised a system that is free from the bureaucracy and
unnecessary delays that led to so much criticism of the panel system. It has been worked over
very carefully in its detail-much more carefully than the proposal put forward by the
Minister of Energy Resources, from which it differs in one essential respect. The decision
will be taken by the medical practitioners selected by the mother from a limited field from
which all extremists have been excluded. That is the essential difference. Both proposals
involve two doctors in the decision making. Both proposals require that the mother shall
make the decision as to who the doctors will be. The difference is that in the amendment of
the member for Franklin the doctor shall be selected from within a limited field from which
the extremists have been excluded. This will do no more than ensure that some weight is
given to the rights of the foetus.
It is accepted that those rights must yield when they come into serious conflict with the
right of the mother to maintain her life and her good health. This concept is in accordance
with the mainstream of our general jurisprudence, which has always accepted the right to
take life in various circumscribed situations such as self-defence, defence of family or
property, or times of war. The usual doctrine of self-defence requires that no more than

reasonable force is applied. In the case of abortion, such fine tuning is simply not possible.
The other party cannot be merely restrained; it must be eliminated entirely. This is justified
not merely to save the life of the mother but to protect her from any serious risk to her life,
whether physical or mental. I believe that this somewhat unequal set of rules can be justified
on the basis of the differing stages of development of the two parties in conflict. However, I

Curiously, the argument already advanced in the House this evening, and probably
advanced most frequently against the control of abortion, is the possibility that individuals
may seek to break the law by resorting to back-street abortionists. In that regard, I would

arguments based on socio-economic grounds that would not be acceptable as a reason for
repealing the laws of theft. I would like to think that New Zealand could be just as high-

A further argument is the contention that there is one law for the rich and one law for
the poor, because the wealthy may travel to Sydney for freely available abortions. The irony

jurisdictions. If we were to follow this course, New Zealand would rapidly become the
lowest common denominator of the world.
It is in this area of abortion that I hope New Zealand will defend its reputation as a
liberal, fair-minded, and enlightened country that is prepared to adopt a leading stance in
the protection of life and the rights of all living, rich or poor, healthy or disabled, very old or
yet to emerge from the womb.
