if one leaves the decision as to when and in what circumstances an abortion should be
performed to any doctor, or even to any panel of doctors, it is seen by many-and it is seen
by me-to allow a risk to exist that two doctors of similar views, which are not the views of
the majority, are able to present the community with a de facto abortion on request
situation. I do not say that that will happen, because I cannot look into the future with
certainty, but I do say it is a very real risk. That is the watershed.
No matter what your views are on abortion or the criteria for it, and no matter what
your feelings are about the foetus or the mother, if you support a system that leaves the
choice to one, two, or even more doctors who are unsupervised in any way there is a risk of
abortion on request. If one decides to institute some system of control, one runs the risk of
developing a counter-balancing risk-the risk of inconsistency of decision, and the danger of
the pregnant woman's being treated with somewhat less consideration. The two risks are the
risk of abortion on request on the one hand, and the risk of inconsistent decisions and
possibly less humanity on the other. That is the watershed that one cannot straddle; one
finds oneself accepting one risk or the other.
For my colleagues who wish to make their decision on the basis of what the public wants
I see a real problem, because on the one hand the public has made it very clear to all of us
that it prefers the machinery proposed by the Minister of Energy Resources in his
amendment, and on the other the public has also made it clear through other surveys that it
is not in favour of abortion on request. Members who try to meet public opinion will fall on
this razor-edged watershed of trying to meet both those requirements of the public: on the
one hand, the preference of the public for the decision to be made by two doctors; and, on
the other hand, the preference of the public, clearly expressed in surveys, not to have
abortion on request. Those whose vote will be determined not by the attitudes of their
electors, but entirely by their conscience, must decide, on their own terms, which risk they
are prepared to live with: the risk of abortion on request, or the risk of some inconsistency in
decision-making.
My view is that, although I should like to be able to straddle both and cover both risks,
in view of the fact that that is impossible, if I am to err I will err on the side of conservatism; I
am not prepared to risk the possibility of abortion on request developing, because in my
view-and it is a personal, conscience view-the risk of abortion on request developing is
more worrying than the risk of inconsistency in decisions.
The amendments moved by the member for Franklin have been subjected to some
considerable inaccuracy of interpretation both in this debate and outside the House. There
has been constant reference in the debate to their being a panel in disguise. It has been
implied that some sort of subterfuge is involved.
Richard Walls: Of course there is.
Mr MALCOLM: The member for Dunedin North is one of those who would claim that
there is subterfuge involved. I refute that. The purpose of the panels outlined in the royal
commission's report was clearly to exercise some mechanism of balance that would aim to
exclude the possibility of a minority of doctors producing an abortion on request situation. In
that sense, the amendment proposed by the member for Franklin seeks to maintain that
principle of balance and to avoid abortion on request. It seeks that objective without
subterfuge, and without disguise-it seeks it quite openly.
However, the form of the royal commission's recommendations placed the decision in
the hands of a panel, and removed the decision from the doctor who would perform the
operation. It reduced the role of the family doctor, and set the stage for the possibile
development of an inquisitorial situation. For those reasons, I find the panel suggestion put
forward by the royal commission unacceptable, and I believe that most other members do,
too. Those dangers are not present in the amendment proposed by the member for Franklin,
so that the claim of subterfuge or deceit is simply not true.
Opponents of the Birch amendment have widely claimed that the decision will be made
by the two certifying consultants, and that the doctor who performs the operation will
become a functionary. That is simply not so. There is absolutely no obligation in the
amendments proposed by the member for Franklin for the operating consultants to have any
sort of a panel inquisition of the woman who is seeking an abortion. In fact, the Birch
amendment goes as far as it possibly can towards enshrining a perfectly normal medical
procedure that the woman, believing herself to be pregnant, would probably present
herself to a general practitioner and ask him to confirm that she was pregnant. Once he had
established that she was pregnant-I suggest this is a perfectly normal procedure-she may


## p. 3561 (#443) ###########################################

11 October
3561
Contraception, Sterilisation, and Abortion Bill
then in some circumstances indicate her desire to have an abortion. If that were so, in most
cases the family doctor to whom she had presented herself would not be professionally
competent to perform the abortion, and would refer her to a person who had a sufficient
degree of medical specialisation to be competent to perform abortions. That is the procedure
proposed in the Birch amendment; it is the procedure of normal medical practice.
It then becomes the prime responsibility of the doctor to whom the pregnant woman has
been referred, who in the Birch amendment is called the operating doctor, to establish
whether he is prepared and willing to perform that abortion—and by "prepared and willing"
I mean that, first, he has to establish that he is not going away next week for a fortnight's
holiday, because he could not then perform the operation, and, secondly, he has to establish
that he is prepared to perform abortions. He has to be prepared to establish also that he has
access to medical facilities, to a hospital, in which to perform the operation; and, most
importantly, he has to establish clearly in his own mind whether he believes that the abortion
is justified within the law, because, if the abortion was not justified within the law, one
assumes that he would not be prepared to perform it. So under the Birch amendment the
basic decision is made by the operating doctor.
The role of the certifying consultants then becomes one of checking out the decision the
operating doctor has made. It is only after he has made that first decision-that he is
prepared to perform an operation on this woman because he believes himself to be
professionally competent to do it and that the operation will be within the law-that the
certifying consultants come into the picture. The certifying consultants are not obliged to see
the woman; in fact, I expect that in many cases they probably would not want to see the
woman. It would depend entirely on the circumstances put forward by the operating doctor.
The Birch amendment in fact follows closely the procedure that is followed under normal
circumstances in medical consultation.
Detractors of the Birch amendment-many of whom, I am bound to say have clearly
not read the amendment; I say that of members who, from the comments they have made in
the House, have not read the amendment, and also of many people outside the House-fail
to recognise the simple realities of the process I have described. They talk about the need to
make three or four visits to doctors. That is not true in the Birch amendment. The procedure
is quite simple and is a fairly normal medical procedure. The member for Porirua indicated
tonight-and I can only quote what he said—that he has been informed that obstetricians
and gynaecologists who have been asked for an opinion about the Birch amendment have
not even had the amendment put to them properly before their opinions are sought. In the
circumstances, it is very important that the House carefully checks any criticisms of the
amendment to be moved by the member for Franklin, as they might have come from ill-
informed sources.
The abortion clinic is in my electorate. Those who operate the clinic have told me that,
if the amendment to be moved by the member for Franklin becomes law, the clinic will no
longer function. I fail to understand why the clinic could not function, if it was so wished.
Having looked closely at the amendment, and knowing that most of the people at the Aotea
clinic are anxious to help those with whom they come in contact, I find it hard to believe that
it could not continue to operate, albeit under a slightly different procedure, if the amend-
ment was passed.
Whatever our moral views on the many issues involved with abortion, on which there is

great and worrisome that I will opt for the amendment to be moved by the member for

There have been instances in history where innocent men have been killed because
people who have had to make a judgment have been prepared to follow the decision of the
majority rather than to follow their own consciences. If anybody wants an example of that, a

I uphold the principles many members have talked about tonight of the standard of the

advocate respect for life on these grounds and at the same time punish the solo mother by
reducing her benefit. Both issues have to be taken to their proper conclusion. We have
community responsibilities, and I intend to see that the community observes those respon-
sibilities if we are to protect the life that has been conceived.

I have a letter dated 6 September, which I received from a person who, until recently,

consisted of four doctors. However, in due course it was found that it was not possible for the
four doctors to meet at the one time. The situation was then changed, so that the details of
the cases were circulated in writing to the four doctors on the panel, and each replied
separately. As I read the letter, it was eventually found that smaller committees could
operate satisfactorily.

Associated with this legislation is also the question of education in schools on the

It has been emphasised that it has long been recognised that pregnancy resulting from
rape may cause a state of severe psychological stress that affects a woman's mental health,
and that has been taken into account in considering whether abortion is justifiable on legal
grounds. In other words, the commission suggested that, rather than make rape itself a
justification for an abortion, mental health must be involved. Where rape is involved, very
often psychological reactions do result in mental strain. If the woman takes prompt action to
ensure detection of the rape, the gentlest and most effective way to relieve that woman of the
risk of pregnancy should be taken immediately. I would certainly consider seriously giving
support to the amendment proposed by the member for New Lynn, but there must be
evidence that rape has actually occurred.
Finally, I wish to make a quick reference to the question of giving education on human
relationships in our schools. The amendment suggested by the Leader of the Opposition,

to prevent young women from having unwanted pregnancies. The report of the Royal
Commission on Contraception, Sterilisation, and Abortion does not go quite as far as the
Statutes Revision Committee did in 1974, but it does state that the commission believes that
the giving of specific contraceptive advice and access to contraceptives is not warranted,
except where some special provision must be made for some girls under 16 years of age.
We cannot have it all ways. Protection of the fetus must be absolute, except where risk
to the health of the mother is involved, as is provided in the present law. I believe in
upholding that principle. We must look seriously at the commission's recommendations on
contraceptives to overcome effectively unwanted pregnancies.

Whatever the consequences, the Royal Commission on Contraception, Sterilisation,
and Abortion has achieved one major aim. It has finally given full importance to an area
which for far too long has been sadly neglected. I refer to contraception and family planning,
which have been regarded as isolated and relatively unimportant for consideration. That has
been borne out by the way in which this debate has gone tonight. Our present lack of
concern in this field and the lack of a population policy have caused problems in almost every
area of Government administration, and in our day-to-day life in New Zealand.
In its recent study in the Hutt, the Department of Health found that 36 percent of all
pregnancies were unwanted, and that ex-nuptial births are currently 17 percent of all live
births. In 1973 there were 9111 ex-nuptial confinements, with 364 of those children born to
girls under 16 years of age and 3745 to unmarried girls aged between 16 and 19 years. Also,
39 percent of first births within marriage occur within 7 months, suggesting pregnancy as a
reason for marriage. How many of these couples start out in a relationship for which they are
ill equipped, and with a partner to whom they are ill suited? We have heard a lot of talk in
this debate about family life and marriage. That is very relevant. The files of many welfare
and related departments show a high proportion of broken marriages amongst those people.
Marriage breakdowns also occur when the children come too soon and too often in
marriage, causing an unbearable strain on both parents. So often in these cases husbands are
unable to cope with the pressures and desert their wives and families, leaving the State to
pick up the pieces, if it can. The problem extends also to the field of education. Any teacher
can tell you of the concern caused by the children of solo parents who cannot cope on their
own, or of the children of large families who are emotionally and financially distressed.
Another far-reaching effect of having a high proportion of unplanned and unwanted children
in the community is in the field of law and order.
According to the Department of Social Welfare, ex-nuptial children who are not
adopted are more likely to appear in court and be referred to the Department of Social
Welfare as the result of child abuse or neglect. During the panel discussion to which I
referred earlier we heard of common instances of children beaten with vacuum cleaner
hoses, placed in rotary clothes dryers, or just left in bed while the parent goes out for 2 or 3
days. Even adopted children are more prone to psychiatric disturbances. One of the saddest
aspects of the situation is that the problem is so often self-perpetuating in that it has been
frequently shown that neglected children usually turn out to be neglectful parents. The real
problem and the costs are in the terms of human hardship and misery, through the trauma of
the pregnant 14-year-old to the distress of the 45-year-old mother of eight who has been
forced to bear yet another child she did not want. Even more important is the misery
experienced by many children who, through no fault of their own, find themselves thrust into
an unwanted and uncaring situation. The problem is there, seriously affecting almost every
aspect of our present life, but, to a large degree, the solution also is there and is far more
readily available and more easily implemented than solutions to many of our other
problems.

This, therefore, obliges me to legislate on any issue so that people can make reasoned

jurisprudence. Before a moral precept should be given the force of law, it needs in my
opinion, the overwhelming support of the public."
So I come to my representation of the public conscience on the abortion issue in

believe the average New Zealander has the inner good sense and strength to make good
judgments when he or she is called upon to exercise a choice and to resolve a conflict of
rights, as must be the case when a decision on such a matter as abortion is faced.

to be moved by the Minister of Energy Resources. We must uphold and respect the views of
those who firmly and conscientiously believe that the termination of pregnancy is a violation
of their moral beliefs, but we have no right to insist in law that every pregnancy reaches its
logical conclusion.

I shall confine my remarks to clause 56, which deals with the teaching of human development
and relationships in State schools. I do not propose to go back over the reasons why clause 56
is worded as it is, nor do I believe there is any need for me to further explain the reasons that

public discussion for the last 2 months.
I want to examine some of the implications of clause 56, and explain to the House what I
see as being the responsibility of the Minister of Education if clause 56 is passed and becomes
part of the Education Act. The first thing to note is that clause 56 is an empowering clause
that would empower the Minister of Education at some time in the future to authorise
syllabuses in human development and relationships. The clause would provide also the
statutory authority by which the Executive Council could make regulations covering the
teaching of human development and relationships.
The second question is whether that would provide a sufficient basis in law for the
teaching of courses in human development and relationships in State schools under proper
safeguards. I believe it is important for members to make the distinction between the
principles that should be stressed in the Act and the administrative details that should be
more appropriately found in regulations. I have tried to identify the principles at stake, and
the amendments I have proposed are intended to cover them. I do not say that they are the
only principles at stake, but I ask members to examine them very carefully. The difficulty
comes in trying to incorporate everything in one Act, and to incorporate by way of
amendment many things that I think should more properly come under regulations. I can
understand the concerns that have prompted the amendment, but it seems to me that the
provisions might be more appropriate to regulations made under the authority of the
Education Act. However, to lay to rest some of the fears, I feel it would do no harm to have
the provisions incorporated within the Act.
My second point is that clause 56, as it now stands, needs four more safeguards. First,
we should make it clear that the law refers to courses in classes; secondly, the decision on
teaching should rest with the schools and not be mandatory; thirdly, we should provide for
prior consultation to ascertain parental opinion before courses on human development and
relationships are taught in schools; and, fourthly, there should be a right of withdrawal of
pupils from those courses. These provisions, if passed, would provide a sufficient basis in law
for us to embark on further consultation to ascertain public opinion, as suggested in the
recommendations of the royal commission. For that reason, the proposed clause 1 (c) as set
out in the Supplementary Order Paper of the member for Oamaru, is in my opinion not
really necessary.
I would not wish to quarrel with the importance of the principle in the proposed
amendment, but it is a principle-one of many-that would have to be kept in mind in
subsequent discussions on the writing of the official syllabus. In my opinion, therefore, it is a
statement more appropriately set out as an objective of the syllabus. It is inappropriate as a
piece of law, and would not really be necessary. However, if it were included there would be
a number of other equally important principles that presumably should be written into the
Act. If honourable members accepted this approach we would very soon find ourselves
writing a syllabus of instruction in an Act of Parliament, and that would be quite inappro-
priate. If the principle is settled by Parliament, the question would then be what the courses
in human development and relationships would mean in practice.
I now turn specifically to clause 56. If it is passed-and the House alone will decide
that-professional and public consultation will begin. There will continue to be a great deal
of public discussion about what might or might not be included in an official syllabus on
human development and relationships. The report of the Ross committee has already been
mentioned. The royal commission has indicated generally the approach it would like to see,
and there is also the report of the Johnson committee on health and social education, which I
have received and which will soon be published. That report will greatly assist members of
the public to become fully informed on what might be appropriate in courses of study on
human development and relationships. I intend to see that the report receives the widest
public discussion. The issues are such that there would be ample time for an expression of
public opinion, and I believe that sufficient time must be taken to allow for the very
important phase of public consultation. During the public consultation phase, views on the
regulations that would need to be written in the public interest would be clarified.
Several important issues will have to be written into regulations, including the condi-
tions that are to be laid down to ensure prior consultation with parents before a school
introduces courses in human development and relationships. It must be decided how
frequently schools should be required to review their mandate with the parent community,
who would be responsible for deciding who would teach the courses in human development,
whether or not teachers should have the right to declare their own conscience, and whether
persons other than school teachers would be permitted to teach the courses.

During that phase the matters raised by the member for Oamaru would be taken up. In

opportunity for public discussion of the drafted or proposed regulations. There is no need for
this clause to be included in the Education Act, as provision already exists for regulations to

remembering that if my own amendment is passed, giving an option, the introduction of such

The member suggests that the length of time given to these discussions should be as the

Those matters would be better built into regulations after full consultation, the results of

and decision at a national level would have been completed. Local implementation would
then follow, and this would be within the guidelines of the official syllabus and according to
the requirements of the regulations. Broad guidelines for teaching human development and
relationships could be prescribed.
The speed with which courses in human development and relationships would be
introduced would be governed by three considerations: first, the wishes of the local parent
community as expressed through the process of consultation required under the regulations;
secondly, the ability of suitable teachers; and, thirdly, the availability of teaching materials
that reflect the New Zealand way of life.
The report of the Johnson committee on health and social education, which will become
a public document next month, proposes a comprehensive scheme for health and social
education, including aspects of human development and relationships of concern in this
debate. The Johnson committee is not asking for an increase in the time allocated to health
and social welfare education, or for any other subject in the school curriculum, contrary to
what the Minister of Social Welfare has implied. It would be unwise to force the pace of
implementation; I think the royal commission went too far too fast.
Public discussion over the last few months has shown that there is a great deal of
uncertainty and quite a bit of misunderstanding about the exact way in which schools will be
expected to teach courses on human development and relationships. For that reason I have
introduced the second Supplementary Order Paper that stands in my name. It replaces' the
word "shall" with the word "may" in clause 56, which will read that "schools may" teach
courses in human relationships. It will be permissive, and not mandatory, and within the
parameters of the regulations, which will be clearly set out beforehand.
An amendment has been suggested that would allow school committees and boards to
choose teachers by some form of inquisitional examination of their morals. I simply say that
no teacher would subject himself to such an examination. In fact, I believe that would be
quite contrary to the recommendations of the royal commission, which has said that the final
responsibility for the choice of the teacher rests with the principal, remembering always that
the principal is responsible to his board or committee. I also feel that teachers should have
the right to seek exemption from any requirement to teach human development and
relationships. I have therefore already given notice that I shall move a further amendment to
provide that nothing in the Act or the regulations will require teachers to teach such courses
or classes.
To sum up, the Bill should produce principle, and provide enough law to empower a
course of action under proper safeguards. If clause 56, amended as I suggested, is passed
there should be sufficient law. With an adequate basis in law, the way would then be open
for public discussion towards the detailed provision of a proper syllabus and the way in which
courses in human development and relationships should be taught in State schools. That may
take one, two, or even more years to complete. Clearly it will not be hurried.

those administered by injection.
As clause 5 stands, there is provision for a registered medical practitioner, when called
by a member of the Police after a complaint of rape, to be required to give the complainant a
contraceptive device and/or advice, or to advise her where she can receive such service from
another doctor or a family planning clinic. Rape, according to this clause, does not need to
be established beforehand by the Police or the courts. I gather that rapes are often not
reported to the Police, and my amendment allows that advice and assistance to be given
without having to report to the Police, so that a person reporting rape can go straight to the
doctor for this assistance.
Clause 6 prohibits the manufacture of condoms that do not meet certain standards. My

implements recommendation 12 on page 114 of the royal commission's report. Recommen-
dation 12 also prompts another amendment in my name-clause 6A-which exempts from
customs duty contraceptives complying with those standards. Recommendations 9 and 10 on

which brings contraceptives in cases of hardship, or where there is a particular medical
condition, or as a pregnancy test, within the Drug Tariff Act 1974 and the 1946 social
security regulations, which relieve the patient of the cost of such services. As I mentioned,
that amendment gathers up another three of the recommendations in the royal commission's
report that have not yet appeared in the Bill. It may be that these recommendations will be
adopted by other means, such as an Import Prohibition Order under section 48 of the
Customs Act, and if I have an assurance from the relevant Ministers, particularly the
Minister of Customs, about those amendments, I may not pursue that matter with an
amendment in the Committee stage.

Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Attorney-General): In the course of his address the member
for Wanganui mentioned certain amendments that have a bearing on my Customs portfolio.
If he would like to discuss them with me, I shall be very happy to see him in my office
tomorrow morning and to offer any assistance I can. I am one of those members-and there
are probably many in the House in this category-who has never derived any satisfaction
from speaking or voting on this issue that just will not go away. The fact that Parliament
must accept its share of the blame for the fact that the issue won't go away makes it no more
palatable to speak on tonight. In the 8 years I have been in the House I have never
encountered a more obtrusive or divisive issue; one that is more conducive of intolerance of
an opposing point of view, or more likely to cut across friendships and loyalties.
I am always amused by the reaction of those who believe we actually want to decide this
issue on behalf of women. They could not be more wrong. Some time ago I accepted an
invitation to appear on a “Dateline" programme on TV1. In the course of the interview I
said—and I quote word for word from the script I obtained from the Avalon studio—“I do
happen to believe that the majority of the people in my electorate share my basic view about
abortion on request"—and by that I meant that they oppose abortion on request. I could not
have anticipated that that statement, made in good faith, would be so misunderstood. Some
people actually thought that I had claimed that all my constituents shared my view. Some
thought that I had quoted from the results of a survey. Further confusion arose from an
advertisement in local newspapers stating, "He"-that is, I-"believes that he has the
support of his rural constituency in not wishing to liberalise the abortion law." Since that
advertisement appeared, I have wondered why those who inserted it did not quote the words
I actually used. Though the result has led to almost endless confusion, I have no reason to
believe that this was deliberately intended. It was the right of anyone to challenge my TV
opinion if they disagreed with it, but I in turn have the right to be quoted correctly.
Subsequently, a group of constituents exercised their right to challenge my statement by
conducting a street survey in Warkworth involving 721 people of voting age who were asked
to indicate their preference among five alternatives relating to the carrying out of an
abortion. I promised I would publish the figures, which are as follows: (1) decision by the
woman concerned, 20.67 percent; (2) by the woman and the doctor of her choice, 65.19
percent; (3) by two doctors supervised by a statutory committee, 4.16 percent; (4) by a panel
of two doctors and a non-voting social worker appointed by a statutory committee set up by
the Government, 3.61 percent; and, (5) never under any circumstances, 6.38 percent. I
should add that I accept that the survey was fairly conducted. Equally, I should add that the
results came as a surprise to me, because they seemed so out of line with the impression I had
formed about opinion on abortion on request. I knew very well that there was opposition to
the royal commission's panel system, and this survey indicated that it ran deeper than I had
expected, but I was still convinced that opposition to abortion on request ran very deep
indeed.
When the issue came up in discussions with constituents, I had noticed for some time, as
no doubt other members have noticed, that some people who strongly supported a decision
by the doctor and woman only were also strongly opposed to abortion on request, without
realising how the two could clash. They can clash, of course, because the spectrum of
opinion within the medical world includes many doctors who firmly support abortion on
request. Without any supervision or restraint, they naturally and understandably would put
their own beliefs into practice. Having been thus challenged, and to ensure that I obtained as
balanced a view of electoral opinion as possible, another questionnaire was circulated on my
behalf. I did this very reluctantly, because I have seen enough of surveys to know their
limitations, and I knew that another survey would just add to the heat of an emotion-charged
situation, but I felt it had to be done.

The wording of this questionnaire was simple, namely, "Do you or do you not want an
abortion on request, yes or no?" A number of people who did not know why the wording
was deliberately confined, without realising how it originated or what I wanted to check,
were critical of the survey. Some said that, because there was no direct mention of abortion
on demand or abortion on request in the Bill, this latest questionnaire was irrelevant. The
questionnaire form was distributed to people in various parts of the northern half of my
electorate. It was impossible to undertake a full survey in the time available, but a number of
volunteers worked wonders and managed to obtain 2136 signatures in a very short time; for
this I thank them most warmly.
I cannot and do not claim-and I underline this-that the survey was done on a
scientific sampling basis. That would have taken far more time than we had available. I must
also say that some reports indicated that the survey had been circulated among interest
groups where there was a heavy predominance of one point of view. On the other hand, the
survey, involving over 2000 adult signatories, is too big to be dismissed, and the survey as a
whole was by no means confined to church or other possible vested interest groups.
Christians are certainly heavily represented among the signatories, but then the churches are
strongly represented in my electorate anyway. I have offered to show the questionnaire
forms to one of the leading organisers of the Warkworth petition, should she wish to see
them.
Of the 2136 signatories to the questionnaire on my behalf, 1566 said no to abortion on
request and 570 said yes. Because of the limitations I have mentioned I do not submit these
figures as being conclusive, but I do believe they indicate there was substance to my claim on
TV about electorate feeling on the abortion on request issue. In addition, 265 letters I have
received from constituents oppose abortion on request, and 137 support liberalisation of the
law to some degree. I predict now that the response of many of my opponents will be, "Why
not have a referendum?" Well, I must admit that if there had been a referendum every
member in this House would have been spared untold effort, anguish and, in some cases, a
considerable degree of disillusionment. Whatever the pros and cons of a referendum—and I
challenge anyone to come up with a generally acceptable form of wording for a ballot; or do
people think that members of Parliament should decide the wording?-it is each member's
duty to vote in this Chamber so long as Parliament is the place where the decision is to be
made. No one can duck that responsibility because he might prefer a referendum or might
see it as the easier way out.
For the rest, I have little to add to what has already been said by others. I personally
cannot vote for a system that would allow abortion on request. If there is one reference point
for all our endeavours in this House, it is life. Most of what we do and plan for is directed
towards protecting lives, prolonging lives, and improving the quality of lives, and, to me, the
passing of a law that would admit abortion on request would run counter to those
endeavours, because I accept that the foetus has life and has the right to live. I also seek a
workable law. We cannot once again go through all the trauma of the drawn-out ritual of yet
another abortion Bill that proves unworkable. If that is subsequently shown, then we will
have to cut our losses, admit that Parliament cannot successfully deal with the issue, and
throw it all on to a referendum. If we do, I hope that we can overcome the problem that a
referendum would entail. I do not want Parliament to be seen to fail on this matter, but I
believe there is a very real danger that it will if we make the wrong decision.
Judging from the trends, from remarks, and from letters sent to me, I have concluded
that the panel system is not workable. I always knew there were opponents of the panel
system inside and outside my electorate, but I underestimated the extent of the opposition to
that system. I now seriously doubt if there would be sufficient public support for the system,
which appears to provoke very real fears in the minds of many women. On the other hand,
the amendment to be introduced by the member for Franklin seems to avoid the dehumanis-
ing effects of the panel system, while being based essentially on the same thinking that
produced the royal commission report. Also, it fits in neatly with normal medical proce-
dures. I am not impressed with the evidence produced tonight alleging non co-operation
from sectors of the medical profession. To take liberties with an observation made by a
former United States Supreme Court judge, this Chamber is neither infallible because it is
final nor final because it is infallible. From the outset we have had to grapple with an
impossible task in finding a generally acceptable abortion law. It is partly our own fault that
we have not made more progress, but it does no harm to remind an increasingly critical
public that we are trying to grapple with an issue which is as intractable as it is unwanted.

MARILYN WARING (Raglan): The Royal Commission on Contraception, Sterilisa-
tion, and Abortion, appointed in 1975 and chaired by Mr Justice McMullin, presented its
report to the Government in March. My research tells me that since 1947 there have been 35
royal commissions in New Zealand, and no legislative action has directly emanated from any
one of them until this time. The position that this House faces, then, is unprecedented,
according to my research. In that respect it is very interesting to look at the performance of
the members of the royal commission.
In June, Mrs Barbara Thomson and Mr Maurice McGregor announced their reserva-
tions about their own proposed panel system. They made those statements as a matter of
principle. Two further members of the commission have in private expressed doubts and
reservations about their findings. They too are persons of principle, but their principles are
otherwise directed than to make those findings public. Having signed their names to a
document, they feel morally obliged to adhere to the recommendations regardless of public
and professional opposition. The only medical member of the royal commission was openly
and publicly opposed to abortion before being appointed as a member, yet I know he has
referred patients to the Auckland Medical Aid Centre.
These facts raise important issues; first, of objectivity, and, secondly, of unanimity on
the royal commission. It is interesting to recall, in the light of those facts, the statement of
the New Zealand Association of Scientists, which in August 1977 stated that unsupported
statements, imprecise definitions, and uncritical evaluation of contradictory research find-
ings are to be found in the report. These scientific shortcomings are serious enough to raise
doubts about the report's recommendations as a basis for legislation.
During the second reading debate I shall address myself to only one issue. There will be
opportunity for further participation on other issues during the Committee stage. The proper
formulation of the issue involved in the abortion question is not whether or to what extent
abortion should be permitted, but whether and to what extent the freedom of decision that
modern medicine now makes possible should be abridged.
If in the final analysis there is one principle that is acknowledged to be the standard by
which the political arrangements as a whole are judged, and by which the fitness of proposed
laws are measured, it is the principle of liberty paraphrased in the 1975 National Party
manifesto as "freedoms". It is the object of the constitution to secure the greatest possible
freedoms for citizens who live and work in the State, and to make whatever sense they can of
their lives with the minimum of interference. Where, from a consideration of personal
freedom, there is doubt about the specific content of legislation-and there is in this
case or substantial disagreement about the broader premise on which the legislation must
be justified-and there is in this case-the presumptions of liberty must prevail. The acid test

Mr MINOGUE (Hamilton West): I have listened with considerable interest to the
speakers who have preceded me in this debate. It is appropriate that my turn to speak should
come at 10 minutes to 2 in the morning. I believe it indicates the approach of this worthy
establishment to serious issues. I seriously question whether it is possible for people to
concentrate on the issues involved in this serious matter at this hour of the morning. I would
question seriously also whether the format of this debate has permitted intelligent discus-
sion. It seems to me to have been a hotchpotch of abortion, education, and other issues, out
of which it is impossible to discern any clear philosophy, or any clear direction as to which
way we should go on any one of the various issues involved.
It is my belief that if the House passes this legislation as it pertains to abortion in
anything like its present form, it will have failed to discharge its responsibilities as a
democratic institution. I say that, not only from the manner in which we have discussed this
matter, but also from the approach to the whole question that is evident in so much of what
has been said. If we pass this legislation in anything like its present form, we will have
opened the way not only to abortion on demand, but also to legislation on the demand of


## p. 3583 (#465) ###########################################

11 October
3583
Contraception, Sterilisation, and Abortion Bill
pressure groups that claim that their views should be imposed on other people who do not
happen to hold those views. It is a pressure group that believes its convictions should be
translated into the law of the land.
Let me illustrate the failure of democracy as I see it. I believe it would be possible for a
woman to say to any member of this House, "I believe in the view expressed by the royal
commission that life begins at conception or implantation. I believe that abortion is totally
wrong. I will not practise it, and I will continually preach against it. What is your view, as a
parliamentarian, to my rights?" I would feel bound to say, "It is your privilege to hold those
views, and my duty to uphold you." On the other hand, another woman could advance the
view that she did not agree with the findings of the royal commission that life begins at
conception or implantation, but adopted the view of the United States Supreme Court—an
even more august institution than our royal commission—that life begins with viability, and
that it is the responsibility of the State to ensure that women are looked after adequately
should they seek recourse to abortion after responsible medical consultation. Such a woman
could claim that she had a view to express that was at total variance with the first. She, too,
could ask a parliamentarian for his views. Again, my reply would be that I would uphold her
right to believe in and the right to practise her conviction.
I believe we are getting close to the essence of democracy in this discussion, because out
of those two conflicting views it is the duty of a democratic parliament to come to a solution
that enables not merely the expression, but also the practice of various opinions. However,
that is not what we are proposing to do. We are proposing to come down on the side, the
only one, that imposes on other people a particular philosophy and belief. The philosophy of
the second woman would in no way preclude the first from carrying out her belief, but the
philosophy of the first is a total denial of the beliefs of the other party. Is this democracy? I
think democracy is dying, and it is appropriate that it should be doing so at five to two in the
morning.
I have very grave reservations about this whole affair. A panel system in any form, open
or disguised, will not work for some very obvious reasons, especially those advanced in the
report of the Canadian committee on the operation of the abortion laws in that country,
published in January 1977. A panel system operates in Canada, and it was the duty of the
committee to report on whether or not the law was operating equitably. A summary of the
committee's findings states: "The procedures set out for the operation of the abortion law
are not working equitably. In almost every aspect there is considerable confusion, unclear
standards, or social inequity involved. There is diverse interpretation of the indications for
abortion. There are sharp disparities in the distribution and acceptability of therapeutic
abortion services, there is a continuing exodus of Canadian women to the United States to
obtain abortions, and there are unacceptable delays experienced by women seeking to
obtain induced abortions in Canada."
That is the result of a panel system, yet we are told that if we establish a panel system
here we will rid ourselves of these self-same uncertainties, disparities, and inequities.
Nothing could be further from the truth. The same problems of interpretation will arise. For
instance, how will a diversity of panels or committees interpret the word "health"? How will
they approach the problem of psychiatric illness? Will they accept the certificates of
psychiatrists, and will there be as many opinions as there are psychiatrists? We are deluding
ourselves entirely if we imagine that the panel system will remove those evils illustrated by
the Canadian system. We are adopting methods that are self-defeating. How could we obtain
a uniform abortion law in this country devoid of those uncertainties? There is only one way,
and that would be if the supervisory committee in fact reduced the panels or the certificated
doctors to the status of mere rubber stamps, carrying out the orders of the supervisory
committee. Is that intended? Is that what people mean when they say we will have
uniformity in the abortion laws? That is totally contrary to any notion of democracy. It is a
total denial of justice in the courts, and is something that I will have nothing to do with even
at this hour of the morning.
I think that the passage of the Bill-the reasoning that is being advanced in respect of
panels-is insupportable. It reflects a state of total confusion that amounts in my view to a
denial of the democratic process that the House should be asserting. I think it very honest of
the people concerned who have said that they are confused, that they do not know how they
should decide this issue. For those who are confused, and wander in the wilderness, I say
that they should decide it on the basis of upholding the democratic institutions of this
country.

Water and Soil Conservation Amendment Bill
WEDNESDAY, 12 OCTOBER 1977
Mr Acting Speaker took the chair at 2.30 p.m.

WATER AND SOIL CONSERVATION AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. W. L. YOUNG (Minister of Works and Development): I move, That the Water
and Soil Conservation Amendment Bill be introduced. The purpose of this Bill and of the
following one, the Soil Conservation and Rivers Control Amendment Bill, is to enable
catchment authorities to raise the revenue required to meet their administrative expenses.
The changes proposed will not necessarily enable all catchment authorities to raise sufficient
revenue to meet the whole of their administrative expenses. Of the 20 catchment authorities
in the country, 3 or 4 will still require some assistance from the Government by way of an
administration grant. However, the grants presently being made by the Government should
be reduced by at least 50 percent. This year $625,000 has been set aside to assist catchment
authorities to meet their administrative costs.
This Bill empowers each regional water board to fix an annual charge not exceeding $10
for each water right. The annual charge is intended to cover some of the costs of monitoring
and supervising water rights. It is most important that the functions of regional water boards
in policing and supervising water rights are carried out, so that the boards can fulfil their
proper role in water management. It is considered that the holders of water rights should
make some contribution to the costs of this activity, and this has led to the provision for an
annual charge. Provision is also made for the Crown to make a grant to a regional water
board in lieu of the annual rate.
Cabinet has also approved an increase in the application fee for a water right from $4 to
$30. Provision for this increase will be contained in an amendment to the Water and Soil
Conservation Regulations that is being prepared. The amount expected to be raised
throughout New Zealand by the increase in the application fee is about $10,000 a year, and it
is expected that the annual charge for monitoring water rights will yield approximately
$37,000 at the maximum charge. Further provision for meeting administrative costs will be
contained in the Soil Conservation and Rivers Control Amendment Bill.
Hon. MICHAEL CONNELLY (Wigram): The Minister said that a charge is to be made
to those who have access to water. Will the charge be uniform on all those who have water
rights, or will there be different charges for large users and small users, and perhaps those
who fit into the domestic category? The increase from $4 to $30 is a large increase-750
percent and while I know that inflation is proceeding apace, it has not quite reached that
rate yet. Is the increase somehow related to future Government policy? Otherwise, how can
the Government justify an increase of that magnitude?
Hon. W. L. YOUNG (Minister of Works and Development): The charge is up to $10 per
right; the maximum is $10 by way of administrative charge. On the question of the increase
from $4 to $30, as the member for Wigram will know, as long ago as 1973 it was said that
extra finance was required, and the Labour Government was going to do something about it
in 1975. It is quite unrealistic to go through the processes of granting water rights,
advertising, and carrying out the attendant investigations, for $4, particularly when the water
right can remain for several years. With that in mind, the member will realise the
appropriateness of the increase, which is not entirely related to inflation but more to the
expenses involved in granting the right.
Hon. R. L. BAILEY (Heretaunga): The proposed new section 24K(2) states, “Nothing
in subsection (1) of this section shall apply to the taking or use of any natural water that is
reasonably required for domestic needs, the needs of animals, or for or in connection with
fire-fighting purposes." Could the Minister explain what this means so far as irrigation is
concerned, in the rural sector particularly? I know that, under the present system, people
who use irrigation must pay a fee. I wonder if this has any overlapping effect. I note that
animals are exempted, and domestic needs, as well as fire-fighting purposes. The Minister
said that the funds would offset some of the investigation work required. How much is being
spent on investigation of water resources now? The Minister may have a ready reference,
and it may even be in the estimates. How far will this go towards meeting some of that cost?
The Minister referred to $10,000 in one instance, and to $30,000 in another.

SOIL CONSERVATION AND RIVERS CONTROL AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. W. L. YOUNG (Minister of Works and Development): I move, That the Soil
Conservation and Rivers Control Amendment Bill be introduced. The Bill is complementary
to the Water and Soil Conservation Amendment Bill, which has just been introduced. The
Bill increases from 0.03472c in the $1 to 0.05c in the $1 the maximum administrative rate that
can be levied by a catchment authority each year on all rateable property within its district.
About half the catchment authorities are already levying the maximum rate permitted by the
Act. Of these, five are being assisted by the Government to meet deficits in the administra-
tion account. The charges proposed in this and the preceding Bill will provide needed
assistance to catchment authorities in meeting their administrative expenses, and further
enable them to carry out efficiently and effectively their important role in salt-water and soil
management.

Oral Answers to Questions
ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTION
Snapper Fisheries Protection
1. Mr COURTNEY (Nelson) asked the Minister of Defence: Does he intend to take any
action to protect foreign fishing vessels from the shots of indignant west coast snapper
fishermen as reported in the New Zealand Herald of 7 October 1977?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Acting Minister of Defence): The Government deplores the
suggestion-and it is no more than that-that New Zealand fishermen would be prepared to
consider using firearms to warn off foreign fishermen or to take the law into their own hands
in any other way. The Government will not tolerate unlawful interference with foreign
fishing operations, and would proceed against any persons using firearms in this manner,
under the appropriate provisions of the Crimes Act or the Fisheries Act. I emphasise also
that, as stated by the Minister of Fisheries when replying to an earlier question by the
honourable member, the Government will be keeping the operations of foreign fishing
vessels in the west coast snapper beds under careful observation, and will be taking whatever
action may be necessary to ensure that the resources of that area are properly managed.
Mr Courtney: Does the Government intend to investigate the situation-the one where
it is said that 140 Auckland share fishermen met and there was talk of fishermen steaming
across foreign trawl lines and putting to sea with rifles to shoot across the bows of foreign
craft-to ensure that it develops no further?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: There is constant patrolling of the area. I cannot say whether
a complaint has been laid officially by any fishermen. The particular matter reported stated
that fishermen were talking of doing so-and-so if something else happened. I suggest that the
member bring evidence that there has been a definite breach before he asks a question that
is, to a certain extent, hypothetical.
Hon. W. W. Freer: What action does the Government contemplate taking to avoid the
development of a situation such as the one referred to in the original question?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: We shall maintain a constant watch over the operations of
both foreign and local fishing vessels.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.
Pregnancy Arising from Rape
2. Mr BRILL (Kapiti) asked the Minister of Police: Has his department had occasion to
investigate the incidence of pregnancy arising from proven rape, and, if so, what was the
outcome of the inquiries?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I reply on behalf of the Acting Minister
of Police. The police investigate complaints of rape, which are usually reported immediately
after the incident. Complainants are medically examined in relation to the rape offence and
are usually advised to discuss the possibility of pregnancy with their own doctor. The police
have had no occasion to investigate the incidence of pregnancy arising from proven rape and
have no statistics on the number of pregnancies attributable to such rapes.
Mr Hunt: Has the Minister any statistics to indicate that, even though there is no police
investigation, there might still be a great deal of evidence of rape occurring in the
community?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: I am not sure whether the honourable member wants me to
reply to that question in my capacity as speaking on behalf of the Acting Minister of Police or
as Minister of Justice. Speaking as Minister of Justice, the only indication of a serious study I
know of is that referred to in the report of the Royal Commission on Contraception,
Sterilisation, and Abortion, which I have no doubt the honourable member will have read.
The commission indicated that it had no evidence of any such pregnancy being reported
since the Bourne case, which, of course, was not in New Zealand.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.

Wellington Hospital-Management Consultants
4. Mr BRILL (Kapiti) asked the Minister of Health: Has he seen recent press reports
about the comments made by the treasurer of the Wellington Hospital Board over the use of
management consultants at Wellington Hospital, and, if so, does he intend to take up with
the board any question as to the accuracy of these comments?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry): The Minister of
Health replies as follows: "I have seen the reports referred to. It is a matter for the board to
decide what action, if any, it may take on statements made by a member of its staff. I should
point out, however, that right from the start of the consultancy in 1973 the activities of the
management consultants have been guided and monitored by a steering committee set up for
this purpose. The committee, which has Mr Alan Atkinson, a former Chairman of the State
Services Commission, as an independent chairman, also includes three members of the
Wellington Hospital Board and top board and Department of Health executives. I under-
stand that this steering committee is satisfied that the work of the consultants has resulted in
the more effective use of the board's services for the benefit of the patients using these
services. Further, in one of the press reports, the chairman of the Wellington Hospital Board
is on record as saying that, on balance, the consultants had provided value for money. The
lessons learnt are also being taken up and applied in other hospital board areas."

Maori Farmers
6. Mr BELL (Gisborne) asked the Minister of Maori Affairs: Can he give the number of
new Maori farmers settled on previously European-owned land in (i) the year ended 31
March 1977, (ii) the 10-year period to 31 March 1977, and the area of land involved in each
case?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Maori Affairs): No statistics are available which can
exactly answer the question. Page 12 of the report of the Department of Maori Affairs for
the year ended 31 March 1977 goes part of the way, but it will be appreciated that the
department can only give information for farmers who have been financially assisted from
that source. There are possibly other Maori farmers who have purchased their properties
with finance raised elsewhere. Departmental statistics for Maori farmers are compiled on a 1
July to 30 June year, and for the year ended 30 June 1976, 7 farmers were assisted into the
purchase of 475 hectares of general land. In the year 1 April 1976 to 31 March 1977, 14 loans
were approved to enable Maoris to purchase 920 hectares of general land. The department
has not maintained records with this information for the past 10 years, but the report shows
that over the past 4 years purchases of general land for Maori farmers and other Maori
interests include: general land purchased by farmers financed by the department, 2213
hectares; general land purchased by farmers financed by the Maori Trustee, 196 hectares;
general land purchased by Maori incorporations and farmers under section 460 of the Maori
Affairs Act, 327 hectares; and general land purchased for rounding off development
schemes, 315 hectares; making a total of 3051 hectares.
Mr Couch: Is it the Government's policy to continue buying general land for Maori
farmers?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE: Yes.
Mr Bell: In cases of European land now being farmed by Maoris, does that land in the
main retain a European title or does it assume the category of Maori land?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE: The term "European" has gone. The term is now “general”
land. The title remains as is when a property is taken over unless it is being added to a piece
of land that is classified as Maori land.

Snapper Fisheries Protection
7. Mr COURTNEY (Nelson) asked the Minister of Fisheries: Has he seen the article in
the New Zealand Herald of 7 October 1977 in which the N.Z. Share Fishermen's Association
president alleges that a number of foreign fishing boats working the area from Albatross
Point northwards to Muriwai beach would cause grave and permanent damage to snapper
stocks if immediate action were not taken, and, if so, is it true?
Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Minister of Fisheries): Yes, I have seen the article in the New
Zealand Herald of 7 October 1977 regarding foreign fishing boats working outside our 12-
mile territorial sea zone, from Albatross Point northwards to Muriwai beach. Consideration
will be given to the need to close other areas on the west coast of the North Island to foreign
trawlers if this is found to be necessary. However, a recent report has indicated that the
foreign fishing vessels in that area were catching mainly barracouta.
Mr Courtney: Was it an oversight that areas on the west coast were not restricted as they
were on the East Coast; will the area of restriction come first; is the Minister aware that most
of the snapper is caught outside the 12-mile limit; and can the fishermen in this area expect
an early decision on restrictions?
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: Order! I remind the honourable member that supplementary
questions are usually just one question. We sometimes have a couple tagged together, but
not a whole string of them.
Hon. J. B. BOLGER: The non-exclusion of this zone to foreign vessels was not an
oversight, but was the Government's policy after it had analysed catch records over the past
few years. The member also asked whether the Government would move quickly on this
matter, and my answer is that action will be taken if and when it is shown that the fishing
taking place is damaging to the fish stocks.
Hon. M. Rata: Will the Minister confirm that foreign fishing boats have been working in
this area, and, if so, what action has been or will be taken?
Hon. J. B. BOLGER: Foreign fishing vessels have been working outside the 12-mile
zone in the area referred to, and the catch was mainly barracouta. The question expressed
some concern about damage to the snapper fishery. I informed the House yesterday that the
latest information shows that many of these vessels have now moved out of the area.

Brockville School-Classrooms
3. Mr MacDONELL (Dunedin Central) asked the Minister of Education: In view of the
fact that two prefabricated classrooms are to be replaced with a transportable classroom at
the Brockville School, how can he justify such a move when the roll is expanding, bearing in
mind that a transportable classroom holds less than half the pupils accommodated in two
prefabricated classrooms and lacks toilet and hand-washing facilities?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied: The prefabricated classrooms
which are to be replaced are a double unit, only one room of which is being used. The
classrooms will be replaced by a transportable unit classroom which will include toilet and
hand-washing facilities. The school at present has 20 classrooms, 4 of which are in
prefabricated double units. The Otago Education Board hopes to replace the other double
unit later this financial year with another unit classroom should funds permit. For its present
roll of 578 only 17 classrooms are required, so the school has ample accommodation for its
current needs. The forecast rolls indicate that expansion will not be as great as previously
expected and the accommodation requirement for 1978 and 1979 is expected to be 18
classrooms.
(22/9/77)
Meat Grading Standards
4. Mr MacDONELL (Dunedin Central) asked the Minister of Agriculture: Can any beef
graded "manufacturing" or "L2" for export in freezing works be regraded for local


## p. 3601 (#483) ###########################################

12 October
3601
Questions and Replies
consumption as "prime" or "choice" under existing regulations, and, if so, would this be in
the public interest?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Agriculture) replied: It would be most unusual for a
beef carcass graded for export as "manufacturing" or "L2" to be graded correctly as
"prime" or "choice" under the local consumption grading standard. Export grading is
carried out by company graders in accordance with standards laid down by the New Zealand
Meat Producers Board, while local consumption grading standards are those specified in the
New Zealand standard specification titled "Grades of Meat and Definitions of Cuts of Meat
for Sale on the New Zealand Market". In freezing works that do not also operate as a local
authority abattoir, local consumption grading is undertaken by works staff, although their
standards are subject to test checking by Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries staff. At
abattoirs, including those operated at freezing works under delegation from a local author-
ity, local consumption grading is carried out by Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries staff.
Export grading is basically aimed at facilitating trade, and is generally a case of putting "like
with like" according to weight and conformation. On the other hand, local consumption
grading is more consumer oriented. With export and local consumption beef grading each
having its own standard it may not be impossible for the grading extremes mentioned to be
obtained, but it is most unlikely. If grading is carried out correctly there seems little chance
of the public interest being adversely affected.
(23/9/77)
Burnside Freezing Works-Meat Grading
5. Mr MacDONELL (Dunedin Central) asked the Minister of Agriculture: What propor-
tion of the beef killed at Burnside Freezing Works is regraded and sold for local consump-
tion?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Agriculture) replied: Since about June last year no
meat produced at the Burnside freezing works has been regraded from an export grade to a
local consumption grade. By arrangement with Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries staff,
the works management now nominates, before the meat is graded, whether or not it is to be
exported or used locally. Grading is then done in accordance with the export or local grading
standards as appropriate. About 28 percent of all beef produced at Burnside is put on the
local market, and the grading of this is supervised by Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries
staff.
(23/9/77)

Education-Itinerant Teachers
8. Mr BRILL (Kapiti) asked the Minister of Education: How many itinerant teachers have
been appointed in this financial year for the purpose of co-ordinating remedial teaching
programmes carried out in primary schools, and how many such teachers are at present
being trained?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied: No additional positions for
itinerant teachers of reading have been created this financial year. A total of 10 such teachers
is employed to carry out and co-ordinate remedial teaching programmes in primary schools
in selected areas. Teachers appointed to these positions are drawn from the general teaching
field. Appointments are made from those teachers who have shown particular strengths in
teaching reading. No specialist training is given prior to appointment, but up to a month of
directed observation and study under the supervision of district advisers on reading is
provided for all appointees. This usually includes a short placement with a reading clinic.
The itinerant teachers are encouraged to continue studies relevant to their work through
courses provided by universities, teachers colleges, and the Department of Education's unit
providing advanced studies for teachers. They are also involved in relevant in-service
training courses for teachers.
(27/9/77)
Education-Literacy and Numeracy Standards
9. Mr BRILL (Kapiti) asked the Minister of Education: Have any surveys been under-
taken to ascertain whether literacy and numeracy amongst entrants to secondary school are
higher today than in earlier decades, and, if so, what were the results of such surveys, and by
whom were the surveys undertaken?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied: There have been no surveys of
literacy and numeracy in the terms specified by the honourable member in his question.
However, national surveys on reading covering a wider age range of pupils have at various
times been conducted by the New Zealand Council for Educational Research. The first
survey, based upon the Australian Council of Educational Research reading test adjusted for
New Zealand conditions, showed that, for most pupils, between 1952 and 1965 there had
been a significant improvement in reading skills. A second survey covering the period 1968
to 1974 used the progressive achievement test in reading comprehension and vocabulary
developed by the New Zealand Council for Educational Research. Results of this survey
indicated that there was no real change between 1968 and 1974. A 7-year study of
computational skills based upon the progressive achievement test in mathematics is currently
being conducted by the Department of Education. This study is not sufficiently advanced to
draw even interim conclusions.
Details of the various surveys are:
Reading (1) The surveys referred to are as follows (a) In May 1952 the New Zealand
Council for Educational Research standardised the ACER reading test on a national sample
of children aged between 8 and 13 years. In 1965 a similar survey, using the schools and a
comparable sample of pupils, was conducted. Two tests were used, a 30-minute reading
comprehension and a 10-minute vocabulary test. The results showed that at age 12 years 80
percent of the children had higher attainment in reading skills than recorded in 1952. It was
also noted that there was some decline in ability among the 20 percent of less able pupils.
Hence the range of reading attainment had widened over the 13-year period; (b) NZCER
established norms in 1968 for the progressive achievement tests of reading which comprised
comprehension and vocabulary, using a national sample of 7000 children aged 8 to 14 years.
The tests were applied to the same age groups from the same schools in 1974. There was a
rise in reading comprehension test scores at the lower age levels and some slight decline in
vocabulary, but overall there was no shift in standards. (2) In the years 1936 and 1968 the
Otis test of mental ability was administered to a 20 percent sample of children in the
9-13-year age group. The Otis test had significant elements of both reading comprehension
and computational skills inherent in the test. Results showed that in the 32-year period there
was a shift upwards of approximately one year of mental age. This is interpreted as a steady
improvement in the skills associated with the test. Mathematics-(3) There is very little
reliable research on which to base statements about changes in mathematical skills. While a
number of studies have been made, the samples have been too small and geographically too
isolated to draw any valid conclusions. However, the evidence available suggests a decline in


## p. 3603 (#485) ###########################################

3603
Questions and Replies
basic computational skills, but there is insufficient evidence to show whether there has been
any change in the ability to handle other mathematical concepts. (4) Because of the paucity
of information, a 7-year longitudinal study of a sample of pupils using the progressive
achievement tests in mathematics has been instituted. The survey is now in its third year, and
an interim report is expected to be available in about 18 months. (5) The International
Education Association surveys have provided baseline data against which to judge shifts in
educational standards. However, the IEA studies are of recent origin and, although they can
be repeated, it is probably too early to draw any valid conclusions on shifts which may occur.

available to all students in such subjects as: remedial reading (at Hamilton); the teaching of
slow learners (at Christchurch and Wellington); and the education of the handicapped (at

Waitangi Trust Board-Income and Expenditure
13. Mr BELL (Gisborne) asked the Minister of Lands: Could he advise how the income
from rentals and from other sources received by the Waitangi Trust Board is utilised?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Lands) replied: The Waitangi National Trust property
covers 480 hectares, and was presented to the nation in the 1930s by a former Governor-
General and his wife, Lord and Lady Bledisloe. The board is charged under the deed of trust
to administer the property as a place of historic interest, recreation, enjoyment, and benefit
for the people of New Zealand. Adjoining the board's property is a 580-hectare endowment
forest managed by the New Zealand Forest Service, and also a gift from Lord and Lady
Bledisloe. The trust board receives timber royalties from the forest. The major source of
income is admission fees to the Treaty House and grounds, and approximately 90 000 people
are expected to visit the property during the Board's 1977-78 financial year (1 July/30 June).
Additional income is received from the sale of books, postcards, coloured slides, a small
grant from Government towards the Waitangi Day expenses, and rentals from five lessees.
Present income is approximately $100,000 per annum. Expenses each year total a similar
amount, and range over such items as wages, expenses for Waitangi Day, and maintenance
and capital expenditure on buildings, plant, vehicles, and grounds. A continuing tree-
planting programme is undertaken and, as finance permits, recreational facilities are
developed. For example, a walking track from the boat ramp near the Waitangi Hotel to
Haruru Falls is planned for construction during the board's 1977-78 financial year, and this is
estimated to cost $7,500. The major project at the present time, however, is the refurbishing
of the Treaty House. This involves structural alterations and the acquisition of period
furnishings. The cost of this in the 1977-78 year is estimated at $20,000. The work is to be
done in stages, and eventually the house will be presented to the public as a dwelling of the
1870s, the period from which most of the present structure dates. The front portion of the
house containing 3 rooms, which is all that existed when the Treaty of Waitangi was signed in
1840, will be given special treatment to recall this earlier period.
(27/9/77)

Monofilament Nets
15. Mr COURTNEY (Nelson) asked the Minister of Fisheries: What measures, if any,
does the Government intend to take to control or ban the use of monofilament nets, the
disadvantages of which are described in the latest issue of Catch 77?
Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Minister of Fisheries) replied: The Ministry has initiated a study on
set-netting, chiefly in the Bay of Plenty, to look at the effects of set-netting as a fishing
method. This will include making recommendations on the future use and control of
monofilament nets. The programme to study set-netting was set up in late 1976–77. It will
probably cover a period of 2 to 3 years, and results will be indicated periodically during that
time. The aims of the study are: (a) to ascertain the most efficient methods of set-netting; (b)
to look at the effects of set-netting on commercial fisheries of inshore reefs; and (c) to
expand set-netting as a technique to other species and into deeper water.
(28/9/77)
Fish Farming
16. Mr COURTNEY (Nelson) asked the Minister of Fisheries: Has he seen the article in
the Otago Daily Times of 19 August in which a scientist, Mr C. D. Wallace, supported the
concept of fish farming, and in particular trout farming, and said that the fear of disease in
wild stock was ill founded, and, if so, does the Government intend to change its stance on
fish farming?
Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Minister of Fisheries) replied: I have seen the article in the Otago
Daily Times of 19 August which reported on Mr C. D. Anderson's address given to the New
Zealand Veterinary Association's symposium at the New Zealand Institute of Agricultural
Science convention. It is the Government's policy to encourage fish farming in New
Zealand. However, except on the Chatham Islands, trout farming is prohibited in New
Zealand, and the Government is not considering any changes to this policy.

Mangapurua and Mangatiti Valleys-Farm Land
18. Mr WETERE (Western Maori) asked the Minister of Lands: Has he seen the article in
the Wanganui Chronicle of 31 August which alleges that farmers leasing land in the
Mangapurua and Mangatiti Valleys, north-west of Raetihi, would be encouraged to give up
their holdings, and, if so, is this a fact, and what sort of encouragement will be given to these
farmers to leave the land?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Lands) replied: I have seen the article to which the
member refers. This mentions in part a land-use study that has recently been completed by
the Department of Lands and Survey of approximately 28 000 ha of Crown land in the
Mangapurua and Mangatiti Valleys. Of this land, 3325 ha are at present leased on a
temporary basis to adjoining farmers, and for continuity the study has also included 1125 ha
of private land situated within the Mangapurua and Mangatiti catchments. When printed,
the study report will be available for public comment. All submissions will be evaluated by
the Land Settlement Board, and my department will then make known to me recommenda-
tions regarding the future land use options. Until this action has been taken I am unable to
comment further on the future of the temporary leases. I can assure the member, however,
that the ownership of the 1125 ha of private land is not threatened. Should the report
recommend accordingly, the Crown would purchase these properties only if the owners were
willing to sell, and then it would be at current market valuation.

Mansion House Hotel
19. Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert) asked the Minister of Lands: Is it correct that action
is being taken to close Mansion House Hotel on Kawau Island and to remove a number of
amenities, including the post office?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Lands) replied: It is correct that the lessee company of
the Mansion House Hotel intends to surrender its lease because it is not profitable.
Arrangements for the surrender are at present being negotiated by the Hauraki Gulf
Maritime Park Board as the hotel is on park-board-controlled land. The board is also
negotiating with the postal authorities on the continued operation of the post office. The
store at Mansion House has not operated for over a year, but the board sees the need for
some retail outlet in Mansion House Bay and is studying the options which are available. In
terms of its approved working plan for Kawau reserves, the park board intends to restore
Mansion House as an historic building for public appreciation and interpretation. It will
ideally become a park visitor centre.
