Mihiwaka Tunnel Derailment
21. Mr MacDONELL (Dunedin Central) asked the Minister of Railways: In view of the
derailment in the Mihiwaka Tunnel on 16 September, the eighth on this section of track this
year, what urgent action is he taking to stop any reoccurrence?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Railways) replied: It is not possible completely
to eliminate derailments. Six derailments have occured this year in the area referred to; of
these two were caused by track conditions, one by improper loading, one by ground
conditions, one by a combination of track and wagon interaction, and the latest by a fault in
a wagon wheel. This area is known to be a difficult area for track maintenance, and work has
been under way for some time on embankment stabilisation and improvement. In addition,
the department's inspectorial staff pay particular attention to the area so that developing
trouble can be remedied at the earliest possible stage.
(29/9/77)
Wairarapa Storm Damage-Government Assistance
22. Mr WETERE (Western Maori) asked the Minister of Agriculture: Can he list the
measures being taken to assist the farmers who are suffering so fearfully in the wet weather
in the Wairarapa?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Agriculture) replied: The Government has approved
the following measures designed to assist farmers who have been adversely affected by
climatic conditions in the Wairarapa: (a) refunds of freight costs by commercial transport up
to $10 per tonne on stock feeds on the customary terms; (b) refunds of freight charges by
commercial transport for livestock from the relief area removed for grazing elsewhere, on
the customary terms; the concession to be limited to the outward journey for a maximum of
160 km; (c) transport subsidy for use of farmers' own trucks for cartage of stock feeds, at the
rate of 6c per tonne-kilometre, up to a maximum of $10 per tonne, and for livestock cartage
at 6c per tonne-kilometre, the concession to be limited to the outward journey for a
maximum of 160 km; (d) regrassing subsidy of up to $25 per hectare on the customary terms;
(e) availability of suspensory loans through the Rural Banking and Finance Corporation in
cases of severe hardship; (f) payment of 50 percent of the cost of helicopter flying time on
farmers' properties where hay and/or supplementary feeding is necessary; and (g) refund of
75 percent of costs incurred by farmers since 1 September 1977 in feeding out dairy meal to
keep stock alive. Consideration will be given to further proposals to be put forward by the
Wairarapa Adverse Climatic Disturbance Relief Committee following its initial meeting on
Monday, 26 September.
(29/9/77)
Lower Wairarapa Valley Development Scheme
23. Mr WETERE (Western Maori) asked the Minister of Works and Development: When
will the Government supply the necessary funding for the Lower Wairarapa catchment
development scheme as outlined in an article in the Wairarapa Times-Age on 16 September?
Hon. W. L. YOUNG (Minister of Works and Development) replied: The Lower
Wairarapa Valley scheme was approved by the Government in 1960 with a 3:1 subsidy on an
estimated cost of $4,898,000. In 1963 the Government agreed to provide a loan of $470,000
over 10 years so that the work could be done in 10 years instead of the original programme of
20 years. By March 1972 several major items of work were largely finished. On 24 November
1975 the Cabinet approved a revised estimate of $7,136,000 for this scheme, with the
provision of a grant amounting to $5,352,000. The Government contribution is made
available to the Wairarapa Catchment Board according to the needs of the board's works
programme. In 1976-77, $200,000 was made available, and at 31 March 1977 the Govern-
ment contribution already made available for this scheme totalled $4,479,000. For 1977-78,
a contribution of $265,000 by the Government has been allowed for. I understand that the
board has been revising its programme, but this has not yet been submitted to the Soil
Conservation and Rivers Control Council. In this programme some of the works are being
brought forward. When the revised programme is received, the allocation of funds will be
reconsidered. The scheme for the Upper Ruamahanga catchment was received by the Soil
Conservation and Rivers Control Council on 17 May 1977. Further consideration was
deferred pending examination of economic, environmental, and other matters. I expect that
provision will be made in next year's estimates (1978–79) for the commencement of this
scheme.

Police Jails-Use as Remand Prisons
28. Mr KIRK (Sydenham) asked the Minister of Police: Arising from his reply to a
question for oral answer on Friday, 9 September, when he indicated that there were police
jails that had previously been used as remand prisons, can he name these jails and specify
the reasons that this practice was discontinued and the reasons for their unsuitability as
remand prisons?
Hon. ALLAN MCCREADY (Minister of Police) replied: Police stations previously gazet-
ted as police jails were: Kaitaia, Opotiki, Gisborne, Wairoa, Nelson, Dunedin, and
Waitangi. Those at Gisborne and Waitangi (Chatham Islands) have been retained at the
request of my department due to their geographical location and the absence of Department
of Justice institutions in the near proximity. The use of police stations as police jails is
historical, and developed because of the lack of Department of Justice prisons and the
difficulties of travel. With the passage of time these problems have largely been overcome.
Lack of facilities such as exercise yards, meal rooms, ablution facilities, and size prohibits the
use of police cells for remand prisoners who could require to be accommodated for periods
of up to 7 days or more. Police cell blocks are now designed for overnight and weekend
custody only.
(5/10/77)

totalled only $303,000. On the basis of this expenditure, provision has been made this year
for $300,000, which is considered to be a reasonable estimate. There has been no change in
the criteria governing the reimbursement of expenses.

Canterbury-Timber Stockpile
35. Mr ELWORTHY (Oamaru) asked the Minister of Forests: What volume of wood is
held in the timber stockpile from wind-thrown forests in Canterbury, and how will this
timber be released on to the market without disrupting normal sawmilling and trading
patterns?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Forests) replied: Approximately 14 800 cubic metres of
logs are stored for trial purposes under water sprinklers at Balmoral forests, and at the end
of August approximately 37 500 cubic metres of sawn timber was stockpiled in the yards of
Timber Stockpile Ltd. in Christchurch. No decision has yet been taken on when disposal of
the sawn timber stockpile will commence, although indications are that sales should be
possible within the next few months. The timing of the commencement of disposal and the
volume to be released will be influenced by the availability of a diminishing supply of
windthrown timber-principally from private sources-and through sales of Forest Service
logs reverting to formal commitment levels from the beginning of October.
(23/9/77)
Housing-Multicultural Bias
36. Hon. M. RATA (Northern Maori) asked the Minister of Housing: Is the Housing
Corporation aware of the need for a multicultural bias in the design and administration of
housing, as pointed out on page 82 of the task force report New Zealand at the Turning
Point, and, if so, what is being done to ensure that this multicultural bias is being introduced?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing) replied: The Housing Corporation has
concentrated its design resources on the production of medium-density and cluster-
development housing. Such groups provide the environment for community co-operation or
communal activity, but are so designed that individuals or nuclear-type families who wish to
follow a separate and private existence may freely do so. In the Auckland area alone, over
half the current year's building programme is committed to this type of development.
Designs have also been produced for use on individual sites which are particularly suited to
the larger or extended family, and are so planned that partitions may be removed or added
as necessary to allow some tailoring to the needs of the family to be housed. A pilot design of
this type, situated in Auckland, was recently viewed by the Pacific Island Housing and
Welfare Committee, and was praised as being well suited to the use of the Polynesian
extended family unit.
(23/9/77)

Social Development Council Report
41. Mr O'BRIEN (Island Bay) asked the Minister of Social Welfare: What steps are
planned by the National Government to deal with the situation revealed by the report of the
Social Development Council, and when can action be expected to abolish the poverty
described in the report?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare) replied: In the 1976 Budget, the first
Budget of this National Government, a substantial measure of tax relief was given to families
with at least one child under 5 years of age and when the principal income earner was in
receipt of a salary of less than $100 per week. The rebate was equivalent to $6 per week, and
phased out when a salary reached $140 per week. In the 1977 National Budget the young
family rebate was extended to $9 per week for children under 10 years, phasing out at a
salary of $240 per week. In addition, a single-income rebate of $4 per week was introduced
and the existing wife rebate of $375 was increased to $520 per annum. All this is in contrast
to the reference on page 3 of the Social Development Council's report which states that the
poverty level referred to was based on the Department of Statistics 1973-74 "Household
expenditure survey", which found that 29 percent of children were likely to have a standard
of living below the pensioner datum level. This, of course, was during the period of the last
Labour Government. Recently the chairman of the N.Z. Council of Social Service and
author of the council's report on "Families and Incomes" wrote congratulating the Govern-
ment on restoring the family economic position to a level equal to what it was before it
deteriorated so drastically under the Labour Government.
(23/9/77)

ORAL QUESTIONS
Sugar Price
47. Rt. Hon. W. E. ROWLING (Leader of the Opposition), on behalf of Hon. W. W.
FREER (Mt. Albert), asked the Minister of Trade and Industry: How does the new price
negotiated with Fiji for bulk sugar compare with fluctuations in the world sugar price, and
what effect will it have on the price for Australian sugar?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Deputy Prime Minister) replied on behalf of the Minister of
Trade and Industry: "The world price for raw sugar is only one of the factors that have had
to be considered in the recent price negotiations with Fiji. Under the terms of the
agreement, approved by the previous Government, Fiji was entitled to argue for price
increases on the basis of prices received in other markets and factors such as increased costs
of production. We, for our part, had to seek a price reasonable in terms of the New Zealand
consumer and the overall balance of the agreement. The price that has been agreed involves
a slight increase in the return to the Fiji grower and is in the Government's view reasonable
in view of all the factors involved. I would not expect the outcome of the negotiations with
Fiji to have any effect on the price for Australian sugar. The Australian agreement operates
until the end of 1978."

EEC and Dublin Declaration
65. Miss DEWE (Lyttelton) asked the Minister of Overseas Trade: Has he seen in the New
Zealand Economist of September 1977 an article on "A Minister For Europe?" in which a
reference is made to "the assertion made in New Zealand that the EEC had, by omitting to
approve the price rise, not honoured the Dublin Declaration", and, if so, has the EEC so
failed to honour the Dublin Declaration?
66
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour) replied on behalf of the Minister of Overseas
Trade: "I have seen the article referred to in the September 1977 issue of the New Zealand
Economist titled "A Minister for Europe?", and the reference in it to “. . . the assertion
made in New Zealand that the EEC had, by omitting to approve the price rise, not honoured
the Dublin Declaration". The EEC has not failed to honour the Dublin Declaration. The
article actually confirms this. In terms of the Dublin Declaration, the Community is obliged
to review periodically and, as necessary, to adjust the prices New Zealand receives for its
exports of butter and cheese to Britain under Protocol 18 to the EEC Treaty of Accession.
While I was in Europe in July, the EEC Commission put a proposal to the Council of
Agriculture Ministers that the Protocol 18 guaranteed prices should be increased by 10
percent. This proposal was considered at the 18-19 July meeting of the council, and will be
discussed again at this month's council meeting, which is scheduled for Monday and Tuesday
of next week. I am hopeful that the council will reach a favourable decision on the
commission's proposal then."

the doctor in charge of the ward, to be present at routine ward rounds to make available
their expert advice. Increasingly, both in the hospital and community settings, the manage-
ment of patients is becoming a team effort, rather than the one-to-one relationship between
patient and doctor which was previously the rule.

Forest Encouragement Schemes
69. Mr ELWORTHY (Oamaru), on behalf of Mr ELLIOTT (Whangarei), asked the
Minister of Forests: What is the total area planted or planned for planting under forest
encouragement schemes, and to what extent has the annual projected planting rate been
met?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Forests) replied: Planting under the forestry encourage-
ment loans scheme and forestry encouragement grants scheme has totalled 45 914 hectares
to 31 March 1977. This is made up of 14 479 hectares under loans which were commenced in
1964, and 31 435 hectares under grants introduced in 1971. It is expected that a further 8500
hectares will be planted under both schemes during the 1977 year. Cabinet approved on 1
July 1974 a target level of 10 000 hectares of new planting per annum under both of these
schemes. Although annual project approvals are made up to this target level, actual
performance has been only 70 percent to 80 percent since the target was introduced. The
reasons for this shortfall by private planters have been both physical and financial. It is
expected that a gradual increase in the level of performance will occur during future planting
seasons.

OECD Economic Survey
75. Hon. R. O. DOUGLAS (Manukau) asked the Minister of Finance: Is it correct, as

## p. 3621 (#503) ###########################################

12 October
3621
Questions and Replies
Zealand were substantially altered for the published version in order to remove all reference
to the work "indexation”, and, if so, can he confirm that the reason for the changes made
which is advanced in that journal is also correct?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Acting Minister of Finance) replied: The reasons are not
correct. As I explained to the Deputy Leader of the Opposition yesterday, the differences

New Zealand, I can only assume the term was removed by the secretariat when it discovered
the error. The reasons given in the National Business Review are therefore incorrect.

Hospitals Geriatric Means Test
76. Mr MINOGUE (Hamilton West), on behalf of Mr MALCOLM (Eden), asked the
Minister of Health: Can he indicate whether, following the decision of 9 February 1977 to
remove the "geriatric means test" as it applied in the Auckland Hospital Board region, any
confusion was caused about the implementation of this policy in practice, and, if so, has he
been successful in overcoming that confusion so that the policy is capable of being
understood and implemented in the fashion intended at the time the original decision to
remove the "geriatric means test" was announced?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare) replied on behalf of the Minister of
Health: There was some misunderstanding about this scheme when it was introduced. The
purpose of the special assistance scheme was to provide financial assistance to geriatric
patients in private hospitals who were over the age of 65, who could not be accommodated in
public hospitals, and who had insufficient income to meet the private hospital fees even after
payment of the $11 a day Government subsidy by way of private hospital daily patient
benefit. The Government has decided that from 9 February 1977 the Government will
subsidise the patients by up to a maximum fee, which will take into account the patient's
income less $5 a week for personal and incidental expenses. On 1 July the maximum fee to
which subsidy would be available was reviewed, and the scheme is now working as intended,
and earlier misunderstandings have been resolved.

Social Welfare Counselling of Unmarried Mothers
85. Hon. MICHAEL CONNELLY (Wigram), on behalf of Mrs BATCHELOR (Avon),
asked the Minister of Social Welfare: Has he seen a report in the Evening Post of 21
September 1977 in which he is quoted as saying that increased counselling would be given to
unmarried mothers who choose to keep their babies, and could he explain what the emphasis
of such counselling will be and what effect it may have on unmarried mothers?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare) replied: Yes, I have seen the report
referred to. The Domestic Purposes Benefit Review Committee recommended that counsel-

Townswomen's Guilds recently. Emphasis will be placed on informing the unmarried
mother of her rights and the likely consequences of any decision she may make. The effect of
the counselling will be that unmarried mothers will be able to make a more informed and
reasoned decision on the future of their children.

Imports-Volume
88. Mr ELWORTHY (Oamaru) asked the Minister of Trade and Industry: Has he seen
the comment by the New Zealand Institute of Economic Research, on page 17 of its latest
report, that "it is difficult to see that the volume of imports could fall much further", and, if
so, (a) does he agree with this statement, and (b) could he indicate what evidence there is to
support this view?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Minister of Overseas Trade) replied on behalf of the Minister
of Trade and Industry: "I have seen the comment referred to. I cannot disagree with this
statement when it is read in its proper context, for the paragraph goes on immediately to
point out that 'Opportunities for import replacement are limited, in the short term at least,
and any marked reduction in the quantity of imports would probably be precipitated only if
there were a substantial fall in the volume of production.' With most of the goods currently
imported into New Zealand being essential inputs into the manufacturing process, the
Government would certainly not consider further restricting the level of imports if, by doing
so, the viability of our economy, in terms of both production and employment, would be
endangered."

Auckland Hospital Board-Surgical Waiting List
109. Mr HUNT (New Lynn) asked the Minister of Health: Has he seen a statement in the
New Zealand Herald of 6 September 1977 that, at a recent meeting of the Auckland Hospital
Board, it was revealed that "in the last 12 months since July last year the general surgical
waiting list increased by nearly 1000, to a total of 2422", and, if so (a) is the statement
correct, and (b) in what way will the Government be assisting the Auckland Hospital Board
to reduce the waiting list?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health) replied: I have seen the statement. There is a
further statement in the New Zealand Herald of 27 September which gives an explanation of
the increased waiting list, and I would draw this to the member's attention. Briefly, the total
increase in the general waiting list is 950, of which 680 are on the surgical list. The remainder
are on the geriatric non-surgical list, and this is considered to be due to the greater eligibility
of geriatric patients to receive a subsidy for private hospital fees. I am advised that many of
these patients are in private hospitals. The paediatric surgical list is composed of patients
with mainly minor conditions, and no urgent cases are on it. The greatest single cause is a
shortage of anaesthetists. This is worldwide. Two extra specialists have been appointed and
approvals have been given for further increases. The situation should improve as further
areas of stage III of the Auckland Hospital are commissioned in the next 9 to 12 months and
by the return of the eye department to the Wallace block, which has been upgraded.

Consumer Price Index
115. Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central) asked the Minister of Statistics: Has he seen the

to including income tax in the calculation of the index?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Statistics) replied: I have seen the article referred
by to by the honourable member. Consideration has been given to including income tax in
the consumer price index whenever the compilation of the index has been reviewed. The
1971 report of the consumer price index revision advisory committee recommended that the
consumer price index cover direct personal expenditure on goods and services only, and in
keeping with this definition the committee recommended the exclusion of direct taxation.
That is in line with international practice.

Export of Manufactured Goods to Australia
121. Mr SCHULTZ (Coromandel) asked the Minister of Trade and Industry: To what
extent has the quota system imposed on the imports of New Zealand manufactured goods
into Australia reduced New Zealand's trade with that market, and will this mean any change
in the spirit of the NAFTA agreement?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry) replied: It is impor-
tant to remember that the quotas recently negotiated for New Zealand through the medium
of article 3:7 arrangements have been for products which Australia already has under global
restriction. The New Zealand quotas constitute a special allocation tied to New Zealand
suppliers. They are additional to whatever sales New Zealand exporters may make by
competing for global quota using their duty preference. Since sales to the Australian market
may still therefore be made outside the special quotas for New Zealand, it is not possible to
quantify in advance the extent to which the sales of New Zealand goods into the Australian
market will be restricted under the new regime. The fact that it has been possible to
negotiate special entitlements for New Zealand within the Australian quota system is itself a
testimony to the spirit of the NAFTA agreement.

NAC-Use of Aircraft
124. Mr KIRK (Sydenham) asked the Minister of Civil Aviation and Meteorological
Services: Will he explain the justification for the sale of ZKNAQ earlier this year for reasons
of non-utilisation when it is reported that NAC is considering the purchase of a further
Boeing 737 as the ninth in its fleet?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Civil Aviation and Meteorological Services)
replied: NAC's ninth Boeing, ZKNAQ, was bought ahead of demand for it in order to avoid
a substantial price increase-NZ$329,929—and to ensure that it was available to meet the
considerable passenger growth forecast at that time. The aircraft entered service in
December 1975. Due to an unforeseen falling off in traffic it was leased to Nigeria in June
1976. This lease expired on 31 March 1977, and because traffic had not recovered by this
time the aircraft was sold to Nigeria on 15 April 1977 for a substantial profit. Traffic growth
on trunk routes is now exceeding predictions, and there is every indication that an additional
aircraft will be required by December 1978. A special arrangement has been negotiated by
NAC with the Boeing Aircraft Corporation whereby NAC will be able to use the cheaper
Dash 7 engines instead of the Dash 15 variety. The Government is at present studying the
whole proposal.

Drugs in Prisons
152. Mr KIRK (Sydenham) asked the Minister of Justice: What immediate action has he
taken to prevent hard drugs entering New Zealand prisons since the death by drug overdose
of an inmate at Addington Prison?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice) replied: Experience both here and overseas
shows that it is not possible to exclude illicit drugs completely from penal institutions, even
those designed for maximum security. For obvious reasons I shall not describe publicly some
of the methods that can be used. It is enough to say that they do not depend simply upon
conveyance by visitors, although that is the usual channel at present. I imagine that,
theoretically, a totally sterile environment could be produced by severing every form of
contact a prisoner has with the outside world. In practice it would be impossible. Prisons are
now dependent upon many incoming supplies and services that can be used to breach
security by those who are so determined. To eliminate every possible channel would mean
disregarding practical difficulties and the enormous cost factor, as well as humanitarian
principles. Small quantities of drugs are easy to conceal, and no prison can be made self-
sufficient and isolated from the community. I am indeed concerned about the recent death of
an inmate by presumed drug overdose at Addington Prison, but a hasty emotional reaction is
17-Vol. 414

unlikely to assist matters. Hence no immediate action has been taken. My department
depends on the continued vigilance of staff and the imposition of salutory penalties by the
courts upon those who are caught introducing contraband into penal institutions.

Down Under the Plum Trees
155. Mr LUXTON (Piako), on behalf of Mr MALCOLM (Eden), asked the Minister of
Education: Is he in a position to give an undertaking that the book Down Under the Plum
Trees will not be used in New Zealand schools, and, if not, can he explain why, although he is
Minister of Education, he cannot give an assurance of that type?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied: It should be obvious that I am
unable to give the undertaking that is sought in the honourable member's question. Part of
the findings of the Indecent Publications Tribunal, as amended by the Supreme Court, read,
"This book is indecent unless circulation is restricted to persons over the age of 18 years." In
my view, this means that the unrestricted availability of the book in any library in New
Zealand, including school libraries, would be illegal and subject to prosecution if this age
restriction is not enforced. It is only necessary to remind members that there are 2525
primary and secondary schools, and it must be apparent why I cannot give a categorical
undertaking that the book referred to in the question will not be found in a school library
somewhere in New Zealand. If any information is available to anyone that might indicate
that the book is at present in a specific school library, that information should be brought to
the attention of the authorities.

entitled Land Information Handbook, and, if so, why did he feel this was necessary, have
other Government publications ever carried this warning, and does this establish a precedent
for the Department of Lands and Survey?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Lands) replied: The Land Information Handbook was
published by the Department of Lands and Survey on behalf of the Land Use Advisory
Council. The council approved the text, which had been prepared in consultation with
agencies which gather and retain information about the land resource. It was the council's
considered view that appropriate notice should be included to advise readers of likely
restrictions on the availability of particular information from some sources. I have been
unable to readily identify other Government publications where specific reference has been
made to restrictions on the disclosure of information. This publication was aimed at
informing readers of the sources of information available on land. Where there is some
restriction on this information it is to the advantage of the inquirers to be informed in
advance. Whether comments on the disclosure of information appear on other departmental
publications will depend on the nature of the publication.

Unemployment-Census Figures
171. Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn) asked the Minister of Labour: Will he confirm that the total
number of persons who indicated that they were unemployed on census night 1976 was
27 210 and that this figure is 5.4 times higher than the 5021 registered that month as being
unemployed?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour) replied: Provisional national statistics from the
1976 census show that 27 210 persons had indicated they were unemployed on census night.
It is also true that the number of registered unemployed at that time stood at 5021. In 1971
the equivalent figures were 16 168 disclosed by the census, and 1121 registered unemployed.
However, it is not valid to compare these two figures. The total of registered unemployed
only includes persons who seek assistance from the Department of Labour's employment
service. As many disengaged persons do not require such assistance they are not included in
the count of registered unemployed. In addition, although my department assists persons
seeking part-time employment, this group is not included in the total of registered unemp-
loyed. In contrast, the census figures include all persons who indicate they are unemployed
whether seeking full or part-time employment.
(5/10/77)
Facial Eczema Research
172. Mr LUXTON (Piako), on behalf of Mr SCHULTZ (Coromandel), asked the Minister
of Agriculture: To what extent is research being conducted into facial eczema in sheep and
cattle, and will further work be continued next year?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Agriculture) replied: Officers of the Ministry of
Agriculture and Fisheries are carrying out extensive research into facial eczema, including
work in the following areas: (1) genetic resistance; (2) relative resistance to sporidesmin; (3)
effects of sporidesmin intoxication on milking cows; (4) incidence of subclinical facial
eczema in dairy herds; (5) zinc residues in milk and general work on fungi. This work is part
of an on-going programme started over 25 years ago, and until the cure has been found it will
not be terminated. The Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries now has a great deal of
evidence to show that controlled procedures are effective in preventing substantial stock
losses.

Mr WELLINGTON (Manurewa): For the purpose of discussing Ministers' replies to
questions, I move, That the House do now adjourn. I turn to questions 109, 103, 92, and 96,
which deal with community health. What the National Government has done has not yet
been fully appreciated; its full significance has not yet been grasped. For the benefit of the
member for Nelson and the member for Auckland Central, who are trying to interject, the
theme of the National Government's approach to health services is that primary health care
should be taken into the community, and that there should be a movement away from
institutionalised medicine. The white paper produced by the Labour Government emphas-
ised institutionalised medicine, but the National Government is moving towards a more
personalised service. We have passed the day when a hospital was sufficient for areas of size
and substance, and when it could be decreed that X doctors were needed in an area.
The National Government wants to establish greater flexibility and mobility in health
services. We have been innovative outside the system and on the fringe of it. An agreement
in principle was recently reached between the Department of Health and the Plunket
Society. As a result of that agreement in principle, at a cost of $1.5 million the Plunket
Society will be responsible for the care of all pre-school children in the south Auckland area,
which has a population of 200 000. The National Government will continue to maintain that
service at an estimated cost of $1 million a year. The Government has been concerned to
deliver health care as best it can by bringing primary medical attention within the reach of
those in isolated areas, among them the new mass housing suburbs the Labour Party thought
were politically safe. We also want to bring health care within reach of those who are
unfamiliar with New Zealand's traditional approach to medicine.
In south Auckland, where there is a considerable multicultural population and a large
child population, a crisis arose 2 years ago. The infant mortality rate was higher in that area
than anywhere else in Auckland, and the question that arises is what the National
Government, in consultation with the hospital board and other interested groups, has done.
A new health structure is planned; it will provide initially for two community-based
hospitals, in East Tamaki and Papakura. The Auckland Hospital Board has opened a base
for its almost unique extramural service at Middlemore Hospital.
The Department of Health is in the process of acquiring the land for a large health
centre that will accommodate doctors and allied health professionals, who will join forces
with those in the field of community care. Moreover, additional health centres will be placed
in needy areas like Otara and Manurewa, but Manukau will be the core health centre and the
others will be satellites providing services on a smaller scale. When we came into office in
1975, we found that the department's office in Papatoetoe was badly run down and that staff
morale was low. The National Government has approved of the appointment of 10
additional public health nurses, and I am delighted that some of those health nurses are
working in the schools in the south Auckland area and are dealing at first hand with some of
the health problems, which are well known to most members. I have already mentioned the
recent agreement in principle with the Plunket Society, which will extend the network of
health services into the pre-school area. These measures are welcome.

HEALTH AMENDMENT BILL
Mr DOWNIE (Pakuranga): I am directed by the Social Services Committee to present
the report of the committee on the Health Amendment Bill. The committee recommends
that the Bill be not allowed to proceed. I move, That the report do lie upon the table.
Members will recall that the purpose of this Bill was to control the practice of acupuncture to
ensure that only qualified persons undertook or practised acupuncture under the supervision
of registered medical practitioners, dentists, or physiotherapists.
The committee was impressed by the quality and content of submissions made on the
Bill, and the very responsible attitude adopted in the submissions from those who are at
present involved in the practice of acupuncture. The restrictions that would have been
imposed by the Bill now appear, in the light of the submissions received by the committee, to
be unduly onerous and could have resulted in the reduction of acupuncture services provided
by responsible practitioners. As well as the submissions from acupuncturists, the committee
received a large number of submissions, both in writing and in person, from those who
believed that acupuncture treatment had been beneficial to them. In their eyes, the Bill
would have deprived them of this form of treatment.
The points of concern that prompted the introduction of the Bill were procedures for
the sterilisation of equipment, the adequacy of diagnostic ability, the danger of symptoms of
serious diseases being masked by acupuncture treatment, and the difficulty of making the
distinction between therapeutic relief from symptoms and the actual cure of a disease. The
submissions were to some extent reassuring on these particular points, and consequently the
need for this restrictive legislation in its present form is not now so apparent.
However, the committee still feels that in the interests of the general public some form
of control over the practice of acupuncture is required. There should be co-operation and
consultation between medical and allied health professionals on the one hand, and the
responsible and qualified acupuncturists on the other. Some co-operation and consultation
could lead to a satisfactory linking of orthodox Western medicine and traditional acupunc-
ture, with resultant benefits to the patients.
Without making any firm recommendations, the committee believes that a suitable
alternative to the Bill could be found in the provisions of the Medical and Dental Auxiliaries
Act 1966. A number of allied health professions, including those of chiropodists, dental
technicians, and medical radiographers, have already obtained recognition as registerable
occupations under the Act. An acupuncture registration board could be established with
functions relating to education, discipline, and registration. However, before proceeding
with such a measure it would be advisable for discussions to be undertaken with the New
Zealand register of acupuncturists and the New Zealand Society of Acupuncturists to reach
agreement on standards of education and professional conduct, and also to make some
provision in appropriate cases for reference of patients to orthodox medical practitioners if
such patients do not respond to acupuncture treatment.

Public Finance Bill
THURSDAY, 13 OCTOBER 1977
Mr Acting Speaker took the chair at 2.30 p.m.
Prayers.
PUBLIC FINANCE BILL
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance): I move, That the Public Finance Bill
be introduced. This Bill consolidates and amends the Public Revenues Act 1953 and the New
Zealand Loans Act 1953, and clause 2 provides for the Bill to come into force on 1 April
1978. The Bill represents a merging of the two existing Acts, which deal with complementary
and closely interrelated financial operations of the Government. It is a forward move to have
all these operations combined in one Act. Over the years the Public Revenues Act and the
New Zealand Loans Act have been amended several times, and a number of provisions of
both Acts have become outdated.
The necessity for a complete revision of the legislation has become apparent in recent
years, and was brought to a head as a result of the findings of a Treasury committee
established in 1973, following an announcement in that year's Budget. The object was to
review the form of the public accounts with the aim of bringing about improvements in
presentation. The principles followed in arriving at the committee's recommendations were:
(a) that the public accounts should show particulars of the Government's taxation revenue
and loan receipts, and how expenditure was to be financed from such revenue and receipts;
(b) that those activities of a trading nature that were intended to be financed as far as
possible from their own revenue should be excluded from the Public Account; and (c) that
the relationship to the Public Account of the main trading departments would be limited to
the funding by way of loans and subsidies of that part of their expenditure that could not be
financed from revenue from their own activities.
As an outcome of the committee's report, it became evident that parliamentary control
over the expenditure of public money should be reinforced by eliminating a considerable
number of permanent appropriations that had crept into the statute book. Approval in
principle to these recommendations and to the revision of the existing legislation was given
by the then Government in 1974, and endorsed by this Government when it came into office.
I shall now deal with the principal changes the Bill makes to the present legislation. The
Works and Trading Account will be abolished. The principal departments that are at present
served by the Works and Trading Account are Electricity, State Coal Mines, and Railways.
As Electricity and State Coal Mines are now merged into the new Ministry of Energy, the
proposal is to establish separate accounts for Energy and Railways as accounts outside the
Public Account, thus bringing them into line with the Post Office.
The principal trading departments will, therefore, join the insurance offices and the
trust offices as accounts outside the Public Account, and will be subject to clause 68 of the
Bill. The remaining votes whose transactions are recorded in the existing Works and Trading
Account will thenceforth be accounted for in the Consolidated Account, which replaces the
Consolidated Revenue Account. Normal estimates of expenditures will continue to be
prepared for these trading departments now outside the Public Account. Balance sheets and
statements of account will be tabled annually in Parliament.
The principal power of the Minister of Finance to raise loans for development is at
present governed by section 11 of the New Zealand Loans Act. This provides that where
money has been authorised to be transferred by any Act from the National Development
Loans Account in any financial year the Minister may borrow the amount so authorised. The
Appropriation Acts in each year empower the transfer of sums from the National Develop-
ment Loans Account, usually to the Works and Trading Account, the Post Office Account,
and the Housing Corporation Account. This sets the amount of the principal borrowing
authority.
However, permanent appropriations in several other Acts extensively augment this
borrowing authority, and enable the Minister additionally to raise loans to cover loan money
advanced to or invested in bodies in which the Government has a proprietary interest. This
existing procedure for determining the borrowing limit has deficiencies that have long been
recognised. It is unrelated to the various contingencies that may have to be faced from a
financial or economic viewpoint and for which borrowing may justifiably be required. The


## p. 3657 (#539) ###########################################

13 October
3657
Public Finance Bill
Bill, therefore, does not provide for any limit on borrowing.
Clause 71 provides that the Minister may, if it appears to him to be necessary or
expedient in the public interest to do so, raise a loan upon such terms and conditions as he
thinks fit. All loan money raised under Part V of the Bill is to be credited to the Loans
Account or the Loans Redemption Account, established under clauses 39 and 40 respec-
tively. The Minister will be answerable to Parliament for his borrowing activities, and
parliamentary control over the application of loan moneys has been tightened. In spite of the
change of name of the National Development Loans Account to the Loans Account, the
proceeds of borrowing in the normal course will be used for capital and development
expenditure.
An important change, however, has been included to allow for transfers of loan money
from the Loans Account to the Consolidated Account. This can be justified in view of the
extent to which capital expenditure is at present being met from loan money in the Works
and Trading Account. Such expenditure would otherwise have to be met from revenue when
those votes, whose transactions are at present recorded in the Works and Trading Account,
will be recorded in the Consolidated Account. The transfer from the Loans Account in any
financial year will be limited to the amount approved by Parliament. This will be achieved by
the inclusion of a new clause in the Appropriation Bills that will allow Parliament the
opportunity to debate the issue.
Clause 53(1) enacts the important constitutional principle that there shall be no
expenditure of public money except pursuant to an appropriation by Act of Parliament. This
provision is not specifically contained in the present Acts. Appropriation of public money is
provided either in the annual Appropriation Bills or by means of permanent appropriations
in this and other Acts. Expenditure under permanent appropriations has increased consider-
ably over the years, thus eroding parliamentary control over a significant area of public
finance. The opportunity has been taken, therefore, to re-enhance parliamentary control by
repealing many of the permanent appropriations that deal in the main with the application of
loan money, and replacing them with annual appropriations.
Clauses 120 to 159 make amendments to other Acts, and a large number of these
amendments include the removal of this type of permanent appropriation. Generally
speaking, the permanent appropriations that remain relate to: (a) civil list and judicial
salaries, (b) superannuation payments, (c) repayments of debt and debt servicing, (d)
payments under Government guarantees, and (e) payment of trust money. The existing
provision in the Public Revenues Act empowering the Minister of Finance to give a
guarantee on behalf of the Crown has been re-enacted in clause 86, which further provides
that a statement of all guarantees given under the clause during any financial year shall be
included in the public accounts for that year, and any payment made pursuant to such a
guarantee shall be disclosed in the quarterly summaries of the public accounts.
A number of other Acts, particularly relating to Government agencies, also include
provisions enabling the Minister of Finance to give guarantees on behalf of the Crown. The
number of these provisions has also grown over the years, and there has been no correspond-
ing requirement of disclosure. To correct this, the third schedule to the Bill includes
amendments to a number of Acts, whereby guarantees given by the Minister of Finance in
accordance with those Acts shall be made pursuant to clause 86. The present provisions in
the New Zealand Loans Act relating to the establishment of the Public Debt Commission
have been retained. The commission's function is to determine what part of the public debt
shall be repaid from the amount of the annual contribution transferred from the Consoli-
dated Account to the Loans Redemption Account.
Section 59 of the New Zealand Loans Act provides a complicated actuarial formula for
calculating the annual contribution charged against revenue for the repayment of public
debt. This procedure is outdated and unduly complicated, and therefore a new procedure
has been devised. Clause 49 proposes a new formula, which is simply that the contribution
shall be a sum equal to at least 1 percent of the public debt outstanding at the end of the
previous financial year. This, however, is only the minimum amount of money available for
repayment of debt in any year. In all of the preceding 10 years, for instance, additional funds
have been transferred to the Loans Redemption Account for this purpose.
Part II of the Bill relates to the important office of the Controller and Auditor-General,
and also to the functions and powers of the Audit Office. The Bill gives statutory recognition
to the independence of the Controller and Auditor-General that is lacking in the Public
Revenues Act. Clause 15 states that neither the Minister of Finance nor the Minister in
Charge of the Audit Office shall be in any way responsible for the exercise by the Audit


## p. 3658 (#540) ###########################################

3658
13 October
Public Finance Bill
Office of its functions, duties, and powers, other than such functions and duties that the
Controller and Auditor-General has as administrative head of the Audit Department. The
clause further provides that when exercising any of its powers in respect of the Audit
Department, the State Services Commission shall have due regard to maintaining the
independence of the Controller and Auditor-General.
Parts I to VI of the Bill were considered by the Public Expenditure Committee during
July. This somewhat unusual procedure was sanctioned by the House on 10 December 1976,
when the House resolved that the draft Public Finance Bill could be referred to the Public
Expenditure Committee before its introduction. I now confirm that I have received a report
from the chairman of the Public Expenditure Committee advising that the committee
considered Parts I to VI of the draft Bill, and in a memorandum listed amendments to the
Bill recommended by the committee. I further confirm that all the amendments so recom-
mended have been incorporated within the Bill now before the House. A few minor drafting
changes have been made since the Bill was considered by the committee, but these changes
were by way of elucidation only, and did not affect any of the amendments recommended by
the committee.
Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition): I take it from the Minister's
last remark that this Bill is substantially the one that left the Public Expenditure Committee.
I wonder why he did not go through the Bill, because it was rather difficult to follow. For
example, although the part of the Bill that deals with the Audit Office starts at clause 14, the
Minister did not mention the role of that office until quite late. Was there any reason for
dealing with that significant part of the Bill in that order? In view of the complexity of the
Bill, the Opposition does not have many comments to make on it. However, in passing I
note that among the statutes repealed in the fourth schedule is one that went through the
House as recently as a couple of weeks ago. It is a very interesting commentary on the rush
that 1977, No. 000-the Finance (Inflation-Adjusted Bonds) Act is repealed by this Bill. I
suppose that must have been one of the shortest-lasting separate enactments in the history of
Parliament. However, it is interesting to see in that schedule a consolidation of legislation
enacted from 1922 to 1977.
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance): I am sure the honourable member
will realise that the Bill he referred to had to be passed as new legislation, whereas this Bill
collects a considerable number of items and brings them together. It would have been
inappropriate simply to have included the Finance (Inflation-Adjusted Bonds) Act in this
legislation, and have a debate on a very small fraction of the Bill as new legislation. As the
Public Finance Bill is the product of the Public Expenditure Committee, I hope the House
will see fit to deal with it expeditiously, especially as it has been given very detailed
examination by the committee. Everything that the committee recommended has been
accepted by the Government, and the Bill is really a Public Expenditure Committee Bill as
much as it is the Bill of the Minister of Finance. I doubt whether we will find very much that
will concern us in the normal procedures of the House, although on closer scrutiny,
something might arise.
Bill introduced and read a first time.
OVERSEAS INVESTMENT AMENDMENT BILL
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance): I move, That the Overseas Investment
Amendment Bill be introduced. This is a short Bill, which contains a small number of changes
of a technical nature to definitions in the interpretation section of the principal Act. In
addition, provision is made for regulations controlling the commencement of business in
New Zealand by an overseas person. Clause 2 contains the following changes to the principal
Act: first, it introduces a definition of "building society", and, where appropriate, inserts
those words after the word "company" in the principal Act; secondly, the definition of
"nominee" is amended in two respects—(a) an anomaly in the principal Act is removed so
that a New Zealand company owning shares in another company that is itself an overseas
person will not also be defined as an overseas person, and (b) the definition of "nominee" is
widened to include the situation where two or more overseas persons get together, and,
acting in concert, individually acquire shares in a New Zealand company; thirdly, the
definition of "overseas person" is changed to include a company in which 25 percent or more
of any class of shares is held by an overseas person. At present, only voting shares are taken
into account. Clause 3 rectifies a printing error. Clause 4 amends the section of the principal
Act relating to the making of regulations, so that a regulation may be made concerning the

commencement of business in New Zealand by individual overseas persons. Companies only
are covered at present.

Mercury Level in Fish
9. Mr COURTNEY (Nelson) asked the Minister of Health: Can he state the level of
mercury allowed in fish by Department of Health regulations, and also the maximum level
recommended by the World Health Organisation?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry): I reply on behalf of
the Minister of Health. The maximum level of mercury allowed in fish sold in New Zealand
is 0.5 parts per million—that is, 0.5 milligrams of mercury per kilogram of fish. The World
Health Organisation has not set a specific recommended maximum level for mercury in fish.
Rather, it has set a provisional tolerable weekly intake for mankind from all sources,
including fish, of 0.3 milligrams per person or 0.005 milligrams per kilogram of body weight.
Mr Courtney: How was our base arrived at, and why is it not the same as that
recommended by the World Health Organisation?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: I have no details on exactly how our base was
reached, but I am assured by the Department of Health that it is safe and that monitoring is
taking place. It has taken place recently in Christchurch and is taking place now in
Whangarei.
Hon. R. L. Bailey: What proportion of the fish sold retail is tested for mercury?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: I cannot give that information precisely, but, as I
said in answer to the previous question, monitoring is taking place and very few samples with
an overpercentage of mercury have been revealed. Those that have been revealed are being
followed up by the department, explanations are being demanded, and action will be taken.
Hon. W. W. Freer: As the Minister has stated that several samples have shown an
overpercentage of mercury and are being followed up, can he tell the House the type of fish
involved?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: Of the 13 suspected samples taken in Christchurch,
only 4 have been higher than the 0.5 parts per million, and they were shark samples. Groper,
sole, ling, elephant fish, and tarakihi samples were all below that level, confirming that they
present no problem. Apparently the problem is with a certain species or a certain age of
shark.

Motorcar Spare Parts
11. Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert) asked the Minister of Trade and Industry: Has he
seen a statement in the Auckland Star of 5 October by an importer of thermostats to the
effect that "motorists are being swindled by the system of snowballing percentages on car
parts", and, if so, what action is being taken by his department to protect motorist
consumers?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry): I have seen the
article referred to. The maximum mark-ups that may be applied to car parts are fixed by the
Stabilisation of Prices Regulations 1974. In terms of those regulations, importers, wholesal-
ers, and retailers are permitted to apply a lawful percentage mark-up to the into-store cost,
which includes duty and sales tax. This year the Government established the Commission of
Inquiry into the Distribution of Motor Vehicle Parts, and included in its terms of reference is
one dealing with the reasonableness or otherwise of the profits realised by distributors of
motor vehicle parts. The commission is required to report its findings by 30 November.
Hon. W. W. Freer: As the control is based on the Stabilisation of Prices Regulations
1974, which the Minister has criticised frequently, when does he intend to alter those
regulations to protect consumers, on which basis he gave assurances before the end of 1975?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: I have always said that, fundamentally, I am not a
believer in this sort of economic control if it can be avoided, but the previous Labour
Government left the country in such a mess that we have to keep the regulations operating in
the meantime.
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: I think the Minister will recall that the Standing Orders
provide that ministerial answers should not infringe in that way.
Hon. W. W. Freer: In view of the Minister's rather lighthearted reply, is it not a fact that
he now has to agree that, without such regulations, competition would not lower prices to
the consuming motorist?
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: That question seeks an opinion, but the Minister may answer
if he wishes.
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: The Government has no intention of amending the
regulations at present, but I believe that, in the long term, when we get the economy on to an
even keel, competition will be the best form of price regulating in many cases. In the present
circumstances, with import licensing obtaining quite tightly in some cases, and economic
difficulties being experienced, the Government has decided that the regulations should
remain.

Wellington Extramural Hospital
17. Mr LAMBERT (Western Hutt) asked the Minister of Health: Can he confirm that
there is a need in Wellington for an extramural hospital similar to the Auckland extramural
hospital, and, if so, are any plans in existence to develop this facility?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry): I reply on behalf of
the Minister of Health. The community health programmes of all hospital boards are at
present undergoing a rapid development as a direct result of the additional expenditure of
$3,369,000 that the Government has recently approved for specific community health care
projects by hospital boards. The Auckland extramural hospital will itself be undergoing a
reorganisation to allow centres to be set up in other parts of the board's area from which
services can be provided. The Wellington Hospital Board has developed its own community
health care programme for Wellington, based on the Wellington Public Hospital. It will
shortly be expanding its activities considerably as a result of the injection of funds mentioned
earlier in this reply. The board considers this type of development more suitable for
Wellington than the establishment of a separate extramural hospital, as has occurred in
Auckland.

Disarmament
20. Mr HUNT (New Lynn) asked the Minister of Foreign Affairs: Since the General
Assembly of the United Nations will in mid-1978 devote a special session to disarmament,
what will New Zealand's role be at this special disarmament session, and will any initiatives
be taken by the New Zealand Government to halt the tragic build-up in military expendi-
ture, especially on nuclear weaponry, that has been evident in the last 30 years?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Acting Minister of Foreign Affairs): New Zealand is
one of the countries which co-sponsored the resolution at the General Assembly last year
calling for a special session. The Government therefore welcomes the special session and will
do everything possible to ensure its success. Our role will be similar to that adopted by New
Zealand in other disarmament discussions—namely, the expression of a sensible and
reasoned voice seeking to assist in establishing a consensus that will set the international
community on the road to more assured progress on disarmament issues in future years. We
are not on the 54-member preparatory committee for the special session and the scope for
any initiatives is limited in the preparatory stages. We do, however, follow the committee's
work in New York closely and have made our views known to the committee. We also
submitted a paper commenting on the agenda and objectives of the special session. The
Government also plans to publish a green paper on disarmament before the special session
with a view to acquainting the public of the various disarmament issues that will be
considered at that session.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.

national superannuation represented 53.99 percent of social welfare expenditure, and 10
percent of total Government expenditure. It is estimated that in the year ending 31 March
1978 net expenditure on national superannuation will represent 52.81 percent of total social
welfare expenditure and 11.32 percent of total Government expenditure.

point out that Government spending in this area has dropped from an increase of 28.6
percent in the last year of the Labour Government to less than 4 percent in the first year of
the National Government.

MANUKAU CITY RATING REPEAL BILL
Mr BIRCH (Franklin): I move, That leave be given to introduce the Manukau City
Rating Repeal Bill. The Bill provides for the repealing of all the legislation that has been
used by the Manukau City Council in recent years to help solve some of the difficult rating
problems experienced. The problems that have been experienced go back to the time when
the district was a county administered under the Counties Act. Since 1967 the Manukau City
Council has come to Parliament with three proposals. In 1967 it approached Parliament with
the Manukau City Empowering (Rates Postponement) Bill, and it approached Parliament
again in 1969 and 1972. That indicates the complexities of the council's rating problems. The
city council is now approaching its rating problems from a different angle, and is confident
that by using differential rating under the Rating Act it will find a solution. The effect of the
Bill is to repeal the earlier local Bills passed by Parliament in 1967, 1969, and 1972.
Motion agreed to.
Bill introduced and read a first time.

in the Bill. The provisions were correctly placed in the Bill, because they were intended to

recommendation, but it became obvious to me that they related to a very complex

more I tried to amend the provisions to make them workable, the more I realised that they
were becoming less and less workable.

completely the reverse of that intended by the House. Although only two clauses in this Bill
relate to that matter, I feel sure the measure that will eventually be introduced will have up

covered, and it will be referred to a select committee, where once again representations can
be made and the Bill given full and thorough consideration. I believe we should not hurry in
legislating on this point. At present the situation is under control.

Contraception, Sterilisation, and Abortion Bill
Mr ELLIOTT (Whangarei): I move, That it be an instruction to the Committee of the
Whole on the Contraception, Sterilisation, and Abortion Bill that it postpone consideration of
clauses 2 to 48 until after consideration of clauses 49 to 54. Clauses 49 to 54 concern
amendments to the Crimes Act; and clause 54 is the most important. The key to control over
abortion is the law pertaining to it. What is legal or illegal, lawful or unlawful, must be
enshrined in the Crimes Act. A tight Crimes Act will restrict abortion; loose definitions will
not. I believe that any procedures for the carrying out of abortions-who shall perform
them, where, under what conditions, with or without panels or supervisory
committees should not be decided until after the law on abortion is put in place.
What happens to clause 54, the key clause amending the Crimes Act, may very well
determine, and should determine, what happens to other clauses of the Bill. In his dissenting
judgment on the Woolnough case in 1975, the Chief Justice Sir Richard Wild said—and I
quote from page 143 of the royal commission's report—that the legislature has never stated
what was lawful and what was unlawful in enacting abortion legislation; it has abdicated this
function to the courts. I believe it is logical, reasonable, and sensible to place the law on
abortion first. I suspect that there may be some who will oppose it, because they fear it might
be too tight or too liberal, according to how they want the Crimes Act to be amended; but
why shy away from the fundamental issue and leave it until after 53 other detailed,
confusing, and perhaps rambling procedural and administrative decisions have been made.
Clauses 49 to 54 should be taken first.
Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson): I find myself unable to support the motion.
When I rose earlier to speak on another motion to vary the order in which the clauses should
be dealt with, my view then expressed, and still held, was that we should proceed with an
orderly consideration of the effective clauses of the Bill, omitting the short title, which of
course enables the whole range of the Bill to be covered, and clause 2, which, with its series
of definitions, in effect encompasses the whole Bill. I believe we should start at clause 3, the
first operative clause, and then go through the other clauses. If we start picking and
choosing, and arguing about whether to start here or there, we shall be in a pickle before we
know where we are.
The Chief Justice, in what I stress was a minority judgment of the Court of Appeal, was
by no means the first to draw attention to the deficiency in the law in the absence of a
definition of the word "unlawful" in another section of the Crimes Act. Mr Justice Henry
made pungent comment on that many years ago; but, notwithstanding that, the law has been
able to live with it, and whatever gap there is, is being filled on the recommendation of the
McMullin commission. The provisions included in the Bill give effect to the commission's
finding, which in turn was based on the majority decision of the Court of Appeal. I see no
reason why we should not assume that the commission's finding is a good one to act upon in
that it reasonably and workably restates the law, proceed with the Bill in the way it is
framed, and consider the clauses before we come to those mentioned by the member for
Whangarei. We will then consider them in their proper place.
Motion negatived.

Contraception, Sterilisation, and Abortion Bill
(1) Every person commits an offence who sells or gives or otherwise disposes of any contracep-
tive to any child under the age of 16 years, or offers to sell or give or otherwise dispose of any
contraceptive to any child under that age, unless that person is-
(1) The parent or guardian of that child, or is acting in the place of a parent of that child; or
(b) A registered medical practitioner; or
(c) An authorised representative of any family planning clinic, or of any agency or association
from time to time approved for the purpose by the Minister of Justice by notice in the
Gazette; or
(d) A registered pharmacist, or a person acting under his supervision and with his authority, and
he sells or gives or otherwise disposes of, or offers to sell or to give or otherwise dispose
of, the contraceptive in accordance with-
(i) The written prescription of a medical practitioner; or
(ii) What he believes to be the written authority of any person referred to in paragraph
(a) or paragraph (c) of this subsection.
(2) Every person commits an offence who directs or persuades or attempts to direct or persuade
any child under the age of 16 years to use any contraceptive unless that person is—
(a) The parent or guardian of that child, or is acting in the place of a parent of that child; or
(b) A registered medical practitioner; or
(c) An authorised representative of any family planning clinic, or of any agency or association
from time to time approved for the purpose by the Minister of Justice by notice in the
Gazette.
(3) Every person commits an offence who sells or gives or otherwise supplies any information
about, or instruction in the use of, any contraceptive to any child under the age of 16 years, or
offers to sell or give or otherwise supply any such information or instruction to any child under that
age, unless that person-
(a) Is the parent or guardian of that child, or is acting in the place of a parent of that child; or
(b) Is a registered medical practitioner; or
(c) Is an authorised representative of any family planning clinic, or of any agency (including any
agency of the Crown) or association from time to time approved for the purpose by the
Minister of Justice by notice in the Gazette; or
(d) Is a registered pharmacist, or a person acting under his supervision and with his authority; or
(e) Does so as part of any course on social relationships, or human biology, or human
development, approved by the Director-General of Education or the Director-General
of Health; or
(f) Does so to any pupils of a school with the prior approval of the principal or head teacher of
that school.
(4) Every person who commits an offence against subsection (1) or subsection (2) or subsection
(3) of this section is liable on summary conviction—
(a) In the case of a first offence, to a fine not exceeding $200:
(b) In the case of a second or subsequent offence to imprisonment for a term not exceeding 3
months or to a fine not exceeding $400.
(5) Every child under the age of 16 years who, knowing its purpose, procures or attempts to
procure any contraceptive from any person other than a person who is authorised under this
section to supply the contraceptive to that child commits an offence and is liable on summary
conviction-
(a) In the case of a first offence, to have a conviction recorded against him; or
(b) In the case of a second or subsequent offence, to a fine not exceeding $4.
(6) The following enactments are hereby consequentially repealed:
(a) Section 2 of the Police Offences Amendment Act 1954:
(b) Section 2(2) of the Police Offences Amendment Act 1967.

INCOME TAX AMENDMENT BILL (NO. 2)
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Associate Minister of Finance): I move, That the Income
Tax Amendment Bill (No. 2) be introduced. The first amendment Bill gave effect to Budget
proposals relating to the increased young family rebate, and the new single-income family
rebate, including the resultant new PAYE tax tables, which operate from 1 October 1977.
This second Bill, comprising 40 clauses, covers additional Budget proposals as well as other
items of tax legislation, and is made up as follows. The short title states that the Bill forms
part of the Income Tax Act 1976, and, unless otherwise provided, it applies to the tax on
income derived during the year ending 31 March 1978, and future years. The remaining 38
clauses are made up as follows: 17 clauses cover the 1977 Budget announcements; 10 clauses
amend existing provisions or add new ones; and 11 clauses simply clarify existing legislation
or are merely machinery provisions.
The Budget announcements are contained in the following clauses. Clause 6 provides
for a rates rebate with maximum of $25 on owner-occupied homes. Clauses 7, 27, and 33 deal
with the announcement that a rebate will be provided as part of the Government's fishing
vessel ownership scheme, which is an extension of the farm ownership savings scheme.
Clauses 8, 10, and 11 contain either an interest exemption, or a rebate in relation to interest
received from certain mortgages. Clause 8 provides a rebate of 20c in the dollar, with a
maximum of $500 for approved home vendor mortgages. Clause 10 extends the scope of the
existing additional $200 interest exemption by including interest received from mortgages
guaranteed by the Housing Corporation of New Zealand. Clause 11 exempts from tax 50
percent of the interest received from farm vendor finance bonds or approved farm vendor
mortgages. Clause 11 also exempts premiums on redemption of inflation-adjusted bonds.
Clause 9 increases the allowable maximum aggregate donations and private school fees
from $200 to $350, and converts the tax benefit from an exemption before tax to a rebate
from tax of 50c in the dollar, subject to a maximum rebate of $175. This clause also adds
World Vision and the Save the Children Fund to those organisations qualifying for this
rebate. Clause 14 adds deer to the "nil" value increased livestock scheme. Clause 15
increases from $6,000 to $7,000 the allowable cost of motorcars for depreciation purposes.
Clause 16 gives an optional 20 percent first-year depreciation allowance to meat export


## p. 3681 (#563) ###########################################

14 October
3681
Income Tax Amendment Bill (No. 2)
houses in the year expenditure is incurred in erecting, extending, or altering buildings to
conform to hygiene standards. Clause 17 permits a supplementary depreciation allowance in
the second, third, fourth, and fifth years of use of plant and machinery normally used in two-
shift or three-shift operations. Clause 19 provides that plant and machinery that is subject to
a Government grant under the special assistance programme for the meat freezing industry,
will not qualify also for the industrial development plan investment allowance.
Clause 20 allows a 100 percent deduction in the year incurred on a wider range of energy
conservation expenditure, and changes the approving authority from the Commissioner of
Energy Resources to the Commissioner of Inland Revenue. Claims of $20,000 or more for
any year are to be supported by a certificate from an appropriately qualified engineer.
Clause 22 covers transitional provisions relating to the transfer from a loan to a grants
scheme in respect of certain types of farm forestry expenditure. Amounts of loans and
accumulated interest written off will not be assessable income, and expenditure covered by
those loans will not form part of the cost of the timber on maturity of the trees. Clause 24
applies to suspensory loans in relation to the cost of fishing vessels and applied technology
investment finance the same tax treatment as applies to other similar suspensory loans.
Clause 25 defines the tax treatment of Government grants for commercial research develop-
ment in priority areas under the pioneer regional development scheme. As with similar
grants they are not assessable income, but the deduction otherwise allowable is reduced by
the amount of the grant.
Of the remaining 21 clauses, the following 10 amend, replace, or add to existing
provisions. Clause 5 extends the retrospective pay rebates to arrears of superannuation in
earnings-related accident compensation. Clause 18 allows 100 percent write-off in the year of
installation of approved safety devices in taxis. Clause 21 permits farming and fishing
development expenditure on assets to be recovered if the asset is sold within 5 years. Clause
23 allows an alternative increased export tax incentive by way of customs duty relief in
certain cases approved by the Minister of Customs. Clause 26 is to prevent what are really
revenue profits from overall group company business activities from being regarded as
capital gains when received by a single company within a commonly owned group. It also
permits losses by one company in a group to be offset against the income of any other
nominated company or companies in the same group. Clause 28 brings present penalties for
offences more into line with present-day values. Clause 29 removes any doubt that late
payment penalties can be charged where annual returns are furnished late. Clauses 30 and 31
increase from $500 to $1,000 the amount of tax or penalty the commissioner may remit in any
one case. Clause 32 permits offence proceedings to be instituted under the general powers of
delegation instead of under the commissioner's specific written authority to the officer or
officers concerned.
The following 11 clauses are routine machinery and drafting amendments. Clause 3
inserts in section 4 of the principal Act the application date for last year's amendment to the
term "dividends". This was omitted in the translation to the Income Tax Act 1976. Clause 4
covers the position of existing and future tax assessments for a year in which the annual
taxing Act has been repealed. Clause 12 clarifies two points relating to employee share-
option schemes. Clause 13 is another clarifying amendment that enables an adjustment for
an incorrect accounting practice to be made when it affects only part of the business profits
or gains. Clause 34 details the terminating dates for tax incentives. Clause 35 provides that
certain losses are to be deductible from employment income. Clause 36 corrects a drafting
omission regarding regional development allowances. Clause 37 removes references to the
former universal superannuation. Clause 38 removes references to non-assessable income.
Clause 39 details amendments resulting from the Human Rights Bill. Clause 40 repeals
redundant provisions relating to non-resident traders.

House instructs me to adopt a different procedure for regulating the introduction of a Bill.
The committee considered the debate on the introduction of Government Bills at
considerable length in 1972. "There was general agreement that the introduction of a Bill,
except in exceptional circumstances, need not be a lengthy process, and that in general all
that is necessary is a brief explanation from the Minister followed by a limited period of
questions. It is unnecessary for the Minister at this stage to give a detailed analysis of the
Bill, as this material is contained in the printed explanatory note attached to the Bill, and it is
also not the appropriate time for members to make impromptu speeches that would be more
suitable on the second reading after they had had an opportunity to study the legislation. The
committee considered suggestions to restrict the number of speeches, and also a proposal to
limit the time for the debate. These were not approved in 1972 as it was felt that the present
rights of members should be preserved to cover the comparatively few cases where matters
of conscience or local interest were affected, or where there was strong opposition to the
Bill."
Then in 1974 the committee considered various proposals to amend the procedure
relating to the introduction of Government Bills, and it was agreed finally that the present
procedure should be retained, but that a time limit of 2 hours should be allocated to the
debate. Therefore I remind honourable members that debate on the introduction of a Bill is
very restricted except in exceptional cases in which matters of conscience are affected—and I
ask the member to examine whether his conscience is affected in this case—or there is local
interest-and I ask him also to consider whether there is local interest in this matter, and
emphasise that it must be local interest and not national interest—or in which there is strong
opposition to the Bill.
If the member has strong opposition to the introduction of the Bill, I expect to hear
some sort of reaction to it from him later on, but except in those cases-that is, the
exceptional cases I referred to—the introduction of a Bill need not be a lengthy process. All
that is necessary is a brief explanation from the Minister, which we have had, followed by a
limited period of questions. In fact, the member was giving us some material that would be
barely relevant for a second reading debate, and certainly not on the introduction of the Bill.
