Aranui-Manning
2. Miss DEWE (Lyttelton) asked the Minister of Railways: Has he seen the report in the
Dominion of Friday, 7 October 1977, on the likely cancellation of the 10 a.m. sailing of the
Cook Strait ferry Aranui due to a crew shortage, and, if so, could he advise: (a) was the
sailing cancelled; (b) how many crew were involved; (c) what were the reasons for the crew
shortage; (d) of which union were they members; (e) what is the total manning scale of
members of that union on the vessel; and (f) how many passengers were inconvenienced?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Railways): Yes, I have seen the report in the
Dominion of Friday, 7 October 1977, concerning the likely cancellation of the 10 a.m. sailing
of the Cook Strait ferry Aranui due to a crew shortage. To answer the specific questions
asked by the honourable member: Yes, the sailing was cancelled. Twenty-three members of
the provedor section of the crew exercised their right under the Shipping and Seamen Act
1952 to give 24 hours' notice to relinquish their positions. After leaving the vessel no other
members of the Federated Cooks and Stewards Union of New Zealand were available to fill
the jobs. The normal complement of cooks and stewards on the vessel is 27. About 267
persons were booked for the sailing, and they had their travel arrangements altered.
However, nearly all the people were conveyed on the Aratika or the Arahanga on the same
day.
Miss Dewe: Will the Minister confirm that four members of the provedor section of the
Federated Cooks and Stewards Union were involved, and, since there has been a disruption
to the vessel, has there been an increase in the number of crew, or has the crew been
consistently four members short?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN: To the best of my knowledge the crew remained four
members short while the ship was held up. I do not have that information with me, but to the
best of my knowledge that is the position.
Mr T. J. Young: As it would appear that action must be taken to have a fully manned
crew, what action is being taken to overcome the shortage?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN: The stoppage occurred because the captain of the Aranui
logged 11 members of the crew for returning late from a stop-work or union meeting. The
crew took exception to that. I am informed that discussions have taken place, that the matter
has now been satisfactorily resolved, and that the ship is sailing once again. That action was

Fishermen-Eligibility for Loans
3. Mr COURTNEY (Nelson) asked the Minister in Charge of the Rural Banking and
Finance Corporation: What qualifications are needed by the individual fisherman himself in
order to be eligible for a corporation loan for the purchase of a boat?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister in Charge of the Rural Banking and Finance Corpora-
tion): It is the rural bank's normal requirement that where loans are granted for the purchase
of fishing vessels applicants must hold a skipper's coastal fishing vessel certificate and a
second-class diesel trawler engineer's certificate.
Mr Courtney: Does the Minister know that all fishermen do not need to have those
certificates? I think particularly of the Kaipara fishermen.
Hon. D. MacINTYRE: There have been isolated cases where loans have been granted to
experienced fishermen who did not meet the minimum requirements at the time, but they
were required to obtain the qualifications within a short period. There is a lesser qualifica-
tion for an in-shore skipper's certificate which restricts the vessel to within 25 miles of its
port. Such a restriction can affect the viability of the venture, and it has been a long-standing
policy of the Fishing Industry Finance Committee to improve the qualifications of fishermen.
It feels that applicants should hold the minimum qualifications of a skipper's coastal fishing
vessel certificate and second-class diesel trawler engineer's certificate. These certificates
enable fishermen to travel up to 75 miles out from the coast.
Mr Lange: Would not the Minister agree that the Kaipara fishery has traditionally
existed without the need for fishermen to venture 70 miles up the coast because the fishing is
done within the habour, and would those conditions disqualify the Kaipara fishermen from
the assistance that is offered to others?
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: The Minister may give a brief opinion.
Hon. D. MacINTYRE: I would need to know the individual fishery, the size of the
individual boats, and the conditions.

Fishing Boats-Loan Refusals
9. Mr COURTNEY (Nelson) asked the Minister in Charge of the Rural Banking and
Finance Corporation: Can he give the reasons of the corporation for refusing to give loans on
fishing boats marginally shorter than the regulation length when the boats are specifically
designed for their operating conditions?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister in Charge of the Rural Banking and Finance Corpora-
tion): To ensure that vessels are properly constructed and seaworthy it has been a long-
standing policy of the Fishing Industry Finance Committee that vessels must be annually
surveyed by the marine division, Ministry of Transport, and this is a condition of any loan
now granted by the Rural Bank. In terms of the Shipping Survey Fishing Boat Order 1969,
only fishing vessels with a registered length exceeding 35ft are subject to survey, and the
marine division does not survey vessels under this length.
Mr Courtney: What is the length of the boat that is eligible for a loan? Is it 40 ft?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE: It is 40 ft, but in the recently introduced Fishing Vessel
Ownership Savings Bill the length of 9 m is mentioned, and the matter is now being discussed
with the marine division to find out whether we can get it to reduce the length of vessels that
it will survey.
Mr Elliott: Is the reason for the refusal of loans not only because the boats are
marginally shorter than the required length, but also because they are built of materials that
are not prescribed such as ferro-concrete?
Hon. M. Rata: What's wrong with ferro-concrete boats?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE: They sink. The Fishing Industry Finance Committee has set a
policy on what boats it will support, and at the moment the support does not include ferro-
concrete boats, a major reason being the great loss of sale value from the time the boats are
launched. Another reason is that, as a result of past experience and advice received from
marine experts, it has been found that the ferro-concrete boats are not as good an investment
as steel or wooden boats.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.
Medical Practitioners
10. Mr DOWNIE (Pakuranga) asked the Minister of Health: What action can his
department take to ensure that only legally qualified medical practitioners set up in practice?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry): I reply on behalf of


## p. 3692 (#574) ###########################################

3692
14 October
Oral Answers to Questions
the Minister of Health. Registration of medical practitioners is a function of the Medical
Council of New Zealand. The Department of Health has no control over medical practi-
tioners wishing to set up in private practice. Nevertheless, district officers of the department
are advised to interview new practitioners not personally known to them and to check their
credentials, particularly in the case of overseas practitioners. In cases of doubt, medical
officers of health are instructed to telex the department's head office so that a check can be
made urgently with the Medical Council. The Pharmaceutical Society has been asked to
advise pharmacists of their responsibility to ensure that prescriptions are written by
registered practitioners, and that, if there is any doubt, the Department of Health is to be
contacted. The legal penalties for posing as a medical practitioner are substantial and should
be sufficient deterrent to bogus practitioners. There can, however, be no foolproof method
of ensuring that the occasional fraud does not occur.

Stock Losses through Poisoning
13. Mr ROGERS (Onehunga) asked the Minister of Forests: How many claims for
compensation for stock losses, including dogs, arising from poisoning operations have been
received, how many claims have been paid, and what was the amount of compensation paid
out in each case during the last two financial years and for the period since?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Forests): For the period embracing the 1975-76 and
1976-77 financial years and to the present, the Forest Service has received six claims for
compensation for the loss of stock and dogs resulting from poisoning operations. A
settlement has been made in each case, and the amounts involved are $4,204, $810, $200,
$10,857, $414, and $200, a total of $16,685, being compensation for 24 cattle, 210 sheep, and
10 dogs lost. These losses relate to the use of poison against opossums, and in two cases also
involve poisoning of wild pigs, both of these programmes to combat the problem of bovine
tuberculosis in cattle.

Nuclear Disarmament
15. Hon. M. RATA (Northern Maori) asked the Minister of Foreign Affairs: In view of
the special session of the General Assembly of the United Nations, which will be devoted in
mid-1978 to the question of nuclear disarmament, will he advise: (a) whether New Zealand
will be participating; (b) what specific proposals the Government intends to initiate; and (c)
whether he proposes to publicise within New Zealand any views to highlight the significance
of this special United Nations session?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Acting Minister of Foreign Affairs): New Zealand
will certainly be participating in the special session next year, as I indicated yesterday in
answer to the question referred to by the member for New Lynn. New Zealand is not on the
54 member preparatory committee for the special session, and, accordingly, the scope for
initiating proposals before the special session itself is limited. However, the Government is
doing everything possible within its resources to make a positive contribution to the session.
At home, the Government is preparing a green paper on disarmament for the special
session, with a view to acquainting the public of the various disarmament issues that will be
considered at that session. The Minister of Foreign Affairs has also proposed that a link be
established between the Government and the public to facilitate the exchange of ideas and
opinions on disarmament issues in advance of the special session. At the special session itself
New Zealand will, of course, be prepared to initiate any proposal it deems is required to
make the special session a success. However, the session will not constitute a disarmament
negotiating forum but rather a general conference devoted to the principles, programmes,
and machinery of disarmament. It will be a success if it provides a better framework for the
progress in disarmament in future years. New Zealand's contribution will be tailored to meet
this objective.

CONTRACEPTION, STERILISATION, AND ABORTION BILL
In Committee
Further consideration of clause 3, and the amendment proposed thereto.
11 a.m.
By leave, further consideration of clause 3 postponed.
11 a.m.
Clause 4. Administering of contraceptives to mentally subnormal females.
(1) Subject to subsection (3) of this section, a parent or guardian of any female, or any person
who is acting in the place of a parent of any female, or any person otherwise having the custody or
care of any female, may, if that female is mentally subnormal, administer any contraceptive to that
female.
(2) For the purposes of subsection (1) of this section, a female is mentally subnormal if she is
suffering from subnormality of intelligence as a result of arrested or incomplete development of
mind.
(3) Nothing in subsection (1) of this section shall apply to any intra-uterine device or to the
administering of any contraceptive by injection.

any female,", the words "or any registered medical practitioner in the course of treatment of

"The Governor”-National Film Unit Involvement
2. Mr H. N. AUSTIN (Hobson) asked the Minister of Tourism: What was the extent of
the financial involvement and the role of the National Film Unit in the television series "The
Governor"?
Hon. H. R. LAPWOOD (Minister of Tourism): The involvement of the National Film

Economic Stimulation—Manufacturing Production
3. Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert) asked the Minister of Finance: Does the
Government have any plans to stimulate the economy sufficiently to maintain manufacturing
production, let alone increase it?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance): The Government has announced on
a number of occasions in the last 2 or 3 weeks that it is examining proposals that will
stimulate manufacturing production. In the light of the fact that all the information that we
can get from overseas suggests that next year the New Zealand economy will not get any
external stimulation, and although manufacturing production, and, indeed, retail sales, have
held up quite well until the last month or so, there are signs of a downturn now and some
stimulation is warranted.
Hon. W. W. Freer: The fact that the Prime Minister has stated that the Government is
examining proposals still does not give a clear indication that positive action will be taken by
the Government at an early stage.
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: That was a statement and there was no question in it.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.

Overseas Loans
4. Miss DEWE (Lyttelton) asked the Minister of Finance: Is it possible to assess the
monetary benefit to the country by repaying loans which were arranged by the Labour
Government with those more favourable loans secured by the present Administration, and,
if so, what is the amount of that benefit?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance): Of the borrowing undertaken by this
Government since coming into office, $194.7 million has been applied in the repayment of
borrowings arranged during the term of the last Labour Government. The savings which can
be accurately ascribed to those repayments totalled $2.5 million.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.
Economic Stimulation-Building Industry
5. Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert) asked the Minister of Housing: What does he
intend to do to stimulate the building industry to save from closure factories such as the
particle board plant at Kumeu, which is currently producing only 3 days a week because of
the drastic fall in demand for its products by house builders?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing): The Government announced in April
that its house-building target for 1978 was 26 000 to 28 000 new dwellings. Since that
announcement a number of measures have been taken to assist the building industry to
achieve that objective, the most recent being on 22 August when savings banks Government
stock ratios were further reduced, construction of an additional 250 State rental houses was
approved, a loan supplement of $3,000 was made available to single-income families, and a
number of other measures were announced. In my opinion it is too early yet to be able to
judge the effect of these measures fully, but I am keeping a day-to-day check on the
situation, and if further stimulation is needed the necessary measures will be recommended.
I remind the honourable member that the need for a reduction in the level of activity by the
building industry has been occasioned by the overstimulation and the demands put on the
industry by his Government in the 1973 to 1975 period.
Hon. W. W. Freer: As the Minister has stated that he is keeping a day-to-day watch on
developments, when does he expect to have to take positive steps to give further impetus to
the building industry?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND: If the honourable gentleman had listened to what I said
he would have heard that it is too early yet to judge the effects of the measures taken within
the last 2 months, and when I consider that the effect of those measures is apparent I will
recommend the course to be taken.
Rt. Hon. W. E. Rowling: Is the Minister satisfied from his day-to-day check of what is
happening in the building industry that it will be able to achieve even the lower level of
26 000 that he suggested, let alone the 28 000 which was the top level?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND: Clearly I am concerned at the level of building activity. At
the same time, it would be foolish to overstimulate an industry which is there to meet the
demand, rather than simply to have the market tailored to meet the industry's requirements.
Mr Hunt: What representations did the Minister receive from the local member
concerned regarding the particle board plant at Kumeu.
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND: I have not discussed this particular factory with the member
concerned, but all industries connected with the building industry are keeping in close touch
with me on developments in those kinds of supporting areas.
Hon. Michael Connelly: In introducing its policy to cut back the building industry what
consideration did the Government give to the impact on associated manufacturing and
servicing industries which supply the building industry?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND: I am sure the honourable member knows the answer to that
question. One of the reasons targets were set at the level they were was to ensure that the
reduction in the level of activity in the building industry was such that it created no drastic
problems for the supporting industries. I emphasise that that is precisely why targets were
set.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.

11. Mr CHRISTIE (Napier) asked the Minister of Police: Can he confirm that the report

situation?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Lands): I reply on behalf of the Minister of Police. In
most establishments where meals are served over a long period to large numbers of people
the quality and quantity of meals fluctuates from time to time. This is certainly the case in
respect of meals served to recruits at the police college at Trentham, despite the fact that
meals and facilities are constantly inspected and reported on by college supervisors. The
kitchen from which meals are provided is not particularly modern, and generally unsatisfac-
tory messing arrangements was one of the factors taken into account by the Government
when it decided to let a contract early this year for the construction of a new police college
just north of Porirua. In the meantime the police are endeavouring to find a satisfactory
solution to messing problems at the Trentham college. One positive step that has been taken
is the recent establishment of a position as police catering officer. Applicants for the new
position have already been interviewed, and, when the person to be appointed takes up his
duties, the situation at Trentham will be high on the list of matters requiring his expert
attention.

to alleviate the position?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: The decision to go ahead with the police training college at Porirua
was approved not by the Labour Government but by this National Government, which has
set aside the necessary funds. As soon as construction of the new college is sufficiently
advanced for movement of the college to Porirua to be completed, the difficulties being
experienced at Trentham will be overcome.
Hon. Michael Connelly: Will the Minister reconsider his statement that the National
Government authorised construction of the police college at Porirua?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: I say again that the funds allocated for the establishment of the
police college at Porirua were set aside by this National Government.
Hon. G. F. Gair: Would the Minister allow me, as chairman of the Cabinet committee
on expenditure, to confirm that it was in fact towards the end of last year that the final
decision was made by this National Government to approve the building of the new police

Free Enterprise
13. Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert) asked the Prime Minister: How does he relate the
statement of the chairman of Tappenden Industries Ltd as reported in the New Zealand
Herald of 7 October that “free enterprise is being whittled away" with the National Party's
traditional claim of unqualified support for free enterprise?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): It is not possible to relate the statement in
question to National Party philosophy in any way; nor do I accept the statement. The same
statement further suggests "the extent of rules and regulations which now enwrap profit-
seeking organisations are getting close to choking them to death", referring to the retail car
trade. The facts simply do not bear this out. The figures released just last week by the
Minister of Trade and Industry show that new car sales are running at an acceptable level
and that used car sales have actually increased for the 9 months ended September 1977. I am
obliged to point out that, while the National Government wholeheartedly believes in free
enterprise, it makes no apologies for the existence of controls in this sector, as these controls
are designed to achieve the most favourable balance between the needs of the commercial
sector, the New Zealand consumer, and the economy as a whole. This was promised in the
1975 National Party manifesto, which stated that the National Government would provide

Customs Revenue from Opium-smoking Equipment
17. Mr KIRK (Sydenham) asked the Minister of Customs: Is it correct that the Customs
Department is collecting revenue from imported equipment which was primarily designed to
be used for the smoking of opium?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Minister of Customs): It is an offence under the Misuse of
Drugs Act 1975 to be in possession of any needle, syringe, pipe, or other utensil, for the
purpose of committing an offence against that Act. The range of equipment which could be
used for the smoking of controlled drugs, including opium, is extremely wide and extends
from simple household items such as tinfoil and household spoons to various kinds of pipes,
many of which can also be used for smoking tobacco. To the extent that any of these goods
are dutiable my department collects revenue on them. Because of the obvious difficulty in
making an effective Customs Import Prohibition Order to cover all goods that might be used
in taking opium, the law enforcement agencies involved in the fight against drugs have in the
past relied on the offence provision in the Misuse of Drugs Act. However, in view of recent
publicity on this matter I have asked my department to re-examine the matter to determine
whether it would be possible to impose a prohibition aimed specifically at such equipment.
Mr Kirk: Will the Minister seek to prevent the importation of equipment such as this?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON: Any equipment which could possibly be the subject of a
prohibition order will be included in the inquiry to be carried out by my department.

fire safety be replaced by statutory regulations?
Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister of Internal Affairs): The recommendation referred to
has not been acceptable to successive Governments, which have preferred that fire safety
standards should be applied through bylaws adopted by territorial authorities rather than
regulations promulgated by the central government. Successive Governments have also
preferred that the standards to be applied should be determined and revised from time to
time through the consultative process of the Standards Association of New Zealand. This
process provides much more flexibility for amendments made necessary by technological
developments and the special requirements of individual districts. Fire safety bylaws must be
adopted by all territorial authorities, and all must have the prior approval of the Minister of
Local Government. I do not consider that there is any indication that the situation is in need

these bylaws, as they are required to do under the present legislation, and I intend to enforce
that legislation.

mentioned?
Hon. D. A. HIGHET: That is correct, and that is why I believe that by working through

remembering that we must have some flexibility because of the circumstances in each
district.

recommendation that a single standard is best achieved by regulation rather than by trying to
persuade local authorities to follow the same pattern?
Hon. D. A. HIGHET: I certainly would not agree. In reply to a similar question from the
member for Petone only a fortnight ago I said that I believed, as did the previous Minister of
Internal Affairs, that it is better to have some flexibility and that this can be handled best by
bylaws and not by regulations.

me or through me as Winston Churchill's secret envoy and as chief of British Security Co-
ordination, BSC. The innocuous-sounding organisation with headquarters in New York was,
in fact, the hub for all branches of British intelligence. Roosevelt was acutely aware that
America, psychologically isolated since World War I, and relying wistfully upon geographi-
cal insularity, was woefully unprepared to meet or counter the onslaught of newly developed
military, propaganda, and espionage techniques. He desperately needed time to alert his
nation and to arm it without plummeting into war. Churchill was in far more desperate need
of arms and supplies to grant severely battered Britain even a modest hope of resistance and
a slim chance of survival. Only a leader who could extend his vision of national self-interest
to the belief that a union of free people was the real defence against totalitarian aggressors
would wager on Britain at such unattractive odds. Roosevelt was such a rare gambler."
It goes on: "We failed to face that critical question prior to 1939. Not one of the
democracies honestly confronted the obvious threat to its survival. They would not unite,
rearm, or consider sacrifice for individual or collective security. There were those who
argued that the sacrifices were not necessary. Today, parallel arguments are heard, similar
responses given. We are rightly repelled by secrecy; it is a potential threat to the democratic
principle and free government. Yet we could delude ourselves if we should forget that
secrecy was for a time virtually our only defence. It served not only to achieve victory, but
also to save lives in that perilous pursuit. The weapons of secrecy have no place in an ideal
world. But we live in a world of undeclared hostilities in which such weapons are constantly
used against us and could, unless countered, leave us unprepared again, this time for an
onslaught of a magnitude that staggers imagination. And, while it may seem unnecessary to
stress so obvious a point, the weapons of secrecy are rendered ineffective if we remove the
secrecy. One of the conditions of democracy is freedom of information." [Interruption.]

18 October
3711
New Zealand SIS Amendment Bill
information. It would be infinitely preferable to know exactly how our intelligence agencies
function, and why, and where. But this information, once made public, disarms us, so here is
the conundrum: how can we wield the weapons of secrecy without damage to ourselves?
How can we preserve secrecy without endangering constitutional law and the individual
guarantees of freedom?"
That in essence was the question that was put to the former Chief Ombudsman when he
was asked to investigate the Security Intelligence Service. After investigating it and finding
things that he had not imagined could be so, he brought down a report last year that stated,
first, that there is need for a Security Intelligence Service, and, secondly, that under proper
legal safeguards it is necessary on rare occasions for that service to engage in acts that would
otherwise be unlawful. This Bill has been brought together in that context-not just the Bill,
but also the administrative action that was proposed by Sir Guy. In the matter of classifica-
tion of documents and the vetting of State servants, it has been necessary to take a longer
time to evaluate Sir Guy's proposals. A committee of senior officials is considering that
matter, but, because of the complexity of the subject, it will be some considerable time
before it completes its examination.
I make the point that, in considering the role and the function of the service, the public
should realise that a great deal of the service's work is involved in this vetting procedure
rather than the investigation of the more spectacular matters with which it is concerned.
There has been a suggestion by the Association of University Teachers of New Zealand that
the universities should be some kind of special sanctuary, not open to the Security
Intelligence Service. While I agree with Sir Guy's proposals that it should be made easier for
members of the service to have university courses that would make them better
members and one would hope that that situation can be improved-the Government does
not accept that our universities can be some kind of special sanctuary. That would clearly be
going too far in the interests of the State.
A member of the press gallery raised a very interesting point about the provision in
section 23 of the principal Act, and clause 7 of this Bill, that exempts restrictions on the
broadcasting or the reporting of proceedings in Parliament in relation to the publication of
information about the decisions of the Commissioner of Security Appeals and service staff
generally. He said that if we make special provision for this we establish the fact that special
provision is needed, and if at some time it was taken away it would be held that this reporting
could not take place. It is his contention that the power is there already, whether by
convention or otherwise, and that this section of the legislation is unnecessary. It is a
constructive approach, but it seemed to me that if we took that out there would be those who
would claim that we are removing a right. I think by leaving it in we are making sure there is
no doubt—and I would not see any Government in this country taking it out at some time in
the future.
There has been a great deal of discussion about the meaning of the word "subversion".
Without going into the detail, which doubtless other speakers will during this debate, let me
make it perfectly clear that, as far as this Government is concerned, “subversion" does not
include those who dissent from the policies of the Government of the day. That is not
subversion, either in terms of the Bill or in terms of the policy of this Government. I quote
from Lord Denning's report on the Profumo affair: "No one can understand the role of the
Security Service . . . unless he realises the cardinal principle of their operations are to be
used for one purpose, and one purpose only-the defence of the Realm. They are not to be
used so as to pry into any man's private conduct or business affairs, or even into his political
opinions, except in so far as they are subversive; that is, they would contemplate the
overthrow of the Government by unlawful means." That has been said over and over again
in the last month, but it has to some considerable extent fallen on deaf ears.
Some amendments to the Bill are contained in a Supplementary Order Paper circulated
today. I made it clear when introducing the Bill that the Government would accept
representations, and consider them carefully. That has been done. As a result of those
representations, some amendments have been made and others are under consideration for
introduction later, before the Committee stage of the Bill, the reason being that representa-
tions are still being received.
We have provided that an interception warrant cannot be used to obtain information
passing between lawyer and client, priest and penitent, or doctor and patient. Some of this is
in the Evidence Act, but in the case of the lawyer it is spelt out separately. We have altered
the section that deals with the addition of terms to a warrant by the Minister in charge. The
wording was difficult, but we now say "such other terms, if any, put into the warrant". The


## p. 3712 (#594) ###########################################

3712
18 October
New Zealand SIS Amendment Bill
purpose of that portion of the Bill is to enable the Minister to put further restrictions on the
warrant-not to make it easier-and this wording has been used with that in mind. Similarly,
we are rewording the Bill by means of the Supplementary Order Paper so that, in his report
to Parliament, the Minister is required to report in a positive sense-not that he shall have
regard to certain things, as was the provision in the original Bill, but that he shall put certain
things in unless they are prejudicial to security. So that portion has been firmed up.
We have put in a new subclause requiring the destruction of any irrelevant material
obtained as a result of the execution or the operation of one of these warrants. Anything
obtained in that way that is not strictly relevant must be destroyed forthwith. I am informed
that that would be the case anyway, and that around the world irrelevant material is
destroyed. However, it is now to be made mandatory and part of the law. As a result of
objections, principally from the news media and publishers, we now propose that it will not
be an offence to disclose the identity of former members of the Security Intelligence Service.
However, the clause will still apply to present members.
Finally, we have accepted the representations of the various State Service organisations,
and are removing the portion of the Bill which gives power to direct State servants to take
certain action in accordance with these warrants. There will be no direction to State servants;
they can only be requested. If they wish to refuse, that is the end of the matter. Those are the
amendments in the Supplementary Order Paper, although there may well be other amend-
ments after consideration of representations that are still coming forward, or possibly from
this debate.
I am bound to say that I am gravely concerned at the attitude of the parliamentary
Opposition to the Bill, especially that of the Leader of the Opposition, who was the Minister
in charge of the service during a particularly important and difficult time in its history. It
seems that he has taken a complete about-face from his attitude at that time, and from the
attitude of the former Labour Prime Minister, the late Mr Kirk, each of whom gave total
support to the service when he was the Minister responsible. I am well aware that at least two
members of the Labour Cabinet took a different view-the then Minister of Justice and the
present Deputy Leader of the Opposition, who have opposed the service, and in one case, at
least, opposed its very existence. The present Leader of the Opposition, however, did not.
It is a matter of fact that in the investigation of the late Dr Sutch illegal methods were
used with the full knowledge and approval of the then Labour Prime Minister and Minister
in charge of the service, the late Mr Kirk. My information is that, on the change of Prime
Minister in September 1974, the present Leader of the Opposition, when being briefed on
this matter, told the director of the service that he already knew about the matter as he had
been told by the former Prime Minister. Why that should be so I do not know, because he
was not the Deputy Prime Minister at the time, but simply a senior Minister. I am informed
that, although fully briefed on the matter, at no time was any opposition expressed to what
was done.
Indeed, the late Mr Kirk told the director of the service to use whatever methods were
necessary to obtain information on the activities of Dr Sutch, who had been communicating
with a man named Razgoverov, in the Soviet Embassy, who had been identified as a KGB
agent before he came to New Zealand. Although the service recommended that he be not
permitted to come to New Zealand, that recommendation was not accepted by the Labour
Government of the day. He came to New Zealand, and was immediately in communication
with the late Dr Sutch. Most of the rest is public knowledge. It is a fact that the service was
not only authorised but also encouraged by the Labour Minister in charge, the former Prime
Minister, to use methods which were then illegal. I am not criticising him in this matter of
espionage; that is one of the reasons why, in his report, Sir Guy Powles said there are times
when this has to be done, but it should be done under proper legal safeguards.
That is what the Bill is all about-doing something that we know was done. I do not
know how many times, but I am not much interested. I am interested, however, in the fact
that it was done in the time of a Labour Government with the knowledge and full support of
a Labour Prime Minister; and we now find his colleagues opposing it. I applaud what he did

I do not think any member on this side of the House gets any pleasure out of the kind of

It has been suggested that clause 3 should be amended because it refers to "potential"
espionage. We have brought in the New Zealand Intelligence Council to consult with the
director on policy. [Time extended.] The great difficulty is that, unless the service interests
itself in potential espionage, it is incapable of carrying out its task, because if it has to wait
until there is actual espionage it will obviously be too late. That is simple logic. If the police
are suspicious that a crime is about to be committed but do nothing, it might well be too late;
and similarly with the Security Intelligence Service. That is the reason for this. Again, if any
New Zealander is not involved in espionage, sabotage, terrorism, or subversion—and
subversion in its very limited definition-then he will not be involved.
We have looked through a great number of representations. Many of them are well
thought out and compelling in their arguments, but some arise from a total misunderstanding
of the purposes of the Bill. The one thing I do want to emphasise is that, after the
Ombudsman's report was received in the middle of last year, a committee of senior officials,
led by the permanent head of the Prime Minister's Department and the Cabinet secretary
and including the Secretary of Foreign Affairs, the Chief of Defence Staff, and one or two
others, has spent virtually the whole of the time since trying to formulate the Ombudsman's
recommendations into workable legislation. Sir Guy has admitted from time to time that
some of his proposals do not finally jell. Indeed, some parts of his report were based on
misapprehensions, but nothing of great importance.
I emphasise that at no time was any recommendation from that committee of officials
dealt with by the small committee of Ministers-myself, the Deputy Prime Minister, and the
Minister of Labour-on a political basis. I hoped that when I introduced the Bill into the
House it would have bipartisan support. That hope was dashed immediately, and I regret it
very deeply, just as I regret the manner in which so many members opposite have turned
through 180 degrees in their attitude to the service. I find it incredible and deplorable that
men who, as Cabinet Ministers, properly supported the service have taken the attitude that
they have taken in the last month-appearing on public platforms with people whose
publicly avowed objective is to bring down this country. It is a sorry day in the history of the
Parliamentary Labour Party, and for none more than the Leader of the Opposition, who
supported the service when he was the Minister.
There has been a suggestion that the National Party caucus is split on the issue. I am
very happy to say that that suggestion is quite wrong. There is no member of the National
Party caucus who does not see the need for a Security Intelligence Service and does not
support it in its difficult work—not one. I am perfectly certain that there are members on the
other side of the House who still take the same view. I know that the former Attorney-

others on that side of the House think, and what they have said publicly. I doubt if they are
in the majority.

politically desperate. I find it deplorable that in a matter that deeply and gravely involves the

settle, and for some of those who are putting on performances such as we have seen up there

would be very happy to leave our political future in the hands of the people on this measure.

In the course of this debate we will demonstrate that the Powles report has been twisted

applied that fills me with alarm. The propensity of the person who can set them in motion to

their very vagueness encourages individual interpretation.
To take an example, we all know that unemployment is rising, and that those who are
out of work or occupied with "made" work now number about 60 000. More than half a
million New Zealanders-half of them children-live below what has been officially
described as the poverty level. All of those people provide fertile ground for protest-and
they have good reason to protest. They are likely to express their protests in demonstrations
and other verbal and visual expressions of their dissatisfaction. They could well be led in that
by the trade unions, speaking for the silent and-I believe in the case of many of them—the
inarticulate majority; and, beyond doubt, the Socialist Unity Party would push its way in,
which would cause the whole affair to be tarred with the brush of subversion and thereby
dismissed as the voice of Moscow.
Sir Guy Powles noted that the Security Intelligence Service is prone to put more weight
on what it regards as subversion than on its true role of counter-intelligence. His recommen-
dations on that point have been totally disregarded and, on the contrary, we have a new and
dangerous dimension of potential subversion dragged in, over which the service may
institute surveillance. The Prime Minister told us it was impossible to avoid the potential,
and that one could not concentrate on the actual. I do not accept that, but in any case he was
talking about the past role of the service; in his speech today he paid singularly little
attention to the new powers proposed to be conferred. I do not know what potential
surveillance is, or what potential subversion is. Indeed, I do not know what surveillance
really conveys. All I know is that it has a chilling sound, and it is an open invitation to probe,
prowl, and pry into the affairs of anyone who raises his voice or, equally likely, anyone who
arouses suspicion by speaking in lower than normal tones, especially about industrial
matters.
The wide scope of subversion itself has attracted much comment. It is defined as "the
undermining by unlawful means of the authority of the State in New Zealand". The Prime
Minister says, "Well, we would not take any action on minor acts of subversion; it is only the
big things that would interest us." Well, let us look at what could be acted on, and there are
two elements in this consideration. The first is an invasion of the authority of the State. That
is all-pervasive; the State interferes and intervenes in every aspect of our lives. Then it must
be unlawful, which requires no more than a contravention of a minor regulation. Radio and
television licences are issued under the authority of the State. To fail to pay them is not only
unlawful, but it also undermines that authority. I do not say that anyone who does not take

What is really aimed at is hijacking and, to a lesser degree, kidnapping. I personally

The Prime Minister claims that the additional powers and the right to invade forbidden

misused. We say no to that. I do not accept it. As to the second of these, I quote from the
New Zealand Herald of 17 October. That is yesterday, is it not? "The course of recent
legislation seems to give the police very large powers and to trust to them to be very discreet
and thoughtful in their working. Experience has shown this to be a mistake." That was on 17
October 1877, not 1977, and, if we read for the word "police" the "Security Intelligence
Service", it would seem that we have learnt very little in 100 years.
I shall mention one or two of the safeguards put forward by the Prime Minister. Others
will be examined in detail by my colleagues. It is said that an interception warrant is not to be
issued unless the information sought advises it and is not likely to be obtained otherwise.
Well, a moment's examination of those words shows them not only to be self-justifying, but
able to be interpreted as the person seeking to interpret them wishes. Like Humpty-
Dumpty, he can make the words mean whatever he wants them to mean. Then it is said the
warrants must contain certain particulars about the type of communication and the identity
of the person concerned, quite apart from the fact that a communication, especially a
telephone communication, implies the involvement of more than one person-so eavesdrop-
ping will involve not only suspects but non-suspects. In this regard we think of the protests of
the Youthline organisation, to which confidentiality is so vital a part of the advisory and
helpful service it gives-the Minister can add additional terms to the warrant as he thinks
necessary.
The Bill goes on to state that the Minister's report can be so vague as to be deceptive. It
need be only a general assessment of the warrants issued during that year. A Supplementary
Order Paper enlarges on that a bit, but it does not get to the root of the criticism I am now
about to make, because both the original and the amended version could readily be satisfied

the original introduction of the Bill." In that one sentence he could cover a range of warrants
against all the 30 organisations I mentioned that made representations against the Bill,
simply grouping them together, and saying, “Oh, they were some of the original opponents

of the Bill. We just issued warrants against them. I need not go into further details." That

However, all safeguards, however real or imaginary, are swept aside by the proposed
new subsections 4A(5) and (7). They enable the Minister and the Security Intelligence
Service to do as they like, and no one can say them nay. By removing the procedure from
judicial scrutiny, they throw overboard the traditional remedies like trespass, conversion,
injunction, mandamus, and all the other legal processes that the common law has evolved to
protect the citizen from the exercise of absolute and dictatorial powers. Going back 300
years or more, it has been the role of the common law courts and their associated
jurisdictions in Britain to evolve remedies against the oppressive weight of the monarchy and
the establishment-the Executive.
This Bill throws the safeguards overboard and enables the Government—the
Executive to ride roughshod over the remedies of centuries. By overriding existing
legislation, it tears up not only all the statutes, the purpose of which is to protect the
individual—and the Human Rights Commission Bill is said to be one of these-but also all
those parts built into other Acts to make sure that they are not used oppressively: the
Wanganui Computer Centre Act, the Income Tax Act, and the Evidence Act, partially
cured I agree by amendments put forward today, but still not fully operative and still leaving
areas of confidentiality that could be overriden by the Bill.
In the last election campaign the present Government, then aspiring for office, put into
the mouth of the present Minister of Agriculture this specific promise, "We will bring in laws
to ensure that your privacy is totally protected from any form of electronic snooping." In the
first instance that promise was quite unnecessary, because the Labour Government had
already introduced to Parliament the Listening Devices Bill, which did just that. The Bill had
been referred to a committee for recess study, but was killed by this Government. The
promise made at that time by the present Minister of Agriculture has been openly, cynically,
and outrageously broken by the Government. I do not know whether it is tragic or comic.
The word "snooping" was used. Well, whether it is Snoopy or the Red Baron, I do know
that it is disastrous and a foretaste of worse things to come.

opposed the Bill. When the Labour Party indicated it was to set up a select committee on the

In recent months the Prime Minister has revealed a complete lack of judicial tempera-
ment for the job to be undertaken. There is an instinct of desire to clobber anyone, whether
it is a group or an individual, who is prepared to question the infallibility of the establish-
ment. Yet this Bill in effect gives power to one person to intrude into the private life of any
New Zealander. Anyone who writes or receives a letter, anyone who uses a telephone or
receives a telephone call, can be the subject of a warrant of which the person or persons
named in the warrant have no knowledge; nor indeed will anyone they are likely to contact
have any knowledge of it. There is no appeal, no matter how false, no matter how damaging,
the premise on which the warrant was originally issued may be. Contrary to the recommen-
dation of Sir Guy Powles, there is no time limit on any such warrant, and there is no limit to
the number of people who can be named in it.
The interception warrant gives power not only to open mail and tap telephones, but also
to break into private premises in circumstances that normally would make a person liable to
a jail sentence of up to 10 years. The Bill provides that an agent may seize any
communication-and since "communication" is not defined in the Bill we have a pretty wide
open proposition. In any event, unlike a search warrant, the interception warrant is not
challengeable in any court of law. As I have already said, it is not subject to any time limit
-again unlike a search warrant, which terminates after 1 month.
The Combined State Service Organisations pointed out that the Bill contained new
conditions of service for 175 000 State employees. I am pleased to see that the Bill has been
altered in that respect. But for very strong and valid protest, those conditions would have put
175 000 people to all intents and purposes under the direction of the Security Intelligence
Service. That would certainly have cut across the relationship of trust between those
employees and their clients, their patients, or their pupils. The Post Office Association
pointed out that the Bill produced double standards of obligation. Once again, at least that
aspect has been set aside. There would have been the situation that public servants would
have been directed.

of not being prepared. We should say to those who have not yet faced reality that in many

Not every critic of the Bill is unaware, or unable to accept reality, but for whatever
reasons-including straightforward political motivation-many other extraordinary things
have been said in the course of attacking the Bill. For example, there has been the objection
to the reference to potential espionage by people apparently unaware that by the time
espionage becomes actual it is invariably too late. There have been those who resolutely
assert that no protest group is outside the ambit of the Bill. It suits them to ignore the fact
that its ambit is restricted to those who advocate the undermining of the State by unlawful
means-this is specifically set out in the Bill. But perhaps the most truly extraordinary point
of all to emerge from the attacks, and the best example of all to show how the anti-SIS
campaign has distorted reality, is the incredible suggestion, advocated apparently by the
member for New Lynn, among others, that judges be dragged into the Executive arena by
giving them, rather than the Minister in charge, the power to issue interception warrants.
Anyone who has advocated this in the course of attacking the Bill has shown, in my view, a
dangerous ignorance of our constitution. They are apparently unaware that it would be as
dangerous to drag the judiciary into the Executive sphere, as it could be for the Executive to
encroach in their sphere.
Hon. Dr A. M. Finlay: Is the issue of a search warrant an Executive act?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON: In the last few weeks, as the member for Henderson well
knows, the highest court in the English legal system has drawn a clear line between the
functions of the Executive and the functions of the judiciary, in the Gouriet case, and thus
we have impeccable legal authority for asserting our point of view. If judges became
involved in interception warrants, obviously they would become involved in decisions that
would attract political controversy, and, if they did, who of the opponents to the
Bill including the member for New Lynn-have stopped to think how they would be
rendered answerable in the process of exercising this discretion? It is no use for anyone to
suggest that because judges issue search warrants they should also issue interception
warrants. The one involves the application of set legal principles; the other would involve
value judgments on matters of State security, which vary from time to time and from place to
place. The other day someone suggested that judges already can make such judgments in the
course of awarding discovery of documents on which a plea of State privilege has been made.
The two are not analogous. In the one case a judgment on State security is made in the raw;
in the other it is essentially in adjudication on a claim. There are, of course, many other
reasons, as I am sure the member for Henderson is well aware, why judges must not issue
interception warrants. Come to that, I do not recall the member for Henderson's clearly
stating what his view is about this, and whether he disagrees with the member for New Lynn.

in electronic surveillance in the United States for the purpose of obtaining foreign intelli-
gence information. I view it as a first step in an on-going effort of this Administration and
Congress to place meaningful restrictions on the largely unchecked power of the intelligence
community. The Bill seeks to end the all too common abuses of recent history by providing
substantive and procedural limitations on the hitherto unchecked power of the executive
branch to engage in electronic surveillance for national security purposes."
Senator Kennedy went on to say that his objective has been "to reach some kind of fair
balance that will protect the security of the United States without infringing our citizens'
human rights and liberties. This Bill goes a long way in striking that balance. It provides


## p. 3740 (#622) ###########################################

New Zealand SIS Amendment Bill
detailed statutory restrictions on the power of the Government to engage in foreign
intelligence electronic surveillance. Its provisions are applicable to all such surveillance.
American citizens and lawful resident aliens, therefore, can be targets of electronic surveill-
ance only if they, first, knowingly engage in 'clandestine intelligence activities, which involve
or will involve a violation of the criminal law'; secondly, knowingly engage in activities 'that
involve or will involve sabotage or terrorism for or on behalf of a foreign power'; and,
thirdly, 'pursuant to the direction of an intelligence service or intelligence network of a
foreign power, and are knowingly and secretly collecting and transmitting foreign intelli-
gence information in a manner harmful to the security of the United States'."
The Bill sets out standards and procedures. In contrast to the provisions in our Bill,
before a warrant can be obtained the Attorney-General must approve each such application.
The court can approve the application for a warrant authorising surveillance only after
making certain detailed findings, and concluding that "there is probably cause to believe that
the target of electronic surveillance is a foreign power, or agent of a foreign power, and
unless the warrant is designated as being for a foreign power, the surveillance can only be for
a 90-day period, or maximum." I have read this extract at some length, because Sir Guy
Powles tells us that, in essence, we need this Bill to protect the secrets of the United States.
The United States itself does not demand restrictions of the sort contained in the Bill before
us.

the Prime Minister will resign if he makes a mistake? Of course he will not. There is no
effective check in this Bill.

Security. The interpretations clause, clause 2, provides that "New Zealand Intelligence
Council' means the council of that name established in accordance with an approval given by
the Prime Minister on the 3rd day of February 1975". The Intelligence Council was set up
without reference to Parliament; Parliament was not sitting at the time, and the then Prime
Minister, who is now the Leader of the Opposition, set up that council under his Executive
power. Although certain amendments have been made to the administration since then, that
shows that both tigers have the same sort of spots.
Since the 1939-45 war New Zealand has been forced to become security conscious. I
remember that at the time the first ANZUS meeting was held in this country we were totally
incapable of receiving people from overseas, because we had no idea at all about security.
We had had no security training; all doors were left open, and we went about our way—a bit
like Parliament at the moment, where I understand that anything marked "Secret" is not to
go below the sweepers. The result was that we were not able to receive information that was
vital for our total defence; we had to take ourselves in hand and realise that something had to
be done. Mind you, during and after the war an SIS had been operated within the Prime
Minister's Department under the powers of the Prime Minister, but without any legislative
authority. We began tightening up security arrangements, and about 20 years ago Brigadier
Bill Gilbert was appointed to build up a small internal force to ensure the security, of New
Zealand. All services were made security conscious and instituted checks.
Members will recall that about 20 years ago we had no security at all at our airports, but
today everyone accepts the arrangements made. We began to realise that a new dimension of
warfare was spreading across the world, and it has finally reached New Zealand. Some
groups throughout the world will stop at nothing-terrorism, hijacking, or whatever. I
believe all members will have read the newspaper report tonight of the final result of one of
those attacks. I emphasise that it could very well have ended the other way round, and that
the hostages could have been shot instead of the hijackers. As a result of our realisation of
what has been happening in the world we have set up security guards at our airports, and we
sincerely hope they will be in the right place at the right time in the event of such a group's
trying to operate in New Zealand.
Many of us consider our country a small land of practically no significance from the
point of view of information. But in this day and age of satellites, nuclear submarines, and
IBMs nothing is secure, and it is vital that we co-operate with our friends and be able to talk
to them. We must be trusted, and therefore we must be seen to be able to keep secrets. We
have decided that this is not the job for the Police, as was indicated by the member for
Henderson in his anti-bugging Bill, and a long time ago we decided it was not a job for the
armed services. Quite frankly, I wonder why we shackle ourselves in the fight against drugs,
for instance. Why should we not be able to catch by any means the white-collar criminals
who are dealing out death amongst our citizens? But no, we have said that New Zealand, as
a democracy, will not stoop to that sort of action.
In 1969 the New Zealand Security Intelligence Service Bill was introduced and passed.
That was the first time the organisation had been given legislative stature, and it is very
interesting to note that on 21 August 1969 the late Norman Kirk-he has been quoted
several times in this House already, but I think it is worth quoting his words again, because
someone outside may be listening now who was not listening before-said "with the present
way of life throughout the world, this type of thing is essential in an otherwise free society".
He was talking about the Security Intelligence Service. Later, he said, "We are discussing a
service which is essential. In an open democratic society there are tremendous advantages
and also some risks attached." The member for Henderson will remember him saying these
words. "To have a free and open society, the proper purpose of a security service is, and
always has been, to do with the maintenance of a democratic open society, but we have to
remember that the freedom conferred by such a society creates the opportunity to abuse the
privileges or destroy the society. This Bill," he said in 1969, “should be a protection against
such an abuse and against both those who would overthrow our free and open society and
those who could in fact inhibit these rights in the name of its protection."
Three years later, Norman Kirk became Prime Minister, the Minister responsible for
administering that particular Act; and he changed neither his views nor the Act. I shall again
quote from Hansard, Volume 360. Mr Kirk supported the Bill, and his opening remarks
were, "This Bill is very much what we expected and, indeed, what we have been seeking for
a long time." Again, he said, "The final point about the Bill is that it will leave the security
service in political control, and this obviously must be so."

Some amendments to the Bill have been proposed. It was suggested that the Public
Service would work voluntarily for the Security Intelligence Service, and therefore the word
"direct" has been deleted. A member of the executive of the Public Service Association has
considered the amendments and believes they still do not meet the objections expressed by
thousands of New Zealanders. The Bill still provides no limit to what the Security
Intelligence Service is authorised to do under a warrant. Any person can be approached by
the service to act for it, and such approach must be kept secret under penalty of a fine.
Complete protection is still provided for SIS agents or their helpers against any legal action
arising from anything they may do under the terms of a warrant. A cloak of secrecy is still
provided for present SIS agents, whatever they may do. They will not be asked to resign, but
will be moved sideways into the Public Service, and that particular amendment makes the
Bill even more obnoxious.
No legal protection is given against interference by the SIS with legitimate political
activity, which Sir Guy Powles said has happened in the past. Certainly I am not confident
that it will not happen in the future. State employees cannot now be directed to work for the
SIS, but they can still be requested to do so and their employer will be informed of the
request. That provision applies to all New Zealanders, not just the 18 percent in the Public
Service. The new clause allowing the service to destroy unwanted information could cut both
ways. It will enable the SIS to destroy documents or erase tapes that could be evidence of
illegal and unwarranted activity. Secrecy breeds suspicion, and suspicion breeds fear-and
the Bill has succeeded in doing that before our eyes this evening.
I believe that a Heylen poll should be taken asking New Zealanders if they are prepared
to put their faith and trust in the Prime Minister to administer the Bill. I should be very
interested in the result. The Bill has wide-ranging powers, but the normal safeguards have
been deliberately removed, as has the private citizen's right of redress through the court. If a
person talks to the press he will suffer persecution as well as being fined, as also will the press
if it publishes his story. To my knowledge no other legislation on the statute book is
protected from the gaze of the press and excluded from judicial inquiry in the courts. When
he introduced his amendments today the Prime Minister said that the proper safeguards are
contained in the Bill. He cannot even properly describe legislation, let alone administer it.
If this Bill goes through, any Watergate situation that arose could not be exposed in the
media, as happened in America, and no New Zealander could do anything about it. Yet the
Prime Minister said today: "We are doing something that has to be done. We are doing it
with the utmost possible safeguards. We are doing it for the good of the future of our
country." I am nonplussed by the subjectivity of his eagerness to wield the power he seeks,
which he will cover with the camouflage of those patently inaccurate and incorrect asser-
tions. This Bill effectively puts above public accountability the Security Intelligence Service
and the Minister in charge of it. I accept that a few words have been changed by the
amendments in the Supplementary Order Paper. None the less, a subjective judgment will

In total, this Bill clearly amounts to an invasion of the privacy of New Zealanders, and I

concerned that the economy is being run down because of mismanagement, with unemploy-

without as deep an inquiry into some aspects as I had wished." And, on the same page: "My

That is not the finished, considered report of somebody who had a great deal of time to look

I remember that when the report was commissioned the present Prime Minister, who
was then the Leader of the Opposition, was furious, as is his wont, because the ultimate full
report was to go only to the then Prime Minister. I well remember the Leader of the

The Ombudsman went on to say that, given the fact that he felt it necessary to suggest
some rather Draconian and severe measures, the whole package needed to be taken and put
into legislation. I quote again from his report: "If you take bits out of it and enlarge them or
change them you destroy the whole balance." That is worth emphasising, because I do not
think that part of the report has been read-or at least it has not been heeded by the
Government. This is the man who wrote the report and on whose report the legislation is
based, saying that if you take bits out of it and enlarge them or change them, you destroy the
whole balance. Can Government members say with straight faces that the Bill as amended,
or even before being amended, is taken straight out of the report, neither amended nor
enlarged? Of course they cannot.
In his report Sir Guy expresses considerable concern about one aspect of the service's
activities and I remind members of that because it is not referred to anywhere in the Bill.
"Virtually every form of protest and dissent-not necessarily either very militant or very
radical-falls within the service's net for one of two reasons: penetration or the possibility of
penetration by subversives, or an inherent potential for subversion. The service has over the
years taken some interest in a diverse range of organisations. Personal files have been
opened on a number of people engaged in political protest activities, which suggests that
they might conceivably in future become subversive or become a target for subversives. The
service has advised me that approximately 10 percent of its work in the field of counter-
subversion is concerned with protest groups."
At the end of that section of his report Sir Guy made the following recommendations:
"That the Act be amended by inserting a proviso in the following terms: 'Provided that
intelligence shall not be obtained regarding any person or body which is not actually engaged
in espionage, sabotage, or subversion, unless the advice of the Intelligence Council has been
obtained; that, until the Act is so amended, the service curtail its counter-subversion
activities in accordance with the spirit of the proposed amendment; that the priorities
attached by the service to espionage, subversion, and terrorism respectively be reconsidered
by the service in consultation with the New Zealand Intelligence Council, but with the object
of allotting higher priorities to espionage and terrorism, and lower to subversion."
Very real concern is being expressed throughout the country that the Security Intelli-
gence Service has given undue attention to protest groups. That is supported by Sir Guy's
observations, and one wonders how many of us who were opposed to the Vietnam war and
involved in protest movements came under the scrutiny of the Security Intelligence Service.
Indeed, one wonders how many people involved in protest groups today still unnecessarily
occupy the time and activities of the Security Intelligence Service.
What has happened to the 90-day warrant suggested by Sir Guy? All we have had is a
rather ridiculous comment by the Prime Minister about the difficulties of undoing the bug. I
should have thought that there were rather easier ways of overcoming the problem. I submit
to the House, and particularly to Government members, that to use the name of one of New
Zealand's most distinguished civil servants as the supporter or the father of the legislation
before us is an insult to a very distinguished and gifted New Zealander-a man who, as I
have said, has given a great deal of service to his country. Who was the person or the body of
people who advised on the differences, the qualifications, or the modifications that ought to
be made to Sir Guy's report before it appeared in the Bill?

I still think that the approach of the former National Prime Minister, the Rt. Hon. K. J.
Holyoake, was right. With his liberal colleague, the Hon. Ralph Hanan, he came to the
House and the House tried to write a statute for the Security Intelligence Service. The House
was unanimous that it was needed, and I believe it still is. There was none of the fear that
there is today; even if it is groundless we should still be concerned. In all the years I have
been in the House I have never seen fear put in such a broad section of the community by a
Bill, which on the surface appears necessary to deal with terrorists. I have never before seen,
and never want to see again, the things that this Bill has made happen in this country. I
belong to a generation that can well remember how another country alien to us impercept-
ibly allowed its freedom to be eroded because people were afraid to stand up and be
counted. I am not going to be one of those.
From time to time I have said, and I will say again, that a Minister-whoever he
is-acting alone in these matters, and not on advice from the New Zealand Intelligence
Council but from the Director of the Security Intelligence Service, can make this kind of
decision. This is bad legislation. It undermines democracy, and we will have no part of it,
although we believe that a Security Intelligence Service is essential to the well-being of our
country.
The National Council of Women made another comment: "We are concerned that the
Minister, and the Minister alone, has the power even if under restricted conditions to issue
warrants for interception. Sir Guy Powles reported that up to 100 memoranda per year were
received by Ministers, and these included particular individuals or groups who were in the
news for instance as candidates for trade union or local body elections, or as visitors to
China." Ministers know this is so. The authority is in the hands of one Minister, and I do not
care whether it is the Prime Minister or any other Minister. The National Council of Women
stated: "We consider if this power is given to the Prime Minister, of whatever party”—and I
agree with that-"the democratic freedom of New Zealand is threatened." Past experience
proves that that has happened. The fact that material that was not very relevant was
dispatched somehow, somewhere, from the Security Intelligence Service during the term of
the Labour Government does not mean that I liked it.
If people think New Zealand is a democracy they are wrong. The House should
carefully read its record of the past 24 months and wonder what it has done to undermine
and erode the right, once taken for granted, that a person's phone and mail were secure
provided he acted within the law. If the Bill becomes law, no matter what safeguards are
provided, that security can no longer be taken for granted.

Hon. MICHAEL CONNELLY (Wigram): The New Zealand Labour Party and Labour
Governments stand second to none in their commitment to parliamentary democracy, law
and order, and the defence and security of New Zealand. Their reliability and performance
in those areas is a matter of record and one of history. Yet in this debate member after
member on the Government benches has questioned our loyalty and implied a want of

weak on terrorism, subversion, and security. He also said that we are unconcerned about the
integrity of the State. Those statements were unworthy of the Minister, and they did neither
the Government nor the Minister himself any credit. No previous Labour Government has,
and no future Labour Government will, imperil the defence and security of this nation or,
for that matter, of our allies.
Likewise, it has been alleged that in this debate the Opposition is attacking the Security
Intelligence Service, but that is totally incorrect. We have said unreservedly that, in the
imperfect world in which we live, a Security Intelligence Service is a necessity. A Labour
Government would ensure that such a service had the resources necessary to undertake its
task effectively. Our objection is not to the SIS but to the manner in which the Government
is handling the legislation, its refusal to send the Bill to a select committee to hear evidence,
the last minute amendments announced when this debate commenced, the further amend-
ments it is stated are being considered, and the still further amendments which might even
follow those. How can any legislation, and especially a measure of this type, be debated
effectively when the House is told that the Bill before it does not represent the Govern-
ment's final thinking on the matter-that there are amendments to follow but their nature is
not disclosed and therefore they cannot be debated at this stage. That alone is sufficient
reason for this Bill still to be referred to a select committee.
Reference has been made to the different approach of this National Government to
legislation of this type. The former National Government welcomed the opportunity to send
its Bill to a select committee and welcomed the suggestions put forward by the Labour
Opposition at that time, but that is not so in the present case. The Government has set its
face against any opinion other than its own on the quality of the Bill. We have read
widespread editorial comments on the measure, and comments in the Christchurch Press and
Christchurch Star are relevant. They, too, offer reasons why the Bill should be sent to a
committee. The Christchurch Press said that efforts should be directed to providing security
against the misuse of security methods and that one answer surely is to define the purpose of
interception warrants in such a way that would minimise the political element and exclude
self-serving political ends. The Christchurch Press is a responsible newspaper, and its view
should be considered before a parliamentary committee.
The Christchurch Star referred to widespread public concern and pointed out that by
refusing to send the Bill to a committee the Government was not only excluding fringe
groups but also responsible bodies such as the New Zealand Law Society and the Ombuds-
man. It made the point that the main matters at issue were the provisions for telephone
tapping and the interception of mail. It indicated that the Law Society wanted a tighter

WEDNESDAY, 19 OCTOBER 1977
Mr Acting Speaker took the chair at 2.30 p.m.
Prayers.
NOTICE OF MOTION-ADMISSIBILITY
Rt. Hon. W. E. ROWLING (Leader of the Opposition): I give notice that next sitting
day I shall move, That this House deeply deplores the fact that the "open Government"
promised by the National Party has turned out in reality to be marked by (1) thousands of
listeners being denied the right to hear debates in Parliament in which there was intense
public interest; (2) the refusal of Government members to participate in such debates when
they were no longer broadcast and, worst of all; (3) numbers of unoffending people being
forcibly evicted from the public gallery of Parliament-[Interruption.]
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: Order! I ask honourable members to restrain themselves and
give the Leader of the Opposition an opportunity to give his notice of motion.
Rt. Hon. W. E. ROWLING: I repeat, (3) numbers of unoffending people being forcibly
evicted from the public gallery of Parliament, thereby being deprived of the right of passive
personal participation in the democratic process.
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Acting Prime Minister): A point of order, Mr Speaker. I invite
you to look carefully at that notice of motion to see whether the reference to the eviction of
people from the gallery is not, in fact, questioning your decision and the ruling you gave last
night.
Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson): I happen to have a copy of the notice of motion
before me, and I can see nothing in it that in any way reflects upon the Chair. [Interruption.]
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: Örder! I do not know what has got into honourable members
this afternoon, but I should not need to remind them again that when a point of order is
being discussed it must be heard in silence by all members.
Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY: The notice of motion assigns no blame and makes no criticism;
it simply records a fact and contrasts it with another fact that was in issue during the last
election campaign.
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): The word "unoffending" suggests that
your judgment is being challenged, Mr Speaker, because if the people were unoffending you
had no cause to order the gallery to be cleared. The very fact that you, as the Speaker of
Parliament, decided that order could not be maintained while the gallery was occupied
indicates that you had decided that people were offending against order. If this notice of
motion were to be debated—and at this stage of the session we know that it will not be-then
the issue of whether or not you had been right and wise in the determination you reached
would come into debate, and I do not believe we should have motions that bring the Chair
into debate.
Rt. Hon. W. E. ROWLING (Leader of the Opposition): As the member for Henderson
pointed out, this notice of motion does not attempt in any way to apportion blame or to point
the finger. It simply states a matter of fact—that a number of unoffending people were
removed from the public gallery. I am not talking about those people who offended against
the House and against whom the Speaker took action, but, as members know, it was
inevitable that when the public gallery was cleared in the way it was a number of people who
were perfectly placid and here to listen to the debate were caught up in the situation and also
,removed, without being given the right to stay.
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: I do not need any further assistance on this matter. It is pretty
clear to me. The gallery was cleared on my orders. As I explained to honourable members
on two or three occasions last night, as a result of references made to the matter during the
course of the debate, several warnings had been issued, both by me and by the Acting
Deputy Speaker when he was in the chair, to the visitors in the gallery that they were not to
take part in the proceedings of the House and were not to interrupt the debate in any way.
Warnings were given that, if they persisted in their interruptions, they would be cleared from
the gallery. On resuming the chair from the Acting Deputy Speaker a further interruption
occurred, and the Prime Minister raised a point of order, suggesting that I clear the gallery. I
