ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS
Standard of Living of Average Wage Earner
1. Hon. R. O. DOUGLAS (Manukau) asked the Minister of Statistics: What increase in
gross wages is necessary to maintain the standard of living of a family consisting of a sole
earner earning the average male weekly wage, including overtime, a dependent spouse, and
two teenage children each eligible for the family benefit, in view of the increase in the
consumer price index over the last 6 months?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Statistics): On the basis of a whole series of
assumptions covering overtime, tax rebates, insurance, superannuation, and end-of-year
rebates, the increase in gross earnings to provide a reasonable equivalence in figure terms
would be $17.30 a week, or about 12.6 percent.
Hon. R. O. Douglas: Has the average wage and salary earner received a wage increase of
$17.30 a week over the past 6 months?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: Clearly, that is a matter in terms of the negotiations that
have been going on. Negotiations have been carried on during this period. I suggest too that
the figure used reflects to some extent the average amount, and that a man in this situation, a
sole earner with a teenage family, would probably be on a higher than average level. The
average leve! is affected by the number of juveniles and part-timers included in the average
figure. That should be borne in mind in relation to the sort of figures that have been
negotiated in recent wage settlements.
Mr D. M. J. Jones: Is it correct that, since 1 October 1977, the average wage earner on
$100 a week with a child under 5 years of age has received a tax rebate increase of $3 a week


## p. 3782 (#664) ###########################################

3782
19 October
Oral Answers to Questions
and a further $4 a week if he has a child aged between 5 and 10 years, with further increases
for people in the higher income brackets?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: It is true that special budgetary measures have been taken to
help those in most urgent need-the people with young families. It is a matter of judgment,
but in the Government's view that is where the most urgent need lay.
Hon. R. O. Douglas: Is it not a fact that the gross income has to increase by $17.30 a
week because the Government takes approximately 50 percent of that increase in taxation?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: Certainly, taxation has an impact on the whole question of
wage claims. Equally, I should hope that in making those claims all negotiating parties
understand the point that excessive claims will bear most heavily on those least able to cope,
certainly in the present economic situation. Restraint should be the order of the day if
excessive claims are not to lead to unemployment.

Security Intelligence Service-Advertisement
2. Mr MALCOLM (Eden) asked the Minister in Charge of the New Zealand Security
Intelligence Service: Has he seen an advertisement in the Dominion of 14 October 1977
headed "Censored" and signed by several journalists, and if so, does he know, of the
number of accredited members in the press gallery of the House, how many signed that
advertisement, and is it correct that many of the top senior press representatives who hold
that privileged position would be in a better position to judge the real need for and purport
of the SIS?
Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson): A point of order, Mr Speaker. I-suggest that this
question does not meet the requirements of Standing Order 87. The question starts off by
asking the Minister whether he is aware of an advertisement, and how many journalists who
signed it were accredited members of the press gallery. Those are both questions of fact, and
are unobjectionable. Then the question goes on to inquire how many of those were in top
senior positions and by virtue of their privileged position would be better able to judge the
real need for and purport of the SIS. That is clearly a matter of opinion. You would not
permit me to ask whether it was because of that position that they found it desirable to sign
the advertisement, which is the converse of the question, and is equally a matter of opinion. I
suggest that the question should be ruled out of order on that score.
Mr LANGE (Mangere): The question should be disallowed because it carries the
implication that the Minister in charge of the service is responsible for the press gallery,
which he must answer to in this House. That would be a most inappropriate stage for this
Parliament to reach, and on that ground the question should be disallowed.
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): If I could take the last point first. The
Minister in Charge of the Security Intelligence Service is also the Minister in Charge of the
Legislative Department, which grants the privilege for certain people to occupy positions in
the press gallery. In regard to the point raised by the member for Henderson, I guess the
question was aimed at the fact that the people alluded to in the second part of the question
would be in close contact with the Minister in Charge of the Security Intelligence Service
during interviews with him. Since he is the Prime Minister, and since there has been
widespread publicity of that fact, the implication is that they would learn a little more than
others. That would be the essence of the second part of the question.
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: We do not need to waste any more time on this. I thank
honourable members for drawing it to my attention. As the member for Henderson has
pointed out, the first part of the question is not objectionable. I cannot sustain the point
raised by the member for Mangere. The second part of the question relates to whether the
questioner is seeking an opinion. This matter was referred to me earlier. It was one of those
borderline cases, and it seemed to me we could leave it to the House to decide. I thought that
if nobody raised the matter it would be all right, but that if it was raised I would probably
have to sustain the objection because the way the question is worded does err on the side of
seeking an opinion rather than seeking information. Having said that, I point out that many
questions asked by members do seek an opinion. In many of our supplementary questions
there is a fine dividing line between seeking an opinion and seeking information. On this
occasion I think we would be doing justice to the House if I disallowed the question in its
present form. I invite the member to submit it in a different form, when we might be able to
accept it.

available.

Unemployment Statistics
7. Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn) asked the Minister of Labour: Has he seen the report by
Robin Turkel in the New Zealand Herald of 13 October on unemployment in New Zealand,
which is summed up in the paragraph, "Since the first step towards solution of any problem
is recognition of its existence, it would seem time for New Zealand to compute its jobless the
way most other developed countries do-as a percentage of the work force rather than
merely registered unemployed", and has he any intention of following this advice?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): The Government has already taken initial
steps to study the feasibility of an alternative measure of unemployment. A technical
working party comprising members of the Department of Labour and the Department of
Statistics is investigating the feasibility of conducting a household labour force survey similar
to those carried out in some other countries. Many technical questions need to be answered
if such a survey is to be reliable. The working party has addressed itself to these questions, as
well as making detailed studies of overseas surveys, and its report is now in the final stages of
preparation. If a decision is made to adopt a household labour force survey to measure
unemployment, the registered unemployment series would continue to be published as a
measure of those unemployed persons seeking the assistance of the Department of Labour.
The system adopted in New Zealand is the same as that in Australia.
Mr Isbey: Would the procedure outlined by the Minister be based upon the figures
arrived at when the census was taken, when it was pointed out that the figure of those
declared unemployed was 5.4 times more than those actually registered as unemployed?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: No, that would be completely fallacious, because the ratio of
those registered as unemployed to those declared unemployed on a census has varied
tremendously in each of the last three censuses. A special section would have to be included
in the census form asking people who say they are not working whether they have ever
worked and whether they want to work. Every possibility must be covered if this survey is
done through the census.

Telephone Service-Emergency Dialling
9. Mr ROGERS (Onehunga) asked the Postmaster-General: Has he seen the comment
on page 13 of the New Zealand Fire Service Commission report that "The introduction of
the emergency (111 dialling) telephone service has not proceeded as speedily as the New
Zealand Post Office equipment allows", and what is he doing to speed up installation?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Postmaster-General): Yes, I have seen the comment about
the introduction of the 111 emergency telephone service. The Post Office makes provision
for the introduction of the 111 emergency telephone service each time a manual telephone
exchange is converted to automatic working, but the introduction of the emergency service is
contingent on all three services-ambulance, fire, and police-being able to accept calls on a
24-hour basis. All three services have not been able to provide a 24-hour answering service in
some cases, and the 111 emergency service has not proceeded in those areas because of that.
It is not possible to introduce the 111 emergency service until exchanges are converted to
automatic operation.
Mr Prebble: How many districts do not have emergency dialling facilities?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON: In 12 districts where automatic exchanges are in operation the
111 emergency service is not available because the police are unable to accept calls on a 24-
hour basis. There are 31 smaller districts with manual exchanges which cannot provide the
service, but at present 93 percent of all subscribers to automatic exchanges are provided with
the 111 service.

Hon. L. W. GANDAR: I do not have a breakdown of the number of applications in

be able to complete the filling of the vacancies. The vacancies are in the fields specified by
the colleges as being the disciplines that require recruitment. We have filled them, and that
was the objective.

revenue? He suggested an investigation by the Department of Trade and Industry.

waiting list would be 36 000. He had received a letter from a person in the Papatoetoe-Otara

Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister for the Environment) said he had not heard any comment

not be planned.

doubling in a period of 3 years, had stabilised.

THURSDAY, 20 OCTOBER 1977
Mr Acting Speaker took the chair at 2.30 p.m.
Prayers.
ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS
Social Welfare Beneficiaries—Allowable Income
1. Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert) asked the Minister of Social Welfare: As people
over 60 can earn unlimited income and receive $2,581.28 per annum on national superannua-
tion, why cannot a widow or other beneficiary with few assets and perhaps greater
responsibilities be allowed to earn more than at present?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare): Widows' benefits and other income-
tested social security benefits are based on need and designed to meet a specific set of
circumstances. It is appropriate, therefore, that the establishment of need be by way of an
income test. Additional benefit of up to $16 per week is also available, as well as telephone
and television licence fee concessions, rates rebates, and so on. On the other hand, national
superannuation is a retirement income, and for this group telephone and television licence
fee concessions are being phased out.
Mr Lange: Would the Minister acknowledge that the Government in its election
manifesto promised to allow the levels of earnings for such beneficiaries to be raised, and, as
the Government is now two-thirds of the way through its term, when will it do something
about that promise?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: Yes, the Government has given an undertaking to increase
allowable income to the difference between the widows' benefit rate and 80 percent of the
average ordinary-time weekly wage. This will be introduced during this Parliament.
Hon. W. W. Freer: Could I bring the Minister back to the supplementary question
asked by my colleague and ask, when will the Government honour its election undertaking
to increase the allowable income for people on widows' and other income-tested benefits?

2. Mr WELLINGTON (Manurewa) asked the Minister of Labour: Did the Government

work had not taken place, the Government would have had to give very serious considera-
tion to any options available to it. Deregistration may have been one of the options, either of
the New Zealand or of the south Auckland branch of the union.

Rail Ferry Wash Damage, Tory Channel
6. Mr LATTER (Marlborough) asked the Minister of Railways: Following his recent
inspection of ferry wash damage at Tory Channel, did the General Manager of Railways
agree to any help for any residents and are further studies being done with the aim of
alleviating shore erosion?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Railways): The Marlborough Harbour Board

University of Canterbury, and an interim report has been received. Although the report

Electoral Rolls
7. Mr T. J. YOUNG (Hutt) asked the Minister of Justice: Has he seen the report of the
comments of the Lower Hutt City returning officer in the Evening Post on 15 October that
"The option voters had of enlisting on either the local body or parliamentary roll for local
authority elections made ‘a bit of a farce' of the enrolment provisions relating to local body
rolls", and, if so, what is he doing to create the joint parliamentary and local body roll
promised?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): The present provisions whereby enrol-
ment on the appropriate parliamentary electoral roll enables a voter in a local authority
election to cast an effective vote is the first step towards a common roll. Facilities will be
available when the next local authority elections are held in 1980 for rolls to be provided for
local authorities from parliamentary electoral roll sources. However, a number of adminis-
trative questions have yet to be resolved. The main problem is that parliamentary electoral
rolls are based on residence alone, and any rolls compiled from them alone can contain
names of only those having a residential qualification. Persons with a ratepayer's qualifica-
tion are also entitled to vote in local authority elections, and ratepayers' rolls cannot be
produced from parliamentary roll sources.

Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Broadcasting): I reply on behalf of the Minister
of Mines. "I find it difficult to find the basis for the honourable member's assertion. As I said
in the House on 26 July, no applications were received for petroleum prospecting licences for
on-shore Taranaki in response to the international advertising of areas carried out late in
1975."
Hon. F. M. Colman: Can the Minister state the closing date for the applications referred
to in the question, and confirm that before the applications closed the Government imposed
a taxing measure that was unacceptable to the industry?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: I can confirm that at the end of its 3-year term the Labour
Government lifted a freeze on applications and called for applications worldwide. Some
interest was shown, but when the applications closed no firm applications had been received.
The Labour Government's freeze occurred because petroleum legislation was under consid-
eration. This Government in turn has reviewed the taxation regime affecting the applica-
tions.
Mr Friedlander: Was there a freeze on petroleum prospecting licences during virtually
the whole term of the Labour Government, and did its Bill not provide a major disincentive
to oil exploration?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: If we want to pick up political points in a matter of national
importance I can confirm that during the term of the Labour Government a freeze was
imposed on applications. Long discussion about legislation did not please the oil companies,
and applications could not be called for until near the end of the Labour Government's term
in office. I trust that the decision was made in the interests of the country. In this difficult
area the Government is dealing with major companies and must protect New Zealand's long-
term interests in the energy field.
Hon. F. M. Colman: Can the Minister confirm that during October and November 1975,
when the licences were available on the international market, there was widespread interest
and indication that they would be eagerly sought by oil prospectors, and that only when the
present Government altered the rules about taxing any discovery did the impasse develop?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: I have tried to point out that exactly the same situation
occurred under the Labour Government. When the Labour Government was reviewing the
legislation there was a lack of interest in applications. The interest did not translate into
action, partly because of the review of the tax regime. In my view that review is in the
interests of the country.
Hon. Michael Connelly: Is it not a fact that before closing the applications for licences
the Government announced its proposals for increased taxation?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: There is no secret about that. The Government has
proposed changes in the taxation system. Everyone is aware of the costs and difficulties of
exploration, and interest does not always translate into action. The taxation measures are
not the only reason why there has been lack of interest. Two or three proposals have come
forward for major areas of interest-off-shore Taranaki and also on-shore. The proposals
are being reviewed. This Government, like the previous Labour Government, will not give
away vital national interests in its energy resources unless it has a taxation regime that is in
the interests of the country as well as the oil companies.

works in early lamb areas, Canterbury and Hawke's Bay, can build up to normal capacity
fairly quickly, the losses should not be great. It is estimated that 2 200 000 lambs will be
ready for the United Kingdom pre-Christmas trade this year. Since the resumption of work
will permit the loading of export beef and mutton, New Zealand should now be able to meet
its obligations to customers in the United States, the USSR, and other markets.

Rodney County Council (Mahurangi Harbour) Vesting and
Empowering Bill
RODNEY COUNTY COUNCIL (MAHURANGI HARBOUR) VESTING AND
EMPOWERING BILL
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Minister of Customs): I move, That leave be given to introduce
the Rodney County Council (Mahurangi Harbour) Vesting and Empowering Bill. The
purpose of the Bill is to secure legislative authority to reclaim a portion of the Mahurangi
Harbour for the purpose of constructing in the reclamation a series of oxidation ponds
designed to service the areas of Snells Beach and Algies Bay and the Warkworth district
community. After treatment, it is proposed that the effluent will be discharged into the sea
south of Martins Bay. The proposed reclamation is in Dawson's Creek in the Mahurangi
Harbour, some 5 kilometres south-east in a direct line from Warkworth.
The ponds are designed with a maximum ultimate capacity of servicing 17 000 persons,
and the area to be reclaimed is 20.3 hectares. Reclamation will be carried out by the
construction of earth bunds, and the ponds will not be in view from boats using the main
Mahurangi River channel. The Bill prohibits the use of the reclaimed land for any purpose
other than that of a sewerage scheme, and the physical work of reclamation will have to be
carried out in accordance with approval from the marine division of the Ministry of
Transport.
The Bill is a fairly standard empowering provision, and vests the land in the county,
gives the power to reclaim, although restricting this for purposes of sewerage, and gives the
council the power to contract out the work. It includes the usual provisions regarding
safeguards against the creation of nuisances and against adverse effects of waste water, silt,
or other debris; there is the usual protection provision regarding the application of the
relevant Acts and bylaw powers for the county, as is usual in these cases.
The east coast of Northland is certainly one of the finest coastlines in the country, and
probably one of the finest in the world. In recent years, as more people have followed the
sun, the subdivision development has encroached, the onus on us to safeguard this superb
environment has become increasingly important. There are areas of this coast where the
provision of adequate sewerage services is well overdue, and the longer the delay in starting
these schemes the more expensive they become. The consequences of delay are serious; but
so also are the consequences of being pushed into making the wrong decision, which could
permanently impair the environment. That is the dilemma now facing us in the largely land-
locked Kawau Bay, one of the scenic gems of this part of the world, with a growing beach
population, a good proportion of which is permanent.
The Bill is presented to provide for the reclamation work required, and to provide for a
conventional oxidation pond scheme, initially, the Snells Beach and Algies Bay area, with a
proposed outfall into Kawau Bay a short distance to the south of Martins Bay. As would be
expected, the question of the location of the ponds and the outfall has provoked the deepest
controversy. Many-probably most-Snells Beach and Algies Bay people do not want
oxidation ponds as close to their areas as is planned by the county. As for the outfall, the
county has looked at several possible locations for discharging effluent into Kawau Bay, and
objections have been to all of them. Many people object in principle to the idea of any water
outfall at all. Although I regard this situation as a warning of the troubles that can come from
seaside subdivision development's proceeding too far too fast, I readily acknowledge the
tough predicament the county council has found itself in.
Not so many years ago, before environmentalism was a real factor and before competi-
tion between various uses in our coastal bays and water bays became intense, any local
authority could install a sewerage scheme with minimal opposition, but the Rodney County
Council has to provide these services at a time when it can expect to face opposition
whichever way it moves, and whichever method it adopts. The provision of a sewerage
scheme has blown up into a major issue, probably one of the most difficult the council has
ever had to face. All people living or planning to live in the district are involved, whether
they are old-established residents, who managed very well with existing disposal methods
suitable for a low-density population until the subdivision development really began to gain
momentum, or new residents who bought their sections on the understanding that sewerage
would be provided, but are still waiting, or prospective residents who cannot even build until
sewerage is provided.
Clearly, the existing situation cannot continue. I have been in regular touch with the
council during the long drawn-out process of deciding on the best locality and method of
sewage disposal, and I publicly acknowledge its honest endeavours to find the best solution.
Now, in effect, the county council is saying, "Here is our proposal in this Bill. Show us a


## p. 3820 (#702) ###########################################

3820
20 October
Selwyn Plantation Board Amendment Bill
better one if you can", and I certainly have no quarrel with that approach. The onus is on
anyone or any group that challenges the scheme to produce a better scheme-one that is not
only better environmentally, but is also practical and stands up to cost comparisons.
In fact, an alternative has been presented: a land-based spray irrigation scheme, details
of which have been examined by the Snells Beach Ratepayers and Residents Association,
with expert assistance. The association has pointed out that land is available for siting
treatment ponds, and that a local farmer is prepared to use the treated effluent for fertiliser.
Treatment would be located well away from any built-up area, and there would be no
discharge into Kawau Bay. The preliminary studies indicate that this may be a viable and
economically attractive alternative, but further studies would be needed to confirm that.
I sincerely hope the Local Bills Committee will give very serious consideration to this
alternative. The county has said, "Here is our scheme; show us a better one", and, if no one
can show a better one, the council's proposal has my full support. But meanwhile an
alternative has been presented and deserves full consideration. At this stage it is my duty
now to formally move the first reading of the Bill, which would enable the county to
proceed.
Motion agreed to.
Bill introduced and read a first time.
SELWYN PLANTATION BOARD AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Transport): I move, That this Bill be now read
a second time. The Bill aims at the general modernisation of aspects of the principal
Act-the Selwyn Plantation Board Act 1953. The plantation board administers plantations
on the Canterbury Plains and foothills between the Waimakariri and Rakaia Rivers. Its area
of jurisdiction is that of the original Selwyn County, which was dissolved many years ago,
and the board consists of representatives of the local authorities whose districts include any
part of the former Selwyn County. The board owns about 7200 hectares, of which about 4800
are in plantations. The original purpose of the board was to establish better shelter
plantations on the Canterbury Plains to protect them from the prevailing westerly winds. It
has a consistent planting programme, and sells a large volume of timber. Through these
activities it makes loan moneys available to the local authorities of the district.
For some time the board has been restricted in its activities because some of the sections
in the original Act have become outdated. This is an appropriate time to bring the Act up to
date. The Bill is not a complex one, but some amendments have been proposed by the Local
Bills Committee. In clause 2, the chief executive officer of the board is designated as general
manager; he will perform the functions of the secretary as set out in the original Act.
Clause 3 gives the board appropriate powers to lease land. At present the board is not
permitted to take land on lease for plantation purposes. However, some land that is suitable
for afforestation is not available for purchase, but is available for long-term lease. It is
thought necessary that the board should be able to enter into leases for this land. In addition,
the board at present leases out land that it does not require for plantation purposes,
but
these leases are limited to 14 years. Clause 4 increases this period to 33 years, which will
allow the board more flexibility and will result in better land use by the board's tenants.
Clause 5 provides for more efficient operations by allowing two board officers to sign
cheques, but designated board members will still have the right to sign cheques. Under the
present Act, cheques can be signed only by the secretary and one board member.
Clause 6 will provide a greater opportunity for the board to invest in research by way of
grant. This amendment brings up to date the amount that can be spent, by increasing it from
$200 to $1,000. The Local Bills Committee has proposed a further amendment, which
requires a Supplementary Order Paper. At the appropriate time I shall move that the board
be empowered to make grants to community projects concerned with recreation, enjoyment,
health, education, and instruction on cultural activities in the district of any constituent
authority. The grants may not exceed $5,000 in any one financial year. The committee has
proposed no change to the limit on unauthorised expenditure.
Clause 8 will ease the difficulties faced in attracting suitable workers, and will bring the
board into line with other local bodies that operate in country areas, such as power boards.
This clause will enable the board to help its employees to own their homes. Housing is scarce
in the Canterbury district, and the power conferred by this clause will enable the board to


## p. 3821 (#703) ###########################################

20 October
3821
Selwyn Plantation Board Amendment Bill
attract good employees by offering housing on reasonable terms. It is mainly concerned with
advancing or guaranteeing loans. A further amendment is proposed to change the basis upon
which interest is to be charged. Instead of allowing a rate not less than that charged by the
Housing Corporation, it was considered more appropriate to allow interest rates of 1 percent
either side of the maximum rate set under section 9 of the Local Authorities Loans Act 1956,
unless otherwise authorised by the Minister of Finance. Clause 9 removes the requirements
to prepare statements of receipts and payments, thus making the annual reports more
precise, and bringing the board into line with other local bodies in the district.
I am sure that the Bill as reported back will be well received by members of the House. I
remind them of the particularly fine function the Selwyn Plantation Board performs, and of
the tragedy that happened during the 1 August gales some time ago, which was a real tragedy
for Canterbury.
Bill read a second time.

According to the report of the Railways Department for the year ended 31 March 1977,
long-distance passenger journeys had decreased by 31.7 percent to 1 288 593, while suburban
journeys had decreased by 5.3 percent to 17 189 541. Long-distance passenger revenue had
decreased from $5,589,421 to $5,577,086, a reduction of 0.2 percent. That illustrated the
effect fare increases had on rail service patronage.
The report had stated that the decrease in long-distance passenger journeys could be
attributed to a marked downturn in travel, some resistance to higher fares, the withdrawal of
some provincial railcar services, and a reduction in the number of special train hires. It was
also stated that certain routes-Christchurch-Greymouth, Christchurch-Picton, Wellington-
Wairarapa, New Plymouth-Taumarunui, and Napier-Gisborne-would be served by

railcar.

BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): As is usual, I shall give the business for next
week. I shall be moving shortly that the House adjourn until the ringing of the bell, because
the hours of sitting on Tuesday will be affected by a parliamentary luncheon. Estimates will
be taken on Tuesday and Thursday, and legislation on Wednesday and Friday.
ADJOURNMENT
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): I move, That this House do, at its rising,
adjourn until the ringing of the bell on Tuesday next.
Motion agreed to.
ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS
Bahrain-Saudi Arabia Causeway
1. Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert) asked the Minister of Overseas Trade: Has he seen
the report in the National Business Review of 5 October that "every assurance has been
given that a causeway between Bahrain and Saudi Arabia will be built", and, in view of the
New Zealand investment in the port facilities, will he advise what stage has been reached in
the construction of the causeway?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Acting Minister of Overseas Trade): The Saudi
Arabian Ministry of Communications has appointed a Saudi-Danish team of consultants for
the $825 million causeway between Bahrain and Saudi Arabia. The Danes are Kampsax
International, which produced the feasibility study, and Christiani and Nielsen, both of
Copenhagen. They will design 12 kilometres of bridges and 10 kilometres of causeway. The
pre-qualification call is expected later this year with an invitation to a short list of
international contractors to tender in April 1978. Construction time is expected to be about 4
years. The Saudi Arabians have agreed to finance the causeway.
Hon. W. W. Freer: Is there definitely no possibility that the causeway project will be
cancelled?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: I have no evidence of the possibility of such a
concellation.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.
Export Killing Season—Opening
2. Mr ELWORTHY (Oamaru) asked the Minister of Labour: What action is contemp-
lated by the Government to enable the export killing season to open at the normal time?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): As my colleague will now be aware, the
dispute involving freezing industry tradesmen has been taken over by the Federation of
Labour, and discussions between the federation and the Freezing Companies Association on

5. Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert) asked the Minister of Housing: In view of his

by the corporation that their rents have been assessed purely on the income going into the
home?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND: The honourable member knows that several bases are used
for calculating State house rents. The unit is valued under the terms and conditions I have

income-based rental, and it is possible that in many cases the tenant is not paying the
maximum rent set for the property but a rent related to his ability to pay.
Hon. W. W. Freer: In cases where a tenant's income is such that he is paying the highest
level of rental, which may exceed the fair rental as assessed by the Department of Labour's
formula, what basis is used by the department in assessing the final rental?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND: The maximum rent that can be charged is the rent that is
assessed according to the formula laid down by the Department of Labour. The maximum
rent is assessed on the value of the particular house, not the tenant's income.

21 October
3841

many private landlords, that 1 week's rent should equate with about 1 day's pay, and is it also

land will not accept our pigmeat. Australia, however, will accept canned pigmeat.

## p. 3842 (#724) ###########################################

department is carrying out extensive trials to see whether the disease can be controlled by
deep freezing the meat for more than 60 days. The trials are continuing.

convinced that there was no disease or possible disease in the South Island. The department
will not be certain of that until all pigs have been tested.

Radioactive Fish and Plankton
9. Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert) asked the Minister of Health: In view of the
statement in the Christchurch Press of 11 October by the director of the National Radiation
Laboratory that it was pure conjecture to suggest that radioactive fish and plankton are
drifting towards New Zealand, will he advise what proof he has that the director is correct,
and upon what tests was his statement based?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry): I reply on behalf of
the Minister of Health. The original question from the paper was based on the claim that
dangerous amounts of radioactive leakage were contaminating marine life and drifting
towards New Zealand, and the particular question related to what programme the National
Radiation Laboratory would mount to measure this. The reply observed that the present
information was conjectural. The National Radiation Laboratory's present monitoring
programme is confined to atmospheric monitoring that could detect some venting from
underground nuclear explosions. Any ocean contamination would suffer marked dilution,
and a programme required to maintain continuous measurements at the lowest limits of
detection is not warranted on the evidence available at present.
Hon. W. W. Freer: As the Department of Health has conducted a number of tests on
the contamination of fish from mercury poisoning, would not the department be justified in
extending those tests to make sure that there has been no increase in radioactivity in our fish
stocks?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: My understanding is that there is a great deal of
difference between the two types of tests. I am prepared to convey the question to the
department and advise the honourable member of the reply.
Hon. W. W. Freer: Will the Minister give an assurance that instructions will be given to
the department to look very closely at such tests being conducted?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: I will consult with the department and communicate
the reply to the honourable member.

body, and interested persons in the community. It gives employment and experience to a
group of young Maori people who are endeavouring to improve their own skills. Many other
local bodies and community organisations are responding with similar initiatives.

Chatham Islands-Forestry Development
16. Miss DEWE (Lyttelton) asked the Minister of Forests: Are there any plans for the
planting and development of forests on the Chatham Islands, and, if so, what areas are being


## p. 3845 (#727) ###########################################

21 October
3845
Oral Answers to Questions
considered and for what specific end use?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Forests): The potential for any large-scale develop-
ment of forests on the Chatham Islands is extremely limited because of the severe climatic
conditions that prevail there, particularly the salt-laden winds that sweep over the islands.
For the same reason there is an obvious need to encourage the establishment of shelter belts
of resistant trees to benefit farming and the community generally. It has therefore been the
policy of the New Zealand Forest Service to encourage the establishment of shelter belts and
assist with designs and species composition. The total area of woodlots that would be
required to make the islands largely self-sufficient in sawn timber and fencing materials has
been estimated to be about 150 hectares. At present the area of woodlots is only about 40 or
50 hectares.

TOWN AND COUNTRY PLANNING BILL COMMITTEE-NOTICE UNDER STANDING
ORDER 89
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: I have to inform the House that I have received an application
from the member for Henderson to move the adjournment of the House under Standing
Order 89. The letter reads: "I propose to move on Friday, 21 October, that the House be
now adjourned for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance.
This is the manner in which the Town and Country Planning Bill Committee is proceeding
with the task entrusted to it, namely that of considering the Bill, and hearing evidence on it.
So far the committee has received 222 formal and general submissions, together with 56
individual representations in respect of one particular clause. Apart from the initial meeting
to appoint a chairman, the committee has met on six occasions (over a time span of 12½
hours), and has heard witnesses in support of 18 of these 222 submissions. Various aspects of
the proceedings have drawn protests from Opposition members of the committee, but the
Standing Orders preclude my going into further details as to these. However, witnesses have
expressed outside the committee room dissatisfaction with the opportunity offered of
developing their submissions and answering questions from members. In addition, other
bodies wanting to make submissions have been denied the right of personal appearance.
(Incidentally, I am of the opinion that many local bodies were unable to formulate views
they would like to put before the committee pending the outcome of the local body elections,
which took place last Saturday.) Quite apart from what has taken place in committee, the
Minister in charge of the Bill has on several occasions expressed the Government's intention
to pass the Bill this year, which will necessarily result in the 204 representations already
lodged and awaiting the attention of the committee being given inadequate consideration.
Moreover, many of the people concerned with this Bill, both as witnesses and members of
the committee, are also closely involved with the Local Government Amendment Bill No. 2,
which is concurrently before the Local Bills Committee, and it is impossible for the two to be
properly considered at the same time. This is a matter which involves the administrative or
ministerial responsibility of the Government, which alone can arrange for the appropriate
remedy, namely to hold the Town and Country Planning Bill over for consideration during
the parliamentary summer recess."
This request was received by me within the time fixed by the Standing Order, and I have
given it careful consideration. As members know, before a motion under Standing Order 89
can be accepted, it must meet the criteria set down in Standing Order 90. These are four in
number: namely, that the matter shall not be framed in general terms; that it shall deal with a
particular case of recent occurrence; that it requires the immediate attention of the House
and the Government; and that it involves the administrative or ministerial responsibility of
the Government. The subject of the application in this instance appears to be the conduct of
the committee dealing with the Town and Country Planning Bill. While the matter is
expressed in specific terms, I have some doubt as to whether it ought to be regarded as a
particular case of recent occurrence. I shall not decide that point, because in my opinion the
application can be decided on the basis of the fourth criterion—that is, whether it involves
the administrative or ministerial responsibility of the Government.
The Town and Country Planning Bill has been referred by the House to a select
committee especially appointed to deal with it. Questions relating to the conduct of a select
committee should be settled in the committee, or they may be brought to the House on
motion, or by an interim report from the committee, but they are not within the administra-
tive or ministerial responsibility of the Government. Committees are responsible to the


## p. 3847 (#729) ###########################################

21 October
3847
Public Expenditure Committee-Interim Report
House, not to the Government, and, accordingly, their proceedings cannot be made the
subject of a motion under Part XIV of the Standing Orders. I therefore rule that the motion
is not one contemplated by the Standing Order, and the application is therefore declined.

CARRIAGE OF GOODS BILL
Mr McLAY (Birkenhead): I am directed by the Statutes Revision Committee to present
the interim report of the committee on the Carriage of Goods Bill, and to advise that, after
careful consideration of the Bill, the committee has decided to recommend to the Govern-
ment that it should establish a working party to consider the present law relating to the
carriage of goods, the Carriage of Goods Bill itself, the report on which it is based, and the
submissions made to the Statutes Revision Committee on the Bill; the working party to have
regard to the purpose and scope of the Bill and to inquire into and report as to what changes
are necessary or desirable to achieve a fair and just balance between the interests of
consumers and operators, and also to achieve practical and workable legislation. The
committee further recommends that the Bill be held over at the end of the present session of
Parliament. I move, That the report do lie upon the table.
The House will recall that the Bill was introduced in August of this year and was
referred to the Statutes Revision Committee for consideration. It provoked considerable
interest among those involved in or directly affected by the carriage of goods both within and
beyond New Zealand. Submissions-25 in all-were received from road carriers, major
consignors of goods such as Federated Farmers, the Retailers Federation, the Manufacturers
Federation, the Timber Merchants Federation, insurance interests, the shipping industry,
both Air New Zealand and the National Airways Corporation, and a number of other
interested persons and organisations.
The reform contained in the Bill was first proposed by the Contracts and Commercial
Law Reform Committee as long ago as 1968. Since then there have been numerous
meetings, discussions, and reports on the proposed changes in the law, the most important
being the work of the Transport Advisory Council. However, it was not until the Bill was
introduced and those interested were required to make submissions on a specific legislative
proposal that the views of the various parties could be brought together in a cohesive form.
In brief, the Bill, in the form in which it was introduced, abolished the differences
between the liability for common carriers and private carriers, and made all carriers,
including freight forwarders, absolutely liable for loss and damage to goods-except loss and
damage resulting from the fault of the consignor-including any loss or delay, except that
resulting from meteorological conditions or an attempt to save life or property. Liability was
to be limited to $1,000 per unit. There were special provisions relating to the definition of the
term "unit" in accordance with modern developments in containerisation, palletisation, and
unitisation of goods. In addition contracts of through carriage, lien rights, and the right to
contract out of the terms of the Bill were all specifically covered.
The Bill creates a separate set of a single legal rules applicable to all modes of carriage
of goods within New Zealand, whether by land, sea, or air. As I have indicated, the Bill
attracted 25 submissions. Although the details of those submissions differed substantially,
these differences are unimportant for the purposes of this report because the majority took
the view that the law relating to the carriage of goods required reform, and that the present
$40 limit on liability in particular, was quite unrealistic. However, with the exception of one
or two submissions, the majority made it clear also that they considered the proposed $1,000
limit to be too high and the terms of liability to be too onerous. It was suggested that the cost
of covering such liability by way of insurance would be very high indeed, and that this cost
would eventually be passed on to the consumer.


## p. 3852 (#734) ###########################################

3852
21 October
Carriage of Goods Bill
It has become clear to the select committee that it is necessary to conduct further
investigation before the reform is finally enacted. The committee concurs with those who see
need for reform, and particularly for an increase in the existing $40 liability, but it believes
that the extent of both the reform and the increase in monetary liability must be most
carefully investigated. We doubt whether such an investigation could be carried out
effectively by a select committee of the House and we therefore recommend to the
Government that a small working party be established to look into the whole matter. We
believe that the working party should use the Contracts and Commercial Law Reform
Committee report and the reports that followed it, together with the Bill and the submissions
on the Bill, as the starting point, and in general terms should address itself to eight major
questions: (1) whether there should be one or more statutes governing all modes of carriage
of goods in New Zealand; (2) whether the monetary limit on liability should be $1,000 or
some other figure; (3) how the term "unit" should be defined; (4) whether contracting out of
the terms of the Bill should be permitted; (5) whether the Bill should impose liability on a
carrier in respect of delay; (6) what the best formula would be for assessing the quantum of
damages arising from loss or damage to goods; (7) bearing in mind that a carrier is at present
absolutely liable for loss and damage, whether there should be any exceptions to that rule;
and (8) the likely cost of any changes to the law to the ultimate consumer. The committee
believes that those matters should be investigated urgently, so that the Bill can be
reconsidered by the select committee during the recess with a view to bringing it back in final
form for passage next year. For that reason we recommend to the Government the
establishment of a working party along the lines I have indicated, and consequentially, to
enable the select committee to consider the matter during the recess, the committee further
recommends that the Bill be held over until the next session of Parliament.
Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR (Timaru): As a member of the select committee and one who
was a party to the decision just conveyed to the House by the chairman of the committee, I
should like to make a few remarks on the motion to present an interim report from the
Statutes Revision Committee, and also to elaborate on one or two points outlined by the
member. It is regrettable that the Bill has to be deferred, because, as has been stated, it is
based on the report of the Contracts and Commercial Law Reform Committee tabled in
1968. It has been under continuous study since that time, and it may well be argued that
there should be no need for further delay after 8 years. I can appreciate the validity of that
argument. However, it was only after the Bill was presented and the select committee began
to hear submissions that the full implications were realised.
As the chairman of the committee pointed out, only 25 submissions were presented, but
they covered all modes of transport, the insurance industry, chambers of commerce, users of
transport, retailers, and others particularly involved in the carriage of goods. Because of the
wide-ranging and differing viewpoints, it was felt that the action proposed would be the best
course to adopt. The member for Birkenhead listed some of the points it is suggested should
be included in the proposed terms of reference of the working party the Government is being
asked to set up. They include consideration of the sizes of the units of goods, the question of
definition of "unit of goods", and so on.
Since the report of the Contracts and Commercial Law Reform Committee was
presented in 1968, there have been real changes in transport generally. Containerisation has
become international and we in New Zealand have been caught up in it. In considering
insurance cover, the question of liability for the carriage of containers, FCLS and LCLs-full
containers and split containers-brings very real problems to the surface. Although the
period between the introduction of the report of the Contracts and Commercial Law Reform
Committee and the presentation of this report spans 9 years, and the delay in implementing
legislation can be criticised-and the committee may well be questioned and criticised for
asking for a further delay-the transport of goods and insurance coverage are changing
rapidly and, as the witnesses agreed, there is need for reform.
For some years there has been general agreement that the level of carriers' liability
ranging from $40 for carriage of goods by rail to a $240 maximum is inadequate. Everyone
agrees that the review is necessary. No matter what maximum was set, someone would not
agree with it. The situation has been further complicated by the coverage of transport and
insurance not only internally but also internationally, particularly through adoption by the
United Kingdom of the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, adopting the protocol of the Hague
Bisley Rules which go back to 1924. The international implications relating to sea carriage
and containerisation involvement must be studied by the committee. Therefore, it is
imperative that the working party cover all modes of transport.


## p. 3853 (#735) ###########################################

21 October
3853
Carriage of Goods Bill
At first the committee thought that the Transport Advisory Council could form the basis
of the working party, but then it was realised that the interests of the insurance industry and
users generally must be represented. There is therefore a real need to go beyond the
immediate personnel of the Transport Advisory Council. A good argument can be made for
covering all modes of carriage and questions of carriers' liability in one statute, but an
equally good argument can be made for dividing these over a range of statutes for the various
modes of transport. A full discussion centred around whether or not carriers should be
permitted to opt out of liability; the total liability concept needs further investigation. All
members on the committee are conscious of the need to update and tighten carriers' liability,
but it is obvious that intensive work must be done by specialists in this field as soon as
possible, so that the select committee can come to terms with this Bill, or Bills, if it is
subsequently decided to cover the question in more than one statute.
Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central): The Statutes Revision Committee has followed an
unusual course in suggesting the setting up of a working party to look at the Bill. The Labour
members on the committee agreed with this action, because transport forms a major part of

present Bill does not meet the position. We received 25 submissions from groups that fell
broadly into three categories, the first being the insurance industry, which will pay the cost
of damaged goods. Its representatives pointed out that, as an industry, it transfers costs from
one party to another, with the eventual cost being paid by the consumer. They made the
point very strongly that the provisions of the present Bill would mean greatly increased
administration costs. I was somewhat sceptical of this argument, as the insurance industry
accepts that it does not pay the costs of damage; the consumer does. It appeared to me that
the insurance industry was fearful that at present the real cost of damage in transport is much
greater than that being met by insurance. The insurance industry itself has not investigated
the costs that would result from this Bill. It is therefore necessary that the Bill be held over
until the true cost of various elements in the transport of goods is known.
The second group to make submissions was the transport operators, who were against
the Bill for a variety of reasons. The third group, made up of those who use transport
operators—the consumers-was mostly in favour of the Bill. If there is to be a choice
between the interests of the insurance industry, the transport operators, and the consumers,
the House should come down heavily on the side of the consumers.

MONEYLENDERS AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. In this year's Budget the Government undertook to make an interim amend-
ment to the Moneylenders Act 1908 to increase the interest rate that may be charged by a
person lending money in the course of his business without his being required to register as a
moneylender under the Act, and that increase was to be from 10 percent to 15 percent. This
two-clause Bill gives effect to that undertaking. When the existing provision was first enacted
in 1901 it was never envisaged that the Moneylenders Act should be a fiscal control measure.
However, the onset of inflation and the corresponding rise in interest rates over the last 4
years has resulted in the Moneylenders Act impeding the orderly development of interest
rates. This Bill ensures that for the remaining short life of the Moneylenders Act it does not
continue to inhibit proper, efficient, financial activities.
It became apparent on the introduction of the Bill that there was some confusion over
the existing provisions of the principal Act, and it may be helpful to members if I explain the
existing law and the effect of this amendment upon it. Section 2 of the principal Act defines a
moneylender as including every person whose business is that of moneylending, but the
section then goes on to exclude any person from this definition who in good faith carries on
any business in the course of which and for the purposes of which he lends money at a rate of
interest not exceeding 10 percent. This does not mean, as some appear to think, that a loan
at less than 10 percent automatically excludes the operation of the Act. Far from it. A person
may be a moneylender for the purposes of the Act although lending at less than 10 percent.


## p. 3855 (#737) ###########################################

21 October
3855
Moneylenders Amendment Bill
Conversely, it is possible for a loan to be made at over 10 percent without the lender falling
within the definition of a moneylender. Indeed, this has been evident since 1973, with
interest rates in the uncontrolled sector going sky high.
The important point to remember is that those who lend at less than 10 percent in the
course of their business may at present lend at a higher rate if they register as moneylenders.
The Bill simply lifts the limit at which they can lend without being required to register as
moneylenders. The reason for this, as I explained during the introduction, is that it is very
difficult to determine whether or not a person is a moneylender for the purposes of the Act.
This has resulted in distortions in the money market and has caused great difficulty,
particularly to stock and station agents in their providing finance for increased primary
production. For that reason alone I hope there will be unanimity in the passing of the Bill. I
do not expect it, though.
Subclause (2) of clause 2 has the effect of retaining the existing law in respect of
transactions entered into by people other than moneylenders before the enactment of the
Bill. If, however, such transactions contain a provision permitting the variation of interest
rates the lender will be eligible, if he wishes, to increase his interest rate above 10 percent
without necessarily needing to be registered as a moneylender. Section 3 of the 1908 Act
permits a court to reopen a moneylending transaction on the ground that the transaction is
harsh and unconscionable. For the purposes of that section, and that section only, a
moneylender is defined as any person lending at a rate exceeding 10 percent. Because the
Contracts and Commercial Law Reform Committee has recommended that this sort of
power should be applied, generally speaking, to all credit contracts, this Bill does not alter
the 10 percent figure in section 3 of the principal Act in any way. It is widely recognised that
the Moneylenders Act 1908 is an anachronism, and for this reason the Government intends
to implement the report of the Contracts and Commercial Law Reform Committee on credit
contracts as soon as possible. I hope to introduce a Credit Contracts Bill later this year for
recess study. Those are the simple facts relating to the Bill.
On the Bill's introduction the socialist members opposite launched themselves into their
usual make-believe world and saw dreadful consequences as a result of the realism of this
Bill. I have no doubt that they will follow the same course of horror promotion in this second
reading debate. Although some unfortunate, gullible, persons may be taken by such stories,
most people will see them for what they are, political monster making. We will be told,
incorrectly, by the socialist leaders that the imbalance in the money market results from the
actions taken by the present Government in March 1976.
Mr Prebble: Of course it does.
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: Here come the stories, and the monster makers. The briefest
scanning of the facts will show that the pressures that led to the imbalance came from the
Labour Government's action in carelessly and foolishly-
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: Order! I am wondering whether the Minister is making life
more difficult for me when I come to deciding what is relevant to the question before the
House-that the Moneylenders Amendment Bill be read a second time. It is a very small
Bill, and I am bound by the Standing Orders as elaborated by Speakers' rulings, which I
think are very sound in this case, that a second reading debate should be confined very

motion. It is not, in my opinion, an occasion for a debate on the financial policies of this

Hon. DAVID THOMSON: In view of that ruling, which clearly confines what I can say

that the same rules will apply to following speakers. The Bill is not a panacea, but it is
necessary to relieve pressures that have developed since 1973, pressures which are working
to the disadvantage of our primary production servicing industries. The broader remedies to
the Moneylenders Act that have been developed in the interests of the consumer will be
found in the credit contracts legislation, which will be introduced at the end of the session for
recess study.

Miss DEWE (Lyttelton): It is always a pleasure to follow the member for Mangere.
Without fail, he refers to the Old Testament, and on this occasion he mentioned
Deuteronomy. I have a very strong feeling-which is reinforced every time I hear him
speak-that he visualises himself as a modern Moses leading the Labour Party out of its
political wilderness. I wish him well; he has a hard task in front of him.
The member made a statement that must be tidied up in the interests of veracity. He
said that all a person had to do to become a moneylender was fill in a form. This Bill is a very
simple amendment to the Moneylenders Act. It has two clauses-one the short title and the
other the amending clause. The member's statement should not be left unchallenged. I
should like everyone to know that it is not a simple matter to become a moneylender; one
does not merely fill in a form. The principal Act lays down some very strict criteria relating
to moneylenders and their eligibility for registration. The member shot his own impassioned
argument down in flames when he said that the Labour Government had allowed lending for
consumer durables at 11 percent. Now he has the audacity to say that he would introduce a
Bill to permit lending at 3 percent or a similar low rate of interest.
The Deputy Leader of the Opposition talked about the cost of money, and said that the
Bill would allow interest rates to rise. The whole problem is related to the old economic rule
of supply and demand. Everything has a price—and that includes investment money. If
investment money is in short supply, its price-which is the interest rate-rises. If it is not in
short supply, the interest rate falls. Investment capital for development of rural and urban
industry and housing has been in short supply for a considerable time.
The Bill's consequences for little people were dwelt on by the Deputy Leader of the
Opposition. I should like to talk about someone whom I consider to be a little person, and
that is myself-an average person, a single person, a working person, who did not have
enough capital to do something related to building her own home, and had to borrow
money. This all happened in 1973, when I embarked upon a subdivision enterprise and
bought a section. I had to fill it and to get approval from the drainage board and the
Christchurch City Council before I could build. Interest rates in 1973 were 7 or 8 percent. It
took me 2 years to complete the subdivision and the building work. In March 1975 I
borrowed money and signed a mortgage. The interest rate I borrowed at was not 7 or 8
percent, but 12 percent-and that was under the administration of the Labour Government.
Members opposite have said in this debate that the National Government will allow interest
rates to rise as a result of this Bill, which is a simple amendment to the Moneylenders Act. I
am still burdened with the mortgage taken out during the term of the Labour Government.
The shortage of money caused the high interest rate. In 1972 the rate of inflation was
about 5.5 percent; in 1973 it had risen to 10 percent; in 1974 to 12 percent; and in 1975 it was
15.7 percent. The high inflation rate meant that money that had traditionally been available
for mortgage investment was being diverted into property speculation, with the resultant
price increases for homes and land. Some people wanted to obtain a high return for their
investment and were not prepared to lend money at the previous prevailing rate. The
shortage of money caused interest rates to rise. In 1973 the Labour Government enacted the
Trustee Securities Amendment Bill, which exacerbated the shortage of money for housing
because it diverted money from the traditional forms of investment. As a result of that
enactment, interest rates rose remarkably.
The Government has to free the money market before there can be any rationalisation
of interest rates. Who are the lenders being spoken about? The amending Bill does not alter
the definition of a moneylender; it merely changes one word. Section 2(d) of the principal
Act reads: "Any person bona fide carrying on the business of banking or insurance or any
business in the course of which and for the purposes whereof he lends money at a rate of
interest... not exceeding 10 percent per annum." The Bill changes the expression "10
percent" to "15 percent". The change is necessary because of the distortion I mentioned
earlier when talking about the drying up of money.
The lack of money has had a disastrous effect, not only on private borrowing for
housing, but for stock and station agents, who were tied to interest rates of 10 percent when
they could not borrow money at that rate. Being unable to borrow money inhibited their
activities in encouraging the agriculture sector, which is the most important facet of our lives.
Stock and station agents need to have money deposited in their coffers to enable them to
finance farmers through the winter months, when they have no income. During the winter
farmers do development and maintenance work on their farms, and this cannot be done

without borrowing.

that interest rates will rise by 50 percent after the enactment of this measure. The legislation

interest rates of more than 10 percent. Wages, and the prices of houses, motorcars, and
other commodities, have not increased by 50 percent; they have increased by 500 percent.

The measure is nothing more than an action to free up the flow of money and to allow
time for the Credit Contracts Bill to be introduced. The Minister has given the reasons for
the Bill to be introduced. The Contracts and Commercial Law Reform Committee took 9
years to study the inadequacies of the principal Act, and its report was received by the
Minister only this year. Because of the distortions in the economy, not in the last 2 years but
in the last 5 years, some tidying up was necessary. This is a holding Bill until such time as that
amendment is put through. I support the Bill.
Hon. MICHAEL CONNELLY (Wigram): The member for Lyttelton said that the Bill

The member for Lyttelton highlighted the fact that National members invest themselves

Hon. MICHAEL CONNELLY: I shall say only that if there is a shortage of investment
funds, let the Government look at its policies, which have created that situation. Another
reason for increased interest rates is the risk factor. When there is a risk in lending, that is a
reason for lenders to increase their interest rates. This Government is ensuring that
moneylenders have the opportunity to charge more. If the Government adopts unsatisfac-
tory policies, they will have consequential effects in other areas. As the Deputy Leader of
the Opposition pointed out this morning, when the Government increased the base interest
rate, which is the Government stock borrowing rate to which all other interest rates are
related, that meant a consequential increase in interest rates throughout the economy.
Whereas 10 percent was formerly a reasonable maximum under the Moneylenders Act,
people now find that they have to pay more for the money they borrow, and, therefore, they
want the rates at which they may lend to be higher.
The member for Birkenhead advocated dear interest rates to overcome an inflationary
cycle; that was his argument in support of the Bill. I suggest that dear interest rates have a
multiplier effect, and boost the rate of inflation because they put up costs. Interest rates
enter costs at every level. If one is buying a house and paying higher interest rates on the
loan, the ultimate cost of buying that house is forced up by those interest rates. It is the same
for the farmer; if the interest rate he pays on borrowed money goes up, his cost of production
goes up. The same applies in the business community.
It is interesting to compare the differences between the two parties. If one looks at
interest rates over the years, under National Governments the interest rate has invariably
climbed at all levels. The expansionary policy adopted by the Labour Government, which
provides for increased output, greater profitability, and higher wages, with their side effects
of increased efficiency and output in industry, makes more loan funds available at the
savings level and at the general investment level, and, as the supply of loan finance
increases as it does under those policies-as the supply increases, the price falls. That is
why the Labour Government was able to pursue a low interest rate policy. I suggest that, in
the long term, that is the only policy that New Zealand, which depends on export earnings
for the buoyancy of its economy, must follow if our exporters are to keep their costs down
and compete on the international market.
When introducing the Bill, the Minister said that the present limit of 10 percent for
moneylending impeded the ordinary development of interest rates. He said that this change
in interest rates—an increase of 50 percent-was to remedy problems affecting the farming
industry. The Associate Minister of Finance said that increasing the interest rates would help
stock and station agents and farmers. About a month ago, the assistant general manager of
Wrightson NMA said: "A reduction in interest rates, giving a return to a lower interest rate
structure and more stable farm costs, is a prerequisite to farm development." So the
Government's Ministers, who are supposed to know all about farming and be the friends of
the farmers, say that the way to help the farmers is to put up the interest rate by 50 percent;
but the assistant general manager of Wrightson NMA says, "Bring interest rates down if you
want to help the farmers and encourage farm development."
He also said, "The lack of suitable finance at reasonable interest rates seems likely to
become an inhibiting factor which will dissuade farmers from endeavouring to increase
production." This is at a time when we have a major balance of payments problem that is
worsening under this Government, and when we want to increase farm production and
exports. Wrightson NMA states that increased interest rates will be a disincentive to export
production. That shows the bankrupt policy the Government is following. The assistant
general manager of Wrightson NMA said that, unless interest rates across the community
fell, farmers with any significant debt burden would have no alternative other than to borrow
at higher interest rates-that is the implication-or to cut production. It is time the public
took stock of the Government, and the policies it is following and their consequences on the
economy.
We are told in New Zealand that we have to have higher interest rates, yet in the United
Kingdom, Germany, and the United States interest rates, as well as the cost of living, are
falling. We are supposed to have economic miracle men guiding this country. Why, then, are

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS
Economy
1. Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition) asked the Minister of

Health-Doctors' Charges and GMS Benefit
7. Mr HUNT (New Lynn) asked the Minister of Health: Are doctors to be required to
deduct the full amount of the increase in the GMS benefit from their normal charge applying
on that date, as was the case in December 1974, and what measures will be taken between
now and January 1978 to ensure that doctors' total consultation charges are not increased?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): Under section 98(4)(b) of the Social Security Act
1964 medical practitioners are required to credit any persons chargeable with the full amount
of any benefit. Failure to do so may be construed as professional misconduct. Medical
practitioners are entitled to charge a fee commensurate with service, and may, therefore,
increase their charges like any other professional group. Under the Stabilisation of Prices
Regulations 1974, Amendment No. 6, specific complaints about increases to doctors' fees
may be referred by patients to the price control division of the Department of Trade and
Industry to establish whether there are any grounds for action.
Mr Hunt: To the Minister's knowledge, have any people supplied information about
this matter to the price control division?
Hon. T. F. GILL: No.
Mr Hunt: By how much was the GMS payment to the doctor increased when the
Minister reviewed the charges, and by how much has the average charge for visiting a doctor
increased since that time?
Hon. T. F. GILL: I cannot answer that question. I do not know the average charge of
doctors. Unless a complaint is to be investigated, that matter is one between the patient and
the doctor concerned, and I am not advised of it.

Health-Doctors' Charges and GMS Benefit
13. Mr HUNT (New Lynn) asked the Minister of Health: Could he inform the House
what a "nominal or minimal" charge above the GMS benefit will be after 1 January 1978 for
children of family benefit age?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): The new GMS benefit rates for children effective
from 1 January 1978 will be $4.75 for a consultation at the doctor's surgery during normal
hours, $6 for a visit to the patient during normal hours, $7 for an urgent consultation at the
surgery outside normal hours, and $8 for urgent visits outside normal hours. The New
Zealand Medical Association has given an undertaking to recommend to the profession that
any charges for services provided for children and young persons over and above these new
benefit rates should be nominal or minimal. This means that although doctors continue to
determine their charges on the principle of a fee commensurate with the service, it is
expected that with the additional benefit payable in respect of children and young persons
after 1 January 1978 many practitioners will accept the new benefits in full satisfaction of
their services and make no extra charge to the patient.
Mr Hunt: Can we take it from the Minister's reply that he is not prepared to put a figure
on the words "nominal or minmal", and that in fact some doctors would regard 25c-taking
$4.75 up to $5-as nominal or minimal, while other people might regard $1.25 or $2.25 as
nominal or minimal?
Hon. T. F. GILL: I agree with the member's sentiment that there is a danger of this sort
of thing happening, but the position is that legally we have no power to enforce a particular
rate on the doctor. The Medical Association has been co-operative to the extent that it states
that in view of the GMS benefit for children having been raised as it has it will recommend to
doctors that any additional charge be merely nominal or minimal. That, at least, is some
progress.
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: Can the Minister inform us whether either the department or the
Medical Association would, as a matter of practice, check these kinds of matters?
Hon. T. F. GILL: I do not know quite what the member includes in “these kind of
matters".
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: Nominal or minimal charges above the GMS benefit.
Hon. T. F. GILL: There is no power, just good will.
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: No power, but just to check?
Hon. T. F. GILL: We will keep an eye on the position as best we can, without laying on
a big administrative machine that requires notification of every individual charge. I think
many doctors will apply their charges on the basis perhaps of ability to pay. In many
instances where there is no charge at all we might not hear about it, but where there is a
charge that somebody feels is excessive we would usually hear about it.

National Superannuitants
15. Hon. R. O. DOUGLAS (Manukau) asked the Minister in Charge of the Inland
Revenue Department: Is it correct that some national superannuitants, former age
beneficiaries, are being taxed at the rate of 40c in the dollar, which is higher than either the
secondary tax or the marginal rate on their highest income, and, if so, can he state if there is
any justification for this?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister in Charge of the Inland Revenue Department): I
cannot confirm that former age beneficiaries are being taxed at the rate of 40c in the dollar.
What I can confirm is that it is possible that one or two superannuitants have applied for a
special tax code of, say, 40c. It would happen in this manner: a single person on national
superannuation without other income would face a tax deduction equalling 14.22c in the
dollar, or, if the superannuation was treated as secondary employment, a rate of 19c in the
dollar. Should he have other income subject to tax it is possible for him to apply to the Inland
Revenue Department for a special tax code. If that other income were of sufficient
magnitude and he wished to have all his total annual tax met by deductions from his national
superannuation then it would be possible for a tax deduction rate of 40c in the dollar to be in
force. That would be the justification.

would not lose any of their present benefits-the rates, telephone, and TV rebates. The
Minister had changed his tune by stating that the benefits would be phased out rather than
removed. Was it any wonder that there was a discrepancy between what the Minister had
said in the Chamber and what members of the Public Expenditure Committee had been told
by the departmental officers? Obviously the officers knew the facts. They had to write to
members of the public every day telling them that they had lost their telephone rebate, their
TV half licence fee, or other concessions. They realised that the Government was applying a
set of principles which were not set out in any of its manifestoes.
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare) said that the official manifesto
stated: "These benefits along with 'additional benefit', will continue as before, subject to
