normal income testing. All TV, telephone and rate concessions which are currently payable
to beneficiaries will continue under National at the same rates and to the same categories of
persons and with the same income tests as apply under Labour when we take over."
Under the Labour Government a married person had automatically lost the concession
when his income exceeded $80.20 a week, and a single person had lost the concession when
his income exceeded $60.80 a week. The National Party had said it would retain that system
of phasing out concessions, and it had. Because of the substantial increases that had been
granted under national superannuation, many people had exceeded those limits and had lost
the concessions. Under the Labour Government the age benefit had been 53 percent of the
average weekly wage, but under the National Government it had increased to 70 percent,
and would rise to 80 percent. The Leader of the Opposition had been quoted as saying that
that figure was extravagant. What would Opposition members do were they ever returned to
the Treasury benches?
Hon. M. RATA (Northern Maori) said that during the 1975 election campaign National
Party candidates had circulated leaflets telling electors that they would not lose telephone
and television licence concessions or rate rebates, but many people had now lost those
concessions. The Christchurch office of the department was to be congratulated because it
had told a widow that she would be $1.23 a week better off with the widow's benefit than she
would be if she transferred to national superannuation. What was the Government going to
do to honour its election promises? The elderly had not benefited from the Government's
policy. The Government should honour its policy so that the elderly could live in dignity.
Mr LITHGOW (Palmerston North) said that Mr Ian Jenkins, the National Director of
the Marriage Guidance Service, had seen the benefit of an early referral system and sound
counselling for marriages that were about to break up. During the past few years he had
worked closely with the Department of Social Welfare. It was excellent to see a voluntary
service and a Government department working closely together. On 31 March 1977 the
Council for the Single Mother and Child had sent every member a "strike kit" containing
scurrilous material. It had contained unsubstantiated references to a departmental officer,
and had claimed that the Minister terrorised women and forced them to give up their
benefits and live with men they hardly knew. It had also contained a disgusting cartoon of
the Minister of of Social Welfare, who was sympathetic to the solo parent problem. The acts
of a few extremely irresponsible people had put all solo parents under unnecessary fire.
The married person who had lost a partner had found that the unwed teenage mother
and her boyfriend came under the solo parent umbrella. Society was concerned that the
unwed teenage mother was eligible for the same domestic purposes benefit as a 30-or 40-
year-old divorced or widowed person with two or three growing children. The commission
had not faced up to the problem of the unwed teenage mother. The Solo Parents Association
quarterly magazine had stated that the backbone of society was the family unit, which
needed protection. People were ripping off the system, and some people were having babies
to dodge joining the workforce. The girls who could not decide whether to sleep with their
boyfriends, use contraception, have an abortion, have the baby adopted, or get married
expected legislators to decide that they receive greater benefits.
Hon. R. O. DOUGLAS (Manukau) said that health, education, and other areas of social
welfare were being robbed because the funds were being transferred to pay for national
superannuation. Most people now paying tax to support national superannuation would not
benefit from the scheme because it would collapse before those people reached the age of 60.
National superannuation was expected to cost $1,240 million for the year 1978-79; the age
benefit, had it continued, would have cost $740 million. Therefore, the estimated extra cost
of national superannuation for the year 1978-79 was $500 million, or $6 a week for every
taxpayer. Those who benefited most were people over the age of 60 with an above-average
income; those who paid were the wage earners, people with young families. In 1977, three
workers supported each superannuitant; in 40 years' time there would be one person over 60
for every two people in the work force.
The country could not afford the scheme now, let alone in the future. He had a letter
from the Department of Social Welfare dated 25 August 1976, setting out what old age
pension a person was entitled to receive in addition to Government superannuation and
other private income. At 25 August 1976 the amount payable each 4 weeks was $126.44. At
22 August 1977 the same person was entitled to receive only $115.56, or $10.88 less for a 4-
week period. He had taken the case up with the Minister, who had said that the explanation
was that the person had a private income.
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare) said the member for Manukau had

3898
25 October
Appropriation Bill-Estimates
deliberately avoided telling the committee that the constituent he had spoken of drew
national superannuation, Public Service superannuation, had other private income, and was
now applying for a benefit for his wife, who did not qualify for national superannuation. It
was another example of Opposition claims that were not substantiated by facts. The man
should apply for a benefit, and if he was entitled to one he would get it, but he was not $10 a

charges in the committee.
The Leader of the Opposition had frequently said that national superannuation was
extravagant. If Labour were re-elected, what would it do about national superannuation?
Had Labour's New Zealand superannuation scheme been in operation this year, it would
have cost more than the national superannuation scheme. New Zealand could afford the
national superannuation scheme, and would continue to be able to afford it, because of the
more prudent management of the financial affairs of the country by the National Govern-
ment. In last year's Budget the Government had introduced substantial tax concessions,
which had been worth $6 a week to any family man with a child under 6 years of age. That
benefit had been extended in the 1977 Budget to $9 a week for anyone in the middle or lower
income brackets with a child under 10 years of age. A single-income benefit of $4 a week had
also been introduced for the family in the middle or lower income bracket, a total concession
of $13 a week.
When the Labour Government had taken office in 1972 it had had in draft form the
Disabled Persons Community Welfare Bill, but had done nothing about it until the week
before the session had ended in 1975, when it had been rushed through the House. Because
of the incompetent management of the Labour Government the disabled had been ignored
for 3 years. The National Government had implemented the Bill, and the disabled had
benefited from its actions.
He endorsed the remarks about Mr Ian Jenkins, the Director of the Marriage Guidance
Council. The council had done wonderful work, and statistics showed how successful its
efforts had been. Of the 5500 cases handled in 1975, 45 percent had been successful, and in
1976 the success rate had been 59 percent of more than 6000 cases handled. There had been a
52 percent success rate for the present year. He expressed gratitude at the way in which
council members had co-operated when the new domestic purposes benefit measures had
been introduced. Although the new measures had been in operation for only a week or two,
the results had been pleasing, and had indicated that early counselling was successful.
Hon. R. L. BAILEY (Heretaunga) said that the National Party's 1975 election manifesto
had stated that all television, telephone, and rate concessions payable to beneficiaries would
continue under the National Government at the same rate, to the same categories of
persons, and with the same income test as applied under the Labour Government. The
present Minister of Health, the then Opposition spokesman for social welfare, had said on 25
June 1975 that those benefits, along with supplementary benefits, would continue as before,
subject to correspondingly upgraded income tests. The people had believed that they would
receive those concessions together with the new superannuation, which would be upgraded.
Although the superannuation payments had been upgraded, the concessions had been lost.
Earlier the Minister's attention had been drawn to the situation of a man who was worse
off under the national superannuation scheme than he had been under the previous Labour
scheme, when he had had Post Office Savings Bank interest of $10.80, Government
superannuation amounting to $2,983.76, and a benefit of $126.44. Although he still had the
same Post Office Savings Bank interest and received Government superannuation, his
benefit had been reduced to $115.56. The RSA was telling its members to continue receiving
their war pensions and not to transfer to the national superannuation scheme, because they
would be worse off if they did so. Yet the Minister had said that no one would be worse off
under the national superannuation scheme.
Hon. H. J. Walker: I confirm that.
Hon. R. L. BAILEY said that figures given to the Public Expenditure Committee by the
Department of Social Welfare had shown that beneficiaries who had an additional taxable
income of $10 a week were worse off under the national superannuation scheme. The
Minister should acknowledge that what the department said was correct.
Mr WELLINGTON (Manurewa) said that the National Party's policy had clearly stated
that war pensioners would retain special advantages over national superannuitants. The
thrust of the Opposition's debate had been that if Labour was returned to the Treasury
benches it would restore the means test. In the 1930s the Labour caucus had been divided on

3899

the question of the abolition of the means test to make universal superannuation possible.
Labour was still divided.
As the level of national superannuation rose it overtook the income level at which
telephone, television, and rates concessions applied. In a dispassionate article in the New
Zealand Herald the editor had stated that the sharp reduction in the number of complaints
received from the elderly had indicated that the scheme was working fairly and well.
Although, on average, there were 1000 national superannuitants in each electorate,
complaints received by members from the elderly had virtually disappeared.
Mr LANGE (Mangere) said that the National Party's election manifesto had stated that
women between the ages of 55 and 60 who received national superannuation because their
husbands were over 60 would be able to revert to the widow's benefit on the death of the
husband, and receive more by so doing. The turnover of social workers in the department
had reached a critical level, and morale was at an all-time low. Why were social workers
trying to extract admissions of paternity? Between January and June 1977, 49 social workers
had resigned as many in 6 months as in the period covering January to December 1975.
From 1 January 1976 to 30 June 1977, 122 social workers had resigned.
What action did the Minister propose to take to relieve the lot of widows and others who
had not been given the benefits promised by the Minister during the election campaign? A
widow was allowed to earn $17 a week, or, if she had a dependent child, $21 a week. They
wanted to be able to earn more, and had been promised that the allowable limits would be
increased, but no suggestion of an increase had been made recently. When did the Minister
intend to increase the dependency allowance from $1.25 to $2 a week, as had been promised
in 1975? Had the Minister changed his mind because the Horn committee had expressed
opposition to an increase in dependency allowances? Had the spouse retention scheme had
any marked results in the past few weeks? Why had the Minister reduced the income of
people looking after children for a period of 6 months, after which they could receive a
higher level of remuneration? Did he believe that the first 6 months of a child's life should be
spent in a situation of gross underprivilege? Was it designed so that children would be cast on
doorsteps? Did the Minister believe that economic impoverishment would cause people to
have second thoughts 9 months after the event?
What would the Minister do to effect improvements to marriage counselling arrange-
ments, particularly to the procedure which pertained under the Domestic Proceedings Act
when application was filed and allegations against one spouse were made by the other? The
lawyer then filled in all the adverse details, and the form was served on the husband or wife.
Having read that form, he or she was then asked to go to a conciliator.
Mr LAMBERT (Western Hutt) said that Opposition speeches reminded him of a
gramophone record being played over and over again. How many times would the Minister
have to hammer into the heads of members opposite that under the Government's national
superannuation scheme no one would be worse off, because a beneficiary could take the
alternative benefit available if he believed that gave him a better deal? The Opposition had
said that one of the scheme's main faults was that people who did not need the benefit were
obtaining it.
One of the major benefits of the Government's scheme was that superannuation was
paid at the age of 60, not 65 as under Labour's scheme. Under Labour's superannuation
scheme the working woman would have obtained a very poor deal, and no one would have
received a full benefit until the next century. Would the Opposition replace the National
Government's superannuation scheme with its own scheme if it regained the Treasury
benches? On 5 August the member for Southern Maori had said that the next Labour
Government would dispense with the present Government's scheme, but no other Opposi-
tion speaker had confirmed that.
Hon. Mrs T. W. M. TIRIKATENE-SULLIVAN (Southern Maori) said that the Minister
looked and sounded more like an auctioneer, bookmaker, or super salesman than a Minister
of Social Welfare. He was another Government apologist for the most ruthless incursions
into the psyche of the lower-income solo parent. He and his Government had become known
as the "shatterers of dreams". No less in times of retrenchment than at other times, policies
must surely be intelligently directed to minimising social and environmental costs, but the
Government's policies had increased social costs. On 20 October the Leader of the
Opposition had released a much more positive policy: to increase the family benefit by 50
percent for children up to the age of 10 years, and by 100 percent for those over 10 years.
The inability to attain even the minimum standard of living had taken many solo parent
families to breaking point. The punitive actions taken by the Government, and especially the


## p. 3900 (#782) ###########################################

3900
25 October
Appropriation Bill-Estimates
Minister of Social Welfare, had resulted in a social stigma being attached to a solo parent.
What evidence did the Minister have that the domestic purposes benefit was the cause of
marriage breakdown? The Government's policies had added much to the stress that many
solo parents experienced. No effective child care had been provided for the solo parent who
was under stress and, because of financial need, had to work. Although it had been stated in
the departmental report that 70 new child care centres had opened in the 6 months to June
this year, 74 had closed for financial reasons in the same period. The totally inadequate
benefit paid to widows had forced many beneficiaries to practise deception.
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare) said that 74 465 national superannuit-
ants were still receiving telephone rental concessions, and 59 827 were still receiving
concessions on television licence fees. He hoped that within 12 months, when the benefit had
increased to 80 percent of the average ordinary-time weekly wage, all national superannuit-
ants would be over the statutory income limit. The case of a gentleman who was said to be
worse off under national superannuation had again been quoted, and he thought he should
repeat the answer that had been given to a question asked in the House. He had said that
calculations in the honourable member's question were based on an assessment of terminal
tax liability, and that could not be assessed until the end of the financial year, having regard
to the variations, the superannuitant's income during the year, his tax exemptions, and the
rebates that he might be entitled to.
He stressed that all former age beneficiaries on national superannuation were receiving
significantly more cash-in-hand payments than they would have received had the age benefit
been retained. Since the removal of the income test beneficiaries had had the opportunity to
increase their income, and were able to place themselves in a better position. He had
received many letters from beneficiaries who had said they were much better off, and he was
convinced they were better off.
In its 1975 election manifesto the National Party had stated that benefits enjoyed by war
pensioners would be maintained. When national superannuation had been introduced
persons who had received an income-tested war pension were given the option to remain on
that pension together with the various fringe benefits, or to transfer to national superannua-
tion and forfeit the special allowances. The decision to change to nationa' superannuation
could be made only by the pensioner. If the pensioner elected to remain on his war pension
the fringe benefits he automatically retained included the age supplement of $1.50 a week on
attaining the age of 65 for both the pensioner and his wife, and a tax-free war veteran's
gratuity paid regardless of financial circumstances and payable for 2 years after the veteran's
death, or in the case of the widow of a war service pensioner either a gratuity payable for 6
months after the pensioner's death or a lump sum equivalent to one-quarter of the annual
rate of war service pensions. There were educational bursaries for the family, and other
benefits.
It had been claimed that the department had told beneficiaries to get off national
superannuation or to stay on other benefits. If the benefit that the person was receiving was
higher than national superannuation the department would not tell him that he should go off
his benefit and on to national superannuation. The department had told people to stay on
the benefit that would leave them better off, but that did not mean that people were worse
off because of the introduction of national superannuation.
Of a staff of 3500 social workers, 122 had left during the 18 months to June 1977, 9 had
retired, 7 had transferred to other departments, one appointment had been annulled, and
105 had resigned. The reasons for the resignations had included returning to teaching, to
nursing, to private employment, to social work with other agencies including hospital
boards, to social work with guidance counselling, to full-time university studies, marriage,
travel overseas, and pregnancy. The contentment of the department's staff was shown in the
quality of their work.
The domestic purposes benefit had been reduced for the first 6 months because the
Horn committee had felt that the generosity of the benefit was a reason for the break-up of
so many marriages. The committee had consisted of a magistrate as chairman, a representa-
tive of the Marriage Guidance Council and the New Zealand Social Workers Association,
the head of the nursing section of the Wellington Polytechnic, a qualified Maori social
worker from Auckland, the former chairman of the Social Security Commission, and a
welfare officer of the Salvation Army. One of the committee's recommendations had been
that the initial payment of the benefit should be at a lower rate, but the committee
emphasised that hardship should not be permitted.
Last year 19 400 women had applied for the domestic purposes benefit, mainly because

3901
Appropriation Bill-Estimates
of marriage breakdown. He felt that at least some of those marraiges could have been saved
if proper counselling facilities had been available. As a result of the Horn committee's report
a new system of counselling had been implemented working in association with the Marriage
Guidance Council, and, although only a few statistics were available, it was considered that
the system would work. Opposition members had said that national superannuation was
costing too much, and they had also said that it was not high enough. Would the Labour
Party cut out national superannuation, thereby depriving 80 000 people of the benefits they
were receiving?
Progress reported.
